Ohio's facility law, Senate Bill 104, the "Protect All Students Act," was signed by Governor Mike DeWine on 27 November 2024 and took effect 25 February 2025. It requires every K-12 school and every college and university, public and private, to designate bathrooms, locker rooms, changing and shower rooms and overnight accommodations for the exclusive use of males or females on the basis of sex assigned at or near birth, and requires students to use the facilities matching their birth certificate. Single-occupancy restrooms with controlled use are exempt. The bill was signed out of public view over the objections of Democrats, teachers' unions and civil rights groups; its sponsor was Republican state Senator Jerry Cirino. The statute contains no enforcement mechanism.

State identity documents are being narrowed. Amendment of the gender marker on an Ohio birth certificate was barred under the 1987 precedent In re Ladrach, challenged by four transgender Ohioans in March 2018 and invalidated as unconstitutional by federal Judge Michael H. Watson in Ray v. McCloud in December 2020; corrections have been officially permitted since 1 June 2021, although some counties continue to refuse them. Transgender people can change name and gender on Ohio driver's licences by court order together with a Declaration of Gender Change signed by a physician, nurse practitioner, social worker, therapist or psychologist, and an X marker has been available since April 2022. In August 2026 the Bureau of Motor Vehicles announced rules allowing only male or female markers and requiring an exact-matching birth certificate or passport.

Care and sport are governed by HB68, the Saving Adolescents from Experimentation Act, which bans puberty blockers, hormones and surgery for under-18s and bars transgender girls and women from women's high-school and college sports. It passed on 13 December 2023, was vetoed by Governor DeWine on 29 December 2023, and was enacted by House override on 10 January 2024 and Senate override on 24 January 2024. A court blocked it in April 2024, allowed it to take effect in August 2024 after finding the regulation of transgender individuals a legitimate state interest, and the Ohio 10th District Court of Appeals re-enjoined it on 18 March 2025, with Attorney General Dave Yost vowing to appeal. The operative position on any given provision should be checked before relying on it.

Protection is patchy. Ohio statutes do not address discrimination on account of gender identity, but gender-identity discrimination in state employment has been barred by executive order since 19 December 2018, and the Sixth Circuit held on 7 March 2018 that discrimination on the basis of transgender status is sex discrimination under Title VII. Thirty-three Ohio cities and counties have ordinances barring gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Iowa (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2007 Iowa prohibited discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations, but in February 2025 the Legislature passed a veto-proof bill removing gender identity from anti-discrimination laws, signed by Governor Kim Reynolds and effective July 1, making Iowa the first state to remove anti-discrimination protections for any class and the first to take a protected group away from civil rights protections. In 2025 Iowa stripped nondiscrimination protections from trans people and in 2026 passed a bill banning localities from maintaining civil rights protections stronger or broader than the state government, after several cities passed their own protections. As of July 1, 2025 under Senate File 418 transgender people may not alter legal gender on government IDs or documents or be legally recognized differently from assigned sex, stripping 2007 gender-transition language and imposing an unchangeable binary legal definition of sex determined at birth based on gametes expected to be produced later in life. Iowa hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes based on sexual orientation but not gender identity; a March 8, 2016 Senate bill to add gender identity passed 27-21 but died in the Republican-controlled House, though federal law has covered gender identity since October 2009. In March 2019 the Iowa Supreme Court required Medicaid coverage of sex reassignment surgery, but the General Assembly passed and Reynolds signed a ban on state funding a month later, a Polk County District Court ruled that ban unconstitutional in November 2021, and in June 2025 Reynolds signed another law banning Medicaid coverage for transgender surgeries and hormone treatments effective July 1, 2025. In March 2022 Iowa limited women's sports to cisgender females based on sex at birth, effectively barring transgender girls and women at all accredited public or private educational institutions including colleges and universities effective July 1, 2022, with civil lawsuit cause for any direct or indirect harm from violation. In March 2023 Senate File 538 banned provision of any gender-affirming healthcare to transgender minors effective immediately with 180-day wind-down for existing patients, and a separate March 2023 bill required written parental permission for students to use a single-person restroom at school. In May 2023 Iowa banned sexual orientation and gender identity lessons in Kindergarten through grade 6 classrooms, and only Davenport has banned conversion therapy on minors by 8-2 council vote April 22, 2020 after statewide Senate and medical and psychology board efforts failed. Iowa Territory adopted Wisconsin anti-sodomy law in 1838 punishable by up to three years, omitted sodomy in its 1843 code making it legal as noted in 1860 Estes v. Carter, re-criminalized sodomy in 1892 with one to ten years for heterosexual or homosexual consensual activity with first conviction in 1900 State v. Todd and fellatio criminalized in 1902, limited prosecution of heterosexual sodomy in a divided 5-4 1976 Supreme Court ruling requiring compelling state interest for private consensual adult opposite-sex conduct, and repealed same-sex criminalization in a 1978 comprehensive code with no mention of sodomy and age of consent 16 regardless of gender and sexual orientation. Iowa provided benefits to same-sex partners of state employees since 2003, recognized same-sex marriages since April 3, 2009 after unanimous Iowa Supreme Court affirmance in Varnum v. Brien, issued licenses from April 27, 2009 as fourth U.S. state to legalize same-sex marriage, defeated constitutional amendment and convention attempts to ban it, and removed three participating justices in November 2010 retention elections while retaining a fourth in November 2012. Joint adoption by married same-sex couples has been legal since a 2008 Supreme Court ruling with individuals and married couples allowed to adopt regardless of sexual orientation, state courts ordered listing of married lesbian non-birthing mothers on death certificates in December 12, 2012 Buntemeyer v. Iowa DPH and on birth certificates in Gartner v. Newton unanimously affirmed May 3, 2013 to ensure support and fundamental legal rights at birth, lesbian couples have IVF access with non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized if married, and courts are generally favorable to gestational or traditional surrogacy despite no defined surrogacy laws. Since 2007 Iowa has outlawed discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, housing and public accommodations with Des Moines protected since 1991, and hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes based on sexual orientation. On March 17, 2015 the Senate voted 26-24 to ban sexual orientation change efforts on LGBT minors but the bill died in the Republican-controlled House, the Board of Medicine and Board of Psychology declined in 2016 to ban conversion therapy by rule, and Davenport became the first city to ban conversion therapy on minors by 8-2 vote April 22, 2020. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in South Carolina (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Changing legal gender on the birth certificate does not require sex reassignment surgery. State anti-discrimination law contains no explicit prohibition of discrimination on the basis of gender identity, but 2020 federal workplace protections against LGBT discrimination apply in South Carolina, with additional local employment protections for gender identity in Mount Pleasant, Myrtle Beach and Richland County and for city employees only in Columbia, Charleston and Latta. South Carolina has no state hate crime law, while hate crimes motivated by gender identity are prohibited federally under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. In April 2016 Governor Nikki Haley said she opposed a transgender bathroom-restriction bill introduced in the Legislature and viewed it as "unnecessary". On May 17, 2022 the governor signed a transgender sports ban. In May 2024 legislation signed into law and effective immediately banned gender-affirming healthcare for individuals under 18 and banned federal funding going directly or indirectly toward gender-affirming care for adults, after which providers including the Medical University of South Carolina stopped providing such care regardless of age. The 2024-25 and 2025-26 budget appropriations bills require students to use bathrooms based on sex "at the time of birth", though on September 10, 2025 the U.S. Supreme Court allowed trans student plaintiff John Doe to continue using the boys' bathroom while his challenge proceeds, with all other trans students required to follow state law. Same-sex sexual activity is legal under the 2003 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Lawrence v. Texas, which invalidated South Carolina's sodomy law making "buggery" a felony punishable by five years in prison or a $500 fine, though the legislature has not repealed it. Voters adopted a November 2006 constitutional amendment defining marriage as the union of a man and a woman, which was overturned in Condon v. Haley on November 12, 2014, with stay denials by the Fourth Circuit on November 18 and by the U.S. Supreme Court on November 20, the first same-sex marriage on November 19, 2014 and general recognition and performance from the next day. South Carolina permits adoption by individuals with no explicit prohibition on adoption by same-sex couples or on stepchild adoptions, and since a February 15, 2017 federal order the state must list both same-sex parents on children's birth certificates without the adoption or Family Court order previously required only of same-sex couples. No state anti-discrimination provision explicitly covers sexual orientation, though 2020 federal workplace protections apply, supplemented by local employment protections in Mount Pleasant, Myrtle Beach and Richland County and for city employees in Columbia, Charleston and Latta. South Carolina is the only state not to include same-sex couples in domestic violence statutes, which explicitly cover only opposite-sex couples, and it has no state hate crime law, though crimes motivated by sexual orientation are covered federally under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. 66186276B65591139260314.name: Florida
66186276B65591139260314.summary:
Florida stands under the United States national framework and adds a state layer a trans visitor meets directly on the ground, most sharply in public facilities. Under the Facility Requirements Based on Sex Act (Fla. Stat. 553.865), in force since 1 July 2023, a trans person may not use a restroom or changing facility consistent with their gender identity in buildings owned or leased by the state or local government: state offices, courthouses, legislative offices, prisons and jails, local immigration detention facilities, state parks, toll-road plazas, state schools, state universities, beaches and airports. The statute purports to cover all schools, public and private. Private businesses are outside its scope.

The statute's mechanics put the decision with an authority figure on site. Gender labels are required, an internal disciplinary procedure applies, and an authority figure may order a person to depart; a non-member who does not leave can be charged with criminal trespass. The ACLU of Florida advises that refusing to leave a sex-segregated restroom or changing facility can amount to criminal trespass and that each situation calls for fact-specific judgment and legal counsel.

There is one documented arrest. Marcy Rheintgen, a 20-year-old trans college student, was charged on 19 March 2025 after police, alerted in advance, arrested her washing her hands in a women's restroom at the Florida State Capitol, where she had declared "I am here to break the law" on entering. The misdemeanor trespass charge carried up to 60 days in jail and was described as the first arrest under Florida's transgender bathroom restrictions. On 20 June 2025 Leon County Judge Lashawn Riggans threw the case out: as a defendant charged under the statute she had no standing to argue that the law itself was illegitimate, so the statute was never substantively tested. No later arrest under the law is documented in this record.

The restriction reaches higher education through administrative rulings. On 23 August 2023 the Board of Education approved firing employees of 28 public community and state colleges who enter the forbidden bathroom, and on 18 October 2023 it voted to apply a similar restriction to private college and university buildings including student housing, with compliance proof due by 1 April 2024. The federal appellate rule moved the other way first: an August 2020 Eleventh Circuit ruling that a Ponte Vedra Beach high school violated the law by refusing a transgender student consistent restroom use was reversed in January 2023 when the court sided with the district to uphold the ban, which was codified on 17 May 2023.

State identity documents diverge from what many visitors hold. In January 2024 the Department of Highway Services and Motor Vehicles stopped issuing any driver's licence bearing a gender marker different from sex assigned at birth, treating holders, users and applicants as criminally guilty of fraud, with suspension and revocation of the document. In July 2024 transgender people born in Florida could not update or change sex on birth certificates despite explicit legislation permitting it. Before that closure, an amended birth certificate required an application to amend a Florida birth record, a notarized affidavit and a physician letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment, without requiring surgery or sterilisation; after 2011 a driver's licence or ID name change required a court order alongside a physician statement.

Gender-affirming care is restricted in state law, and the restrictions reach adults as well as minors. On 31 October 2022 the Medical Board required a 24-hour waiting period for adults before sexual reassignment surgery; on 4 November 2022 it approved a ban on gender-affirming healthcare for minors, effective 16 March 2023 and codified 17 May 2023, which prohibits hormone replacement therapy for transgender minors and adds adult barriers including a bar on insurance coverage and a requirement that treatment be administered by a physician rather than a nurse practitioner. Minors under 18 cannot receive puberty blockers, hormone therapy or confirming surgeries unless intersex, and a board memo stated that social transition should not be a treatment option. Senate Bill 254's Physicians Only provision prohibited nurse practitioners and physician assistants from providing gender-affirming care to transgender adults, which the Human Rights Campaign reported disrupted care for an estimated 80 percent or more of transgender clinic patients, with temporary or permanent suspensions after signing. A May 2023 law allows medical practitioners to refuse treatment on grounds of conscience, religion or belief. Litigation has partly checked these rules: three plaintiffs obtained a preliminary injunction on 6 June 2023 limited to themselves, the Eleventh Circuit stayed it on 26 August 2024, and a federal judge permanently blocked provisions banning care for minors and adults in June 2024.

Protection machinery at state level is thin. Florida's statutes do not address discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing or other areas, and nursing home and hospital protections in force since 2000, amended in 2007, cover sexual orientation but not gender identity. The state hate-crime law provides harsher penalties for crimes based on sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity. Since February 2021 the Florida Commission on Human Relations has announced enforcement of Bostock v. Clayton County (15 June 2020) to investigate employment, housing and public accommodations claims. Counties and cities comprising about 55 percent of the population, among them Jacksonville, Miami, Tampa, Orlando, St. Petersburg, Tallahassee and West Palm Beach, prohibit discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity in private and public employment, housing and public accommodations.

Two advocacy organisations have warned travellers directly. On 12 April 2023 Equality Florida took what it called the unprecedented step of issuing a travel advisory on risks to the health, safety and freedom of those considering short or long-term travel or relocation to Florida, citing laws hostile to LGBTQ people alongside reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety rollbacks and book bans and curriculum censorship; the organisation reports events and conferences cancelling. The Human Rights Campaign joined with an updated Florida travel advisory in May 2023, citing recently signed legislation, stopping short of a boycott. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Florida since 6 January 2015, when Brenner v. Scott held the state's ban unconstitutional.

66186276B65591139260314.blindSummary:
The state/province stands under the national framework and adds a layer a trans visitor meets directly on the ground, most sharply in public facilities. Under the state's 2023 public-facility statute, in force since 1 July 2023, a trans person may not use a restroom or changing facility consistent with their gender identity in buildings owned or leased by state/province or local government: state/province offices, courthouses, legislative offices, prisons and jails, local immigration detention facilities, state/province parks, toll-road plazas, state/province schools, state/province universities, beaches and airports. The statute purports to cover all schools, public and private. Private businesses are outside its scope.

The statute's mechanics put the decision with an authority figure on site. Gender labels are required, an internal disciplinary procedure applies, and an authority figure may order a person to depart; a non-member who does not leave can be charged with criminal trespass. A state/province civil-liberties organisation advises that refusing to leave a sex-segregated restroom or changing facility can amount to criminal trespass and that each situation calls for fact-specific judgment and legal counsel.

There is one documented arrest. A 20-year-old trans college student was charged on 19 March 2025 after police, alerted in advance, arrested her washing her hands in a women's restroom at the state capitol, where she had declared "I am here to break the law" on entering. The misdemeanor trespass charge carried up to 60 days in jail and was described as the first arrest under the state's transgender bathroom restrictions. On 20 June 2025 a county judge threw the case out: as a defendant charged under the statute she had no standing to argue that the law itself was illegitimate, so the statute was never substantively tested. No later arrest under the law is documented in this record.

The restriction reaches higher education through administrative rulings. On 23 August 2023 the state board of education approved firing employees of 28 public community and state colleges who enter the forbidden bathroom, and on 18 October 2023 it voted to apply a similar restriction to private college and university buildings including student housing, with compliance proof due by 1 April 2024. The national appellate rule moved the other way first: an August 2020 ruling by a national appeals court that a high school violated the law by refusing a transgender student consistent restroom use was reversed in January 2023 when the court sided with the district to uphold the ban, which was codified on 17 May 2023.

State/province identity documents diverge from what many visitors hold. In January 2024 the state motor-vehicle agency stopped issuing any driver's licence bearing a gender marker different from sex assigned at birth, treating holders, users and applicants as criminally guilty of fraud, with suspension and revocation of the document. In July 2024 transgender people born in the state/province could not update or change sex on birth certificates despite explicit legislation permitting it. Before that closure, an amended birth certificate required an application, a notarized affidavit and a physician letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment, without requiring surgery or sterilisation; after 2011 a driver's licence or ID name change required a court order alongside a physician statement.

Gender-affirming care is restricted in state law, and the restrictions reach adults as well as minors. On 31 October 2022 the state medical board required a 24-hour waiting period for adults before sexual reassignment surgery; on 4 November 2022 it approved a ban on gender-affirming healthcare for minors, effective 16 March 2023 and codified 17 May 2023, which prohibits hormone replacement therapy for transgender minors and adds adult barriers including a bar on insurance coverage and a requirement that treatment be administered by a physician rather than a nurse practitioner. Minors under 18 cannot receive puberty blockers, hormone therapy or confirming surgeries unless intersex, and a board memo stated that social transition should not be a treatment option. A 2023 state/province bill's Physicians Only provision prohibited nurse practitioners and physician assistants from providing gender-affirming care to transgender adults, which a national LGBTQ advocacy group reported disrupted care for an estimated 80 percent or more of transgender clinic patients, with temporary or permanent suspensions after signing. A May 2023 law allows medical practitioners to refuse treatment on grounds of conscience, religion or belief. Litigation has partly checked these rules: three plaintiffs obtained a preliminary injunction on 6 June 2023 limited to themselves, a national appeals court stayed it on 26 August 2024, and a national judge permanently blocked provisions banning care for minors and adults in June 2024.

Protection machinery at state level is thin. The state's statutes do not address discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing or other areas, and nursing home and hospital protections in force since 2000, amended in 2007, cover sexual orientation but not gender identity. The state hate-crime law provides harsher penalties for crimes based on sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity. Since February 2021 the state human-relations commission has announced enforcement of a June 2020 national supreme court holding that employment discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity is sex discrimination, to investigate employment, housing and public accommodations claims. Counties and cities comprising about 55 percent of the population prohibit discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity in private and public employment, housing and public accommodations.

Two advocacy organisations have warned travellers directly. On 12 April 2023 a national LGBTQ advocacy organisation took what it called the unprecedented step of issuing a travel advisory on risks to the health, safety and freedom of those considering short or long-term travel or relocation to the state/province, citing laws hostile to LGBTQ people alongside reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety rollbacks and book bans and curriculum censorship; it reports events and conferences cancelling. A national LGBTQ advocacy group joined with an updated travel advisory in May 2023, citing recently signed legislation, stopping short of a boycott. Same-sex marriage has been legal in the state/province since 6 January 2015, when a state court ruling held the state's ban unconstitutional.
66186276B65591139260314.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Florida's facility statute would survive a direct constitutional challenge is unresolved in this inventory. The single prosecution was dismissed on standing grounds on 20 June 2025, so the statute was never substantively tested, and no later prosecution is documented here.

The current appellate status of the gender-affirming care provisions is unresolved. The inventory records a preliminary injunction of 6 June 2023 limited to three plaintiffs, a stay by the Eleventh Circuit on 26 August 2024, and a federal judge permanently blocking provisions banning care for minors and adults in June 2024, without documenting what happened on appeal after that.

Whether the January 2024 driver's licence marker rule or the July 2024 birth certificate practice has been litigated is not sourced here. The inventory also does not document how the facility statute is applied at Florida airports in practice, nor any screening or document check specific to Florida ports of entry; those layers sit with the national record.

The Equality Florida travel advisory is dated 12 April 2023 and the Human Rights Campaign's update May 2023. No later reissuance or withdrawal by either organisation appears in this inventory, so their current status is unresolved.
66186276B65591139260314.tangentialFactors:
Florida's facility law is not isolated. At least 14 states have adopted laws barring trans women from women's bathrooms at schools and some government buildings, and the Equality Florida advisory places Florida's statutes within a wider set of measures on reproductive health, guns and school curricula that the organisation treats as travel-relevant for reasons beyond LGBTQ policy.

The state's approach to trans participation in sport predates the facility statute. A law of 1 June 2021 excluded transgender girls and women, defined as students of the male sex based on sex assigned at birth, from female school sports. In early 2023 the Florida High School Athletics Association recommended that female athletes supply menstrual cycle information to a school-accessible database, a measure speculated to serve both abortion-enforcement and detection of trans women. The Attorney General threatened competitions including an Irish step dancing competition and Miss America for allowing transgender competitors, describing them as deceptive and as depriving women of fair competition.

The Human Rights Campaign's description of the facility statute covers publicly owned or leased airports, government buildings, convention centres, parks, school campuses and stadiums, and imposes criminal penalties on visitors and residents alike who refuse to leave when asked, which is the wording a traveller is most likely to encounter.

66186276B73402293045483.summary:
Nebraska's state-level framework for trans visitors is set by Executive Order No. 23-16, signed by Governor Jim Pillen on 30 August 2023. The order establishes a Women's Bill of Rights and defines sex, female, male, woman, girl, man, boy, mother and father for use by state agencies, stating that biological sex is determined at birth and that biological differences between males and females in athletic ability and safety warrant sex-based segregation in some athletic, social and educational spaces. The order backs single-sex spaces for women's sports, bathrooms and changing rooms. Pillen was the second U.S. governor to sign such an order. Opponents questioned the order's scope and legality.

State documents are correspondingly restrictive. A legal gender marker change on a Nebraska birth certificate requires a notarized affidavit from the physician who performed sex reassignment surgery together with a certified copy of a court order changing the applicant's name. A driver's licence or state ID change requires a court order certifying the change and/or a physician-signed form confirming sex reassignment surgery. A name change requires district court paperwork, a court date, and publication for four consecutive weeks, or two weeks for minors. These requirements apply to state-issued documents; a visitor holding an out-of-state or foreign passport is not directly governed by them, but a trans person resident in Nebraska or seeking Nebraska-issued identification faces them.

Participation rules for trans students in Nebraska athletics have tightened in stages. The Nebraska School Activities Association requires transgender students to show evidence of hormone replacement therapy and/or sex reassignment surgery. In June 2025 Legislative Bill 89, banning transgender athletes from any sports, passed the unicameral legislature by a two-thirds majority and was signed by Governor Pillen; ten transgender athletes were identified as affected.

Gender-affirming healthcare for people under 19 is barred in Nebraska. The legislature passed the ban 33-15 in May 2023 and Governor Pillen signed it effective immediately. The Nebraska Supreme Court upheld it 6-1 in July 2024. A trans visitor under 19 cannot obtain this care in the state, and a visitor of any age cannot obtain it for a minor in their care.

Custody is a documented site of harm specific to Nebraska. A transgender woman diagnosed with gender dysphoria and transitioning while held in Nebraska's men's prison sued prison officials and workers; on 10 August 2022 U.S. District Judge Brian C. Buescher ruled for the defendants, dismissing her claims of failure to treat her dysphoria, denial of gender-conforming surgery, and failure to protect her. Nebraska had housed her by assigned sex at birth among male prisoners and placed her in a cell with a convicted male sex offender who sexually assaulted her. The judge had earlier dismissed the failure-to-protect claim over that placement, wrote that without medical evidence no reasonable jury could conclude the providers were deliberately indifferent to her serious medical need, and said she had not plausibly alleged more than de minimis injuries from the assault. He found no support for inferring a substantial risk from a prospective cellmate's sexual-offence conviction coupled with the alleged vulnerability of a transgender inmate transitioning to a woman in a men's prison. The placement followed her within the system.

Protection machinery is uneven. Nebraska's 1997 hate crime law guarantees the right to live free from violence or intimidation by threat of violence and enhances sentences for manslaughter, assault, terroristic threats, stalking, kidnapping and false imprisonment, rape and sexual assault, arson, criminal mischief and trespassing. It does not address gender identity. Federal law has covered gender identity under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act since 2009. The state Supreme Court upheld the hate crime law in April 2016, in a case protecting even a straight victim in the company of gay friends.

Discrimination protection for trans people in Nebraska rests on federal rulings and municipal ordinances rather than statewide statute. Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity became illegal under Bostock v. Clayton County, decided 15 June 2020. In August 2020 the Nebraska Equal Opportunity Commission announced it would investigate and resolve housing discrimination claims on account of sexual orientation or gender identity, applying the same ruling to housing. Federal enforcement followed: from 11 February 2021 the Fair Housing Act prohibition on discrimination because of sex was enforced to include sexual orientation and gender identity, with HUD accepting, investigating and enforcing complaints of anti-trans housing discrimination covering sale, rental, terms, conditions and services. Omaha has prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment and public accommodations in both the public and private sectors since 2012, when the City Council voted 4-3 on 13 March to amend the city's anti-discrimination laws to add sexual orientation and gender identity as protected classes, with an exemption for religious institutions. Lincoln passed a 5-0 ordinance in February 2022 covering employment, accommodation and housing, but the protections were removed in June 2022 after a petition drive. In November 2021 the Nebraska State College System voted 4-2 to include gender identity in its policy.

Conversion therapy aimed at changing gender identity is outlawed in Lincoln under a 2021 ordinance and remains lawful in the rest of Nebraska. Statewide ban bills were reintroduced in 2021 and 2025 but have not passed.

Marriage and family recognition are settled in Nebraska as a matter of federal law. Same-sex marriage has been legal since Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015, with then Attorney General Doug Peterson directing compliance and non-enforcement of contrary Nebraska laws. That replaced a constitutional ban adopted in November 2000 by 70 per cent to 30 per cent defining marriage as the union of a man and a woman. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can marry and have that marriage recognised. Nebraska permits adoption by same-sex couples and single LGBT individuals: the Lancaster County District Court ruled for the plaintiffs in Stewart v. Heineman on 5 August 2015, the Nebraska Supreme Court upheld that ruling in April 2017 striking down the ban on same-sex foster parents, and in March 2021 it held that state adoption law clearly allows a same-sex married couple to adopt.

Sodomy prohibitions in Nebraska were repealed by a revised criminal code enacted in June 1977, effective 1 July 1978, by a veto override of 32-15 against Governor J. James Exon.

This division's state-level framework for trans visitors is set by Executive Order No. 23-16, signed by the governor on 30 August 2023. The order establishes a Women's Bill of Rights and defines sex, female, male, woman, girl, man, boy, mother and father for use by state agencies, stating that biological sex is determined at birth and that biological differences between males and females in athletic ability and safety warrant sex-based segregation in some athletic, social and educational spaces. The order backs single-sex spaces for women's sports, bathrooms and changing rooms. The governor was the second in this country to sign such an order. Opponents questioned the order's scope and legality.

State documents are correspondingly restrictive. A legal gender marker change on a birth certificate of this division requires a notarized affidavit from the physician who performed sex reassignment surgery together with a certified copy of a court order changing the applicant's name. A driver's licence or state ID change requires a court order certifying the change and/or a physician-signed form confirming sex reassignment surgery. A name change requires district court paperwork, a court date, and publication for four consecutive weeks, or two weeks for minors. These requirements apply to state-issued documents; a visitor holding an out-of-state or foreign passport is not directly governed by them, but a trans person resident in this division or seeking identification issued here faces them.

Participation rules for trans students in this division's athletics have tightened in stages. The schools athletics association requires transgender students to show evidence of hormone replacement therapy and/or sex reassignment surgery. In June 2025 Legislative Bill 89, banning transgender athletes from any sports, passed the unicameral legislature by a two-thirds majority and was signed by the governor; ten transgender athletes were identified as affected.

Gender-affirming healthcare for people under 19 is barred in this division. The legislature passed the ban 33-15 in May 2023 and the governor signed it effective immediately. The highest civil court upheld it 6-1 in July 2024. A trans visitor under 19 cannot obtain this care in this division, and a visitor of any age cannot obtain it for a minor in their care.

Custody is a documented site of harm specific to this division. A transgender woman diagnosed with gender dysphoria and transitioning while held in this division's men's prison sued prison officials and workers; on 10 August 2022 a federal district judge ruled for the defendants, dismissing her claims of failure to treat her dysphoria, denial of gender-conforming surgery, and failure to protect her. The division had housed her by assigned sex at birth among male prisoners and placed her in a cell with a convicted male sex offender who sexually assaulted her. The judge had earlier dismissed the failure-to-protect claim over that placement, wrote that without medical evidence no reasonable jury could conclude the providers were deliberately indifferent to her serious medical need, and said she had not plausibly alleged more than de minimis injuries from the assault. He found no support for inferring a substantial risk from a prospective cellmate's sexual-offence conviction coupled with the alleged vulnerability of a transgender inmate transitioning to a woman in a men's prison. The placement followed her within the system.

Protection machinery is uneven. This division's 1997 hate crime law guarantees the right to live free from violence or intimidation by threat of violence and enhances sentences for manslaughter, assault, terroristic threats, stalking, kidnapping and false imprisonment, rape and sexual assault, arson, criminal mischief and trespassing. It does not address gender identity. Federal law has covered gender identity under a national hate crimes prevention statute since 2009. The highest civil court upheld the hate crime law in April 2016, in a case protecting even a straight victim in the company of gay friends.

Discrimination protection for trans people in this division rests on federal rulings and municipal ordinances rather than statewide statute. Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity became illegal under a national supreme court ruling decided 15 June 2020. In August 2020 the state equal opportunity commission announced it would investigate and resolve housing discrimination claims on account of sexual orientation or gender identity, applying the same ruling to housing. Federal enforcement followed: from 11 February 2021 the federal fair housing prohibition on discrimination because of sex was enforced to include sexual orientation and gender identity, with the national housing agency accepting, investigating and enforcing complaints of anti-trans housing discrimination covering sale, rental, terms, conditions and services. The second city passed a 5-0 ordinance in February 2022 covering employment, accommodation and housing, but the protections were removed in June 2022 after a petition drive. In November 2021 the state college system voted 4-2 to include gender identity in its policy.

Conversion therapy aimed at changing gender identity is outlawed in that second city under a 2021 ordinance and remains lawful in the rest of this division. Statewide ban bills were reintroduced in 2021 and 2025 but have not passed.

Marriage and family recognition are settled in this division as a matter of federal law. Same-sex marriage has been legal under a national supreme court ruling of 26 June 2015, with the then state attorney general directing compliance and non-enforcement of contrary state laws. That replaced a constitutional ban adopted in November 2000 by 70 per cent to 30 per cent defining marriage as the union of a man and a woman. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can marry and have that marriage recognised. Sodomy prohibitions in this division were repealed by a revised criminal code enacted in June 1977, effective 1 July 1978, by a veto override of 32-15 against the governor.

The practical weight of Nebraska's state measures depends on how long a visitor stays and what they need from state institutions. A short-stay visitor using only federal documents and private accommodation encounters the state framework mainly through facilities practice and the absence of a statewide gender-identity discrimination statute. A trans person resident in Nebraska, or a visitor needing Nebraska-issued identification or care, meets the marker requirements, the under-19 care ban and the athletics rules directly.

A trans visitor in a relationship that Nebraska authorities would read as same-sex under birth-sex status has full marriage and adoption recognition, so the usual concern about partner recognition in hostile jurisdictions does not arise here. The exposure lies elsewhere: in facilities, in custody if arrested and held in state or county detention, and in the absence of a statewide hate-crime or anti-discrimination provision naming gender identity.

Enforcement of the 1997 hate crime law is documented in a case the state Supreme Court decided in April 2016 protecting a straight victim in the company of gay friends, which indicates the statute is applied to perceived-association bias, but nothing in the state's own law extends that to gender identity. Federal protection under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act covers gender identity, so a bias-motivated offence against a trans person can be charged federally even where state law is silent.

Senate Bill 150, enacted on 29 March 2023 after the General Assembly overrode Governor Andy Beshear's veto, carries Kentucky's restriction on which bathrooms transgender students may use in public schools alongside its ban on gender-affirming medical care for transgender minors. It is the single 2023 statute containing the K-12 facility restriction, and the Movement Advancement Project's equality map lists it among state-level bans on transgender people using public facilities according to gender identity. The facility provision is written for public school students; the sources reviewed identify no statewide rule governing adult use of bathrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Responsibility for carrying out the school restriction sits with local districts. The Kentucky Department of Education issued guidance in April 2023 for districts implementing the state's 2023 rules, advising them to remove sex education from the fifth-grade curriculum and to proceed cautiously with the bathroom provisions.

The care ban took effect on 14 July 2023, when U.S. District Judge David Hale lifted the injunction he had issued the previous month, barring transgender minors from puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Seven transgender children and their parents had sued to block the law, and the ACLU of Kentucky described the ruling as a temporary setback. On 28 September 2023 a federal appeals panel allowed the ban to remain in force while challenges proceed. Minors already receiving care were given no phase-out.

Birth certificates can be amended only for post-operative applicants: a doctor's letter stating that gender-affirming surgery has been performed goes directly to the Department of Vital Statistics in Frankfort. A court order was previously required for a Kentucky-born person.

School sport is closed to transgender girls under Senate Bill 83, which passed the General Assembly in March 2022, was vetoed by Governor Beshear in April 2022 on constitutionality and vagueness grounds, and was enacted over that veto the same month with immediate effect. House Bill 470, carrying the minors' care ban among other provisions, advanced on 2 March 2023 and passed on 17 March 2023, was vetoed, and was overridden on 29 March 2023 by simple majority votes; police arrested 19 capitol protesters for criminal trespassing that day.

Employment protection derives from federal appellate and executive sources rather than from statute. On 7 March 2018 the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, which covers Kentucky, held in EEOC v. R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes that Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 bars firing an employee for being transgender or for transitioning, because it penalises failure to conform to birth-assigned sex stereotypes, and that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act does not permit a private employer to dismiss a transgender worker on religious grounds. The case arose from funeral director Aimee Stephens, dismissed in 2013 after disclosing her planned transition. A June 2008 executive order barred hiring or firing state employees on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, restoring protections first issued in 2003 and removed in 2006. Nineteen cities maintain Fairness Ordinances covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations.

Kentucky's hate-crime statutes cover sexual orientation and expressly exclude gender identity, so bias-motivated violence against a transgender person falls outside the state's hate-crime enhancement. The sexual-orientation provision was used in the April 2011 beating of Kevin Pennington at Kingdom Come State Park near Cumberland, which produced arrests on 15 March 2012 by Kentucky State Police working with the FBI and guilty pleas from two defendants after advocacy by the Kentucky Equality Federation.

Conversion therapy on minors has been illegal statewide since Governor Beshear's executive order of 18 September 2024, following city bans in Covington (March 2020, 5-0), Louisville (September 2020, 24-1) and Lexington (May 2021, unanimous).

Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since the Kentucky Supreme Court struck down KRS 510.100 in Kentucky v. Wasson in 1992 on state constitutional grounds, a result reinforced by Lawrence v. Texas in 2003. The unenforceable statute remains on the books; it formerly punished specified sexual acts as a misdemeanour carrying up to 12 months in jail and a $500 fine, with solicitation punishable by up to 90 days and $250.

Religious-exemption and service-access rules cut against those protections. The 2013 Religious Freedom Act requires the state to show clear and convincing evidence before burdening a sincerely held religious belief; Governor Beshear vetoed it over vagueness and the risk of overriding local non-discrimination ordinances, and the General Assembly overrode him 79-15 in the House and 32-6 in the Senate. Senate Bill 17, signed by Governor Matt Bevin in March 2017, allows religious student organisations use of school facilities and control of their internal affairs. In August 2020 a district court held that a Christian photographer, as a public business, could not be compelled to photograph same-sex weddings because the photographs are art and speech protected against compulsion.

Employment protection derives from federal appellate and executive sources rather than from statute. On 7 March 2018 a federal appeals court covering this division held, in a case concerning a funeral home, that the national employment-discrimination statute bars firing an employee for being transgender or for transitioning, because it penalises failure to conform to birth-assigned sex stereotypes, and that the national religious-exemption statute does not permit a private employer to dismiss a transgender worker on religious grounds. A June 2008 executive order barred hiring or firing state employees on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, restoring protections first issued in 2003 and removed in 2006. This division's hate-crime statutes cover sexual orientation and expressly exclude gender identity, so bias-motivated violence against a transgender person falls outside this division's hate-crime enhancement. Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since this division's highest court struck down the relevant statute in a 1992 case on state constitutional grounds, a result reinforced by a 2003 ruling of the highest court of this country. 66186276B6801956407400.name: North Carolina
66186276B6801956407400.summary:
North Carolina stands under the United States framework, and national rules on passports, entry screening, federal custody and federal health funding apply in the state as they do elsewhere in the country. The state layer is where the facility, identification, care and bias-crime questions are decided.

Facility rules are the subject of live legislative conflict rather than settled prohibition. House Bill 2, passed in an emergency 2016 session after the Charlotte city council allowed transgender people to use facilities matching their gender identity, required public bathroom use according to the sex listed on a birth certificate and barred cities from enacting anti-discrimination ordinances covering gay and transgender people. The birth-certificate bathroom provision was repealed by the General Assembly on 30 March 2017, and no state statute now bars a trans person from using the facility matching their gender identity, nor criminalises facility use. Republican legislators revived a bathroom bill in the 2025 session, so the position remains open and could change within a legislative term.

Identification documents are narrowing. A federal ruling of 26 June 2022 removed the undefined sex-reassignment-surgery requirement from the state's birth-certificate amendment process after Lambda Legal's November 2021 suit. House Bill 805, enacted over veto on 29 July 2025 and effective 1 January 2026, recognises only male and female sexes and requires an amended certificate to keep displaying the sex originally assigned alongside any change, which means a corrected state document still carries the original marker.

Care for minors is closed. Three veto-overridden laws effective 16 August 2023 ended the prescription of puberty blockers and hormone therapy and the provision of gender-affirming surgery to people under 18, and House Bill 574 barred individuals assigned male at birth from female sports and athletic teams. House Bill 805 additionally bars state funds for gender-transition care for minors and for people in prison, so a trans visitor held in state custody would not obtain transition care at state expense. A trans athlete visiting or competing in the state falls under the sports restriction.

Recourse after violence is limited. The state hate-crime statute covers neither gender identity nor sexual orientation, so an assault on a trans visitor may not be charged as a bias crime under state law even where bias is evident.

Non-discrimination coverage outside public employment is municipal and county-level. A state prohibition on local ordinances covering gender identity expired on 1 December 2020; Charlotte and Wake County ordinances explicitly covering gender identity took effect 1 January 2022, and roughly 30 per cent of the state's population lives under a local ordinance covering sexual orientation and gender identity. A trans visitor therefore has no statewide protection in private employment, housing or public accommodations, and the answer depends on the particular city or county.

sources.summary: In March 2016 the Public Facilities Privacy & Security Act (HB2) barred local governments from enacting contrary hiring and bathroom-facility policies and required bathroom use according to gender listed on birth certificate, with the birth-certificate bathroom-use portion repealed by the legislature March 30, 2017. A prior state ban on local non-public-employment ordinances prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity expired December 1, 2020, and Charlotte (August 2021) and Wake County (October 2021) ordinances explicitly covering gender identity took effect January 1, 2022, with the article reporting about 30% of the state population covered by local sexual-orientation and gender-identity ordinances. For public employment, an April 12, 2016 executive order barred LGBT discrimination including gender identity and an October 2017 extension applied protection to state contractors, while the University of North Carolina system and most listed campuses maintain gender-identity non-discrimination policies for employment and students. On August 16, 2023 three veto-overridden laws took effect requiring educators to notify parents if a student requests a different name or pronouns, banning trans girls from team sports, and banning gender-affirming care for transgender minors, with House Bill 574 specifically banning individuals assigned male at birth from female sports and athletic teams. Since August 2023 minors cannot be prescribed puberty blockers or hormone therapy or receive gender-affirming surgery, and under HB 805 veto-overridden July 29, 2025, effective January 1, 2026 the state recognizes only male and female sexes and disallows state funds for gender transition care for minors and people in prison. On gender-marker documents, a June 26, 2022 federal ruling removed the undefined sex-reassignment-surgery requirement for North Carolina birth-certificate changes following a November 2021 Lambda Legal suit, but the July 29, 2025 HB 805 override requires amended certificates to continue displaying originally assigned sex alongside any change. Effective August 15, 2023 SB49 Parents' Bill of Rights bans K-4 instruction on gender identity, requires parental notification if a child requests a different name or pronoun in records or by personnel, and grants inspection and objection rights over instructional materials, while the state hate-crime statute does not cover gender identity. Private consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized by Lawrence v. Texas (2003), but N.C. G.S. section 14-177 remains unrepealed and unenforceable for that conduct after State v. Whiteley (2005) upheld it facially only for minors, non-consensual or coercive conduct, public conduct, and prostitution. A prior state ban on local municipalities prohibiting sexual-orientation discrimination outside public employment expired December 1, 2020, while Durham and Guilford counties and Bessemer City, Durham, and High Point prohibit sexual-orientation discrimination in local public employment or discrimination and Charlotte and Wake County ordinances effective January 1, 2022 explicitly ban sexual-orientation discrimination. In public employment, the April 12, 2016 executive order and October 2017 extension bar sexual-orientation discrimination for state employees and contractors, with University of North Carolina campuses and the Housing Finance Agency maintaining sexual-orientation non-discrimination policies. The state hate-crime statute does not cover sexual orientation. In January 2021 a federal judge struck down North Carolina's exclusion of same-sex couples from domestic-violence protection, extending protections to them, and a 2008 Patients' Bill of Rights provision granted hospital visitation via designated visitor statute. In November 2021 a law banning sexual-orientation discrimination in foster-parenting placements was signed effective January 1, 2022, and on August 3, 2019 an executive order banned state funding of conversion therapy on minors.

66186276B80192890672447.name: Montana
66186276B80192890672447.summary:
Montana stands under the legal framework of the United States and under a state constitution whose equal-protection and dignity guarantees state courts have repeatedly applied to block or enjoin anti-trans legislation. In the July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment, Montana is the only state whose standing improved, on the strength of that court record, even though the statutes that would otherwise place it among the most restrictive states remain enacted.

Senate Bill 458, signed in May 2023, codified sex as an immutable male-female binary determined at birth and unchangeable. District Judge Leslie Halligan struck it down in February 2025, holding that it violated the equal-protection clauses of the Montana Constitution by leaving a gap in sex-discrimination protection. Senate Bill 437, signed 24 March 2026, codified biological definitions of gender, male, female, man, woman, mother and father based on primary sexual anatomy, provides that gender means that sex definition and not gender identity, experienced gender, expression or role, and applies across more than 60 sections of state law including driver's licences, marriage licences and anti-discrimination protections, with applicants for driver's and marriage licences required to list sex as so defined. Representative Zooey Zephyr stated that the bill erases transgender, intersex and Two-Spirit recognition; in April 2026 plaintiffs sought to add it to the ongoing litigation as fundamentally identical to SB 458.

Changes to sex markers on Montana identity documents have been blocked in court since 2022. A rule of 9 September 2022 barring changes to sex identification on birth certificates absent proof of data-entry error or a DNA test was blocked by court order on 15 September 2022, which the Department of Public Health and Human Services complied with. A bill of 22 February 2023 prohibiting gender-marker changes on all identity documents, signed 19 May 2023, was stopped by a December 2024 injunction from District Judge Mike Menahan; after an April 2024 suit by two trans women unable to update driver's licences and birth certificates, Judge Menahan issued a preliminary block on 16 December 2024 pending trial on sex-discrimination grounds, which the Montana Supreme Court upheld on 15 April 2026, holding that the constitution requires treating individuals with dignity. A Helena district court's December 2024 order also enjoined the 2022 health department rule, the Motor Vehicle Division policy requiring a birth certificate to change a driver's-licence sex marker, and portions of SB 458, finding the plaintiffs likely to succeed on the claim that the restrictions constitute sex discrimination under the state constitution.

Facilities access is governed by a statute that is not in force. House Bill 121, passed in February 2025, requires bathrooms, locker rooms and sleeping areas in publicly funded facilities to be segregated by biological sex assigned at birth; the ACLU of Montana sued immediately, and on 2 April 2025 District Judge Shane Vannatta issued a temporary restraint, finding the law motivated by animus and supported by no evidence that the restrictions advance women's safety and privacy. A proposal to forbid trans people from using Capitol bathrooms aligned with their gender was voted down by the Montana House on 3 December 2024, and a 2018 ballot initiative requiring public bathroom use to match birth-certificate gender failed to gather signatures.

Gender-affirming care for minors is not prohibited in Montana. Senate 99, signed 28 April 2023, banned such care and was described as the most comprehensive prohibition in the United States; District Judge Jason Marks preliminarily enjoined it on 27 September 2023, ruling that discrimination against a person for being transgender inherently constitutes sex discrimination under Bostock v. Clayton County and served no compelling governmental interest in protecting minors. The Montana Supreme Court kept the injunction in place on 11 December 2024 on privacy grounds, with Justice Laurie McKinnon adding that transgender status should be treated as a suspect class, and Judge Marks permanently struck the ban down on 14 May 2025 for failure to establish a bona fide health risk clearly and convincingly or to show a change in the stance of major U.S. medical organizations.

A 2021 law barring transgender athletes from public school sports, contingent on continued federal education funding and signed the following month by Governor Greg Gianforte, was struck down in September 2022 by District Judge Rienne McElyea as unconstitutional on administrative grounds for infringing the authority of the Regents of the Montana University System.

Protection against discrimination is thinner than the court record suggests. By executive order Montana prohibits gender-identity discrimination in state employment and by state contractors and subcontractors, originating in 2000 personnel rules, broadened by Executive Order 41-2008 in November 2008 and expanded to gender identity and contractors in January 2016; federal Title VII protection for gender identity under Bostock v. Clayton County applies in Montana, and ordinances in Bozeman, Butte-Silver Bow County, Helena, Missoula and Whitefish prohibit gender-identity discrimination in public and private employment, housing and public accommodations, with Missoula County covering county employees only. Montana hate-crime statutes do not include gender identity, leaving prosecution to federal courts under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. In April 2021 Governor Gianforte signed legislation granting a right to discriminate where religious beliefs are substantially burdened, widely viewed as a licence to discriminate against LGBTQ people.

Same-sex marriage has been recognised in Montana since 19 November 2014, when Judge Brian Morris enjoined the state ban effective immediately, a ruling mooted by Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015; the Montana Supreme Court recognised a common-law same-sex marriage as retroactively valid in Adami v. Nelson on 10 December 2019. This division operates under the legal framework of this country and under a constitution whose equal-protection and dignity guarantees its courts have repeatedly applied to block or enjoin anti-trans legislation. In the July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment, this division is the only state whose standing improved, on the strength of that court record, even though the statutes that would otherwise place it among the most restrictive states remain enacted.

Bill 458, signed in May 2023, codified sex as an immutable male-female binary determined at birth and unchangeable. A district judge struck it down in February 2025, holding that it violated the equal-protection clauses of this division's constitution by leaving a gap in sex-discrimination protection. Bill 437, signed 24 March 2026, codified biological definitions of gender, male, female, man, woman, mother and father based on primary sexual anatomy, provides that gender means that sex definition and not gender identity, experienced gender, expression or role, and applies across more than 60 sections of state law including driver's licences, marriage licences and anti-discrimination protections, with applicants for driver's and marriage licences required to list sex as so defined. A member of the legislature stated that the bill erases transgender, intersex and Two-Spirit recognition; in April 2026 plaintiffs sought to add it to the ongoing litigation as fundamentally identical to Bill 458.

Changes to sex markers on identity documents issued in this division have been blocked in court since 2022. A rule of 9 September 2022 barring changes to sex identification on birth certificates absent proof of data-entry error or a DNA test was blocked by court order on 15 September 2022, which the health department complied with. A bill of 22 February 2023 prohibiting gender-marker changes on all identity documents, signed 19 May 2023, was stopped by a December 2024 injunction from a district judge; after an April 2024 suit by two trans women unable to update driver's licences and birth certificates, that judge issued a preliminary block on 16 December 2024 pending trial on sex-discrimination grounds, which the highest court upheld on 15 April 2026, holding that the constitution requires treating individuals with dignity. A district court in the capital city's December 2024 order also enjoined the 2022 health department rule, the vehicle-licensing agency's policy requiring a birth certificate to change a driver's-licence sex marker, and portions of Bill 458, finding the plaintiffs likely to succeed on the claim that the restrictions constitute sex discrimination under this division's constitution.

Facilities access is governed by a statute that is not in force. Bill 121, passed in February 2025, requires bathrooms, locker rooms and sleeping areas in publicly funded facilities to be segregated by biological sex assigned at birth; a national civil-liberties organisation sued immediately, and on 2 April 2025 a district judge issued a temporary restraint, finding the law motivated by animus and supported by no evidence that the restrictions advance women's safety and privacy. A proposal to forbid trans people from using the legislature's own bathrooms aligned with their gender was voted down by the lower house of the legislature on 3 December 2024, and a 2018 ballot initiative requiring public bathroom use to match birth-certificate gender failed to gather signatures.

Gender-affirming care for minors is not prohibited in this division. Bill 99, signed 28 April 2023, banned such care and was described as the most comprehensive prohibition in this country; a district judge preliminarily enjoined it on 27 September 2023, ruling that discrimination against a person for being transgender inherently constitutes sex discrimination under a leading national precedent and served no compelling governmental interest in protecting minors. The highest court kept the injunction in place on 11 December 2024 on privacy grounds, with a justice adding that transgender status should be treated as a suspect class, and the district judge permanently struck the ban down on 14 May 2025 for failure to establish a bona fide health risk clearly and convincingly or to show a change in the stance of major national medical organisations.

A 2021 law barring transgender athletes from public school sports, contingent on continued national education funding and signed the following month by the governor, was struck down in September 2022 by a district judge as unconstitutional on administrative grounds for infringing the authority of the governing body of the division's university system.

Protection against discrimination is thinner than the court record suggests. By executive order this division prohibits gender-identity discrimination in state employment and by state contractors and subcontractors, originating in 2000 personnel rules, broadened by an executive order in November 2008 and expanded to gender identity and contractors in January 2016; national employment-protection provision for gender identity under a leading national precedent applies here, and ordinances in five local government areas (four cities and one consolidated county) prohibit gender-identity discrimination in public and private employment, housing and public accommodations, with one county's ordinance covering county employees only. This division's hate-crime statutes do not include gender identity, leaving prosecution to national courts under the national hate-crimes statute. In April 2021 the governor signed legislation granting a right to discriminate where religious beliefs are substantially burdened, widely viewed as a licence to discriminate against LGBTQ people.

Same-sex marriage has been recognised in this division since 19 November 2014, when a judge enjoined this division's ban effective immediately, a ruling mooted by a national ruling on 26 June 2015; the highest court recognised a common-law same-sex marriage as retroactively valid in a case decided on 10 December 2019. This division permits adoption with no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples or second-parent adoption, affirmed 6-1 in a case decided on 7 October 2009, which granted parental rights and set precedent for stepparent adoptions by same-sex couples.

66186276B13694661525286.name: Missouri
66186276B13694661525286.summary:
Missouri's Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act, enacted in 2023 as Senate Bill 49, has been in force since 28 August 2023. It prohibits anyone under 18 from starting gender-affirming hormones or puberty blockers, allows those already in treatment to continue, and bans all transition-related surgery for minors. A state judge denied a preliminary injunction on 29 August 2023, and the statute took effect on schedule.

The same law bars MO HealthNet, the state Medicaid programme, from paying for gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, and exposes providers who violate it to loss of their Missouri medical licence and to patient lawsuits brought up to 15 years after treatment.

Litigation began with a complaint filed 25 July 2023 in Cole County Circuit Court by Lambda Legal, the ACLU of Missouri and Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner, acting for three families of transgender young people, medical providers, PFLAG National and GLMA. Following a trial in September 2024, Judge Robert Craig Carter upheld the ban on 25 November 2024 and the plaintiffs announced an appeal. The Missouri Supreme Court affirmed unanimously on 13 January 2026, quoting the 2025 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that upheld Tennessee's comparable ban. The statute sunsets in 2027, lawmakers have stated they want it made permanent, and a November 2026 ballot initiative seeks to bar such care indefinitely.

Care in custody is separately restricted. Governor Mike Kehoe signed HB 2009, effective 2 July 2026, providing that no funds shall be expended for any cross-sex hormones or gender transition surgery undertaken for the purpose of any gender transition, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. Missouri became the seventh state to deny gender-affirming care to incarcerated people and the second in 2026 to do so. Florida, Kentucky and North Carolina have near-identical laws, while comparable measures in Idaho and Georgia were blocked by federal courts.

Trans athletes are barred from female sports. Senate Bill 39, signed 7 June 2023, requires public and private schools through college to restrict sports participation to sex assigned at birth; the ban carries a sunset clause repealing it automatically on 28 August 2027.

Identity documents carry a surgical requirement. A change of sex on a Missouri birth certificate requires a court order with certified proof on hospital letterhead, signed by the attending physician with licence and contact details, stating that the petitioner's physical sex has been altered and the surgical changes are irreversible, under Mo. Ann. Stat. § 193.215(9). Two 2013 cases that had permitted an exception were invalidated and reversed in May 2022, leaving no route around the surgical requirement. The Department of Revenue accepted Form 5532 for changing the gender designation on a licence or ID after policy review between 2016 and 2024, then reverted to requiring surgery documentation or a court order after an unspecified incident.

Protection machinery is uneven. Missouri's hate crime statutes explicitly cover gender identity, defined as "having a self-image or identity not traditionally associated with one's gender," while state non-discrimination legislation does not address gender identity at all.

66186276B13694661525286.blindSummary:
An act enacted in this division in 2023 as a senate bill, protecting adolescents from experimental treatment, has been in force since 28 August 2023. It prohibits anyone under 18 from starting gender-affirming hormones or puberty blockers, allows those already in treatment to continue, and bans all transition-related surgery for minors. A state judge denied a preliminary injunction on 29 August 2023, and the statute took effect on schedule.

The same law bars this division's Medicaid programme from paying for gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, and exposes providers who violate it to loss of their medical licence in this division and to patient lawsuits brought up to 15 years after treatment.

Litigation began with a complaint filed 25 July 2023 in a county circuit court by two national advocacy organisations and a law firm, acting for three families of transgender young people, medical providers, and two support organisations for families and clinicians. Following a trial in September 2024, a circuit judge upheld the ban on 25 November 2024 and the plaintiffs announced an appeal. The highest civil court of this division affirmed unanimously on 13 January 2026, quoting the 2025 ruling of the highest court of this country that upheld a comparable ban in a neighbouring jurisdiction. The statute sunsets in 2027, lawmakers have stated they want it made permanent, and a November 2026 ballot initiative seeks to bar such care indefinitely.

Care in custody is separately restricted. The governor signed a legislative bill, effective 2 July 2026, providing that no funds shall be expended for any cross-sex hormones or gender transition surgery undertaken for the purpose of any gender transition, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. This division became the seventh jurisdiction in this country to deny gender-affirming care to incarcerated people and the second in 2026 to do so. Three other jurisdictions have near-identical laws, while comparable measures in two further jurisdictions were blocked by federal courts.

Trans athletes are barred from female sports. A senate bill, signed 7 June 2023, requires public and private schools through college to restrict sports participation to sex assigned at birth; the ban carries a sunset clause repealing it automatically on 28 August 2027.

Identity documents carry a surgical requirement. A change of sex on a birth certificate issued in this division requires a court order with certified proof on hospital letterhead, signed by the attending physician with licence and contact details, stating that the petitioner's physical sex has been altered and the surgical changes are irreversible, under a numbered provision of this division's annotated statutes. Two 2013 cases that had permitted an exception were invalidated and reversed in May 2022, leaving no route around the surgical requirement. The licensing agency accepted a standard form for changing the gender designation on a licence or ID after policy review between 2016 and 2024, then reverted to requiring surgery documentation or a court order after an unspecified incident.

Protection machinery is uneven. This division's hate crime statutes explicitly cover gender identity, defined as "having a self-image or identity not traditionally associated with one's gender," while state non-discrimination legislation does not address gender identity at all.
