66186276B35012827062242.blindSummary:
This division's anti-discrimination act prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity and gender expression in employment, housing, public accommodations, education and credit, a coverage in force since 2008 and expanded again by the 2025 legislature, as documented in the legislature's own 2025 summary of gender-affirming-care and transgender legislation.

Bill 1312 was signed by the governor on 16 May 2025 after passing on 6 May. It requires employers and schools to use a person's chosen name and pronouns, prohibits deadnaming and misgendering in workplaces and schools with immediate effect, and requires schools with dress codes to allow a student to choose from any uniform option. Its provisions simplifying changes of gender identity on birth certificates and driver's licences, and changes of name on marriage licences, take effect on 1 October 2026.

Gender markers on state documents are changeable without surgery. The board of the public health department removed the surgical requirement unanimously in February 2019, ending a rule that had applied since 1 January 1984. A change is made by request, using a Change of Sex Designation form to the motor vehicles agency for licences and IDs and Birth Certificate Correction and Sex Designation forms to the health department for birth certificates. Birth certificates offer M, F, Intersex and X markers; IDs and licences offer male, female and X. Minors need parent or guardian consent plus confirmation from a medical or mental health professional.

Facilities access is protected. In 2013 the civil rights division ruled that a transgender six-year-old child could use the girls' restroom at her elementary school in a town in this division, and in 2023 this division implemented a law granting full access to bathroom facilities for all genders. The state anti-bullying law prohibits bullying on the basis of gender identity and requires school districts to adopt prevention policies.

The hate-crime law has covered gender identity or expression since 2001, with penalty enhancements for bias-motivated crimes. In 2009 a jury in a city in this division convicted a man of first-degree murder with a hate-crime finding in a case described as the first murder trial applying a hate-crime law where the victim was transgender. The gay panic defence was abolished by a bipartisan bill passed in June 2020 and signed in July 2020, effective immediately.

Gender-affirming care is protected at state level but is under direct pressure. Legislation signed in April 2023 was enacted to protect, defend and guarantee gender-affirming healthcare services and to guarantee safe passage of transgender individuals from other jurisdictions. Since the beginning of 2023 basic health insurance coverage in this division must explicitly include sexual reassignment surgery as a basic policy, and a July 2026 assessment counts this division among jurisdictions with comprehensive health-insurance laws covering facial-hair removal and expanded gender-related coverage. On 18 May 2026 the highest civil court ruled 5-2 that a children's hospital in this division violated state anti-discrimination law when it suspended gender-affirming care for transgender youth under federal pressure, and ordered a lower court to issue an injunction requiring the hospital to resume puberty blockers and hormone therapy. One justice wrote that continuing such treatment for cisgender children while stopping it for transgender youth meant the decision denies the petitioners the full and equal enjoyment of services based on gender identity; two justices dissented, citing federal threats that could shut the hospital system.

Conversion therapy has been banned statewide on minors since a bill signed on 31 May 2019. After the highest civil court's 8-1 ruling of 31 March 2026 in a case requiring strict scrutiny of that ban, Bill 26-1322, passed on 8 May 2026, redefines conversion therapy as direction toward a pre-determined gender identity or sexual orientation outcome and removes the statute of limitations for claims.

Custody is governed by litigation rather than statute. A 2019 class action on behalf of transgender women held in men's prisons alleged that the prison service subjected them to sexual and physical violence and denied medically necessary care. The court-approved 2024 consent decree in a case, entered in a trial court in the division's principal city, required the prison service to expand health care, create voluntary specialised housing comprising a 100-bed unit at a men's facility in the division and an integration unit at the women's prison, and pay about $2.1 million to roughly 400 class members without admitting liability. A separate 2019 settlement paid a transgender inmate $170,000 over the safety of a transgender inmate held in a men's prison. No identity-based-housing statute governs placement in this division; trans women were historically held in men's prisons, with relief won through consent decree rather than a baseline housing rule.

66186276B35012827062242.tangentialFactors:
Three ballot measures certified for the November 2026 vote would, if passed, write restrictions on transgender minors into Colorado law. Initiative 109 would ban transgender children from gendered sports that do not align with their biological sex, and Initiative 110 would prohibit surgery on a child for the purpose of altering their sex characteristics; a third certified measure, Initiative 108, concerns child sex trafficking. The measures were pushed by conservative activists and signatures were certified by state elections officials on 17 March 2026.

Restrictions on transgender students in school sport have been adopted at district level. In April 2025 the D49 school board voted 3-2 to advance a policy banning biologically male students from female sports and the reverse; the D-11 Board voted 6-1 in June 2025 for a similar policy, with Academy District 20 following suit. In December 2025 an undisclosed lawsuit settlement was reached over the banning of trans individuals from playing on female sports teams within some association governing districts, and the terms of that settlement are not public.

Colorado's protective framework is operating under direct national funding pressure. The state's own Medicaid agency has said that restoring coverage suspended under a federal rule will require legislative action, which indicates that state-level protection does not by itself hold when national funding conditions change. A visitor assessing Colorado should read its protections together with that constraint rather than as a fixed ceiling on what the state can deliver.

66186276B10610315112087.name: Minnesota
66186276B10610315112087.summary:
Minnesota sets its own civil, health-care and criminal law within the federal framework of the United States; federal rules on passports, visas, entry screening and federal custody are fixed nationally and are not restated here. On the matters a trans visitor encounters at state level, Minnesota law runs in a protective direction.

Minnesota Session Law 2023 ch. 29 (HF 146) declares that gender-affirming health care as defined in the Act "is against the public policy of this state and must not be enforced or applied" in pending cases, and amends state provisions on warrants, arrests and extraditions that arise from other states' laws on gender-affirming health care. The House passed the bill 68-62 on 24 March 2023 after a late-night debate, and Governor Tim Walz signed it. It followed a March 2023 executive order directing the Minnesota Department of Health to summarise the scientific literature on the safety and effectiveness of gender-affirming care and confirming that providers could bill insurance for such care.

The shield reaches out-of-state process. Minnesota authorities may not enforce subpoenas, arrest warrants or extradition requests issued elsewhere over gender-affirming care that is legal in Minnesota, and may not comply with out-of-state court orders to remove children from parental custody for having obtained such care. Families travelling to Minnesota for treatment fall inside that protection.

Anti-discrimination law covers gender identity. Minnesota has prohibited discrimination based on gender identity since 1993 in employment, housing, public accommodations, insurance, goods and services, contracts, health benefits and hospital visitation rights, and in that year became the first state to outlaw discrimination based on sexual orientation in the same fields. A May 2023 omnibus community justice bill protected "gender identity" as a category separate from sexual orientation and repealed exemptions for nonpublic service organizations, effective immediately. The same act repealed residual statutory language stating that the state "does not condone homosexuality or bisexuality" and did not authorise its promotion in educational institutions.

Hate-crime law has provided additional penalties for offences committed because of gender identity since that category was added in 1993; sexual orientation was added in 1989. The trans panic defence was abolished by the omnibus justice reforms signed on 29 May 2024 and effective 1 August 2024, which passed the Senate 34-33.

Identity documents are relatively open at state level. Changing the gender marker on a Minnesota birth certificate does not require sex reassignment surgery: it requires a physician's letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition, or a court order for gender change, plus a notarised Birth Certificate Application and a fee, and the previous certificate is kept confidential. Driver and Vehicle Services updates a driver's licence or state ID on individual request with no documentation required, and since October 2018 licences and state IDs offer M, F or X on request, with no documentation needed for intersex, non-binary and ambiguous-sex applicants. Birth certificates carry no X option.

Care coverage is written into state policy. State Medicaid covers transgender-related care, and Minnesota law bars health insurers from excluding transgender-specific coverage or discriminating against transgender patients. Gender-affirming services were protected by the March 2023 executive order and codified by the legislation signed in April 2023. Conversion therapy is banned for minors and vulnerable adults under a law signed by Governor Tim Walz on 26 April 2023 and effective 1 August 2023, following a July 2021 executive order and city bans beginning with Minneapolis in November 2019. Practitioners may not advertise LGBTQ identities as a mental disease, disorder or illness or promise to change sexual orientation or gender identity; violations are subject to discipline by health licensing boards, and insurers and health plans may not pay for conversion therapy.

Private consensual conduct between adults is not criminalised. Minn. Stat. 609.293, which punished voluntarily engaging in or submitting to sodomy by the anus or by or with the mouth with up to one year's imprisonment and a fine of up to $3,000, was declared unconstitutional on 15 May 2001 as applied to private, consensual, non-commercial acts of adults, on privacy grounds under the Minnesota Constitution, in an unappealed class action decided two years before Lawrence v. Texas. The prohibition had been carried since the 1849 territorial adoption of Wisconsin law and the 1851 code, was raised in 1909 to 20 years' imprisonment, was expanded in 1921 to include fellatio, and was reduced in 1967 to a misdemeanour punishable by up to one year in jail or a $1,000 fine; a 1973 repeal attempt failed 46-69 with 19 abstentions, and formal repeal came in May 2023 through the Omnibus Judiciary and Public Safety Bill signed by Governor Tim Walz.

Marriage is recognised for relationships read locally as same-sex. Same-sex marriage became legal in Minnesota on 1 August 2013, after House passage 75-59 on 9 May and Senate passage 37-30 on 13 May, signed by Governor Mark Dayton on 14 May, following the defeat of a constitutional ban by 51.5% to 47.5% on 6 November 2012. A trans visitor married to a partner of any birth-sex configuration is recognised on that footing.

Custody placement practice has been documented along birth-sex lines. CeCe McDonald, a transgender woman, pleaded guilty to second-degree manslaughter and was sentenced on 4 June 2012 to 41 months; her attorneys acknowledged there was "no way" she would be sent to a women's prison and "really no history of transgender people being placed according to their gender identity" in the state. The Minnesota Department of Corrections placed her in an adult male facility, Minnesota Correctional Facility - St. Cloud, after a state gender assessment concluded she would be held in a men's facility, and although she was later transferred to a second facility she remained quartered with men throughout her imprisonment. She was held in segregated custody while awaiting trial. In May 2012 a fellow inmate attacked her with a glass, causing a wound that required eleven stitches; the attacker pleaded guilty in April 2013 to third-degree assault and received six months' jail time plus probation. A petition filed during her imprisonment led the department to administer the correct hormone regimen.

66186276B73434888205604.summary:
New Jersey's Law Against Discrimination, amended in 2006 to cover gender identity and expression and in 1991 to cover affectional or sexual orientation, bars denial of goods, services, facilities and lodging on those grounds in places of public accommodation, which state materials describe as including hotels, restaurants, stores and transportation, as well as in housing and employment. A trans visitor refused service or lodging can complain to the Division on Civil Rights, which investigates and can grant relief.

Bias-motivated crimes carry enhanced penalties where the bias rests on gender identity or expression, with sensitivity training available as a sentencing condition. A bill extending bias and intimidation protections to gender identity passed the lower house 71-0 in March 2021. The FBI's New Jersey division has reported gender X in its data since June 2021, a July 2022 police licensing system carries gender-identity protections, and state-run hospital patient records are required to protect sexual orientation and gender identity data.

State identity documents are comparatively open. Since 1 February 2019 a transgender person may obtain an amended birth certificate with corrected name and sex without surgery or any medical procedure, under three laws signed in June 2018; those laws also created an X marker on official documents and put transgender and intersex people on death certificates. Since February 2020 no doctor's note is required to change the M or F marker on a driver licence or state ID, and since April 2021 the X, M and F markers are all available. A November 2022 executive order provides privacy and confidentiality in legal name changes. These are state documents; passport and visa issuance is governed separately by federal rules.

An April 2023 executive order directs state agencies to protect and defend gender-affirming healthcare within New Jersey's borders, including access by people travelling in from other states.

The state has recognised and performed marriages of same-sex couples since 21 October 2013, following a 27 September 2013 court decision whose appeal was rejected on 19 October 2013; the legislature codified the position in December 2021 and the governor signed it on 10 January 2022, effective immediately. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can marry and have that marriage recognised here.

A January 2020 law bars the gay and transgender panic defence, providing that provocation is not objectively reasonable when based on actual or perceived gender identity or expression, including an unwanted non-forcible romantic or sexual advance. The bill passed both chambers 73-0 and 39-0.

A July 2026 legal-risk ranking built from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills places New Jersey in the fifteen-state Most Protective tier, alongside California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington.

66186276B83663796884405.name: Connecticut
66186276B83663796884405.summary:
Connecticut sits in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, an assessment built from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, including youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition. The ranking finds the state's laws have gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

A 2022 shield law protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is lawful in Connecticut was banned in the patient's home state. That protection is directly relevant to a visitor arriving from a state that has criminalised gender-affirming care.

State law bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in public places, in public and private employment, in governmental services and in the receipt of goods and services; gender identity and expression were added to the statute in 2011. The state hate-crime law covers gender identity or expression and carries additional penalties, consolidated and strengthened by legislation signed in June 2026 and effective 1 October 2026.

Identity documents are comparatively open. Since 1 October 2015, under H.B. No. 7006, a birth-certificate sex marker can be changed without surgery on a notarised affidavit from the applicant plus a notarised affidavit from a licensed physician, advanced practice registered nurse or psychologist stating that the person has received appropriate clinical treatment such as hormone therapy. That change replaced an earlier surgery requirement, which the Senate voted 32-3 to remove on 1 June 2015. Driver's licences and state identification can be changed on request, and birth certificates, IDs and licences offer M, F and X options.

Since 1 July 2018, people in Connecticut custody are treated consistent with their gender identity, including in strip searches and in access to clothing, commissary items and educational materials, and in housing based on recognised gender.

The state anti-bullying law prohibits bullying on the basis of gender identity and expression, explicitly covering cyberbullying and harassment, and applies to all school premises. In April 2021 a federal judge dismissed the lawsuits seeking to block transgender female athletes from competing in Connecticut girls' high-school sports, leaving their eligibility intact.

Conversion therapy on minors was banned with immediate effect after signing in May 2017, following House passage 141-8 on 2 May and Senate passage 36-0 on 10 May. The gay panic defence was repealed after unanimous passage in June 2019, signed by Governor Ned Lamont and effective 1 October 2019. Consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised with effect from 1971, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, having been lowered to 15 in 1975.

A 2022 shield law protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is lawful in Connecticut was banned in the patient's home state, directly relevant to a visitor arriving from a state that has criminalised gender-affirming care. State law bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in public places, in public and private employment, in governmental services and in the receipt of goods and services; gender identity and expression were added to the statute in 2011. Identity documents are comparatively open. Since 1 October 2015, under H.B. No. 7006, a birth-certificate sex marker can be changed without surgery on a notarised affidavit from the applicant plus a notarised affidavit from a licensed physician, advanced practice registered nurse or psychologist stating that the person has received appropriate clinical treatment such as hormone therapy. That change replaced an earlier surgery requirement, which the Senate voted 32-3 to remove on 1 June 2015. Driver's licences and state identification can be changed on request, and birth certificates, IDs and licences offer M, F and X options. Since 1 July 2018, people in Connecticut custody are treated consistent with their gender identity, including in strip searches and in access to clothing, commissary items and educational materials, and in housing based on recognised gender. The state anti-bullying law prohibits bullying on the basis of gender identity and expression, explicitly covering cyberbullying and harassment, and applies to all school premises. In April 2021 a federal judge dismissed the lawsuits seeking to block transgender female athletes from competing in Connecticut girls' high-school sports, leaving their eligibility intact. Conversion therapy on minors was banned with immediate effect after signing in May 2017, following House passage 141-8 on 2 May and Senate passage 36-0 on 10 May. The gay panic defence was repealed after unanimous passage in June 2019, signed by Governor Ned Lamont and effective 1 October 2019. Consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised with effect from 1971, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, having been lowered to 15 in 1975.

66186276B99594608635082.name: Hawaii
66186276B99594608635082.summary:
Hawaii is a state of the United States and stands under the US federal framework; the national record carries federal law, passport rules and entry screening. The findings below concern Hawaii's own statutes and their application.

A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition, places Hawaii in a fifteen-state Most Protective tier and describes the laws of that tier as having gone above and beyond in safeguarding transgender rights. The assessment is a rubric-based ranking of legislation rather than a measure of enforcement.

Hawaii holds a healthcare shield law or executive order, recorded as current on 27 September 2026, which protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where care that is lawful in Hawaii was banned in the patient's home state. For a trans visitor travelling from a state with a youth-care ban or another care restriction, this is the provision most directly relevant to obtaining care while in Hawaii.

State law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in housing and public accommodations since 2005 and 2006, in employment since 2011, in insurance contracts since 1 July 2016, and in jury selection under legislation signed in June 2022 and effective 1 January 2023. The same 2022 legislation created a state LGBTIQ+ commission and mandated state health insurance coverage for sexual reassignment surgery.

The hate-crime statute covers actual or perceived gender identity or expression, defined to include a person's actual or perceived gender, gender identity, gender-related self image, appearance or expression, whether or not it differs from that traditionally associated with the person's sex at birth. The gay and trans panic defences were abolished by a bill passed in April 2019, signed on 26 June 2019 and effective immediately.

Changing a gender marker on state documents does not require surgery. Since a law passed on 5 May 2015, signed 14 July 2015 and effective immediately, transgender people may change the marker by request; an updated birth certificate requires a completed Application for Amendment to Birth Record and an affidavit from a licensed physician, and an updated driver's licence or state ID requires a Gender Designation Form completed by a medical or social professional confirming gender identity. An X sex option on driver's licences and birth certificates, passed in May 2019, signed 26 June 2019 and effective 1 July 2020, is available by request with no medical documentation required.

Health insurance provisions include coverage of sex reassignment surgeries under the 2016 insurance nondiscrimination rule, mandatory coverage effective 1 January 2023, and the inclusion of transgender individuals in health insurance planning under a bill passed in May 2022 with an emergency clause signed a month later and effective immediately, replacing male-only and female-only planning in place since 1980. Conversion therapy on minors has been banned since 1 July 2018.

Marriage is open to couples regardless of gender under the Hawaii Marriage Equality Act, passed by the Senate 20-4 on 30 October 2013 and by the House 30-19 on 8 November 2013, given final Senate approval 19-4 on 12 November 2013 and signed on 13 November 2013, with marriages beginning 2 December 2013. The 1998 constitutional amendment that authorised the legislature to reserve marriage to opposite-sex couples was repealed by referendum on 5 November 2024, with 55.94 per cent voting to delete the opposite-sex limitation from Article I Section 23. Reciprocal beneficiary relationships have existed since 1997, civil unions were signed on 23 February 2011 and effective 1 January 2012, and benefits for the partners of state employees have been provided since 1997.

Parentage rules have moved toward gender neutrality. A bill passed in April 2021 and signed in July 2021 recognised unmarried same-sex parentage with immediate effect, and Act 298, effective 1 January 2026, implements gender-neutral parentage by voluntary acknowledgment or court adjudication.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since the 1972 repeal took effect in 1973, replacing an 1850 anti-sodomy statute; the age of consent has been 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation since 2001.

The national inventory of bathroom restrictions does not list Hawaii among the nine states and one territory that bar transgender people from sex-segregated facilities in schools or government buildings.

Illinois is placed in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking compiled from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, which describes the tier's laws as having gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

The exemption for employers with fewer than 15 employees was removed by legislation signed in August 2019 and effective 1 July 2020, following a 2018 veto, and discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in jury selection was banned effective 1 January 2020.

Hate-crime penalties were extended to gender identity by HB 3930, passed unanimously on 16 April and 20 May 2015, signed by Governor Bruce Rauner on 20 July 2015 and effective 1 January 2016; before that, such offences were covered only as perceived sexual orientation. The state's hate-crime statute has provided enhanced penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived sexual orientation since 1991. The gay and trans panic defence was repealed by SB1761, passed unanimously in June 2017, signed on 25 August 2017 and effective 1 January 2018.

Gender-affirming care is protected by legislation signed on 13 January 2023 and effective immediately, covering care provided within Illinois, including for people who travel from outside the state to obtain it. Under the shield law, patients and providers are protected from civil or criminal charges where care lawful in Illinois was banned in the patient's home state. Conversion therapy on minors under 18 by mental health providers has been banned under the Youth Mental Health Protection Act since 1 January 2016; a federal court dismissed a challenge brought by pastors on 15 February 2017, holding that private religious counselling is not trade or commerce.

Birth-certificate gender-marker changes no longer require surgery, under legislation passed on 31 May 2017 by 63-43 in the House and 32-22 in the Senate, signed on 25 August 2017 and effective 1 January 2018. An X option has been available since July 2020, and a self-attestation reform passed in January and February 2023 took effect on 1 July. Since 1 July 2024, people born outside Illinois can change the sex designation on an Illinois birth certificate. Driver's licences and state identification are corrected on a Gender Designation Change Form, with an X option available from 2024.

Single-occupancy public restrooms were designated gender-neutral by legislation passed 109-5 in the House and 53-0 in the Senate, signed in July 2019 and effective 1 January 2020. Chicago's Human Rights Ordinance, as amended in 2016, provides that each person determines their own gender identity, with no proof required beyond expression for bathroom access, and all Chicago public schools have had all-gender bathrooms by signage since December 2021. A May 2023 bill permitting use of multi-occupancy facilities consistent with a person's gender identity passed both chambers but had not been signed or vetoed.

Marriage equality was enacted by statute signed by Governor Pat Quinn on 20 November 2013 and effective 1 June 2014, after House approval 61-54 and Senate approval 32-21, superseding a 1996 statutory ban. Gender-neutral marriage certificates have been available under a July 2021 law, and 2023 legislation repealing out-of-jurisdiction null-and-void provisions took effect in 2024. Civil unions have been recognised since 1 June 2011 under a law signed on 31 January 2011, with out-of-state marriages of same-sex couples recognised as civil unions. The Illinois Domestic Violence Act is written in gender-neutral terms and applies to partners who share or have shared a dwelling or a dating relationship.

Private consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since 1 January 1962, when a new criminal code eliminated the state's sodomy law, making Illinois the first state to do so. The age of consent is 17, raised from 16 effective 1 January 2012.

Gender-affirming care is protected by legislation signed January 13, 2023 effective immediately covering care within Illinois including for individuals coming from outside Illinois to seek services, Illinois Medicaid covers reassignment surgery costs for applicants aged at least 21, and in June 2024 the Department of Human Services and Public Health Institute of Metropolitan Chicago announced expansion through the Transgender and Gender Diverse Wellness and Equity Program. Birth-certificate gender-marker change no longer requires operation(s) after legislation passed May 31, 2017 by 63-43 in the House and 32-22 in the Senate, signed August 25, 2017 effective January 1, 2018, requiring an Affidavit and Certificate of Correction Request plus Declaration of Gender Transition/Intersex Condition by a licensed health or mental health professional plus $15 fee, with X option available since July 2020 and self-attestation reform passed in January-February 2023 effective July 1, plus since July 1, 2024 persons born outside Illinois can change sex on a birth certificate, and driver's license and state ID correction upon Gender Designation Change Form with X available from 2024. Single-occupancy public restrooms were designated gender-neutral by legislation passed 109-5 in the House and 53-0 in the Senate, signed July 2019 effective January 1, 2020, Chicago's Human Rights Ordinance as amended in 2016 provides each person determines his or her own gender identity with no proof required except expression for bathroom access, and all Chicago public schools have all-gender bathrooms by signage since December 2021, while a May 2023 multi-occupancy permissive-use bill had passed both houses but awaited governor signature or veto. Funeral and burial instructions may specify gender identity and preferred pronouns under HB 3552 signed August 20, 2015 effective January 1, 2016 after passage 79-34 in the House and 49-0 in the Senate, Des Plaines repealed its opposite-sex clothing ban in July 2021, and transgender students are protected by a June 30, 2019 executive order establishing a task force and procedures for names, pronouns and dress codes. On intersex rights, Lurie Children's Hospital in July 2020 apologised for past non-consensual infant surgeries to make genitalia appear more typically male or female and announced cessation unless medically necessary. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since January 1, 1962 when a new code eliminated sodomy laws making Illinois the first state to do so, with the age of consent set at 18 then lowered to 16 in 1984 and raised to 17 effective January 1, 2012, and public lewd fondling language changed from 'same sex' to 'either sex' in 1963 then repealed in 1984. Same-sex marriage was banned by statute in 1996 under SB 1773 then legalized by statute signed November 20, 2013 by Governor Pat Quinn effective June 1, 2014 after House approval 61-54 and Senate approval 32-21, with gender-neutral marriage certificates available under July 2021 law and 2023 repeal of out-of-jurisdiction null-and-void provisions effective 2024, and civil unions recognized since June 1, 2011 under law signed January 31, 2011 with out-of-state same-sex marriages recognized as civil unions and surviving sex reassignment surgery. Discrimination on sexual orientation has been banned in employment, housing, public accommodations and credit since June 1, 2006, expanded by removal of the 15-employee loophole signed August 2019 effective July 1, 2020 after a 2018 veto, jury-selection discrimination on sexual orientation banned effective January 1, 2020 after unanimous passage in May 2019, and anti-bullying law expanded in 2014 to include sexual orientation. Hate-crime legislation since 1991 provides harsher penalties for crimes based on actual or perceived sexual orientation alongside race, religion, sex and other categories. Conversion therapy on minors under 18 by mental health providers was banned under the Youth Mental Health Protection Act passed 68-43 in the House on May 19, 2015 and 34-19 in the Senate on May 29, 2015 and signed August 20, 2015 effective January 1, 2016 after a 2014 bill failed 44-51, with a federal court dismissing pastors' suit on February 15, 2017 as private religious counseling is not trade or commerce. The Illinois Domestic Violence Act in gender-neutral language applies to same-sex partners sharing or having shared a dwelling or dating relationship, the state permits adoption by gay individuals or partners including second-parent adoptions with IVF and gestational surrogacy access, and a May 2021 bill repealed the 1983 HIV infection public health law effective immediately upon governor signature.

The exemption for employers with fewer than 15 employees was removed by legislation signed in August 2019 and effective 1 July 2020, following a 2018 veto, and discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in jury selection was banned effective 1 January 2020.

Hate-crime penalties were extended to gender identity by a bill passed unanimously on 16 April and 20 May 2015, signed by the governor on 20 July 2015 and effective 1 January 2016; before that, such offences were covered only as perceived sexual orientation. The hate-crime statute has provided enhanced penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived sexual orientation since 1991. The gay and trans panic defence was repealed by a bill passed unanimously in June 2017, signed on 25 August 2017 and effective 1 January 2018.

Gender-affirming care is protected by legislation signed on 13 January 2023 and effective immediately, covering care provided within this division, including for people who travel from outside it to obtain it. Under the shield law, patients and providers are protected from civil or criminal charges where care lawful in this division was banned in the patient's home jurisdiction. Conversion therapy on minors under 18 by mental health providers has been banned under youth mental health protection legislation since 1 January 2016; a federal court dismissed a challenge brought by pastors on 15 February 2017, holding that private religious counselling is not trade or commerce.

Birth-certificate gender-marker changes no longer require surgery, under legislation passed on 31 May 2017 by 63-43 in the lower chamber and 32-22 in the upper chamber, signed on 25 August 2017 and effective 1 January 2018. An X option has been available since July 2020, and a self-attestation reform passed in January and February 2023 took effect on 1 July. Since 1 July 2024, people born outside this division can change the sex designation on a birth certificate issued here. Single-occupancy public restrooms were designated gender-neutral by legislation passed 109-5 in the lower chamber and 53-0 in the upper chamber, signed in July 2019 and effective 1 January 2020. A large city's human rights ordinance, as amended in 2016, provides that each person determines their own gender identity, with no proof required beyond expression for bathroom access, and all public schools in that city have had all-gender bathrooms by signage since December 2021. 66186276B15934532614691.summary:
Massachusetts prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity and expression in credit, public and private employment, union practices and housing under legislation enacted on 23 November 2011 and in force from 1 July 2012, following an executive order of 17 February 2011 that barred state government and its contractors from discriminating against transgender state employees. Public-accommodation coverage was added by a Senate vote of 33-4 on 12 May 2016 and a House vote of 117-36 on 7 July 2016, signed by Governor Charlie Baker and effective 1 October 2016, and was retained at the ballot on 6 November 2018 by 67.8 per cent to 32.2 per cent, the first statewide popular vote of its kind in the United States. For a visitor these are the operative rules in hotels, restaurants, shops, transport and other places open to the public.

Gender identity was written into the hate-crime statute with effect from 1 July 2012. The framework defines a hate crime as a criminal act accompanied by overt actions motivated at least in part by prejudice, including on grounds of gender and sexual orientation, and requires incidents to be collected, summarised and publicly reported through the Crime Reporting Unit created by the 1990 Hate Crimes Reporting Act, involving the State Police, the Attorney General and legislative committees, alongside a Governor's Task Force on Hate Crimes established in 1991.

The state issues its own identity documents on self-declared terms. Birth certificates may be amended to reflect gender identity without sex reassignment surgery. Non-binary X markers on driver's licences and state identification cards have been available since November 2019 under a Registry of Motor Vehicles regulation, and non-binary X birth certificates and amendment of gender on marriage certificates were authorised by law signed on 29 July 2024 in the FY25 budget. Marriage licence forms in Boston have carried no gender or sex field since August 2023. Name changes can be obtained confidentially without public notice under An Act Protecting Personal Security, signed on 25 November 2025.

Health care is protected in two directions. A shield law in place since 2022 protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where care lawful in Massachusetts was banned in the patient's home state; this is the provision most likely to matter to a visitor travelling from a state that has banned the care. In July 2022 both chambers passed and the Governor signed a bill codifying gender-affirming healthcare protections, which took effect immediately under an emergency clause rather than after the usual 90-day period. Conversion-therapy practices on minors were banned by legislation passed 147-8 in the House on 13 March 2019 and 34-0 in the Senate on 28 March 2019, enacted on 4 April 2019 and signed on 8 April 2019 with immediate effect, making Massachusetts the sixteenth state with such a ban.

Marriage is open to same-sex couples following the Supreme Judicial Court's ruling of 18 November 2003, with licences issued from 17 May 2004 after the 180-day legislative window; attempts at a constitutional amendment failed and ended in 2007. The 1913 bar on non-resident marriages was repealed on 31 July 2008, so a couple travelling to Massachusetts can marry there, and 2012 rulings treat out-of-jurisdiction civil unions and California registered domestic partnerships as equivalent to marriage.

Two provisions of the criminal code remain on the books unrepealed: section 34, criminalising the abominable and detestable crime against nature, and section 35, covering any unnatural and lascivious act. Private consensual adult conduct has been outside their reach since the Supreme Judicial Court's 1974 decision in Commonwealth v. Balthazar, and the provisions are unenforceable as applied to such conduct. Repeal attempts repeatedly stalled in committee, including through the 2018 session that removed the abortion, adultery and fornication laws but left the sodomy, anal-sex and oral-sex provisions; the Senate passed repeal unanimously in January 2024, the House advanced it in June 2025, and a Senate committee scheduled it for floor consideration on 24 July 2025. Massachusetts is the only New England state, and one of two northern states, that still carries legislative criminalisation of same-sex conduct. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status falls nominally within the statute's wording, though it is not enforced against private consensual conduct.

In a national legal-risk ranking published in July 2026, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's-licence restrictions and removal of legal recognition, Massachusetts sits in the fifteen-state Most Protective tier.

Conversion-therapy practices on LGBT minors, encompassing lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender minors, were banned by legislation passed by the House 147-8 on March 13, 2019 and Senate 34-0 on March 28, 2019, enacted April 4, 2019 and signed April 8, 2019 effective immediately. Discrimination against LGBTI individuals within nursing homes was prohibited by a bill passed by the General Court in August 2024 and signed September 6, 2024. Private consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the 1974 Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court decision in Commonwealth v. Balthazar holding the 'unnatural and lascivious act' prohibition inapplicable to private consensual adult conduct, with current private behavior unrestricted as permanently enjoined by that decision and Lawrence v. Texas, although sections 34 and 35 criminalizing the 'abominable and detestable crime against nature' and 'any unnatural and lascivious act' remain on the books unrepealed. Same-sex couples may adopt through second-parent adoption allowed since In re Adoption of Tammy in 1993 and visitation rights recognized July 1999, after 1985 foster-parent exclusionary regulations were rescinded April 1990 in settlement of suit by Gay & Lesbian Advocates & Defenders and the ACLU, while birth-certificate forms were changed from mother/father to mother/parent and father/parent under Governor Deval Patrick in 2007 with standardized electronic hospital forms announced February 2011, and legal parentage from IVF and surrogacy regardless of marital status was passed unanimously August 1, 2024, signed August 8, 2024 effective January 1, 2025. Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since 1989 in credit, public and private employment, union practices, housing and public accommodation as the second such state law after Wisconsin in 1982, with sexual orientation added to the 1983 hate-crime law in June 1996 and recognized as a protective class for jury selection by August 2021 Supreme Judicial Court ruling, alongside May 2010 anti-bullying legislation requiring schools to adopt reporting, investigation and anti-retaliation procedures. Conversion therapy on minors was banned after House passage 137-14 in June 2018 failed in the Senate, followed by House passage 147-8 March 13, 2019, Senate passage 34-0 March 28, 2019, enactment April 4, 2019 and signing April 8, 2019 effective immediately, while Catholic Charities of Boston ceased adoption services in March 2006 rather than comply with law prohibiting discrimination against homosexuals.

66186276B2592965416524.summary:
New Mexico sits in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, compiled by applying a rubric to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition. The ranking's authors describe the laws of this tier as having gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

State law effective 1 July 2003 prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership. The public-accommodations limb is the one a visitor interacts with directly: it covers restaurants, hotels, shops and other places serving the public. The 15-or-more-employees exemption was repealed effective 1 July 2019, and 2023 legislation explicitly extended coverage to local entities, counties, schools, universities and government-run agencies under an emergency clause; Albuquerque amended its Human Rights Ordinance in May 2024 to align.

Since 1 November 2019 transgender people may change legal gender without surgery. Legislation passed 26-13 in the House and 33-14 in the Senate and signed by Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham repealed the 1984 surgery requirement and provides male, female and X neutral designations on birth certificates, driver's licences and state IDs. An applicant submits a Request to Change Gender Designation on a Birth Certificate form with fees, with parental consent for minors, or a Request for Sex Designation Change form to the Motor Vehicles Division for licences and IDs. This replaced a prior requirement for a perjury statement from an institution or physician attesting surgical change plus a certified name-change order.

Since 1 July 2019 businesses and public facilities with single-occupancy restrooms must mark them gender-neutral and available to any person regardless of gender identity or sex, under legislation passed 54-12 in the House and 23-15 in the Senate and signed by the Governor. The state has no law prohibiting transgender girls' sports participation; eligibility is determined by birth certificate, original or amended, and the New Mexico Activities Association has issued no further guidance.

Gender-affirming care is protected rather than restricted. In March 2023 House Bill 7 codified protection for gender-affirming care and sex-reassignment surgery for adults on request without restrictions, including for interstate travellers, and is cited as establishing New Mexico as a refuge for transgender youths. The Movement Advancement Project's Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, data as of 27 September 2026, lists New Mexico as a state holding a shield law or 2023 executive order: the shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where the care is legal in New Mexico but banned in the patient's home state, which is directly relevant to a visitor travelling from a ban state. In 2026 the state health care authority announced use of state funds to maintain Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming care after a federal rule moved to exclude it.

Since 2003 New Mexico's hate-crime law has explicitly covered violence committed on the basis of actual or perceived gender identity. In February 2022 the Legislature passed omnibus crime bill HB68 repealing the common-law gay and trans panic defence, signed 9 March 2022. March 2019 school-bullying legislation protects students on the basis of gender identity and requires districts to adopt prohibition, reporting, investigation, disciplinary, prevention and staff-training policies, effective 1 July 2019.

Same-sex couples have had the same marriage rights as different-sex couples since the 19 December 2013 state Supreme Court ruling requiring equal marriage rights, making New Mexico the 17th state to recognise same-sex marriage; statutory codification passed 62-0 in the House and 39-0 in the Senate in March 2019 and took effect 1 July 2019. A trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore has that relationship recognised here.

sources.summary: State law effective July 1, 2003 prohibits discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership, later expanded by repeal of the 15-or-more-employees exemption effective July 1, 2019 and by 2023 legislation explicitly covering local entities, counties, schools, universities and government-run agencies under emergency clause, with Albuquerque amending its Human Rights Ordinance in May 2024 to align. Since 2003 hate-crime law explicitly covers violence committed based on actual or perceived gender identity, and March 2019 school-bullying legislation protects students on the basis of gender identity and requires districts to adopt prohibition, reporting, investigation, disciplinary, prevention and staff-training policies effective July 1, 2019. Since November 1, 2019 transgender people may change legal gender without surgery under legislation repealing the 1984 surgery requirement and providing male, female and X neutral designation on birth certificates, driver's licenses and state IDs, passed 26-13 in the House and 33-14 in the Senate and signed by Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham. Applicants need only submit a completed Request to Change Gender Designation on a Birth Certificate form with fees, with parental consent for minors, and a Request for Sex Designation Change form to the Motor Vehicles Division for licenses and IDs, replacing the prior requirement for a perjury statement from an institution or physician of surgical change plus certified name-change order. Since July 1, 2019 businesses and public facilities with single-occupancy restrooms must mark them gender-neutral available to any person regardless of gender identity or sex under legislation passed 54-12 in the House and 23-15 in the Senate and signed by the Governor. In March 2023 HB7 codified protection for gender-affirming care and sexual reassignment surgery for adults on request without restrictions even for interstate travellers, making New Mexico a sanctuary state for transgender youths, while HB31 repealed the requirement to publish a legal name change in a newspaper that risked privacy, safety and lives of transgender individuals, and in 2026 the health care authority announced use of state funds to maintain Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming care after a federal rule to exclude it. In February 2022 the Legislature passed omnibus crime bill HB68 repealing the common-law gay and trans panic defence, signed March 9, 2022, and there is no state law prohibiting transgender girls' sports participation with eligibility determined by birth certificate original or amended and no further guidance from the New Mexico Activities Association. Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal since repeal of the anti-sodomy law in 1975, with a 1986 attempt to reinstate it failing. Same-sex couples have had the same marriage rights as different-sex couples since the December 19, 2013 state Supreme Court ruling requiring equal marriage rights, making New Mexico the 17th state to recognize same-sex marriage, with benefits for same-sex partners of state employees since 2003 and statutory codification passed 62-0 in the House and 39-0 in the Senate in March 2019, signed in April by Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham effective July 1, 2019. Single persons, same-sex couples and second-parent adoptions are permitted with no prohibition, lesbian couples may access in vitro fertilization and donor insemination regardless of sexual orientation or marital status with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized as legal parent, and no statute or case law prohibits gestational or traditional surrogacy which courts generally recognize. State law effective July 1, 2003 prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership, supplemented by a 1985 executive order barring sexual-orientation discrimination in public employment, with enforcement upheld unanimously in Elane Photography v. Willock in 2013 for refusal to photograph a same-sex commitment ceremony. Since 2003 hate-crime law explicitly covers violence based on actual or perceived sexual orientation, and March 2019 school-bullying legislation protects students on the basis of sexual orientation effective July 1, 2019. Sexual orientation change efforts on minors are prohibited under SB121 passed 32-6 in the Senate and 44-23 in the House, signed April 7, 2017 by Governor Susana Martinez effective July 6, 2017. The common-law gay panic defence was repealed through omnibus crime bill HB68 passed in February 2022 and signed March 9, 2022 after unanimous Senate-only passages in 2019 and 2021 that died without House action. Historically the Navajo recognized four gender roles including nadleehi defined as a male-bodied person with a feminine nature, who due to perceived balance between sexes were typically chosen for certain societal and communal roles such as spiritual healers. They would traditionally wear female clothes and do female work, and some would have sexual relations with men which was accepted by the tribe, with similar recognized roles including Zuni lhamana and katsotse and equivalents among Mescalero Apache, Tiwa, Tewa and pueblos. As a result of colonization much of this cultural acceptance has disappeared, Navajo nadleehi became the subject of ridicule, and Christian converts among the Hopi were prohibited from attending the traditional snake dance because male cross-dressing could be observed. Will Roscoe is documented as writing about the "tolerance or even respect of transgender people" as fueling Spanish explorers' argument for colonization of native peoples and their lands in the name of Christianity. Today LGBTQ Navajo may find it difficult being accepted by family, with 70% of LGBT Navajo youth reportedly attempting suicide. Statewide polling showed 73% supported anti-discrimination legislation protecting LGBTQ people in 2018 and 64% supported a law covering sexual orientation and gender identity in 2017, while Santa Fe is cited as a gay capital and Albuquerque including its metropolitan area as a gay-friendly city.

66186276B43575054209436.summary:
New York sits in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's-licence restrictions and withdrawal of legal recognition. The same ranking places the least protective states at the opposite end, with prison terms of up to five years for youth-care provision and arrest policies for gender-identity bathroom use.

Gender identity and expression have been protected statewide in credit, housing, employment, education and public accommodations since the Gender Expression Non-Discrimination Act was signed in January 2019 and took effect in February 2019, building on a 2009 executive order barring gender-identity discrimination in state employment and Division of Human Rights regulations issued 4 November 2015, effective 20 January 2016, covering transgender harassment and discrimination in those domains. A 2024 constitutional amendment explicitly bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity.

The Hate Crimes Act has covered gender identity and expression since 1 November 2019, with further anti-bias reform bills signed in November 2022. The gay and transgender panic defence was repealed in June 2019, effective immediately, making New York the sixth state to abolish it. Conversion therapy on minors has been banned effective 25 January 2019.

Since 2014 transgender adults could change the gender on birth certificates with a notarized medical affidavit verifying surgery or a gender dysphoria diagnosis; this was updated in 2020 to allow self-affirmation, with parental consent required for those under 17. The June 2021 Gender Recognition Act allowed an X marker on driver's licences and eased sealing of name- and gender-change records. An X marker on New York City birth certificates took effect 1 January 2019 and on death certificates from 2 January 2020; X was reported for state court and jury documents in November 2019 and in healthcare data from August 2020; X on all state forms was approved in April 2022 for 2023, with some organizations until 2024, alongside updatable marriage certificates. A November 2021 law effective 1 January 2022 requires utilities and municipalities to use preferred names and pronouns.

Shield protections apply. The MAP Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, data as of 27 September 2026, lists New York as a state with a shield law or executive order from 2023: the shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care legal in New York was banned in their home state, which is directly relevant to visitors travelling from ban states. Nationally, 16 states and the District of Columbia, covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, hold shields, while 32 states and five territories, covering 56%, hold none. New York City issued an executive order on 12 June 2023 barring city resources from being used to detain, prosecute or investigate the provision or receipt of gender-affirming care. A state law of 25 June 2023, making New York the twelfth shield state, bars courts from enforcing out-of-state laws removing custody over youth gender-affirming care, bars treating such care as child abuse, and bars law-enforcement cooperation with out-of-state agencies. A September 2023 Ithaca ordinance and April 2025 City Council bills expanded provider protections.

Former Penal Law Section 240.37, in effect since 1976 and used by police to harass and arrest transgender individuals, was repealed in February 2021, effective immediately. Gender-neutral bathrooms were mandated by a law signed in December 2020, effective 23 March 2021. The anti-bullying law covers gender, including gender identity and expression, including cyberbullying, in all public elementary and secondary schools, with a 2019 loophole closure. A June 2023 law explicitly includes gender identity in drug treatment and addiction programmes, and a November 2020 law requires annual judiciary statistics by gender identity.

Nassau County remains the only county in New York banning transgender athletes from women's sports on county-run facilities, with a 2025 ruling finding no clear violation of anti-discrimination laws and an NYCLU lawsuit seeking inclusion.

Same-sex marriage became legal statewide under the Marriage Equality Act, passed 24 June 2011 and effective 24 July 2011, following a May 2008 directive recognizing out-of-jurisdiction marriages. Consenting adult same-sex sexual activity was legalized by New York v. Onofre in 1980, with defunct sodomy provisions affecting National Guard employees repealed effective 2000. A 2019 law granted state veterans benefits to those dishonorably discharged under Don't Ask, Don't Tell from 1993 to 2011.

On 16 December 2009 New York barred state agencies from discriminating on the basis of gender identity in all state-employment matters including hiring, termination, retention, appointment, promotion, tenure, recruitment and compensation, defining gender identity as having or being perceived as having a gender identity, self-image, appearance, behavior or expression whether or not different from sex assigned at birth, and ordered equal-opportunity efforts, consistent guidelines and swift confidential complaint investigations, effective immediately.

66186276B97229519707655.summary:
Oregon sits in the fifteen-jurisdiction "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking compiled from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, among them youth care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's licence restrictions, and measures removing legal recognition. The rubric describes the laws in this tier as having gone beyond baseline safeguarding of trans rights.

Statewide anti-discrimination law covers the settings a visitor uses daily. The Oregon Equality Act, signed 9 May 2007 as Senate Bill 2 and in force since 1 January 2008, prohibits discrimination in employment, housing, public accommodation, public education and public services on the ground of gender identity. Sexual orientation is defined to include gender identity regardless of whether a person's identity, appearance, expression or behaviour differs from what is traditionally associated with sex assigned at birth. The protections apply uniformly across the state and do not depend on the locality; religious employers, organisations and institutions are exempt.

Bias-motivated violence carries enhanced penalties: state hate-crime statutes add punishment for crimes committed because of the victim's gender identity. SB704, passed and signed in May 2021 and effective 1 January 2022, abolishes the gay panic and trans panic defences in murder, manslaughter and hate-crime cases.

Identity documents are comparatively accessible. The driver-licensing agency has offered an X marker for neutral or non-binary identity on licences and state IDs since 1 July 2017, and X is also available on birth certificates. Sex reassignment surgery has not been required to change the gender marker on a birth certificate by request since 2014. Legislation in May 2017 abolished the 1991 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before a legal change of sex. A circuit court ruling on 10 June 2016 allowed a resident to change gender to non-binary, which the Transgender Law Center believed was the first ruling of its kind in the country. An October 2019 executive order added gender identity to a 1987 policy barring state agencies from unlawful discrimination and required a third gender option X; legislation signed in June 2021 updated the 2008 definition of gender identity.

Care is shielded for people arriving from states that have banned it. Oregon's shield law, signed by Governor Tina Kotek on 13 July 2023, protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges or investigation when care that is legal in Oregon was prohibited in the patient's home state. The House passed the bill in May 2023; the Senate passed a version with amendments after a Republican boycott.

Partner recognition does not turn on the parties' birth sex. State hate crime statutes provide additional penalties for crimes committed based on the victim's gender identity, and SB704 passed and signed in May 2021 effective January 1, 2022 abolishes the gay panic and trans panic defenses in murder, manslaughter and hate crime cases. Since 2014 sex reassignment surgery has not been a requirement to change the gender marker on a birth certificate solely by request, a June 10, 2016 circuit court ruled a resident could legally change gender to non-binary in what the Transgender Law Center believed was the first ruling of its kind in the U.S., and since July 1, 2017 the Department of Motor Vehicles has offered X designating neutral or non-binary identity on licenses and IDs with X also available for birth certificates, while May 2017 legislation abolished the 1991 requirement for transgender people to publish names in newspapers before legal change of sex. In January 2013 as part of a discrimination settlement the state agreed to provide full medical insurance coverage for gender-affirming surgeries, drugs and related treatments for individuals on public employee health plans, and in August 2014 officials announced Medicaid would shortly begin covering gender-affirming hormone therapy and other gender-affirming healthcare. In May 2023 amid national backlash the House passed a bill to protect and defend gender-affirming healthcare especially for those entering Oregon from other states, frozen then passed in the Senate with watered-down amendments after a Republican boycott, signed July 13, 2023 by Governor Tina Kotek. A transgender-inclusive public schools policy survived challenge after the District Court ruled against plaintiffs July 24, 2018, the Ninth Circuit upheld February 12, 2020, and the Supreme Court denied certiorari in December 2020 in Parents for Privacy v. Barr, while April 2019 legislation signed May 6 amended a 1951 mental health law that equated transvestites with pedophilia after 58-2 House and 29-0 Senate votes. In July 2025 the 9th Circuit ruled the State adoption requirement to respect, accept and support a child's gender expression and sexual orientation was unconstitutional after the Department of Human Services prevented a woman seeking to adopt, and in June 2025 the U.S. Department of Education announced a Title IX investigation into the Oregon Department of Education for allowing transgender women to compete in women's sports. Oregon decriminalized same-sex sexual activity in 1972 after the 1971 repeal of the consensual sodomy law with an age of consent of 18, and a controversial lewd solicitation provision making it criminal to invite a person in a public place to have sexual intercourse was declared unconstitutional on free speech grounds in a unanimous 1981 Oregon Supreme Court decision. Same-sex marriage was legalized May 19, 2014 after Judge Michael McShane ruled the 2004 constitutional amendment banning such marriages via Ballot Measure 36 unconstitutional under the Equal Protection Clause, with same-sex marriages from other jurisdictions recognized since October 16, 2013 per Department of Justice opinion and gender-neutral marriage codified effective January 1, 2016, while domestic partnerships have been available since February 4, 2008 under the Family Fairness Act and benefits to same-sex partners of state employees have been provided since 1998. Since January 1, 2008 Oregon has banned unfair discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations based on sexual orientation under the Equality Act signed May 9, 2007, and the anti-bullying law prohibits bullying including cyberbullying and harassment on the basis of sexual orientation among other categories in all public schools. State hate crime statutes provide additional penalties for crimes based on the victim's sexual orientation, and SB704 passed and signed in May 2021 effective January 1, 2022 abolishes the gay panic defense in murder, manslaughter and hate crime cases. Oregon became the third state to ban conversion therapy on minors after House 41-18 on March 17, 2015 and Senate 21-8 on May 7, 2015 votes, signed May 18, 2015 by Governor Kate Brown effective July 1, 2015. Same-sex couples whether unmarried or married may apply to adopt and lesbian couples have access to assisted reproduction such as in vitro fertilization with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized as legal parent if married, while surrogacy is neither expressly prohibited nor permitted but courts are generally favorable including for same-sex couples.

66186276B98073251815399.summary:
A July 2026 anti-trans legal risk assessment map lists Rhode Island among its 'Most Protective' states for gender-identity nondiscrimination. The same map reports erosion at the federal layer and concludes that its top tier can no longer be considered most protective nationwide, so the ranking describes Rhode Island's own statute rather than conditions a visitor will meet at every point of the journey.

Discrimination based on gender identity or expression has been unlawful in Rhode Island since 2001 in employment, credit, housing and public accommodations under R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 28-5-3, 28-5-7, 34-37-4, 34-37-4.3 and 11-24-2. A bill signed in June 2023 added explicit bans covering patient care, nursing and related healthcare, and the long-standing housing exemption for dwellings with three occupants or fewer was repealed with effect from 1 January 2023.

Rhode Island hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by the victim's actual or perceived gender identity or expression, with the gender-identity coverage placed in statute at R.I. Gen. Laws § 42-28-46. The gay and trans panic defense was repealed in June 2018 by votes of 68-2 in the House and 27-0 in the Senate, signed by Governor Gina Raimondo the following month and effective immediately.

Identity documents are changeable on a self-declaration-plus-clinical-confirmation basis rather than a surgical one. Since 23 October 2014 a birth certificate gender change has required a Birth Certificate Request Form together with an affidavit from a physician, certified nurse practitioner or physician's assistant confirming transgender status, replacing the earlier sex reassignment surgery requirement. The Division of Motor Vehicles issues a corrected driver's licence on a Gender Designation Form signed by the applicant. A third gender marker, X, was announced for driver's licences and birth certificates in August 2019 with availability from July 2020, and a June 2018 law requires transgender people to be recorded correctly on death certificates.

Single-occupancy toilets may be designated gender-neutral with effect from 1 January 2022 under a bill signed in July 2021. Rhode Island also appears on the transgender healthcare equality map among jurisdictions covered by shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches, which are drafted to make those protections enforceable against out-of-state action.

In March 2025 the Rhode Island Interscholastic League revised its transgender athletes policy. Transgender athletes remain able to compete, but member schools now carry responsibility for ensuring compliance with all applicable state and federal law when they determine gender-based eligibility, replacing the prior rule that allowed participation consistent with gender identity.

The gay and/or trans panic defence was abolished and repealed by legislation passed 144-1 in the House in March 2021 and 29-0 in the Senate in April 2021, signed May 5, 2021 by Governor Phil Scott and effective July 1. Use of conversion therapy on LGBT minors, which includes transgender minors, was banned by a bill approved unanimously in the Senate March 17, 2016, approved with amendments in the House April 26, accepted by the Senate April 29, signed May 25 by Governor Peter Shumlin and effective July 1, 2016. Vermont permits both preoperative and post-operative transgender individuals to change the gender marker on birth certificates and other state-issued documents upon court order supported by a letter from a licensed medical or mental health practitioner of surgical, hormonal, or other appropriate treatment for gender transition, while effective July 1, 2022 individuals born in Vermont can legally change sex marker to male, female or X based on self-determination without court order, mental health diagnosis, surgery, divorce or medical permission under a bill signed in April 2022, and since July 1, 2019 the Department of Motor Vehicles has offered X on driver's licences and state IDs with no documentation needed. Texas. 66186276B98555229882405.name: Washington
66186276B98555229882405.summary:
Washington operates under the United States framework on passports, entry screening, federal facilities and federal custody, which are set nationally. State law and state institutions govern health care, insurance, the state prison system and state ballot measures.

A July 2026 legal-risk assessment of United States anti-trans measures places Washington among the most protective states in the country. The same assessment flags two Washington ballot initiatives, I-001 and I-638, due for a November vote, as targeting transgender residents; whether they pass decides whether that protective posture holds.

Washington has shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches that are enforceable against out-of-state action, and a nationwide tracker of such measures lists the state among those covered. For a trans visitor who travels to Washington for gender-affirming care, these measures bear on whether another state's action can reach care provided in Washington.

State correctional practice carries a documented reversal. Washington state prisons have been legally required since October 2023, under court order and rulings, to provide gender-affirming healthcare and, where indicated, sex-reassignment surgery to inmates. In July 2024 a transgender woman prisoner was transferred out of a women's prison back to a men's prison as punishment for consensual sex with a cisgender inmate of the women's prison, so housing assigned by birth sex functioned as the disciplinary sanction.

12653393B40111500734429.name: Kandahar
12653393B40111500734429.summary: Kandahar is the Taliban movement's historic spiritual and political heartland, where the movement's supreme leader, senior leadership and Kandahari clerical establishment are based and where the Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice has a particularly strong local presence. It is a deeply conservative Pashtun region with strict gender segregation, and it is generally described as more socially conservative and less permissive than Kabul, with morality officers operating under fewer constraints than in the capital. The area provides no legal protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity; same-sex conduct remains punishable by death under Sharia provisions, and virtue-and-vice surveillance duties under the 2024 law are enforced intensively, alongside documented flogging, beatings, arbitrary detention, physical and sexual abuse in custody, and systematic pursuit of people perceived as gay or transgender. Public corporal punishments for moral offences are staged prominently, with Ghazi City's Ghazi Stadium having a historical record of public punishments, and religious police and checkpoints give frequent opportunities for scrutiny. There is no meaningful tourism or foreign-visitor infrastructure, no functioning civil-society, NGO, diplomatic or consular presence able to intervene for a foreigner, and the few foreigners present are conspicuous; suspicion of foreigners runs high amid insecurity and an ISIS-K presence that also targets perceived moral deviants. Local tribal and clerical authority reinforces rather than moderates the national system. For a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed, these conditions combine with the national regime at greater intensity and with less discretion than the national average: detention by Taliban security or morality officials, exposure of documents, physical or sexual abuse in custody, imprisonment, violent interrogation, referral to moral courts, corporal punishment administered publicly, and a credible pathway to capital moral-crime charging are all foreseeable consequences, while no local protection, sanctuary or remedy exists to offset them. Nothing in the region distinguishes it favourably from the national picture; conditions are, if anything, harsher, and local conditions plausibly intensify rather than reduce the danger, with fewer mitigating channels than in Kabul.

12653393B56617740339660.name: Zabul
12653393B56617740339660.summary: Zabul is a remote, strongly conservative rural southern province with deep Taliban roots, where the national regime applies in full: no legal protection or recognition of gender identity, Sharia-based criminalisation of same-sex conduct carrying exposure to capital punishment, and the 2024 Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice Law imposing a preventive surveillance duty over gender and sexual conduct. Documented enforcement includes arbitrary detention, custodial sexual abuse, beatings, public flogging — including a near-doubling of floggings in 2025, confirmed by the Taliban Supreme Court — and expulsion of visibly transgender and LGBT people. Zabul adds no mitigating layer: it is among the most conservative provinces in the country, with virtue-and-vice enforcement operating at street level, consolidated Taliban administration and no independent judiciary, no urban queer community, no tourist or foreign-facing economy, no NGO shelter or rights infrastructure, and negligible rule-of-law recourse. Conservative Pashtun social norms reinforce family and community reporting, and the low foreign presence reduces privacy, so outsiders attract attention and are more likely to be handled through family, community, or vice-and-virtue channels than through any impartial process. Enforcement is plausibly at least as strict as in Kabul but with far less visibility and fewer outside actors, leaving a visitor with less recourse than in provincial capitals; no known local exception or protective institution has been identified.

12653393B46006342616872.name: Uruzgan
12653393B46006342616872.summary: Uruzgan is a remote, predominantly Pashtun province where Taliban authority is exercised locally through commanders, tribal elders and local courts with almost no foreign presence, tourism infrastructure, independent institutions, NGOs, advocacy organisations or media outside Tarin Kowt. A deeply conservative Pashtunwali and religious social order, together with the absence of urban anonymity, means a visitor is conspicuous on sight and there is no tolerant local counterweight to the national regime: no legal recognition or protection for gender diversity, Sharia-referenced criminalisation of same-sex conduct including a clause permitting death, and the 2024 Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice Law's moral surveillance duties enforced by the same authorities who carry out arrests. Conditions are known to be equal to or somewhat harsher than the Kabul-centric national picture, with no documented local tolerance or exceptions, stricter community, family and militia involvement in enforcement rather than protection, and no documented operational safeguards, complaint mechanisms or protective state facilities. For a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed, these local conditions combine with the national regime to expose them to arbitrary detention, public flogging, beatings, sexual abuse and coercion in custody, and severe violence, with a credible threat to life — though execution is not shown to be inevitable after discovery. Enforcement rests with unelected local officials acting without independent oversight or effective consular access, and there is no functioning recourse. Region-specific case records for Uruzgan are sparse, and the absence of reports should not be read as safety; no local protective incident or exception is established. The consequences of discovery go substantially beyond questioning, service denial or brief detention.
