67827341B91073241467510.name: Sangha
67827341B91073241467510.summary: Sangha is a remote, sparsely populated and heavily forested department in the far north of the Republic of the Congo, centred on Ouesso along the Sangha river, with logging towns, safari lodges serving the Nouabalé-Ndoki area, and a border with the Central African Republic that brings customs scrutiny. Police and court presence, legal aid, NGOs and oversight are thinner than in Brazzaville, services are concentrated around Ouesso, and practical assistance can be harder to reach; no trans community or advocacy infrastructure is known locally. A visibly transgender outsider can be highly conspicuous in small towns, where checkpoints or local authorities can mean prolonged questioning, harassment, extortion, denial of services or family and community pressure, with little realistic remedy. Tourist-facing accommodation likely cushions everyday treatment, but no local trans-specific law, campaign or documented visitor-targeting has been identified, and the absence of documented local incidents does not establish safety. Otherwise conditions follow the national framework: consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised, though an unequal age-of-consent provision (Article 331) has been invoked by police as a pretext for bribery, with no prosecutions recorded; there is no procedure for legal gender recognition, so foreign-issued documents may not match a visitor's presentation, no statutory protection against gender-identity discrimination, and no hate-crime law. Harassment and extortion of LGBTQI+ people by state and non-state actors, largely within families, is documented and rarely reported, and violence is documented but is not shown here to be trans-specific; no custodial targeting or capital punishment of transgender visitors is documented locally. Social attitudes are conservative and hostile — the surveys recording strong anti-homosexual sentiment (about 73% in one Brazzaville survey) cover the capital, not Sangha — so a visitor who is outed or discovered faces the national exposure with greater visibility, more conservative rural communities, little outsider familiarity with gender diversity, and less recourse than in Brazzaville, while falling short of the custodial targeting documented elsewhere in the country.

35879248B49116351933928.name: Maio
35879248B49116351933928.summary: Maio, a small, sparsely populated rural island of roughly 3,000 residents whose main town is called Porto Inglês in some accounts and Vila do Maio in others, is governed by Cabo Verde's national framework: consensual same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 2004, no law criminalises gender expression, and the state has endorsed UN statements against criminalisation and transphobic harassment, including the 2025 declaration on those issues. Public-attitude polling is comparatively high — around 80% acceptance of homosexual neighbours — but it reflects tolerance of gay and lesbian people rather than of transgender people specifically. The only documented trans-specific violence is reported nationally in a 2016 interview describing verbal abuse and two physical attacks, accounts also characterised elsewhere as undated and without an established pattern. No region-specific ordinances, protections or incidents are documented for Maio, and no local pattern of police targeting, detention or violence appears in the record; the absence of reported border or police targeting should not be read as proof of safety, since foreign passport mismatches and officials' responses are undocumented. Fishing and agriculture matter more here than mass tourism, and the island offers none of the anonymity available in Praia, Sal or Mindelo. In a tight-knit, socially conservative setting with no visible trans community or local advocacy resources, a gender-nonconforming visitor stands out, so being read as transgender or being outed is more likely to draw sustained curiosity, gossip and social friction. Policing is light and health, administrative, police, media and complaint channels are fewer and slower to reach than on larger islands, with health and administrative services concentrated elsewhere and possibly not trained in transgender-related care. The practical exposure is therefore social and bureaucratic — visibility, document handling and friction that is harder to remedy informally — rather than any documented state detention, criminal charge or violence.

35879248B41743840760019.name: São Vicente
35879248B41743840760019.summary: São Vicente operates under Cabo Verde's national framework, with no island-level law changing the rules for visitors: consensual same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 2004, transgender identity and expression are not criminalised, and there is no trans-specific criminal offence. There is, however, no legal gender-recognition procedure, no gender-identity employment protection, no recorded trans-specific hate-crime recourse, and no precedent for documentary flexibility when a passport marker differs from presentation — so a visitor's exposure turns on documents, street attitudes and the discretion of police, clinics and accommodation providers rather than on statutory penalty. Trans visibility there has deep roots: Tchinda Andrade, Cabo Verde's first publicly out trans woman, has lived openly since the late 1990s without documented state persecution, and trans women have taken part publicly in Carnival preparations, including those documented in the film Tchindas, alongside a history of LGBT organising. 73172107B58641114734330.summary: Středočeský kraj (Central Bohemian Region) surrounds Prague and consists of commuter suburbs, small towns, rural countryside and some tourist towns, with notably less anonymity, thinner LGBT services, advocacy groups and specialist care than the capital, lower trans visibility and somewhat more conservative everyday attitudes. Otherwise the region applies the national framework: no criminalisation of transgender identity or expression, anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity in employment, housing and services, court rulings ending surgical and sterilisation requirements for legal gender recognition, and a Supreme Administrative Court safeguard requiring vulnerability assessment for detained trans foreigners — set against unresolved prison-placement rules, inconsistent lower-court and immigration practice, a pending bias-motivated crime amendment, documented high levels of reported discrimination and harassment among trans people nationally, and hostile political rhetoric at the highest level. 73172107B81289681513643.name: Jihomoravský kraj
73172107B81289681513643.summary: Jihomoravský kraj has no region-specific law or enforcement practice on gender identity, so a transgender visitor is governed by Czechia's national framework: no criminal offence targets transgender status or presentation, the 2009 Anti-Discrimination Act covers gender identity in services, employment, housing and education, and legal gender recognition no longer requires surgery or sterilisation following the 2024 Constitutional Court ruling and the subsequent ECtHR judgment. Hate-crime recording and prosecution function through police and courts, though bias statistics remain poorly disaggregated and remedies are not consistently specialised. Alongside this rule-of-law setting, prison placement for trans people remains unresolved, immigration-custody safeguards for trans foreigners are inconsistently applied (a Supreme Administrative Court ruling requires a vulnerability assessment before such placement), and high-level political hostility is documented, alongside survey evidence of high discrimination rates among trans respondents and the ongoing risk of official misgendering or weakly remedied discrimination. None of these national conditions is altered by any documented local legal difference, enforcement pattern or incident pattern in the kraj. Local conditions within the region vary mainly in social atmosphere. Brno, the regional capital and a major university and technology centre, has a visible LGBTQ+ community, recurring Pride events, active NGOs, visible venues and specialist care, with generally tolerant everyday attitudes across hospitality, transport and public services; a visitor who is discovered or outed there is more likely to encounter curiosity, stares, awkward misgendering or isolated service friction than police action or state detention. Smaller towns, rural areas and the region's Catholic wine-country villages are more socially conservative, with little anonymity, thinner support infrastructure and uneven access to informed clinics, shelters or accommodation outside Brno, though no pattern of targeted enforcement against visitors has been documented anywhere in the kraj.

73172107B12746720248776.name: Olomoucký kraj
73172107B12746720248776.summary: Olomoucký kraj has no regional criminalisation of transgender identity or presentation, no facility ban, no border-disclosure requirement, no hostile regional legislation, and no documented local pattern of anti-trans violence, police targeting or official hostility; nor are there local protective measures beyond the national framework, and no distinct regional enforcement regime is known. Under Czechia's national regime, gender identity is covered by the 2009 Anti-Discrimination Act in services, employment, housing and education, and the Constitutional Court ended surgical sterilisation and surgery as conditions for legal gender recognition in April 2024, with foreign documents generally accepted. National gaps carry over: hate-crime recording exists but undercounts and under-distinguishes bias offences, with a gender-identity hate-crime amendment still pending; bias-crime provisions remain incomplete; prison placement for trans people lacks clear binding rules; immigration detention must consider vulnerability, but practice below the Supreme Administrative Court is inconsistent; and senior politicians have made transphobic statements, alongside survey findings of substantial discrimination and harassment in which trans and non-binary respondents are worst affected and of rising social intolerance. Olomouc itself is a university city with a comparatively cosmopolitan, student-led culture, a visible queer scene, modest community organisations, hospital, tourism and university infrastructure, and experience hosting Prague Pride, which should ease urban encounters. The surrounding hinterland — smaller towns, rural districts and the Jeseníky and Prostějov areas — is more socially conservative, older-skewing and less exposed to gender diversity than Prague or Brno, with fewer specialist health, legal-aid and support services and less immediate institutional help than in the capital. If outed or discovered, a visitor there may face curiosity, misgendering, service hesitation or friction, and, particularly when travelling with a child, bureaucracy or ward- and school-related exposure; the main risk is social friction rather than severe punitive state action, though the thinner local community recourse can make such encounters harder to resolve. 25444519B7681288134121.name: Ali Sabieh
25444519B7681288134121.summary: Ali Sabieh — a small rural southern town and regional centre on Djibouti's road and railway route toward the Ethiopian border, a garrison and trading town with a predominantly pastoral, clan-structured hinterland — inherits the national framework: no express offence criminalises consensual same-sex conduct, transgender identity or gender expression, but vague public-morality provisions (Sections 353 and 354) are applied de facto against public same-sex or gender-nonconforming conduct, and the practical legal boundary is unclear. There is no legal gender recognition, so a visitor's foreign documents are assessed without a domestic equivalent and rejection of foreign documents is not documented; anti-discrimination protection is narrow and limited mainly to employment; complaints run only through police or the national human-rights commission, which is sited in Djibouti City, whose effectiveness outside the capital is undocumented, and for which no pathway via the capital is documented. Disclosure is treated as taboo and the social climate is recorded as strongly intolerant, shaped in particular by Afar and Somali customary and religious conservatism, while no trans-specific official violence or targeting is documented. No region-specific evidence distinguishes the town: there are no documented local protections, exceptions, trans-specific enforcement or facility rules, recorded incidents, local trans community or known protective practice, and no organised anti-trans campaign — nor is any harsher state-level targeting documented. However, markedly less tourism and hospitality infrastructure, fewer institutions, a thin institutional presence, limited anonymity and close-knit community networks mean a visibly transgender visitor stands out, especially where presentation does not match local expectations or foreign documents; border and gendarmerie checkpoints, a visible security presence and tight community scrutiny raise the chance that such mismatches become public. Discovery or outing could bring shunning, harassment, community exposure, denial of services, questioning, extortion, violence or discretionary police action including detention or prosecution under the morality provisions, with little realistic recourse. Documentation is thin and the near-total absence of incident-level reporting leaves the outer limits of enforcement unbounded — the absence of recorded incidents does not establish safety.

25444519B1274960689098.name: Arta
25444519B1274960689098.summary: Arta is a small, largely rural and semi-rural, Muslim and tribal region immediately west of Djibouti city on the Gulf of Tadjoura coast, with the Arta Plage beach strip drawing weekend visitors, tourists and expatriates. The beach-resort economy brings visitors into contact with hospitality staff and drivers but offers no documented protection, and Arta-specific police practice, service access, health treatment, detention or facility conditions are not documented, with no local incident record or case law defining the limits of the morality provisions. Over that setting Djibouti's national regime applies: there is no express offence criminalising consensual same-sex conduct, but vaguely worded public-morality provisions (Sections 353 and 354) are treated as de facto prohibitions and can be invoked against visible gender nonconformity, though their application to transgender visitors is unclear and direct trans-specific enforcement is not documented; there is no legal gender recognition, so foreign documents are assessed without a domestic equivalent and may attract extra scrutiny; anti-discrimination protection extends only to employment, with no general remedy for gender identity. If a visitor is discovered or outed, the vague morality provisions, closer community surveillance and thinner institutional protection can plausibly combine to produce questioning, accommodation refusal, family or community outing, harassment, extortion or police action, with no established recourse; social and religious intolerance, including strong family and religious pressure against disclosure, is documented. 25444519B52373268249817.name: Dikhil
25444519B52373268249817.summary: Dikhil is a sparsely populated, largely rural inland region of southwestern Djibouti centred on a small town near the Ethiopian border, predominantly Afar and Issa Somali, with a conservative Muslim social order, limited hotel, transport and clinic infrastructure, few foreign visitors and little anonymity. No documented local law, protection, exception or distinct enforcement pattern differentiates it from Djibouti's national picture: there is no express offence naming consensual same-sex conduct or transgender identity, but vaguely worded public-morality provisions (Sections/Articles 353–354) are treated in practice as making such conduct de facto illegal, with no case law bounding their application to a visibly transgender visitor. There is no legal gender recognition framework and no general non-discrimination protection beyond employment, no specific remedy for refusal of service, housing or facilities, and no region-specific remedy or protection for visitors; recourse runs through police or the national human-rights commission (CNDH), whose channels, along with civil-society complaint routes, are concentrated in the capital. The evidence base for the region is thin, and the effect of its smaller, less anonymous setting on trans visitors is uncertain, though it offers no basis for lighter protection than the national baseline. Combined with that regime, an outed or discovered transgender visitor in Dikhil faces the same unbounded exposure under the morality provisions together with tight-knit community and clan surveillance, conservative scrutiny of a visible stranger, and police who are socially embedded locally: reported possibilities include detention or extortion, service difficulties, social hostility and family shunning, with pervasive societal and religious taboo treating gender status and conduct as such. Formal police discretion and community pressure can operate with little distance from the state, while fewer functioning remedies, practical isolation and the distance of the CNDH make neutral complaints harder to reach than in urban areas. Societal and religious intolerance is described as pervasive, with fear of shunning, but no documented pattern of official violence, state-directed targeting or capital punishment appears nationally or locally, and no documented official protective enforcement is recorded either.

25444519B6046592555533.name: Tadjourah
25444519B6046592555533.summary: Tadjourah is a small, remote coastal region of northern Djibouti, overwhelmingly Muslim and organised around Afar and Issa clan networks, whose towns are small enough that a visibly foreign or visibly gender-nonconforming visitor attracts immediate notice and community comment. It inherits Djibouti's national regime in full: no express statutory offence for consensual same-sex conduct, but vague public-morality and 'good morals' provisions (Sections 353 and 354) that authorities can apply to visible or same-sex-read conduct in public, with no case law bounding their use; no legal gender recognition for anyone's documents, so a visitor's foreign identity papers have no domestic equivalent; no general prohibition of discrimination based on gender identity, with protection limited to employment and recourse limited to police complaints or the national human rights commission; and no general remedy for refusal of service, lodging or facilities. Social and religious intolerance is documented and disclosure is treated as taboo, while the 2023 US State Department report records societal intolerance and no documented state violence against LGBTI people. No region-specific record of official violence, trans-targeting, rejection of foreign identity documents, protective exceptions, or local safeguards distinguishes Tadjourah from the national picture, and documentation is thin and dated. Locally, the exposure is sharper: anonymity is scarce in a small, tightly knit coastal and Afar community where strangers are noticed, informal community surveillance and word of mouth can out a visitor faster, religious and clan authority is strong, and police, courts, the national human rights commission and any advocacy infrastructure sit far away in Djibouti City, making practical recourse harder and complaint handling less likely to be effective. Thin local police capacity means fewer documented enforcement actions, but also weaker protection. Some tourism activity along the Gulf of Tadjourah and limited seasonal diving and beach travel provide a modest counterweight, and a discreet, spending visitor may receive some leeway, but a transgender visitor who is outed faces likely questioning, lodging or service friction, pressure to leave and possible police attention; social conservatism makes informal exposure more consequential than formal arrest, and the absence of reported local incidents does not demonstrate safety.

25444519B8926294731251.name: Obock
25444519B8926294731251.summary: Obock is a remote northern coastal region on the Gulf of Tadjoura centred on the small port town of Obock, with an Afar-majority population alongside Somali and Yemeni-influenced communities, a conservative Muslim social character, a small tourism economy, and a role as a migrant transit area toward Yemen. There is no legal gender recognition, so foreign documents would be assessed against a framework with no domestic equivalent; anti-discrimination protection is limited to employment, with identity-based service denial not generally covered and complaints routed to police or the national human-rights commission. A visibly transgender foreigner in this small, tightly knit setting would be conspicuous and quickly known, with less anonymity and a higher probability of being outed than in the capital, and thinner practical recourse if that happens — no specialised police, legal aid or trans-specific services exist, and complaints would likely be handled informally or not at all, while police attention under the morality provisions and community hostility are plausible. 25444519B34443348585704.name: Djibouti

Police and the national human-rights commission are the stated complaint channels, but their effectiveness is unrecorded and no functioning recourse for a visitor refused service, questioned, detained or harassed is established. Documentation is thin and largely dated, so current enforcement practice cannot be confirmed, and the absence of recorded incidents should not be read as proof of safety. 96108325B47785236493574.name: Saint Andrew

Uusimaa is Finland's most urban, internationally diverse and socially liberal region, holding the country's largest concentration of foreign visitors, public services, hospitals, LGBTQ venues, trans advocacy organisations, the central gender identity units, and large Pride events with official participation, alongside Seta-linked services. 13066534B65630723466818.summary: Imereti operates under Georgia's 2024 family-values package, which bans gender-reassignment surgery and medical intervention at any age (including for minors, with the wider package also affecting travelling families), bars registering a gender different from that on state documents, prohibits public promotion of a different gender and pride events, and undercuts labour rules framed around biological sex; a companion foreign-agents law has sharply reduced LGBTI services. A visitor's own passport remains the only recognition available — the law sets out no documented procedure for handling foreign-issued documents, so any mismatch between papers and presentation invites scrutiny — while hate-crime and anti-discrimination provisions covering gender identity exist on paper but are documented as unenforced, with police homophobia, withdrawn complaints, and slow or absent protection as public LGBTI assembly has repeatedly been violently suppressed nationwide amid attacks on public events and anti-trans rhetoric. Locally, Imereti is a largely rural, strongly Orthodox and socially conservative western region centred on Kutaisi, with less international and NGO presence, no visible trans community, few LGBTI-friendly services, little local advocacy capacity and limited anonymity; outside tourist routes around Kutaisi, its airport and cave sites the environment is markedly more traditional and church-influenced than in Tbilisi. Kutaisi saw far-right violence against an LGBT-linked venue in 2023, while documented assaults, police hostility and pride-event violence concentrate in Tbilisi, and no comparable incidents, region-specific raids or lethal enforcement are documented locally. A visitor discovered in a hotel, clinic or police stop may face gossip, service refusal or hostility, with bureaucratic checks or emergency care more likely to expose them and with police accountability, victim support and recourse all thinner than in the capital and local enforcement unaccountable if they are outed; foreign visitors are not singled out and there is no evidence of region-specific organised targeting, though accounts differ on whether local friction sits at or slightly below the already restrictive national baseline or, given the absence of safe infrastructure, leaves a visitor more exposed than in Tbilisi.

69750345B67040307067067.name: Central Region
69750345B67040307067067.summary: The Central Region — centred on Cape Coast and spanning coastal and interior districts including Elmina, Winneba and Kasoa — is governed by the same police service, criminal law and pending legislation as the rest of Ghana, with no documented region-specific enforcement pattern, exemption, protective practice or regional protection for transgender visitors. Colonial-era provisions criminalising same-sex conduct remain on the books, and parliament passed the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill on 29 May 2026, awaiting presidential assent, with Supreme Court review deferred or dismissed pending assent; an earlier version lapsed unsigned in 2024. The bill would sharply increase penalties and criminalise advocacy, though its present legal force is uncertain, and the campaign around it contributes to a hostile climate. Legal gender recognition does not exist, foreign documents are not recognised, police recourse for transgender complainants is unreliable, unenforced common-law morality offences remain available as a police lever, and there is no documented effective remedy amid strong public and religious opposition to gender diversity. Locally, Cape Coast and Elmina form a visitor-facing heritage-tourism and university corridor where foreign visitors are routine and a traveller can move with relative anonymity, and hotel and heritage-site staff may try to avoid public disputes with foreigners; however, the surrounding fishing districts and smaller towns are more socially conservative and tightly networked, and conservative churches, customary authorities and under-resourced municipal police create more discretionary, reputation-sensitive encounters. This local mix offers no documented legal protection, and no local facility bans, organised morality-police sweeps or documented pattern of trans-specific violence are known. If discovered or outed, a transgender visitor would face social hostility, service refusal, document challenges, bribes or extortion, possible police detention, humiliation, misgendered custody and violence, with hostility amplified by religious pressure and no effective remedy.

69750345B3295588325057.name: Ashanti Region
69750345B3295588325057.summary: Ashanti Region operates entirely under Ghana's national framework: consensual same-sex conduct remains criminal under colonial-era provisions, there is no trans-specific offence, no legal gender recognition and no trans-specific protection, and the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill — passed by parliament in May 2026 and awaiting presidential assent, with one account noting that an earlier passage was sharply expanded in 2024 — would sharply raise penalties and criminalise advocacy; the Supreme Court has declined to block or has deferred review of the bill before assent, while religious and political leaders actively press for enactment. A transgender visitor who is outed or discovered therefore faces likely police harassment, extortion, detention under public-order or morality provisions, public humiliation, social rejection and community confrontation, with thin recourse; police and courts function, but complaints touching gender nonconformity are read through a morality lens and rarely protect the person who is outed, and documentation of hostility toward visibly gender-nonconforming people is established at the national level. Region-specific enforcement records are sparse, and the extent of trans-specific police targeting locally is uncertain — which is not evidence of safety. Ashanti adds a distinctly conservative local layer: Kumasi and its hinterland are a heartland of traditional chieftaincy and the Asantehene's authority alongside assertive Pentecostal, evangelical, Christian and Muslim moral influence, with active anti-LGBT campaigning, dense community surveillance, and anti-LGBT sentiment broadly socially licensed rather than confined to officials. There is no documented local protection regime or enforcement exception. Discovery in hotels, transport or through vigilant community reporting can escalate quickly: risks include denial of rooms, transport scrutiny, hostile treatment in hospitals, eviction, and denunciation or possible mob confrontation in a market, lorry station or Zongo neighbourhood. Kumasi's larger urban, commercial and tourism character offers some anonymity compared with rural areas, foreignness buys some eccentricity allowance in hotels and transport, and a historical Asante tradition of feminine-identified men exists, but none of these offsets police discretion, arrest, extortion or hostile public confrontation once a trans visitor is identified; the region has less visible support infrastructure and less cosmopolitan tolerance than Accra, and is among Ghana's most socially and religiously conservative areas.

385441B21537995001042.name: Labe
385441B21537995001042.summary: Labé, Guinea's second-largest city in the Fouta Djallon highlands, is a predominantly Fulani and conservative Muslim centre where religious and family norms are stricter than in Conakry and visible gender nonconformity draws close scrutiny. The national regime applies in full: Article 274 of the Penal Code criminalises consensual same-sex conduct with imprisonment of six months to three years and fines, and police have arrested people on the basis of clothing or appearance, used the law for extortion, held people for five days beyond the legal limit before releasing them against bribes, and placed transgender women in male prisons where sexual violence is reported. Guinea provides no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection in health, housing, education or employment, and no operative hate-crime recourse; surveys show widespread hostility to gay neighbours, and most LGBTQ Guineans do not disclose publicly because of threats of violence and stigma. In Labé itself, anonymity is harder to maintain in a mid-size highland city with limited tourist infrastructure, which makes a visibly transgender visitor more identifiable, and there are fewer LGBTQ organisations, legal-aid options, anonymous urban spaces, independent services and functioning complaint mechanisms than in Conakry; no local protection, sanctuary or LGBTQ infrastructure is documented. Stronger family and community monitoring means discovery could quickly involve relatives, local religious authorities or police, and local practice appears more likely to escalate disclosure into moral or security enforcement with limited recourse, so an outed transgender visitor faces conditions somewhat below the national picture. Region-specific police practices, border treatment and incidents involving transgender visitors are not documented, and that uncertainty is not evidence of safety; no execution pathway is documented.

31243875B86288540800273.name: Banjul
31243875B86288540800273.summary: Banjul is Gambia's small administrative capital and seat of government, police headquarters and main port: a compact, devoutly Muslim city with a concentrated police and immigration presence, identity checks around the airport, port and ferry terminal, and limited anonymity, in a society where LGBT identity carries strong taboo and media and religious hostility toward gender nonconformity is documented. A visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner is conspicuous, discovery can come through passports, hotel registration, checkpoints or hospitals, and reporting of enforcement is sparse while official discretion is high; police have conducted sweeps of venues and couples in the 2014–2015 era, and there is no Banjul-specific tolerance, protective machinery, trans community infrastructure or documented relief for people targeted by police. Its tourism role is described differently: it is presented both as a main tourism hub with greater foreign visibility and some commercial caution in guest-oriented areas, and as separate from the tourist economy, which sits across the ferry in Kanifing and along the coast, with the capital's cosmopolitan buffer and tourism infrastructure limited by comparison. Partial offsets are that the city offers more urban anonymity and tourist-facing services than rural areas, enforcement against tourists is sporadic rather than systematic, civil-society organisations operate locally, and its concentration of embassies may improve consular access after detention — none of which alters the national picture. Under the national regime, same-sex conduct remains criminalised by the 2025 Criminal Code, which sets a mandatory five-year minimum for unnatural offences and three years for gross indecency, with gross-indecency provisions covering private acts and the 2014 aggravated-homosexuality provisions now removed; there is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection, and trans identity or gender expression is not itself a separate offence, though the sexuality law can raise scrutiny and hostility toward a gender-nonconforming visitor. If outed or discovered, a visitor faces intrusive questioning, humiliation, extortion, arbitrary detention and arrest, with prosecution risk under broad indecency or unnatural-offence framing and severity increasing if police or community actors treat gender nonconformity as sexual immorality or public nuisance, and with no reliable local remedy. Lethal punishment is not credibly expected: former president Jammeh's era of explicit extermination rhetoric ended in 2017 and no executions for gender or sexuality offences are credibly documented since. Patterns of targeting trans visitors specifically, document or border problems, facility rules and effective remedies in the city are not established.

Basse itself offers little tourism infrastructure, no trans or LGBT organisation, no specialist legal aid, few health and lodging providers, distant courts and advocacy groups, and fewer independent oversight bodies than larger cities; the nearby border crossing adds document scrutiny, and a foreigner is conspicuous in a town where anonymity is limited. For a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed, these conditions combine with the national regime: national provisions can operate in a more discretionary local setting, raising the practical likelihood of police suspicion, morality-law application, extortion, public shaming, service refusal, informal mediation or detention rather than formal protection, alongside community hostility and weak recourse if detained or mistreated, including limited medical continuity options and remedies. Remote geography and weaker accountability increase exposure compared with national averages, while imprisonment or mob violence remain possible but not certain. No Basse-specific pattern of police targeting or violence against transgender visitors is established and such evidence is limited, a gap that is not evidence of safety, and the precise treatment by local officials remains uncertain.

31243875B72482523363184.name: Janjanbureh
31243875B72482523363184.summary: Janjanbureh is a small, comparatively remote riverain town on MacCarthy Island in the Central River Region of the Gambia River, with tight social networks, strong conservative religious authority in a Muslim-majority community, limited tourism infrastructure, and far less internationally oriented visitor environment than Banjul. No region-specific reports of targeting or official pattern of targeting have been documented, but the small size of the community means discovery would spread quickly through family, community leaders and police networks, and the absence of reported incidents is not evidence of safety. A visibly transgender visitor would attract attention quickly, with local police and officials unlikely to offer protection and no evidence of local recourse. The town inherits Gambia's national criminal regime, under which the 2025 Criminal Code sets a five-year minimum for unnatural offences, defined to include any homosexual act, and three years for gross indecency, while the 2014 aggravated-homosexuality framework signals sustained legislative hostility toward gender and sexual nonconformity; these provisions target conduct rather than transgender identity itself, though visible gender nonconformity could be misread or draw attention in a hostile climate, and gender-expression or trans-specific enforcement is not documented nationally. No trans-specific legal recognition, document protection or hate-crime recourse is documented. A transgender visitor who is discovered or outed therefore faces arrest exposure, prosecution, police detention and discretion, birth-sex custody placement, extortion, public exposure, shaming and community hostility, with limited anonymity accelerating the spread of discovery, rural policing and informal authority increasing unpredictability, and families facing added pressure around identity and privacy — conditions that leave thinner practical support than the coastal areas and that local isolation makes somewhat worse than the national picture.

31243875B42421745591684.name: Kanifing
31243875B42421745591684.summary: Kanifing, the dense urban municipality around Serekunda and Bakau adjoining Banjul and taking in Kololi and the Senegambia tourist strip, is Gambia's main urban, tourist, NGO and expatriate hub and its most commercially developed district. No local exception, sanctuary or protective regime distinguishes it from the national picture: police and courts there apply the same statutes, and no documented local tolerance programme or gender-identity protection was identified. The national regime it inherits criminalises same-sex conduct under the Criminal Code, with the 2025 code providing a five-year minimum and no stated maximum for unnatural offences and a three-year penalty for gross indecency, the latter provisions reaching private consensual acts. There is no transgender-specific law, no legal gender recognition or anti-discrimination or hate-crime recourse, and visitors' documents are issued at home with no marker-change process available to them. While these provisions do not expressly criminalise transgender identity, they may expose a visitor if officials interpret their relationship or presentation through the statute, and gender-nonconforming visitors may be treated as evidence of prohibited conduct; enforcement history elsewhere in the country includes arrests and police raids of queer venues and gatherings, official statements legitimising hostility, and courts showing no record of relief. Everyday conditions locally are milder than in rural areas: the transient, internationally exposed population, hospitality employment and the tourist strip around Kololi give visitors more anonymity, foreigner visibility and somewhat greater tolerance of gender nonconformity, reducing casual scrutiny and the frequency of village-level enforcement. That shielding is modest only, and social conservatism remains strong, with the tourist economy not translating into protection. The same urban corridor has historically concentrated police and National Intelligence Agency attention to gender-nonconforming and queer people, and police operate from urban stations amid denser deployment, hotel registration and airport proximity, so risk of extortion and arbitrary detention without effective remedy remains documented; a visitor's casual exposure may be lower, but the operative legal regime, social hostility and documented enforcement risks remain live if they are discovered or outed, and the frequency of enforcement against trans visitors specifically is uncertain with no established local pattern.

31243875B21899311231896.name: Kerewan
31243875B21899311231896.summary: Kerewan is a small rural administrative and market centre on Gambia's North Bank, a ferry-crossing, agrarian and close-knit community with a predominantly Muslim, socially conservative population. Nothing region-specific has been identified that gives Kerewan protections, ordinances or institutional exceptions differing from the national picture on the positive side, and no local incidents, enforcement patterns or trans-targeted campaigns are documented. Discovery would most plausibly come through documents, lodging registration, visibility or small-town gossip, with local religious and community leaders and thinly staffed police rather than courts shaping the response. Because local discretion sits with those gatekeepers, harassment, extortion or brief detention appear more likely than formal prosecution, though institutional remedy is thinner than in Banjul or on the tourist coast. Nationally, same-sex conduct remains criminalised under the 2025 Criminal Code with a five-year mandatory minimum, and gross indecency and public morality provisions have historically been applied to gender-nonconforming people, so a transgender visitor who is outed faces police questioning or arrest under those provisions, including possible custody harms if assigned-sex procedures are applied. There is no legal gender recognition pathway, no trans-specific statute, no anti-discrimination or hate-crime coverage for visitors, and no recourse operating through foreign documents; combined with reduced anonymity and lower international monitoring than in major hubs, this makes family or community outing more consequential and raises the practical severity of discovery.

31243875B86283726287100.name: Kuntaur
31243875B86283726287100.summary: Kuntaur is a small, rural, inland river town and administrative centre in the Central River Region, near the Wassu stone circles, with no tourist-facing economy and distance from the capital, tourist infrastructure and any LGBTQ support services. These provisions do not expressly criminalise transgender identity but can be applied to a trans visitor whose relationships or presentation officials or others read through them, and are often used as a lever for suspicion, questioning, extortion or detention rather than as a narrow sexual-offence matter. The country has no legal gender recognition, no gender-identity anti-discrimination or hate-crime coverage, and no documented trans-specific border or facility protections or reliable remedy. In a close-knit, socially conservative and observant Muslim community with no trans community, advocacy group or consular presence nearby, a visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner is immediately conspicuous and readily identifiable; discovery or outing can bring intense local hostility and rapid reporting by neighbours, with police and customary and religious authorities acting as the operative arbiters under less scrutiny than in the Banjul area, and with local courts able to impose custodial sentences or tolerate abuse in holding. Inland districts also have fewer tourist-facing institutions and less English-language support than coastal resorts, raising the likelihood of discovery while lowering recourse: legal help, medical care and consular assistance are limited until Banjul is reached. Rural distance from specialist advocacy increases uncertainty, and while no local evidence shows organised state targeting, the precise consequences of discovery remain uncertain rather than reassuring.

Trans identity itself is not identified in the law as a criminal offence, and no executions of trans visitors are documented. For a gender-nonconforming foreigner in a small, tightly knit community, reduced anonymity means immediate attention and intense curiosity, documents likely examined and little privacy, with community and religious pressure making discovery riskier than in more urbanised areas; discovery would likely mean being reported to elders or police, bringing police involvement rather than protection — detention by birth sex, arbitrary questioning, extortion, harassment, hostile handling and abuse in custody — with no functioning recourse for a foreigner detained or prosecuted on morality or public-order grounds. The credible worst case is imprisonment and abuse in custody rather than lethal state targeting; reduced anonymity makes discovery more consequential but does not establish a higher rate of targeting, while these conditions together leave a trans visitor somewhat worse off than the national picture.

76643164B96925829526723.name: Bissau

No region-specific ordinance, enforcement campaign, trans-specific protection, sanctuary regime or targeted policing is known in Bissau, and no border, facility or custody rule targeting trans visitors is documented. As the most urban, ethnically mixed and internationally connected place in the country — concentrating government offices, police, and a small NGO, embassy and tourist presence — the capital is more socially familiar with foreign visitors and carries less of the conservative pressure found in the interior, where traditional and religious authority and weaker state reach prevail, though routine ID checks and hotel registration make Bissau more administratively visible and police document checks are common. Stigma and taboos around gender expression persist in dated accounts, including a local NGO director's 2018 report of some violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity, while reporting of anti-trans violence is sparse and does not establish current frequency. Because institutions are weak and the rule of law thin, discovery is unlikely to bring arrest but may produce intrusive questioning, mockery, refusal or delay of services, harassment, extortion or arbitrary holding, particularly at borders or checkpoints; a visitor who is outed should expect friction, discrimination and possible impunity for perpetrators rather than state targeting, with effectively no institutional recourse and social stigma surfacing through curiosity, ridicule or refusal of service rather than official action.

73500413B28210658685043.name: Demerara-Mahaica
73500413B28210658685043.summary: Demerara-Mahaica contains Georgetown, Guyana's capital, port, main tourist and administrative centre and the location of the international airport, and it inherits the national regime: consensual same-sex conduct remains criminalised under inherited colonial offences (the 1893 Criminal Law (Offences) Act) carrying sentences of up to two years and life, prosecutions are rare but the provisions retain police relevance, and can be used as leverage if a discovery escalates into allegations of sexual activity. The cross-dressing offence was struck down in 2018, but Guyana has no legal gender-recognition procedure, no hate-crime law covering gender identity, and no documented trans-specific border, airport, facility, custody or care rules. Residual loitering, vagrancy and public-order clauses remain usable by police. Regionally documented harms cluster in Georgetown: police harassment and extortion, threats and bribe-seeking under public-order provisions, discrimination at stations when complainants come forward, trans women attacked in the city, a 2017 Georgetown magistrate refusing a trans woman entry to her own assault case because of her clothing (effectively dismissing it), and an LGBT advocate beaten there in 2019 after harassment. For a visitor, this means elevated exposure to harassment, service friction and inadequate recourse if discovered or outed, though not systematic imprisonment. Countervailing conditions also concentrate here: urban anonymity, a more tolerant everyday climate than rural areas, Georgetown's strongest NGO presence including SASOD and Blossom, foreign embassies, hotels, tourism-linked norms, formal complaint routes, official condemnation of anti-LGBT conduct and civil-society advocacy, together with national polling showing rising acceptance and a 2022 national poll indicating 72.4% accepting or tolerating LGBTQ people — all giving a trans visitor somewhat greater access to support, consular help and everyday safety than elsewhere in the country. That oversight and recourse are tempered by the region's concentration of border, police, court and nightlife contact points, where discretionary policing, public-order abuse and court bias remain the principal exposures.

10453824B39335940856231.name: Bay Islands
10453824B39335940856231.summary: The Bay Islands (Roatán, Utila and Guanaja) fall under Honduras's national regime: gender identity is not criminalised, discrimination on that basis is prohibited and treated as an aggravating factor in crime, and denial of services is punishable — but a 2001 police provision against conduct 'going against modesty and public morals' has been used to harass and detain transgender women, with documented extortion and abuse, and investigations of anti-trans violence are weak. Transgender people are held in men's prisons on the basis of birth sex, where assaults and impunity are reported, and killings of trans activists on the mainland have drawn institutional failure to investigate. No Bay Islands-specific protections, remedies, or police protocols exist, and Roatán's airport police and customs practice is governed by the national regime with no documented local exception; detention on the islands may involve transfer to mainland facilities. Conservative and evangelical currents also persist locally. What does differ is the setting: a tourism- and diving-driven, expatriate-oriented economy with cruise-port life, English-speaking Caribbean and Creole communities, visible LGBTQ nightlife, and a visitor-facing service culture, along with a thinner local police presence. Everyday interactions and resort-zone policing are therefore generally less hostile and less targeted than on the mainland, and no trans-specific violence is documented on the islands — though that silence is thin evidence, and the small, close-knit communities mean privacy is limited. Local healthcare is also limited, with serious needs referred to the mainland. If a transgender visitor is outed or comes to police attention, the national custody and impunity risks follow: harassment, service friction, humiliation, extortion, or harm in custody with limited recourse. Imprisonment or death are not the routine expectation, but consequences can be severe if authorities interact negatively.

10453824B73363653217090.name: Copán
10453824B73363653217090.summary: Copán is a rural, socially conservative department in western Honduras near the Guatemalan border, distant from Tegucigalpa and San Pedro Sula where legal-aid and LGBT organisations are concentrated. It inherits Honduras's national regime: gender identity and same-sex conduct are not criminalised, and the Penal Code contains anti-discrimination and incitement provisions and aggravates offences motivated by gender identity, but enforcement is weak; the 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs public-morals clause is used by police to harass and detain gender-nonconforming people, investigations of anti-trans violence routinely fail, and documented killings of trans people (including cases in Tegucigalpa) occur amid widespread impunity. Transgender detainees are held in men's prisons, where forced haircutting, clothing seizures, denial of feminine presentation and sexual violence with guard complicity have been documented. Same-sex marriage and adoption by same-sex couples are barred. No local protections, exceptions, facilities or remedies are documented for Copán, and the absence of a documented local pattern of trans-specific violence should not be read as safety. Santa Rosa de Copán and the Copán Ruinas Maya-ruins tourist zone receive foreign visitors, and that economy brings familiarity with outsiders and business incentives for discretion, which may soften street-level scrutiny; but tourism is not evidence of trans-specific protection, local trans visibility is low, and the wider department remains poor with thin institutional presence, weak police training and under-resourced national institutions. Police and military checkpoints near the Guatemalan border increase document scrutiny, though smaller-town and rural settings may mean fewer formal document checks, at the cost of slower emergency response and greater reliance on individual officers' attitudes. For an outed or discovered visitor, exposure therefore remains essentially the national one — humiliation, service refusal, extortion or short detention are more likely than severe violence, and police discretion, hotel or health-staff conduct and prison placement risks are not visibly better than the national record, leaving thinner practical recourse.

10453824B86429592273305.name: Cortés
10453824B86429592273305.summary: Cortés, Honduras's commercial and industrial heartland centred on San Pedro Sula and the Puerto Cortés port, offers no local legal exception or protective ordinance for a transgender visitor: gender identity and same-sex conduct are not criminalised, and the Penal Code's anti-discrimination articles with bias treated as an aggravating factor apply, but no shield ordinance or protective policing practice was identified here, and local enforcement may in places sit slightly below the national picture. Regional conditions make those national weaknesses more consequential — San Pedro Sula's extreme general homicide rate, entrenched gang territorial control and extortion across parts of the metropolitan area, police corruption reported as more pervasive than in the capital, strained or abusive policing, conservative churches, and high violent-crime levels — while transit points around Puerto Cortés and the airport add document-mismatch exposure and coastal tourist areas lack visible specialised safeguards. On the other side, urban anonymity, large hotels and transport hubs, a comparatively visible LGBT civil-society and nightlife presence, and access to community or advocacy resources offer some everyday respite, though there is no evidence these reliably protect visitors or alter police and custody practice; information on region-specific trans cases is thin, and current local variation is uncertain rather than evidence of safety. If discovered or outed, the national pattern governs: police can stop and detain people under the 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs modesty and public-morals provision, a power documented as used against transgender women alongside police rape, assault and extortion with persistent impunity. Transgender detainees are placed in men's prisons, where forced haircuts, denial of feminine presentation and sexual assault with guard complicity are reported, and prosecution of violence against trans people remains weak, including unremedied killings of trans activists. These local pressures may raise the likelihood of hostile questioning, unsafe custody placement, denied healthcare, extortion and public violence above the national baseline, although no local divergence — protective or more punitive — is documented beyond the national regime; there is no known execution pathway, and courts, prisons and remedies offer little reliable recourse.

10453824B24427405220616.name: Francisco Morazán
10453824B24427405220616.summary: Francisco Morazán is Honduras's capital department, centred on Tegucigalpa and also containing the Tamara national penitentiary, so it inherits the national regime: gender identity is not itself criminalised and same-sex activity is legal, while the Penal Code treats hatred based on gender identity as an aggravating circumstance and penalises discriminatory refusal of services. In practice, police have repeatedly used a 2001 public-morals provision to harass and detain transgender women, hate-motivated offences and discrimination penalties are undermined by under-reporting, poor training and weak investigations, and impunity for anti-trans violence is documented. Documented killings of transgender activists Cynthia Nicole and Thalia Rodriguez occurred in Tegucigalpa in 2022; these establish serious local harm but do not show current frequency or a trans-specific rate. Gang-controlled neighbourhoods and higher general violence in the capital add exposure a visitor may not be able to avoid. As the capital, Tegucigalpa offers greater anonymity, foreign visitors, a denser concentration of LGBTQ organisations, legal aid, consular and international scrutiny and a more visible urban community than rural areas of the department, but the record does not show this changing outcomes for visitors, and no distinct local remedy or legal exception protects an outed one; rural municipalities in the department offer less anonymity and fewer support structures. Transgender women are held in men's prisons — including at Tamara, within this department — where haircuts, forced masculine presentation and concealment of presentation, and sexual violence involving guards have been documented, alongside inadequate protection despite human-rights intervention. A transgender visitor who is discovered or outed therefore faces police harassment, extortion, violence and abusive, invasive and hostile custody with significant uncertainty about effective recourse: the capital may be marginally more navigable than the rest of the country, but it is not safer overall.

A visibly foreign transgender visitor faces heightened visibility and document checks in Mosul and rural districts, and discovery — at checkpoints, hospitals or lodging — would likely be handled by local actors with effective impunity. Combined with the national regime, this can expose a visitor to arrest, detention under the 2024 law, invasive searches or imprisonment inconsistent with identity, severe imprisonment or deportation, extortion, honour-based violence, extrajudicial harassment and killing, with little reliable recourse; documented impunity for anti-LGBT violence leaves little assurance of protection. The population is tourism-oriented and English-speaking, accustomed to foreign visitors and to handling diverse documents, with generally high institutional trust and high social acceptance, and public services in the region are oriented toward international visitors. Because Keflavík concentrates the region's routine border and security checks, it is the likeliest point of discovery: a mismatch between documents and presentation may prompt ordinary questions, but such checks operate within national protections and trained officer practice rather than targeted hostility, and no mistreatment or trans-specific screening is known. If outed elsewhere, discovery carries no credible risk of imprisonment or execution and complaints have functioning recourse; police-recorded hate crimes nationally remain a small number, in the low double digits, with active investigation, and acknowledged gaps in protection remain relevant. The area is less socially diverse and less anonymous than Reykjavík, so small-town familiarity may bring stares, curiosity, bureaucratic unfamiliarity or awkwardness in smaller, more working-class areas — described as a minor friction rather than hostility — and the peninsula's greater number of routine screening interfaces makes this somewhat more likely to arise than in Iceland overall. Volcanic disruption in Grindavík affects travel generally rather than trans-specific exposure.

53860390B85658391135359.name: Southern Region
53860390B85658391135359.summary: The Southern Region has no distinct local rules for transgender visitors and inherits Iceland's national framework in full: self-determined legal gender recognition with a non-binary/X marker, anti-discrimination and hate-crime law covering gender identity, protected bathroom and facility access, a ban on conversion practices, and functioning complaint and reporting routes through the Equality Complaints Committee and 112/police hate-crime guidance. Descriptions of it vary between a heavily urbanised, tourist-facing area with a large transient foreign population and routine international travel, and a largely rural, sparsely populated, small-town corridor whose economy rests on visitor hospitality; either way, no region-specific restriction, facility exclusion, ordinance, enforcement pattern, targeting or organised hostility toward trans visitors is documented, and police and service providers operate under the same national legal framework, which treats police and courts as protectors rather than a threat. For a transgender visitor who is out or discovered, exposure in the smaller and closer-knit communities is limited to thinner anonymity than in Reykjavík and possible curiosity, awkwardness, isolated social discomfort or minor service friction, with some rural pockets along the south coast described as socially conservative; there is no known criminalisation, forced detention, systematic denial of services or institutional hostility, and the national remedies apply in full. Social reactions in individual encounters can still vary, the national record does not establish that discrimination never occurs, and localized information is sparse, leaving some residual uncertainty.

19161824B24193204184747.name: Southern District
19161824B24193204184747.summary: Southern District follows Israel's national framework with no district-specific legal regime and no local statutes altering border, police, custody or health-care rules: same-sex conduct and gender identity are not criminalised, discrimination in services and employment is prohibited, bias-motivated violence carries hate-crime penalties (doubled for gender identity), legal gender recognition is available without surgery and has been since 1986, police have a national regulation adopted in 2023 on searching transgender people, and courts have granted remedies — including a Beersheba order awarding compensation after a print shop refused service to an LGBTQ group. What differentiates the region is social rather than legal: outside Eilat, a secular, tourism-oriented and foreigner-friendly resort city, the Negev interior and southern towns including Beersheba, Dimona and Ashkelon are more religiously and socially conservative than Tel Aviv and central Israel, with large Haredi, Bedouin and settler-adjacent communities, a small LGBTQ scene, fewer visible venues, thinner support networks and trans-aware resources and specialist care concentrated at Sheba Medical Center in the centre — though Beersheba's university-hospital character and Eilat's tourist economy do offer some anonymity and more professional service settings. No district-specific hostile legislation or targeting pattern is known. For a visitor whose trans status becomes known, the likely exposure is social disapproval, service friction, intrusive questioning or harassment, with police and courts generally available but unevenly responsive; because the rule of law is strong, state prosecution is unlikely, and serious local violence against trans visitors is not documented as a regional pattern, though extortion, app-based luring and street hostility are plausibly somewhat higher in the south's more conservative towns than in the national centre, where discovery may also mean less support. National exposures can still reach the district: airport gender-identity screening has subjected trans travellers to humiliating questioning and outed them, border and security screening including at Eilat crossings can force disclosure, documented custody practice has isolated trans prisoners or placed them inconsistently with their gender identity, and 2025 official data records anti-LGBTQ violence at a high level, including organised dating-app ambushes, against a volatile wider social climate. District-specific trans violence, facility rules, border practices and risks for travelling minors are not documented — that is uncertainty rather than evidence of safety.

19161824B470428506180.name: Central District
19161824B470428506180.summary: Central District, the country's most densely populated region, takes in the Sharon plain and cities including Netanya, Kfar Saba, Ra'anana, Herzliya, Petah Tikva, Rehovot, Rishon LeZion and the towns of Lod and Ramla, along with Arab localities, and it contains Ben Gurion Airport, the main international gateway. The 2009 Tel Aviv shooting falls outside this district. Because the airport sits here, arriving and departing transgender visitors meet the national border screening directly: documented gender-identity screening has involved intrusive questioning and searches, demeaning remarks, and an officer disputing a traveller's gender on the basis of surgery status, creating a concrete outing risk at the district's main entry point. National official data records rising homophobic and transphobic violence in 2025, including dating-app ambushes, though no district-specific trans-violence pattern is documented; prison practice defaults to isolating trans prisoners, and no separate rule affecting a travelling minor is documented. Urban settings offer no established local remedy that offsets these national exposures.

11528761B60518956675191.name: Portland
11528761B60518956675191.summary: Portland, a small rural eastern parish centred on Port Antonio, Boston Bay and Frenchman's Cove, inherits Jamaica's national regime in full: consensual same-sex conduct remains criminalised under the Offences Against the Person Act's buggery provision, which carries hard labour, there is no legal gender recognition so foreign documents may not match a visitor's presentation, no statute prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no recognised partnership status. The criminal law is not itself a trans-identity offence, but it sits within a documented pattern of police leaks, failure to investigate or intervene in anti-LGBT violence, and weak state protection, alongside consistently hostile recorded public opinion, mob violence including an unsolved mob killing of a gender-nonconforming teenager, family violence and extortion by non-reporting, and identity-targeted abuse in detention, including in prison and hospital settings. Portland's tourism economy along the coast — Port Antonio's small eco-tourism, Boston Bay and Frenchman's Cove — is used to foreigners, and its relatively lower level of violent crime and laid-back, visitor-oriented character, plus welcoming statements from tourism officials, may soften everyday friction in hospitality settings; these do not displace national law, provide recourse, or establish safety, and the absence of known Portland-specific incidents does not establish safety. Conditional on being outed or discovered, the parish's character works against the visitor in other ways: it is tight-knit and church-dominated, small enough that an outed or outable visitor becomes known quickly, and attitudes can be more conservative than in tourist-centric areas, while constrained health, policing and legal services and smaller communities reduce anonymity and recourse. There is no LGBT venue, advocacy office or crisis support in the parish to call on, no documented local protective exception or enforcement reform, and no tolerant institution or trans community infrastructure distinguishing it — meaning discovery offers thinner recourse even than Kingston's sparse services. Detention would fall to rural lockups and, on transfer, to Kingston facilities where identity-targeted violence is documented, leaving the visitor facing the national exposure set — hostile public, unreliable police, and identity-targeted violence in custody — with no local offset.

50493656B62478729305943.name: Balqa
50493656B62478729305943.summary: Balqa governorate — taking in Salt, Mahis, Fuheis, the Jordan Valley and the Dead Sea corridor — is a predominantly rural, tribal and small-city area west of Amman, with tighter community ties and far less anonymity than the capital, and its settings vary. Within Balqa, Jordan's national regime applies in full: same-sex conduct and gender expression are not expressly criminalised, but vague public-morality and debauchery provisions and the 2023 cybercrime law have been used by security forces to harass LGBT people and to chill digital expression of gender diversity; gender-affirming surgery for transgender people is criminalised under Article 8 of Law 25 of 2018 with penalties of up to ten years' imprisonment; no clear legal gender recognition pathway exists; security forces have intimidated LGBT activists and pressured community spaces to close, and a 2023 crackdown targeted queer organising; a 2019 Arab Barometer survey found 93% of Jordanians said society should not accept homosexuality. 16772668B94173460365652.name: South Kazakhstan Region
16772668B94173460365652.summary: South Kazakhstan Region — centred on Turkestan and Shymkent, also referred to as Turkistan Region — inherits Kazakhstan's national framework: consensual same-sex conduct is decriminalised, and neither gender presentation nor the use of public facilities is restricted for visitors. No region-specific pattern of police targeting, anti-trans violence, or a distinct trans-visitor law is documented here — an absence of evidence rather than assurance of safety — and no local protective practice is documented. The region's more conservative, religiously observant, rural and less internationally exposed character, with stronger family and community norms, very low trans visibility, few trans-specific services or advocacy, and police and public unfamiliarity with gender diversity, is a general cultural cue rather than a documented driver of trans-specific enforcement; recourse is weaker outside Shymkent's university and student milieu. If a transgender visitor is discovered or outed, these conditions combine with the national regime: stigma, social hostility, harassment, outing, refusal of services, extortion, and hotel or clinic awkwardness are more likely, alongside police discretion that can bring questioning or short administrative trouble if expression is treated as propaganda. 16772668B79240574567699.name: North Kazakhstan Region
16772668B79240574567699.summary: Kazakhstan does not criminalise transgender identity, cross-dressing or use of facilities matching a person's presentation, no trans-specific clothing or facility ban has been documented, and consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 1998. There is no statutory anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity in employment, housing, health care or public accommodation, and no hate-crime reporting system, with no hate-crime data reported to the OSCE since 2018; documented violations against LGBT people include a 2019 Supreme Court case in which two women fled for eight months over fear of harm. Legal gender recognition is medically gatekept — requiring surgery, hormone therapy and sterilisation — and is effectively centred on Almaty, making it practically unavailable elsewhere. No organised state targeting or lethal pattern against trans visitors is known. North Kazakhstan Region is rural, agricultural, small-city and predominantly Russian-speaking, bordering Russia, with deeper social conservatism and homophobic and transphobic attitudes more pronounced than in the south. Compared with Almaty and Astana it lacks LGBTQ organisational, legal-aid and medical infrastructure, has no local trans support and no functioning gender commission, so anonymity is thinner and remedies for harassment or service refusal are correspondingly sparse; local enforcement practice here is undocumented, and its location or social character alone does not establish a documented pattern of targeting distinct from the national picture. Document checks, hotel registration and police spot-checks can out a traveller. A visibly trans visitor who is outed or discovered may face staring, gossip, scrutiny in housing, services, policing and medical settings, service refusal, misgendering or refusal of care, questioning, possible detention under the propaganda law and an unsympathetic police response, with local disapproval more likely to escalate into administrative harassment and little practical recourse.

32016919B83281423333591.name: Narok
32016919B83281423333591.summary: Narok is a largely rural, pastoral, Maasai-majority county in southwestern Kenya bordering Tanzania, whose main visitor economy is the Maasai Mara safari circuit; beyond the lodges and tourist corridor it is sparsely populated with strong customary and patriarchal norms. It inherits Kenya's national regime: same-sex conduct remains criminalised under Penal Code sections 162 and 165 with penalties up to 14 years, upheld by the High Court in 2019; decriminalisation litigation is unresolved; there is no statutory anti-discrimination protection and no legal gender-recognition pathway, with a May 2026 High Court ruling on document markers unimplemented as legislation and the Family Protection Bill stalled. The national record documents police detention of gender-nonconforming people on pretexts, on-the-spot extortion, and custody placement by birth sex, with a 2025 High Court finding that a trans prisoner suffered rights violations and nonconsensual procedures. The criminal provisions do not specifically target transgender identity, but the documented treatment of gender-nonconforming people makes them a relevant secondary concern; Kenya's lack of a domestic gender-marker process is not itself a visitor-facing exposure. Narok offers no local ordinance, protective practice, documented tolerance toward trans visitors, LGBTQ organisation, or trans-specific services, and region-specific documentation of trans incidents here is limited — the absence of local reports is not evidence of safety. Maasai customary norms include documented traditional roles for gender-variant men, which may offer some familiarity but no legal protection. County policing is thinner and less professionalised than in Nairobi or Mombasa, courts and legal aid are distant, and the tourist corridor toward Maasai Mara lodges is comparatively shielded and brings international visitors and some external scrutiny, with lodges offering a discreet setting but not a protective system; transit through Narok town and Kilgoris is not comparably shielded, and visibly gender-nonconforming strangers in small-town settings may attract immediate public attention. Conditional on being outed, a transgender visitor would combine these conditions with the national exposures, facing heightened public hostility, elder or community humiliation, more arbitrary local policing and community-level confrontation or mob exposure, reduced access to supportive services and legal recourse than in Nairobi, and heightened risk of detention or violence — with remote areas potentially worse than the national picture, though Narok-specific practice cannot be confirmed either way.

32016919B11020559484650.name: Kiambu
32016919B11020559484650.summary: Kiambu is a densely populated, largely Kikuyu county bordering and wrapping Nairobi, made up of commuter and dormitory towns such as Thika, Ruiru, Juja, Kikuyu and Limuru alongside a more rural interior. It is a strongly Christian and socially conservative setting, and no county-level statute, protective ordinance, policing directive, enforcement practice, documented incident involving a transgender visitor, or distinct treatment on border or document checks, facilities, custody placement or access to remedies is known to apply — so proximity to Nairobi alone does not establish safer conditions. The county operates under Kenya's national regime: colonial-era Penal Code provisions on same-sex conduct remain in force (with a 2019 High Court validation still on the books), no Kenyan statute recognises gender identity, there is no statutory gender-recognition pathway pending the May 2026 document-marker ruling, civil registration has refused most gender-marker corrections, there are no anti-discrimination protections, and the Family Protection Bill — which proposes capital penalties — remains stalled rather than enacted. Court remedies are slow and uncertain, and recent rulings on document markers and prison treatment still await implementing legislation. For a transgender visitor who is outed or discovered, these conditions combine as follows. Although the same-sex provisions do not criminalise transgender identity, they are used in practice as a police lever, with documented detention on pretexts such as drunken and disorderly conduct, on-the-spot extortion and bribes, and, in reporting by Kenya's human rights commissions and 2025 High Court findings, sexual coercion and rape by security officers; a court has also found serious violations of a trans person's rights in prison, while appellate rulings against forced examinations provide limited positive evidence. Trans detainees face unresolved placement in male or female cells, sex-designated facilities and bathroom use are documented flashpoints, and barriers to gender-affirming care persist. The urbanised edges closer to Nairobi offer a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor more anonymity than upcountry rural areas and put them nearer both those documented police practices and reachable Nairobi-based legal and advocacy support, while small-town and market-centre policing remains conservative and local police stations and county hospitals provide no trans-specific recourse; there is no locally documented additional exposure for travelling families or minors.
