32016919B39119671019936.name: Machakos
32016919B39119671019936.summary: Machakos County — a largely rural and peri-urban, closely knit Kamba-majority area just southeast of Nairobi, centred on Machakos and Athi River — operates entirely under Kenya's national framework: Penal Code sections 162, 163 and 165 criminalising same-sex conduct (upheld by the High Court in 2019, with a Court of Appeal decision still pending), no trans-specific criminal offence identified, and no gender-identity statute or codified recognition pathway for visitors, though a May 2026 High Court ruling allows changes to gender markers on identity documents and other recent court rulings have supported marker changes and barred forced anal examinations. A Family Protection Bill that would impose severe penalties has been stalled in committee for about two years and is not law, and no trans-specific killing rate is available. Locally there is no protective ordinance, no trans-specific organising, and no LGBTQ legal-aid, NGO or service infrastructure comparable to Nairobi's or Mombasa's, where most documented harassment cases originate; county courts and hospitals may be less accustomed to gender-identity disputes, social attitudes are broadly conservative with strong church influence, and there is little anonymity for visibly foreign or gender-nonconforming visitors, so legal and medical recourse lies with Nairobi-based lawyers and NGOs rather than locally. For a trans visitor who is outed or discovered, national police practices apply through the same system: harassment, pretextual detention (such as on 'drunk and disorderly' grounds), on-the-spot extortion, remand abuse, unresolved questions about cell placement for trans detainees, and misgendered custody — exposure that may rise after a passport, incident or medical request draws attention. A local case in which two men were taken from Kakuyuni to Kangundo Level 4 Hospital, where a magistrate halted a proposed anal examination, and a subsequent Court of Appeal ruling that forced examinations are unconstitutional with compensation awarded in 2024, alongside a 2025 High Court finding recording mistreatment of a trans prisoner including nonconsensual procedures, are meaningful signs of judicial relief but do not establish reliable protection from police harassment or abuse in custody. Discovery would most plausibly produce gossip, service refusal, police shakedowns or short detention rather than prosecution for identity itself; local conditions may therefore sit slightly below the national picture, though nothing county-specific distinguishes Machakos from Kenya overall, and any recourse would be thinner than in the capital.

32016919B31527762068828.name: Kajiado
32016919B31527762068828.summary: Kajiado has no documented county-specific law, enforcement pattern, protective ordinance or restrictive measure for transgender visitors, so Kenya's national framework governs: same-sex conduct remains criminalised under unrepealed Penal Code sections 162 and 165 and is sometimes used by police as a lever against gender-nonconforming people; there is no enacted statutory protection against gender-identity discrimination or hate crime, and no codified pathway for a visitor to change documents, so identity papers usually do not match presentation — a High Court ruling on gender recognition has issued, but no protective legislation has been enacted. Documented national risks include police detention on pretexts such as 'drunk and disorderly', on-the-spot extortion, remand beyond constitutional limits and intrusive custody practices, plus an Eldoret High Court finding of abusive prison treatment; court-ordered protections exist but enforcement is uneven. A pending Family Protection Bill would make 'aggravated homosexuality' punishable by death, but it is not law. Court rulings on documents and prison conditions have not produced enacted protections, barriers to affirming care persist, and no region-specific information on entry, policing, facilities or healthcare distinguishes Kajiado — such local practices are simply undocumented, which is not evidence of safety. Overall exposure remains well below routine arrest or torture for gender presentation, but substantially above a setting with operative protections and effective remedies; no specific additional exposure for travelling with a minor is documented. Locally, Kajiado is Maasai-majority and socially conservative, with strong patriarchal customary norms, Maasai age-set and pastoral gender segregation, small-town visibility and weaker legal-literacy and support infrastructure than central Nairobi, particularly outside Kajiado town and Kitengela. The northern commuter-belt towns of Kitengela, Ongata Rongai and Ngong offer relative anonymity and routine foreign-tourist traffic, and Amboseli's tourism economy increases exposure to visitors, but neither adds documented hostility nor documented protection, and tourism and conservancy employment do not guarantee safe facilities or privacy; trans-specific support is limited to Nairobi-linked networks. If discovered or outed, a visitor may face social scrutiny, humiliation, service refusal, and police questioning, extortion or arbitrary detention with thin and inconsistent local recourse, while sex-segregated ward or cell placement and border or document checks follow observed sex rather than identity, making emergency health and custody encounters especially exposed.

38789647B49701521312730.name: Chuy Region
38789647B49701521312730.summary: Chuy Region surrounds Bishkek and takes in Tokmok, Kant and the Manas International Airport corridor — the country's main international gateway — so national entry and document rules, including migration-service registration and the busy Kazakh border crossings, apply to most arriving visitors. It is the country's most urbanised, Russian-speaking and transit-oriented area, and anonymity plus proximity to the capital's small NGO, expatriate and community scene offers some discretion; at the same time, that community life is contracted (the capital's only gay club closed in 2017 and public LGBTQ venues in the wider capital area have largely disappeared), while the surrounding Chuy valley outside the immediate capital area is rural, agricultural and markedly more conservative, with family and community ostracism reported as especially acute and fewer protective networks. No region-specific enforcement practice or trans-specific exposure beyond the national picture is documented, nor is any distinct local protective effect; police and social hostility remain the main risk, illustrated nationally by an MP's call after the 2019 pride march for participants to be beaten. 37992800B48601233133149.summary: Preah Sihanouk, centred on Sihanoukville, is Cambodia's main coastal port and a tourist and casino hub; since 2019 a Chinese-run casino and construction boom has shifted it from beach resort toward a transient, gambling-heavy economy with guesthouse, nightlife and informal entertainment work. The policing and justice environment is weakly accountable, with organised-crime presence, corruption and extortion of vulnerable visitors known concerns, and police treatment of transgender entertainment workers follows patterns documented nationally: harassment, arrests tied to presentation, sex-worker raids and extortion practices. Nationally, street harassment of transgender women is documented, roughly a third of surveyed transgender women report arrests linked to their identity, and custody placement is informally governed; how often such conduct affects visitors in Preah Sihanouk is not documented. 97431129B55805139245338.summary: The Gilbert Islands are Kiribati's main inhabited archipelago and include South Tarawa — the capital and most urbanised, institutionally dense area, with government offices, the main airport and the country's highest concentration of outsiders and visitors — along with Betio and the outer atolls, so the national regime applies directly. Public concealment is the documented norm, with LGBTQ life confined largely to private, advocacy-supported spaces concentrated in Monrovia (where groups such as SAIL and TNOL operate) and not documented in Bomi, and no gender-affirming hormone therapy or surgery is available anywhere in the country. Repeated legislative attempts to impose harsher penalties have not become law. The Decent Work Act (2015) bars employment discrimination on grounds including gender identity, though that offers little to a short-stay visitor. For a transgender visitor, being outed does not mean trans identity itself is criminalised, but exposure in Bomi runs through tightly knit communities with little anonymity, where a visibly trans person is a rarity and social scrutiny is high, with police, landlords, clinics and community authorities the likely points of discovery. A trans visitor therefore meets Liechtenstein's national framework — same-sex relations and marriage are lawful, but gender identity and expression carry no anti-discrimination or hate-crime coverage (harassment and hate-incitement protections cover sexual orientation only), no domestic legal gender-marker change procedure exists (a visitor's home-issued documents are unaffected by that), and no law in force restricts access to sex-segregated facilities on the basis of gender identity. No trans-specific violence, police targeting, arrest, custody risk or border friction is on record, and functioning police and courts remain available, though the absence of local incidents is not itself proof of safety and gender-identity-specific recourse is limited. Official posture is socially conservative: senior public figures and the Roman Catholic Church, the state religion, have voiced opposition to marriage equality and rainbow families, registering as social climate rather than a traveller-facing restriction. Locally the difference is visibility rather than law: an unfamiliar face draws notice in a compact, traditionally Catholic, agrarian community where anonymity is low and privacy limited, and Catholic conservatism runs deeper than in Vaduz. This raises the chance of social discovery or being outed without raising its severity — the likely consequences are friction, stares, gossip, misgendering, service friction or privacy exposure rather than official action. Nothing indicates deliberate targeting, and no region-specific protective distinction or documented local hostility is known either way.

The area's tourism character neither adds protection nor raises risk, and local attitudes and specific trans visitor experiences remain uncertain. Institutions operate predictably, so ordinary travel, lodging and public presence carry friction rather than severe consequence, and the risk of detention, prosecution, violence or denial of emergency care remains low. Because harassment and incitement protections run only along the sexual-orientation axis, there is no protected ground to invoke if such friction occurs, but no documented local pattern of hostility, targeting, or service denial toward visitors exists. Prison placement defaults to birth sex with only a discretionary, medicalised exception and no statutory gender rule, while gender recognition certificates have been available since a 2016 Health Ministry circular allowing certification without surgery; gender-affirming care remains hard to access, with some clinicians showing ignorance or ridicule. Public opinion is mixed. Locally the province is largely rural, poorer and more socially and religiously conservative than Colombo, with predominantly Tamil and Muslim communities (conservative Muslim, Tamil and Sinhalese norms), stronger moral policing in Muslim-majority areas such as Kalmunai and Ampara, tighter-knit communities offering less anonymity for visibly gender-nonconforming people, and a dense post-war military and police checkpoint presence that raises document-check exposure, alongside police forces with a heavy security mandate and poor accountability culture. NGO, legal-aid and LGBT infrastructure is thin beyond national groups, with no visible trans community and comparatively limited trans-focused health and advocacy services, so an outed visitor has fewer allies and weaker practical recourse than in the capital; encounters with police, medics, prison officials or service providers can become more adversarial. No province-specific protective regime, shield practice, remedy, trans-targeted campaign, venues or documented pattern of trans violence distinguishes the region, and the absence of such documentation reflects uncertainty rather than evidence of safety. Tourist areas such as Trincomalee (with naval and tourism activity) and Arugam Bay are more used to foreigners and may offer some anonymity or foreigner leniency and moderated street friction, but this does not offset the inherited state response: discovery or being outed is likely to bring harassment, extortion, detention risk, service denial and denial of protection rather than lethal outcomes.

Locally, the province is anchored by Kandy, the cultural-religious heartland and seat of the Temple of the Tooth, with socially conservative Sinhala Buddhist and Tamil hill-country communities, strong temple influence, and rural and plantation districts around Nuwara Eliya and Matale where social policing runs deeper than in Colombo. Police presence is thinner and more traditional than in the Western Province, and there are fewer LGBTQ-specific services, community organisations or predictable complaint-handling channels than in the capital. Kandy's established tourism economy offers some foreigner tolerance and service-sector familiarity, but no province-specific exception or recourse against police abuse is documented. A transgender visitor who is discovered or outed here therefore faces the national pattern — questioning, extortion, public humiliation, short or arbitrary detention, and potential custody exposure — combined with a modestly harsher local social climate and weaker support infrastructure. Kandy hosts Bogambara Prison, so an arrest there means the same birth-sex placement default and discretionary medical assessment applies. Tourist-facing normalcy does not remove document or detention mismatches. The main exposure is police-driven harassment, extortion and detention rather than routine imprisonment for identity alone; severe outcomes such as execution are not credible.

Provincial health facilities offer no gender-affirming care, and staff have been reported as uninformed or ridiculing. Imprisonment or lethal harm is not the typical outcome for a discovered visitor and would be less common than in more severe jurisdictions, but custody, extortion and assault risks are real, and outed visitors should expect elevated social attention with minimal community support or informal recourse.

64170238B96397749018979.name: Monaco
64170238B96397749018979.summary: Monaco is itself the national jurisdiction, so there is no separate local variation from the country's overall picture: the conditions below are both local and national. Entry is via French Schengen arrangements, in a compact, wealthy, privacy-conscious and tourism-oriented principality with strong property and crime controls, dense policing, professional and functioning courts, and a low-crime environment; the US State Department reports no torture, arbitrary detention or abuse. No criminal offence targets gender expression or transgender presentation, and no targeting of trans travellers by border officers, police or facilities is documented, nor are raids, extortion, arrests, facility exclusions or trans-specific violence. Legal gender recognition does not exist, so a visitor's foreign-issued documents stand alone and match no local procedure — a resident-facing gap that does not itself invalidate foreign documents, though no specific visitor document practice is described. Public life is discreet and socially conservative, shaped by a Catholic majority that regards trans identity as immoral, with very low visibility (roughly ten openly out residents), no Pride, no dedicated queer venues and no community infrastructure, while private luxury hotels and the hospitality sector are generally non-confrontational; proximity to France and Italy offers broader LGBTIQ facilities nearby. If outed or discovered, a visitor is most likely to face awkwardness, misgendering, service friction or a discreet hotel problem — social and bureaucratic friction rather than state punishment, including possible awkward service, school or health-care treatment — with no anti-discrimination recourse on gender identity; custody placement and hospital-ward practice are undocumented, as is any family-specific enforcement rule affecting a minor travelling with a family. Given the policing and rule of law, arbitrary detention or custodial harm is unlikely, but strong public institutions are context rather than a demonstrated trans-specific remedy, and the lack of documented incidents rests on limited visitor evidence rather than a guarantee. The small, tightly policed and touristic setting likely reduces everyday confrontation compared with a larger hostile jurisdiction, without compensating for the absence of trans-specific protections.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (last updated 12 March 2026): same-sex intimacy legal but very few protections — hate crimes and hate speech on sexual orientation are penalised, while discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned (reported discrimination is described as rare); same-sex couples have no marriage or adoption, and LGBTIQ visibility in the principality is limited.

French gay travel guide Monaco page: no gay Pride is held anywhere in Monaco (visitors are sent to France or Italy for one); the ~200-hectare state is pitched as a luxury/relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Monaco: no significant changes; significant issues limited to libel and lèse-majesté laws (not enforced); no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses reported.

Nice-Matin via Monaco Haut Commissariat (March 2025, French): homosexuality decriminalised since the 18th century, yet Monaco ranks near the bottom of European LGBT-rights rankings — no equal succession, survivor pensions or parental leave for same-sex partners; roughly 10 people dare to be openly out; Council of Europe rapporteur Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo: "C’est le triste bilan de Monaco".

Queer In The World Monaco guide (updated 3 December 2023): homosexuality legal and SOGI discrimination illegal only in certain contexts — limited protections with room for improvement; advises visitors to stay current with local laws and customs.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Hate-speech protection rests on Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression, which bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence based on sexual orientation. Article 234-2 of the Civil Code, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016 (technological crime law), punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2–5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months–3 years. In July 2010 a Monegasque court jailed a man for 5 days and fined him €5,000 for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man. Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 added 'sexual orientation' to Civil Code articles 238-1 (6 months–1 year for violent acts not causing total incapacity), 239 (10 years for attacking a partner or co-resident) and 421 (5 years' probation for unprovoked attacks on a person or group). 25212430B51059014460141.name: Cahul
25212430B51059014460141.summary: Cahul, a small socially conservative district centre in southern Moldova near the Romanian and Gagauz boundaries, is subject to the same national rules as the rest of the country: same-sex conduct has been legal since 1995, gender identity is named in the 2023 equality law and 2022 hate-crime provisions, legal name and marker change is available with a psychiatric diagnosis, and gender expression carries no criminal penalty. National enforcement, however, is weak — a trans woman's bank denial was confirmed only after Equality Council review, hate speech has drawn no meaningful state response, Amnesty reported commonplace discrimination and impunity in 2025, and a transgender prisoner's prolonged isolation and humiliation was documented (a 2025 case of a trans detainee held in prolonged isolation is on record nationally); public attitudes are broadly hostile, with 79% saying they would not accept LGBT neighbours. Local conditions add to this: Cahul was one of the southern localities that enacted a 2012 local 'propaganda' ban on homosexuality and transness, which carried no administrative sanctions, was later overtaken nationally, and saw comparable bans struck down as unconstitutional — whether it remains operative or enforced is uncertain — but it signals local official hostility relative to Chisinau. The city has strong Orthodox influence, limited anonymity for a visibly trans visitor, no local Pride, no trans support organisations or nearby Equality Council presence, and fewer trans-aware medical, hospitality and police staff than the capital, so remedies generally require reaching Chisinau. A visitor who is outed can therefore expect curiosity, staring, disapproval, misgendering, refusal of service, ID or document friction, and awkward passport or border checks, with local police less likely than Chisinau's to handle a complaint robustly and poorer outcomes than in the capital. No arrests, violence, imprisonment or lethal risk specific to Cahul visitors are documented, and no trans-specific border checks, checkpoint system, facility restrictions, detention rules or campaigns against visitors are known — nor are distinct rules for travelling families or minors established — though the absence of such records is not evidence that this exposure cannot occur.

25212430B74275153833775.summary: Ialoveni is a largely rural district in Moldova's commuter belt just outside Chișinău, with Orthodox-majority, socially conservative small-town and village life, and no documented local ordinance, enforcement pattern, incident or trans-specific protection that distinguishes it from the national picture; the local "propaganda" bans on record concern other districts (Balti, Drochia, Cahul and Ceadir-Lunga), not Ialoveni, though courts have struck such bans down nationally, and Gagauzia and Transnistria rules do not apply here. Under Moldova's framework, consensual same-sex conduct is legal with no trans-specific criminal offence, gender identity is a protected ground in anti-discrimination and hate-crime law, hate speech and hate crimes are offences, and legal document change is possible but requires a psychiatric diagnosis. Enforcement nonetheless lags behind the law: a trans woman was denied bank service over a document mismatch and received only an Equality Council recommendation, officials have not responded meaningfully to anti-LGBT hate speech, discrimination and violence are reported as commonplace with impunity, a trans detainee endured years of solitary isolation and humiliation in custody as recently as 2025, and surveys show a large majority of people would not accept LGBT+ neighbours. For a transgender visitor in Ialoveni who is discovered or outed, the district's smaller, less anonymous setting means service staff, landlords and police are more likely to react with curiosity, disapproval or refusal than with organised targeting, and complaints are likely to be mishandled; conservative norms increase everyday risk of outing and pressure, and the district has fewer supportive services and probably lower official responsiveness than the capital. Proximity to Chișinău nevertheless allows relatively quick access to GENDERDOC-M, legal help and capital-based advocacy and health services, while remedies for service discrimination would likely require travelling there. The main exposure after discovery is social hostility and unreliable recourse rather than imprisonment or lethal risk, and there is no known local law or enforcement practice that worsens punishment beyond the national regime — but also no documented local remedy that would reduce it. Trans-specific border screening, facility rules, visitor access to care and consequences for travelling minors are not documented. Assumptions about relevant anti-trans violence patterns in Moldova in general remain uncertain in their application to visitors.

25212430B5738533784066.name: Nisporeni
25212430B5738533784066.summary: Nisporeni is a small district town surrounded by rural communities with no large urban centre, little tourism, no local LGBT organisation or visible queer infrastructure, and a strongly Orthodox, socially conservative population in which strangers are quickly noticed. No local law, facility rule, documented incident, or institution concerning transgender visitors distinguishes the district from Moldova's national picture, and the national framework applies unchanged: gender identity is named in anti-discrimination law, hate-crime and hate-speech offences exist, gender expression is not criminalised and consensual same-sex conduct is legal, but enforcement is weak and Equality Council findings are not systematically acted on. Legal aid, community organisations and police-protected Pride marches are concentrated in Chișinău, while district-level police are untrained and unlikely to treat harassment of a trans visitor as a priority; Pride protections and relevant court rulings concern the capital and other cities rather than this district. Local documentation is sparse, so the absence of reported incidents is not evidence of safety, and reduced recourse compared with the capital follows from distance from urban legal aid and NGO support rather than from any documented local pattern. For a transgender visitor, exposure stems less from local rules than from everyday friction: being conspicuous and quickly read as an outsider, staring, informal hostility, and bureaucratic difficulty such as service refusal when documents and appearance do not match, as in a documented 2024 case of a trans woman denied bank service. No local statute, ban or morality enforcement imposes harsher penalties than the national regime, and arrest is not what is typically documented; the greater concern is if detention occurs, given documented custody practices including reports of humiliating and isolating treatment of a trans detainee and a 2025 case of prolonged isolation in a penitentiary. National conditions carry over as well: hate speech and discrimination are commonplace with little meaningful state response, surveys record 79% would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, legal gender change still requires a psychiatric diagnosis, and Amnesty reported arbitrary assembly restrictions and impunity in 2025. Practical recourse here is limited, so discretion is advisable.

25212430B26910735221199.name: Anenii Noi
25212430B26910735221199.summary: Anenii Noi is a small, largely agricultural district east of Chișinău — about half an hour from the capital and lying along the Transnistria boundary — with a socially conservative local culture and no known trans-specific services, venues, advocacy or other local institutions. No distinct local statute, enforcement pattern, protective measure or documented incident distinguishes it from Moldova's national picture, so the national framework governs: consensual same-sex conduct is legal, anti-discrimination law since 2023 names gender identity and sexual orientation, and hate speech and hate crimes have been criminal offences since 2022, while changing legal gender on documents requires a psychiatric diagnosis (a process foreign visitors do not use). Rural district centres outside the capital typically show deeper social conservatism, less exposure to diverse gender presentation and greater reliance on informal authority, which can increase the severity of outing and social hostility relative to Chișinău; anonymity and community support are weaker, and practical support would mostly require travelling to the capital. Enforcement of those national protections is weak: documented cases include a trans woman refused bank service over a mismatch between her documents and appearance (a decision confirmed by the Equality Council), commonplace anti-LGBT discrimination and hostile treatment in state institutions, recurring hate speech and hostile political rhetoric that has drawn little state response, and inconsistent police protection of Pride events in Chișinău alongside failures to investigate attacks. Public acceptance is very low, with a 2022 survey finding 79% of respondents would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, and a 2025 account describes prolonged isolation and degrading treatment of a trans detainee in Penitentiary No. 6. For a trans visitor, discovery in this district would likely become known quickly locally and draw curiosity, disapproval, harassment or service refusal rather than state prosecution, with uncertain police recourse and thin practical remedies; no local organised targeting, additional local restriction or documented local incident is known, but nor is there reliable local support.

Legal name change aside, arrest or criminal penalty is not the expected consequence of discovery; the likely harms centre on discrimination, harassment and weak protection. In Criuleni's small-town setting an outed or visibly trans visitor would be highly visible as an outsider, with limited anonymity and no documented LGBT community infrastructure, Pride activity or NGO presence, making gossip, misgendering, staring, service refusal, harassment and uncomfortable police or medical encounters more likely, alongside an indifferent or unsympathetic official response. The national Equality Council and police remain the main recourse, but remedies are slow and uneven, and specialised advocacy, legal-aid and complaint mechanisms are weaker than in Chișinău, leaving a traveller dependent on capital-based institutions. Conditions broadly track the national picture but are somewhat less protective than in Chișinău and slightly below the national baseline, with no evidence of a local crackdown on transgender visitors.

For a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed, the likely exposure is therefore service refusal, intrusive questioning, harassment and hostile local attitudes rather than prosecution for identity alone: police response has been historically inconsistent, formal recourse would likely depend on institutions concentrated in Chișinău, and police involvement or detention may bring poor responsiveness.

25212430B23943377724140.name: Ungheni
25212430B23943377724140.summary: Ungheni is a small, socially conservative Orthodox border and railway town on the Prut crossings to Romania, and no local incidents, protections, or sanctuary policy for trans people are documented there. No specific pattern of targeting trans visitors is established, and local border, facility and visitor-service practices are undocumented rather than known to be safe. Against Moldova's national framework — anti-discrimination and hate-crime provisions naming gender identity that are weakly enforced, legal gender change requiring a psychiatric diagnosis, a documented denial of banking service to a trans woman whose documents did not match her appearance, anti-LGBT hate speech left with no meaningful state response, very low public acceptance (about four in five would not accept LGBT neighbours), and the isolated detention and humiliation of a trans man in state custody through 2025 (Penitentiary No. 6, Soroca) alongside reported prolonged isolation and humiliating treatment of trans prisoners — an outed or outable visitor in Ungheni is likely to face friction, misgendering, service denial and bureaucratic humiliation with unreliable police response, and emergency or routine health care may involve misgendering or refusal. Authorities have acknowledged homophobia in institutions and police have at times failed to investigate attacks on rights defenders; prison or violence remain possible if contact with police escalates, though there is no evidence of imprisonment for gender expression, no documented local ordinance or pattern against trans visitors, and custody or lethal threat is not the expected daily exposure.

25212430B70495112373630.name: Calarasi

Gender marker change requires a psychiatric diagnosis. For a transgender visitor who is outed or discovered, these conditions combine as social hostility with thin practical recourse: low anonymity, limited LGBT visibility and few support structures mean gossip, staring, hostile comments, service refusal, and informal questioning or discretionary local police handling are more likely than in the capital, where most NGO and Pride activity is concentrated, and practical remedy would largely require travelling to Chisinau. Document mismatches can prompt refusal of services or questioning. National social acceptance of LGBT people is documented as very low — including 79% rejection of LGBT neighbours — and is likely deeper locally. No organised or state-directed targeting, no known local trans-specific ban, and no harsher local enforcement are documented; the main exposure is social hostility, service friction and, should custody arise, Moldova's national document and custody shortcomings, which the local record does not resolve either way.

25212430B1615629371845.summary: Rîșcani is a small, predominantly rural district town in northern Moldova with limited tourism and no visible LGBT or transgender organisations, so a visitor who is outed or read as different may face intrusive questioning, misgendering, service refusal and local curiosity or hostility with less anonymity and fewer community support options than in Chişinău; rural northern conservatism and Orthodox norms compound weak institutional responsiveness, meaning police help can be slow or dismissive and recourse slower than in the capital. The district lies outside Russian-occupied Transnistria, so entry, documents, facilities and custody follow Moldova's national regime and that territory's harsher 'non-traditional relations' promotion legislation does not apply. No documented local anti-trans legislation, propaganda ban, violence, policing pattern, facility rule or protective measure distinguishes the district from the national picture, and there is no known local tolerance or local hostility exceeding it; region-specific border treatment, healthcare access and police conduct are simply undocumented, which is not evidence of safety. Document–appearance mismatches can surface at border checks, in clinics or in detention, and families or children may face added school and health-service inquiry, though no local law criminalising presentation is known. Under the national regime a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed meets anti-discrimination law naming gender identity (Law No. 2 of 2023), hate-crime provisions criminal since 2022 and hate-speech provisions, with same-sex conduct not criminalised, complaint bodies including the Equality Council, and Pride marches proceeding openly under police protection in Chişinău — but enforcement is weak and uneven, discrimination and impunity are commonplace, and public acceptance is extremely low, including survey data showing 79% would not accept LGBT+ neighbours. Documented failures include a 2024 bank service denial over an identity-document mismatch, the Equality Council confirming document-mismatch discrimination, cases of institutions siding with discriminators, inadequate official responses to hate speech and attacks, humiliating and isolating custodial treatment of a trans man documented through 2025 and trans-specific mistreatment in custody at Soroca — indicating limited recourse if state services become involved, alongside legal gender recognition that requires a psychiatric diagnosis. Local 'propaganda' bans have been struck down by courts but remain a documented past feature of public life, and the gap between paper protection and everyday acceptance is felt more sharply in a small northern town than in the capital.

25212430B36697629718061.name: Rezina
25212430B36697629718061.summary: Rezina is a small, largely rural and socially conservative district on the Dniester, with its main town directly facing Transnistria and lying far from Chisinau's concentration of advocacy groups, legal aid, Pride events and police experience with LGBT events. The district has no LGBT or trans organisation, no visible community and little anonymity, so a visibly trans visitor would draw sustained local attention and gossip-driven exposure would spread quickly; there is no local Pride, no documented protective infrastructure, no local police training or documented recourse, and local police are unlikely to pursue harassment complaints seriously. Border checkpoints and adjacency to Transnistria, where legislation bans promotion of 'non-traditional sexual relations', add an external regime that can draw scrutiny of a visitor's documents or presentation, with no independent remedy. There is no local 'propaganda' ban, no local exclusion regime, no organised local targeting or enforcement sweeps, and no universal facility restriction documented here. The national framework applies in full: consensual same-sex conduct and gender expression are not criminalised, Law No. 2 of 2023 names gender identity in anti-discrimination law, and hate-crime provisions have existed since 2022, though enforcement is weak and concentrated in the capital. Documented failures include a 2024 bank-service refusal over document-appearance mismatch, confirmed by the Equality Council, hate speech receiving no meaningful state response, and discrimination reported as commonplace with impunity; legal gender recognition requires a psychiatric diagnosis. Surveyed acceptance is extremely low, with 79% saying they would not accept an LGBT neighbour, and Pride events in Chisinau have faced attacks and bans. Documented mistreatment of trans detainees in the penitentiary system — including prolonged solitary confinement and humiliation, and abuse of a transgender man in Penitentiary No. 6 in 2025, with no later instance recorded — is a national rather than local exposure. For a trans visitor who is outed or discovered in Rezina, these national conditions combine with thin local institutions and conservative attitudes: the likely outcome is staring, gossip, service refusal, humiliation and unhelpful police rather than criminal detention or lethal punishment, though recourse is thinner than in the capital.

25212430B52468939139965.name: Soldanesti
25212430B52468939139965.summary: Soldanesti is a small rural district seat in northern Moldova — recorded in some accounts as a district town and in others as a commune in Sîngerei District — with sparse tourist services, no tourist-facing infrastructure, no local LGBT organisation, no local Pride, no visible trans community and no local equality infrastructure: the Equality Council and GENDERDOC-M both operate from Chișinău, and a complaint would fall to district police described as under-trained, with documented poor handling of trans complaints. Nothing locally contradicts national law — no local criminalisation, trans-specific ban, checkpoint, hostile ordinance, service-discrimination record, anti-trans violence or organised targeting is known — but equally no local protection or mitigation is documented, and traditional northern small-town attitudes in a predominantly Orthodox setting are less accepting than the capital, where institutional and civil-society support is concentrated. A visibly trans visitor would be conspicuous in hotels, markets and police encounters, so discovery or being outed is near-certain and each outcome rests on the discretion of individual officials. Moldova's framework, which applies in full, names gender identity in its anti-discrimination law (Law No. 2 of 2023) and in hate-speech and hate-crime offences in force since 2022, permits consensual same-sex conduct, has no trans-specific criminal statute, and allows document changes with a psychiatric diagnosis; enforcement is weak and inconsistent, with discrimination and violence described as commonplace, widespread hate speech drawing little state response, 79% of the public rejecting LGBT+ neighbours, and a trans woman's bank refusal over documents not matching her appearance confirmed by the Equality Council. Amnesty reports arbitrary assembly restrictions met with impunity; police have recently protected Chișinău Pride marches, but earlier failures and a refused arson investigation show protection is uneven; and a 2025 penitentiary case recorded a trans detainee held in prolonged isolation, subjected to strip searches and staff humiliation, with no effective remedy. In Soldanesti these inherited conditions combine with rural thinness of recourse: the realistic consequences of discovery are hostility, refusal of service, document-mismatch friction in banking, lodging and routine services, unsympathetic policing and slower protection than in Chișinău — social and institutional harm rather than prosecution or imprisonment.

25212430B38040597710669.name: Floresti
25212430B38040597710669.summary: Floresti, a small rural commune in northern Moldova, has no documented local legislation, protections, institutions or incidents distinguishing it from the national picture, so Moldova's national framework governs: same-sex relations have been legal since 1995, gender identity is named in the 2023 equality law and in hate-speech and hate-crime provisions criminalised since 2022, and residents can obtain legal name and gender-marker change, which requires a psychiatric diagnosis — none of which directly protects a visitor. Enforcement is inconsistent: a 2024 refusal of bank service to a trans woman was confirmed as discrimination by the Equality Council without a meaningful state response, hate speech is pervasive with no meaningful state response, and a 2022 national survey found 79% of respondents would not accept LGBT+ neighbours. Floresti is not among the localities named in the 2012 local 'gay propaganda' bans — neighbouring Drochia district enacted such a ban, later invalidated by a court — and no local sanctions or enforcement records were found for it. No local hostile law is in force, and no Floresti-specific border screening, facility restrictions, police targeting, violence patterns or visitor remedies are documented, nor are district-level exposures or protections for minors; that absence does not establish safety. Locally the district is poorer, more socially conservative and less visible than Chișinău, with thin LGBT community infrastructure and legal aid, limited anonymity, rural communities more attentive to outsiders, and Equality Council and police responsiveness harder to reach than in the capital. For a transgender visitor who is outed, these conditions mean staring, possible misgendering in clinics, refusal of services, and indifferent or discretionary local policing that is unlikely to treat harassment as a priority, with recourse concentrated in Chișinău or NGOs — materially worse than the capital, where police have protected recent Pride events though protection has been uneven and earlier attacks went uninvestigated. The principal exposures are discrimination, harassment, service denial and possible custodial misplacement rather than imprisonment or lethal state punishment, and no organised local targeting is documented, though isolated hostility cannot be excluded. Arrest carries a severe custody exposure: abuse of a trans detainee was documented at Soroca penitentiary in the same northern region as recently as 2025, and penitentiary treatment of a trans man through 2025 has included isolation and forced strip searches.

25212430B3857280687737.name: Drochia
25212430B3857280687737.summary: Drochia, a rural northern district, inherits Moldova's national framework: no criminal statute targets same-sex conduct or gender presentation, gender identity is a protected ground in anti-discrimination and hate-crime law, and legal document change requires a psychiatric diagnosis — but enforcement is weak, hate speech has gone without meaningful state response, and documented discrimination includes denial of bank service over a document/appearance mismatch, confirmed by the equality council. Custodial conditions elsewhere in the country are a documented concern: a transgender detainee was held three years in isolation at Penitentiary No. 6 in nearby Soroca, with authorities conceding that homophobia persists in state institutions, and other records describe isolation, forced strip searches and misgendering of a trans detainee in Moldovan custody. Locally, Drochia is a conservative, low-anonymity, Orthodox-majority town where 79% of surveyed residents said they would not accept LGBT neighbours — markedly less tolerant than Chisinau — with no visible trans community, no local Pride, no trans-specific services or specialist or legal-aid presence, and no documented local protective practice. It was among the localities that passed a symbolic 2012 'propaganda' ban carrying no administrative sanctions; that measure was unenforced and dated, and while similar bans were struck down elsewhere, no Drochia-specific invalidation is documented. Police and courts are the national system, and no region-specific pattern of violence or visitor targeting is recorded: discovery here is more likely to mean staring, questioning, refusal of service and slow-moving complaints than organised targeting, with document/appearance mismatch friction and humiliation as the standing exposures, and adults travelling with a minor may face heightened scrutiny in family, schooling or health settings. There is no evidence of routine arrest, detention or lethal punishment for gender presentation in this setting.

25212430B65458906379390.name: Edinet
25212430B65458906379390.summary: Edineț, a small agrarian district centre in northern Moldova near the Ukrainian border, has no documented local laws, incidents, sanctuary practices or protective mechanisms that distinguish it from the rest of the country, and local authorities are expected to follow central rules. It operates under Moldova's national framework, in which gender identity is a protected ground under Law No. 2 of 2023, consensual same-sex conduct is legal, and hate-crime provisions (criminalised since 2022) and hate-speech offences exist; no criminal offence targets trans identity, while legal gender recognition requires a psychiatric diagnosis. Enforcement is weak: the Equality Council can only recommend measures, though it has confirmed discrimination, including a trans woman denied bank service over a mismatch between her documents and her appearance, and a documented case shows a trans detainee held in isolating, humiliating penitentiary conditions. Nearby northern localities, including Bălți and neighbouring Drochia district, previously passed local 'gay propaganda' bans that courts later invalidated. Edineț itself has no documented LGBT organisations, no local advocacy or trans-specific support and no Pride protections outside Chișinău, with legal assistance effectively available only in Chișinău. The social climate is strongly conservative and Orthodox, acceptance is very low (79% would reject LGBT neighbours), and discrimination and anti-LGBT hate speech are commonplace and often inadequately addressed by authorities, so a foreign trans visitor in a small town would be highly visible. If a visitor's trans status becomes known, they should expect gossip and staring, possible refusal of services, accommodation or care, questioning and misgendering, and an unreliable police response with little practical recourse. Offsetting these conditions, statutory protections for gender identity and sexual orientation and the 2023 anti-discrimination amendment apply, police have protected Pride in Chișinău in recent years after earlier failures and Pride now proceeds openly, and no documented local pattern of organised anti-trans targeting exists.

25212430B46101437811477.name: Briceni
25212430B46101437811477.summary: Briceni is a small, agrarian district centre in northern Moldova near the Ukrainian and Romanian borders, not a major tourism hub, and it lies far from Chisinau, where legal aid, Pride protection and advocacy are concentrated. No region-specific information distinguishes it from the national picture: there are no documented trans-specific incidents, local ordinances or protective measures, no local 'propaganda' ban of the kind once enacted in Balti or Cahul (courts have struck down some local propaganda bans), and no documented border, facility or criminal ban targeting transgender visitors. There is likewise no local evidence documenting how trans visitors are treated at borders, in facilities or custody, or when seeking care, and no protective tourist infrastructure is documented; a small population, visible social networks, Orthodox conservatism and fewer accessible complaint mechanisms mean anonymity is absent and a foreigner is conspicuous. A trans visitor therefore inherits Moldova's national regime: identity expression is not criminalised, consensual same-sex conduct is legal, Law No. 2 of 2023 names gender identity as a protected ground, and hate-crime and hate-speech offences covering that ground have been on the statute book since 2022 — but enforcement is uneven and institutions have limited reach outside the capital. Documented conditions include a trans woman denied bank service over a document-and-appearance mismatch, confirmed only through an Equality Council recommendation; commonplace discrimination and impunity in Amnesty's documentation; an Equality Council record of extreme social non-acceptance, with 79% saying they would not accept LGBT neighbours; and widespread social rejection with a limited response to anti-LGBT hate speech. Police have protected some Pride events in Chisinau but failed to protect others, and officials have declined to investigate attacks on LGBT-linked targets. If discovered or outed, a visitor in Briceni should expect service denial, harassment, mockery or a shrug from police or clinic staff rather than a remedy, friction at border, hotel, medical or banking document checks, and unreliable recourse — the practical ceiling being harassment, denial of service and administrative friction rather than arrest or custody — along with stigma that can affect a family with a minor. Beyond the district, custody for trans detainees is documented as isolating and humiliating, with a 2025 case of identity-based abuse recorded in the penitentiary system at nearby Soroca.

25212430B70903588336793.name: Soroca
25212430B70903588336793.summary: Soroca is a small, socially and religiously conservative northern town on the Dniester, with tourism centred on its fortress, a large Roma community, and conditions that make a visibly trans visitor highly conspicuous. It has no local LGBT organisation, no Pride events or activist infrastructure, no protective local policies or ordinances aimed at visitors, and no documented evidence of better treatment than the national picture — recourse rests on the national Equality Council, while police and service staff practice is largely discretionary. The nearby Transnistrian boundary adds restrictions on promoting non-traditional relations if crossed, though no traveller-facing border or accommodation refusal specific to the district is documented. As elsewhere in Moldova, gender identity is a protected ground under the 2023 anti-discrimination law, gender expression and same-sex conduct are not criminalised, hate speech and hate crimes have been criminalised since 2022 with the ground named in hate-crime provisions, and legal name and marker change is available (with a psychiatric diagnosis requirement) — but enforcement lags the statute: a trans woman was denied banking services in a case confirmed by the Equality Council, 79% of people say they would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, political hate speech persists with impunity for past violations, and the state response to hostility is weak, even though police have shown some capacity to secure public events in recent years. Soroca's own record adds institutional hostility: its Penitentiary No. 6 held a transgender man for around three years in solitary, rat-infested isolation with strip searches, forced humiliating searches, misgendering, denial of a requested protective placement and staff homophobia, with authorities acknowledging as recently as 2025 that homophobia persists in state institutions while disputing his discrimination complaints. That case concerns custody rather than documented treatment of ordinary visitors, but harsh treatment is documented for a trans person in local detention, so a visitor detained or brought before local authorities is especially exposed; outside custody, service refusal and street hostility remain plausible, and nothing specific to Soroca remedies the country's enforcement failures.

25212430B39831138215863.name: Donduseni
25212430B39831138215863.summary: Donduseni is a small, rural district town in northern Moldova with a predominantly Orthodox, socially conservative population, high emigration, very low LGBT visibility and low tourism. Outsiders, especially gender-nonconforming foreign visitors, are highly visible and quickly noticed, so anonymity is absent; the district has no local trans community, no documented LGBT civil-society presence or Pride protection, no documented Equality Council action, and thinner police, judicial and service infrastructure than Chisinau, with the nearest support in the capital. No region-specific legal regime, trans-specific campaign or documented incident of violence or police targeting distinguishes Donduseni from the national picture, and the local 'propaganda' bans adopted in 2012 did not name Donduseni; northern rural areas are reported as more conservative than the capital, with strong Orthodox-clergy influence. Undocumented matters — including Donduseni-specific border treatment, facility access, police conduct, visitor service denial and conditions for travelling families — are not known, and that uncertainty is not evidence of safety. The national framework applies in full: consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised, gender identity and sexual orientation are named in anti-discrimination law (Law No. 2 of 2023) and in hate-crime provisions in force since 2022, and legal gender change is possible on a psychiatric diagnosis, but enforcement is weak, the Equality Council works slowly, and anti-LGBT hate speech commonly goes unaddressed. Documented national exposures include a 2024 denial of bank service to a trans woman over a document-appearance mismatch, recorded violence and police inaction in Chisinau, and surveys showing pronounced social rejection (roughly four in five people would not accept LGBT neighbours). For a transgender visitor in Donduseni who is outed, these national gaps combine with local thinness: likely close scrutiny, gossip, service refusal and police indifference rather than organised targeting, with remedies harder to reach and support further away than in the capital. Imprisonment or state violence for identity itself is not a credible outcome, but anyone entering custody faces serious documented risk — a transgender detainee was held in prolonged isolation subjected to degrading searches and misgendering, including a trans man in a northern penitentiary in 2025 — and the psychiatric-certification requirement for document change remains operative.

27540722B39676432794686.name: Diana
27540722B39676432794686.summary: Diana, Madagascar's northernmost region centred on Antsiranana (Diego Suarez) and including the Nosy Be resort islands, has no local ordinance, protection or documented incident setting it apart from the national picture. Madagascar does not criminalise being transgender or cross-dressing; adult same-sex conduct is lawful only from age 21, with unequal penalties for partners under that age (an indecent-assault provision applies to acts with anyone under 21), and there is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime statute. Marriage law does not recognise a trans person's gender, names gender identity as grounds for nullity, and offers no civil-union recognition, and in 2025 the government rejected UN recommendations on anti-LGBT violence and equalising consent. The only documented violence against gender-nonconforming people dates from 2011 — abuse, stone-throwing and murder of transgender sex workers — with no later instance recorded. Social disapproval remains deep enough that many LGBT Malagasy conceal their identities. Diana is described as the country's most tourism-dependent area, with a French-influenced, foreigner-facing visitor economy around Antsiranana and Nosy Be; some accounts find that this anonymity and regular contact with foreign travellers, along with service staff accustomed to diverse visitors, modestly reduces everyday exposure and makes some businesses and officers less inclined to police visitors' presentation. Others note that the port city's beach and bay tourism is modest and its social norms more conservative and less cosmopolitan than Antananarivo's small queer networks, and point to conservative coastal Muslim and Christian norms, discretionary police stops, gendarmerie and military presence, distance from national institutions and the small-town character outside main tourist hubs. Tourism is not evidence of acceptance of transgender people: no trans-specific support, community or protective infrastructure is visible, and effective recourse for a harmed visitor is thin. Should discovery or outing occur, a visitor may face harassment, accommodation denial, invasive questioning or extortion; the main exposure is social and bureaucratic severity rather than any documented campaign of imprisonment or execution. A trans minor or family would face stronger school and community pressure with fewer protective channels.

27540722B68428456346892.name: Atsinanana
27540722B68428456346892.summary: Atsinanana, centred on Toamasina — Madagascar's main port and a tourism and commercial centre — is more urban and foreign-facing than rural districts, giving a trans visitor greater anonymity in daily movement; hotels and businesses there may be reluctant to confront international travellers, and routine checks are more accustomed to nonconforming visitors. Beyond this, no region-specific information distinguishes the area: there is no documented local trans-specific protection, added exposure, harsher enforcement or tourism-facing tolerance, and no recent organised anti-trans targeting is documented in the region. This commercial caution may modestly reduce post-discovery confrontation, but it does not alter national law or provide reliable protection. In the port city, transactional-sex dynamics similar to those behind the documented 2011 targeting of transgender sex workers plausibly persist. Unlike the isolated resort islands, where behaviour is largely tolerated and tourist enclaves are sheltered, the capital offers little insulation from ordinary civilian public life: Sharia-based social norms and the Penal Code's same-sex conduct and marriage offences, carrying penalties up to eight years plus lashes, apply in full, alcohol is barred outside resorts, facilities are gender-segregated, and street culture is conservative and religiously observant with a standing police presence. No transgender-specific criminal provision, document rule, facility rule or care restriction has been identified, and no transgender prosecution is documented, but the same-sex offences are framed by sex with no guidance on how a trans person's gender would be classified. Executions have been suspended since 1953, though flogging remains a stated penalty, and there is no gender-identity anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection, with an official posture that rejects such protections. In Malé, gender-nonconforming presentation can draw attention from police, residents and officials under public morality, indecency or sexual-offence provisions, and a trans visitor who is discovered or outed faces social hostility, questioning, possible detention, fines or prosecution, and vulnerability to blackmail or violence with limited formal recourse. The record documents the 2013 stabbing of a gay blogger in Malé and UNFPA-reported hate crimes against people perceived as transgender or homosexual, with stigma discouraging reporting and no documented relief. There is no documented recent enforcement against visitors, no trans-specific screening or police targeting, and no trans-specific local statute or facility rule identified, so the direct consequences of discovery for an outed visitor remain uncertain; tourism and a large foreign-worker presence provide some anonymity and services, and greater anonymity than on small islands partly offsets the stricter capital environment, though tourist-facing tolerance does not apply in ordinary public local life.

51498476B37587528585643.name: Alif Alif
51498476B37587528585643.summary: Alif Alif (North Ari Atoll) combines enclosed resort islands with small inhabited islands, including guesthouse-tourism islands such as Rasdhoo, Ukulhas, Himmafushi and Thoddoo, and no atoll-specific legal exception or local protection is documented — the Maldives' national regime applies. Same-sex conduct and same-sex marriage are criminalised, with Sharia-framed provisions (sections 410–412) carrying penalties up to eight years plus lashing, while no transgender-specific offence, legal recognition, document or screening rule, facility or custody rule, or gender-identity anti-discrimination protection exists and official posture at the UN rejects gender-identity protections. Enforcement generally follows complaints, stigma discourages reporting, alcohol and dress rules remain restrictive, and the one documented enforcement action in the atoll was the 2015 arrest of two men on Dhaandhoo for private same-sex activity after a public complaint. Resort islands operate as separated tourist enclaves where foreign guests are generally tolerated and privacy is stronger, and national guidance describes private resort islands as generally welcoming to LGBTQ tourists — but this is not trans-specific evidence and does not remove the national legal regime. If a transgender visitor is discovered or outed at a resort, the likelier outcomes are private-sector ones: staff misgendering or gossip, refusal of service, eviction, and security reporting, with domestic-transfer document checks adding exposure and no enforceable remedy. On the inhabited islands a trans visitor would be visible to a close-knit, socially conservative Muslim community, its guesthouses and local police, risking stigma, harassment, moral complaints, public hostility, community pressure, possible police questioning or referral under the national same-sex provisions, and little practical recourse; travel companions may be expelled or questioned, and a 2015 advocacy warning told tourists they could face the threats residents face. Guidance advises caution outside tourist areas.

51498476B1749361850718.name: Alif Dhaalu
51498476B1749361850718.summary: Alif Dhaalu (South Ari Atoll) applies the Maldives' national regime in full: same-sex sexual conduct and same-sex marriage are criminal under the Penal Code and Islamic law, with penalties of up to eight years' custody and flogging under Sharia provisions, though no capital punishment applies. No transgender-specific criminal offence, document rule, screening, facility rule or custody rule is documented, and there is no gender-identity anti-discrimination protection, no trans-specific recourse or support infrastructure in the atoll, and a restrictive official posture internationally. The atoll combines isolated resort islands — where alcohol is permitted and resorts are described as operating outside Islamic law in practice, isolated from civilian centres and comparatively tolerant or welcoming to LGBTQ guests — with inhabited, close-knit, socially conservative Muslim islands and a growing guesthouse sector that apply stricter religious and social norms, including council and police authority over public morality. Morality and public-order provisions can be used against people perceived as gender-nonconforming, so a visitor outed or discovered outside a resort setting faces heightened risk of intrusive questioning, harassment, ejection, referral, detention, prosecution or deportation, and on inhabited islands identity is more likely to be noticed and reported than at resorts. On resorts, discovery by hospitality staff is likely to be handled discreetly to avoid scandal, though service refusal and questioning remain possible, and resort spaces still remain governed by the same national law and conservative social norms. The only documented enforcement case in the record for this atoll involved two men arrested on Dhaandhoo island in 2015 following a public complaint, and the documented enforcement and violence cases generally concern homosexuality rather than transgender status. No region-specific record of violence against transgender visitors, no documented local tradition of either trans acceptance or hostility toward transgender visitors as a distinct group, and no documented trans-specific local practice distinguish this atoll's treatment of outed transgender visitors from the national picture.

64602211B48349945606013.name: Tagant
64602211B48349945606013.summary: Tagant is a remote, sparsely populated desert and rural interior region of Mauritania with no tourism economy and, per different accounts, centred on either Kiffa or Tidjikja. Its communities are small, tightly knit, socially conservative and religiously observant, with a predominantly Moorish and Maliki character and, in places, a strong Islamic scholarly and Sufi influence. There is no visible LGBT or transgender infrastructure, no local protections or institutional recourse for transgender visitors, and little anonymity for outsiders; policing capacity is limited while informal community social control is strong. Different accounts describe local conditions as closely tracking the national picture, with no region-specific evidence documenting trans-targeted enforcement or violence, though the isolation, thinner institutional presence and distance from Nouakchott plausibly reduce restraint on hostile local actors and leave fewer working remedies. Mauritania's national laws apply throughout Tagant: Penal Code Article 264's debauchery provisions can reach gender-nonconforming expression and carry one month to two years' imprisonment plus fines, while Sharia-based provisions retain a possible death penalty for same-sex conduct, held under a de facto moratorium confirmed in 2021. Enforcement is uneven rather than systematic, but arrests and detentions under these provisions have continued in recent years, and reports describe violence and threats against LGBT people alongside official impunity and unreliable official protection. A transgender visitor who is outed or discovered here would therefore face official scrutiny and possible debauchery charges, likely detention, community hostility amplified by close social scrutiny and local religious authority, and negligible recourse — with legal aid, advocacy and consular access all distant in this remote setting.

65221844B99203907341133.name: Black River
65221844B99203907341133.summary: Black River, on Mauritius's western coast, covers the Flic en Flac, Tamarin and Le Morne resort corridor — a tourism, tours and long-stay economy with an expatriate presence where foreign visitors are routine, hospitality venues are accustomed to international guests, and everyday scrutiny is lower than in residential or inland areas. No distinct Black River hostile regime is known: no local trans-specific border or document practice, checkpoint gender check, lodging raid, police sweep or pattern of anti-trans enforcement or violence is documented here, and no Black River-specific enforceable safeguard or remedy is documented either. The resort sector is generally described as welcoming and non-discriminating toward LGBTQ guests, with no reported problems for couples sharing hotel rooms, but that hospitality attitude does not establish trans-specific protection; the district's inland and rural parts are more conservative than the resort strip, so discovery risk and social reaction vary by setting. Mauritius's national framework governs: consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2023 and no trans-specific criminal statute targets visitors, but there is no legal gender recognition — a resident-facing gap rather than a direct visitor restriction, though travellers must carry home-issued documents and mismatched passports, hospital placements or local bureaucracy can still expose them — and the Equal Opportunities Act covers sexual orientation but not gender identity. A visitor outed here would most likely encounter curiosity, discretion, service friction, social stigma or possible harassment rather than state action or organised targeting, but police or medical recourse after harassment is uncertain, formal remedies for gender identity are thin, prompt and reliable visitor remedies are not established, and emergency medical care and ID friction remain the main risks. 65221844B12885462064369.name: St. Brandon
65221844B12885462064369.summary: St. Brandon (Cargados Carajos) is a remote Mauritian archipelago of reefs and islets administered under Mauritian sovereignty with no separate local legal regime. It is described either as having no permanent civilian population or as holding at most a few hundred mostly fishing inhabitants, with fishing stations, a small warden/fishing and coast guard presence, small fly-fishing tourism lodges, and only transient staff plus occasional yacht, sport-fishing and supply-vessel visits arriving by sea under permit; there is no airstrip, no police station or courts, no clinic or hospital, and no hospitality or public facilities beyond those sport-fishing and supply visits, so medical or official matters require a voyage to the main island. The inherited national regime therefore applies unmodified: consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2023; there is no trans-specific criminal offence, state targeting, or documented local ordinance, facility ban or targeted police practice; legal gender recognition is unavailable (a resident-facing gap rather than a visitor restriction, so foreign documents govern); the Equal Opportunities Act 2008 covers sexual orientation but not explicitly gender identity; gender-affirming care is limited and uneven, with documented discrimination in public hospitals; and stigma and harassment coexist with police having protected Pride marchers at times, growing acceptance among younger Mauritians, and religious and political leaders condemning anti-LGBTIQ protests, against a backdrop including a 2018 Pride march annulled after death threats and anti-LGBTIQ campaign rhetoric in 2024. No region-specific incident of anti-trans hostility or documented local protection is known, no pattern of coercive arrest or custody abuse is documented, and no operating visitor safeguard or minor-specific protection exists. Conservative religious attitudes documented nationally may be plausibly stronger in this isolated setting, and while no visitor document checks are documented — whether foreign documents cause friction is uncertain — they may draw scrutiny in an intensely small, visible community where anonymity is nearly impossible. Discovery is close to inevitable aboard a small, closed, transient company where a visitor depends entirely on crew and skippers for shelter, food, medical help and evacuation; being outed or discovered could bring informal curiosity, misgendering, awkward service or harassment, remaining broadly within the national range of consequences but with dedicated on-site protections absent, no complaint mechanism or authority present, and practical recourse available only after evacuation to the main island.

82672581B12520625652479.name: Central Region
82672581B12520625652479.summary: The Central Region, which includes the capital Lilongwe and the districts of Kasungu, Ntchisi, Dedza, Ntcheu, Salima, Nkhotakota and Mchinji, has no separate legal regime: Malawi's Penal Code sections 153–156 criminalise consensual same-sex conduct with penalties of up to fourteen years and corporal punishment, and they were upheld by the Constitutional Court in June 2024, while a 2012 moratorium on prosecutions was annulled in 2016, leaving enforcement active and contested. Those provisions have been applied directly to gender-nonconforming people: a trans woman, Jana Gonani, was convicted under section 153 and served eight years in a men's prison (a trans woman in Mangochi was likewise sentenced under section 153). Custody placement follows birth sex, a 2015 marriage law assigns gender at birth, and forced marriages or unions confer no recognition. Documented patterns of arbitrary police arrest and detention, assault, extortion, mob assault, forced stripping and forced medical examinations, custodial abuse and refusal of medical treatment on gender-expression grounds apply as they do nationally, and reports of arbitrary arrests and assault of transgender people in Lilongwe itself confirm the exposure is present locally. No local protection, ordinance or enforcement exception is known anywhere in the region. Lilongwe's diplomatic missions, NGOs, legal-aid services, hotels and greater urban anonymity may offer some practical buffer and more room than the villages, but these institutions are not trans-protective and no effective visitor-facing remedy is documented; rural and park-area communities are more conservative, less accountable and thinner in recourse, with community denunciation and checkpoint exposure noted along the Mchinji border post. For a trans visitor who is outed or discovered, this means the same criminal exposure, detention, abuse and lack of legal recognition found nationwide, with no region-specific evidence of a safer regime, including for travelling families or minors.

82672581B33227208107325.name: Northern Region
82672581B33227208107325.summary: Northern Region sits entirely under Malawi's national regime: Penal Code sections 153 and 154 criminalise consensual same-sex conduct, with the Constitutional Court upholding them in June 2024 and penalties reaching fourteen years' imprisonment, and section 156 has also been used against gender-nonconforming people. 33880854B30097931647986.name: Caprivi
33880854B30097931647986.summary: Caprivi, now the Zambezi Region, is Namibia's most remote and sparsely populated north-eastern panhandle, entered mainly through Katima Mulilo and the Botswana and Zambia crossings and taking safari traffic toward Chobe, Bwabwata and Victoria Falls; its small towns, lodges and clinics lie far apart and far from the Windhoek courts, legal aid, specialist care and the LGBT advocacy and pride infrastructure where acceptance is most visible. Gender identity is not named in the constitution and no national gender-identity anti-discrimination law exists, gender recognition comes through individualised orders rather than a general process, mental-health regulations still pathologise gender identity, and officials can challenge documents, marriage or gender markers; meanwhile health-professional and patient-charter rules bar discrimination in care, courts function, civil society is active and LGBT public assembly has proceeded without impediment. 87150794B47488127174201.name: Dossa
87150794B47488127174201.summary: Dossa is a small, rural, agriculture-based district in the Dosso area of southern Niger, overwhelmingly Hausa and Zarma and socially conservative, where neighbours know one another and an unfamiliar foreigner draws immediate attention. No region-specific information distinguishes Dossa from Niger's national picture: there is no documented local tolerance, protective exception, tourist-facing immunity or different enforcement practice, and no local trans community, NGO, legal-aid clinic or other protective infrastructure is known. Rural policing is thinner than in Niamey, but small-town visibility, community reporting and the absence of any working remedy raise rather than lower the chance of discovery, while distance from Niamey's limited legal and consular resources only reduces options for help. There is also no documented local evidence about the treatment of transgender visitors, border encounters or enforcement intensity, and that lack of detail is not evidence of safety. Niger's revised penal code, in force since February 2026, applies in full. Article 390 punishes 'indecent, unnatural and LGBTQIA+ acts' and anyone who changes or attempts to change their sex at birth — which places transition-related medical and legal steps inside criminal law — with five to ten years' imprisonment and heavy fines, with no suspended sentences and no mitigating circumstances; further penalties apply to same-sex marriage and to creating or financing LGBTQIA+ organisations, and Article 392 reaches clubs and social venues. Enforcement has taken the form of a coordinated national campaign with dozens of arrests (the reported figures do not establish a trans-specific rate or a local pattern), judges have reportedly been reassigned or sanctioned after lenient rulings, organisations have been driven underground, and prosecutions of women predate the code. There is no broad legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity or sexual orientation; HIV prevention services for men who have sex with men have stopped operating and care services for affected populations have collapsed nationally; and public officials frame the measures as contrary to social and cultural values. A transgender visitor who is outed or discovered therefore faces arrest, detention and prosecution under an actively enforced statute with no meaningful recourse, alongside possible extortion or informal pressure and minimal protection.
