Health policy (Law No. 13/2022) and child-protection rules bar discrimination on gender identity, and 2024 ministerial decrees expressly protect transgender people, including a prohibition on revealing a person's gender identity without authorisation. Entry is governed by the passport issued in the country of origin, with no domestic route to change a gender marker. These protections sit alongside gaps: general anti-discrimination and hate-crime law covers sexual orientation but not gender identity, no case of those protections being enforced for a transgender person is documented anywhere in the country, and verbal abuse and discrimination in public services is reported nationally. Documented violence against transgender people is family- and community-based rather than state-directed, while senior officials publicly endorse Pride. There is no documented history of police hostility or organised targeting in Baucau itself, but equally no local record showing the protections operating there.\n\nWhat differs locally is the setting: Baucau is smaller, more provincial, predominantly Catholic and closer-knit than Dili, with minimal tourist infrastructure, no visible trans community, and few trained service providers, so a visibly transgender visitor is conspicuous and has less anonymity. Pride marches, NGO presence (including CODIVA and Rede Feto) and other diversity visibility are concentrated in the capital, leaving Baucau with thinner specialist support, fewer tourism accommodations, less visible LGBT organisation and less frequent public endorsement of diversity. Consequently, if a transgender visitor is discovered or outed, the combination of national legal gaps and local social conservatism raises the likelihood of gossip, direct community scrutiny, harassment or service refusal, with limited formal recourse — though discovery carries no risk of arrest, state violence or facility exclusion, and severe legal punishment is unlikely. For a travelling family, the child-protection provisions apply, though their local implementation is uncertain.

58719522B43373882655947.name: Dili
58719522B43373882655947.summary: Dili, Timor-Leste's capital, operates under the national framework: no criminalisation of same-sex conduct or transgender identity, no anti-trans statute, no documented police targeting, and no facility, border or care bans, so a visitor's home passport governs throughout and there is no local gender-recognition route. What sets Dili apart is its concentration of visible acceptance: the annual Pride march has been held there since 2017 (marches in 2017, 2018 and 2019, the last drawing about 3,000 people), publicly endorsed by the President and Prime Minister, alongside the main LGBTI organisations (CODIVA and Rede Feto), the diplomatic community, NGOs, tourism services and the country's largest international presence — giving trans visitors more places where staff have encountered gender-diverse travellers than in more socially conservative districts. Countering that, the same city is where studies document family and community abuse of transgender people — corrective violence, including corrective rape reported in a Dili study, along with ostracism and bullying — as well as verbal abuse and discrimination in public services and medical centres, in a society that remains strongly Catholic and socially conservative outside these circles. Anti-discrimination and hate-crime coverage reaches sexual orientation but not gender identity, enforcement of police conduct rules in a trans-specific case is undocumented, reported practice in health services is uneven, and no Dili-specific visitor remedy or protection infrastructure is established. If discovered or outed, a trans visitor would more likely face questioning, misgendering, refusal or delay of accommodation or health care, and private harassment than arrest or deportation: social hostility and discrimination with limited formal recourse, under residual uncertainty about informal police discretion and service friction.

58719522B88874257219633.summary: Viqueque shares Timor-Leste's national framework: same-sex conduct and transgender expression are not criminalised, no trans-specific offence or documented police or facility targeting exists, national health policy bars discrimination on gender identity, and 2024 ministerial decrees expressly name transgender people in protection services and prohibit unauthorised disclosure of gender identity. Viqueque itself is a rural, largely agrarian district in the east, distant from Dili, predominantly Catholic and shaped by customary lisan authority, with small tight-knit Makasae-speaking villages, limited tourism and minimal tourist traffic. It has no LGBTI organisation, Pride presence, or Dili's advocacy, legal-aid and trans-friendly health infrastructure; clinic staff and district police have little relevant training, and services are thinner than in the capital, where Pride endorsements and NGO protections are concentrated. A visibly gender-nonconforming or outed visitor would be conspicuous and exposed to staring, community scrutiny and service friction, with remedy usually limited to referral to Dili. 12702645B14719640472686.name: Ha'apai
12702645B14719640472686.summary: Ha'apai is a remote, dispersed outer-island group whose small, close-knit and largely rural communities sit under strong church influence (Free Wesleyan/Methodist conservatism as described). A visitor's gender presentation is conspicuous, anonymity is limited, anonymous services and private lodging are fewer, and news of a person's identity travels faster than in the capital; policing, courts and services are fewer and further away, and there are no LGBTQ-specific services or advocacy, so compared with Nuku'alofa there are fewer resources, less privacy and slower access to legal or medical support. Tourism spots such as Uoleva and Pangaimotu bring some visitor familiarity, and church and kinship networks may extend courtesy to foreigners while also enforcing conformity — yet no documented local exception, protection, tolerant practice, or pattern of police targeting or anti-trans violence distinguishes Ha'apai from the national picture, and no family-specific restrictions are documented. Reported hostility toward LGBTQ people has risen, and the 2021 murder of LGBTQ activist Polikalepo Kefu (cited in one account as occurring near Mu'a) is pointed to as showing that hostility can become violent, with weak accountability. The national regime applies in full: the Criminal Offences Act retains a same-sex activity penalty of up to ten years' imprisonment — unrepealed, with no recent documented enforcement — and, more directly relevant, a public-solicitation offence covering intent to deceive as to sex, whose wording may reach visible gender presentation, though its application to transgender people and its enforcement in Ha'apai are uncertain. There is no legal gender recognition, so passports and identity documents carry birth-sex markers with no change route available to visitors, and no statute protects against discrimination on gender identity or orientation in services or employment, meaning services can refuse without recourse. For a transgender visitor who is outed or whose birth-sex marker is discovered, the small community scale means rapid local spread of the information, discretionary police handling, possible arrest under the public-deception provision and no practical remedy; reported consequences include questioning, humiliation, refusal of lodging or care, community outing and police involvement under public morality provisions, though not a credible threat of execution. These conditions mainly heighten uncertainty and reduce options for remedy rather than evidencing greater local hostility than the country as a whole.

12702645B16834523743175.name: Niuas
12702645B16834523743175.summary: The Niuas (Niuafoʻou, Niuatoputapu and Tafahi) are Tonga's small, remote northern islands, with tiny close-knit village populations, church-centred and devoutly Wesleyan community life, very little tourism, sparse services and limited police presence, health services and formal institutions; there is no LGBTQ organisation or advocacy presence, and courts, police and healthcare are dispersed, with practical recourse short of a long journey to Tongatapu. They inherit the national framework in full: same-sex conduct remains criminalised with up to ten years' imprisonment (with no documented recent enforcement and no pattern of arrests of trans visitors), a separate public solicitation or 'immoral purpose' offence turns on deception as to true sex and can reach visible gender expression, there is no legal gender recognition (a visitor's foreign documents are not subject to Tonga's resident gender-recognition process and documents carry birth-sex markers), no statutory protection against gender-identity discrimination, and no relationship recognition. Conservative social attitudes and documented religious hostility toward LGBTQ people and fakaleiti prevail, though traditional familiarity with fakaleiti is said to soften street-level reaction somewhat. Niuas-specific document treatment, police practice, facilities rules, violence patterns and protective measures are not documented; little region-specific information exists beyond the national framework and general island community structure, and no local raid or official targeting of visitors is recorded. Because outsiders are highly visible in such small communities, a visitor's documents and presentation are quickly noticed and gossip spreads fast, so discovery or outing is more likely than in better-institutionalised parts of Tonga, and discretion is harder to maintain. If outed, an openly transgender visitor may face intrusive questioning, community pressure, service refusal or awkwardness in everyday and emergency care, and possible police involvement under the morality or presentation provisions; customary and religious leaders shape daily life alongside these limited formal institutions. No local protections, tolerant exceptions or documented enforcement by local officials against visitors operate there, while formal enforcement capacity is thin but the inherited regime's severity caps any benefit from local hospitality; any custody would follow birth sex without protective protocol, and remedies remain thin because police, courts and healthcare are largely untested for gender-identity protection, making discovery more consequential than elsewhere in Tonga.

12702645B50986277851262.name: Tongatapu
12702645B50986277851262.summary: Tongatapu, home to the capital Nukuʻalofa and Tonga's main international airport and cruise port, carries the national regime in full and adds no local laws, protections or ordinances of its own: same-sex activity between men and women remains criminalised on the books with no recent enforcement documented, a public-solicitation offence framed around deception as to true sex can reach visible gender presentation in streets and venues, there is no legal gender recognition so documents carry birth-sex markers with no route to change them, and there is no anti-discrimination protection in lodging, services or employment. As the main island it offers more urban anonymity, a foreigner-facing tourist economy in which hospitality staff deal regularly with foreign visitors, an expatriate presence, and Tonga's largest and most visible fakaleiti community — a tradition that signals cultural familiarity with gender diversity but supplies no legal protection, and which may increase exposure at security, lodging or emergency-care checks. Against that, the island concentrates border screening, police stations, courts, government institutions and hotels alongside socially dominant churches, including Wesleyan and rising fundamentalist influence, within a national climate of fear and discrimination toward LGBTQ people and fakaleitis; complaints about police conduct or service refusal have little prospect of remedy. No documented enforcement against visiting trans people was found, and no Tongatapu-specific visitor protections or targeting practices are documented, so how these operate locally remains uncertain. The 2021 murder of LGBTQ activist Polikalepo Kefu at Muʻa on this island is Tonga's most documented anti-LGBTQ killing and signals real hostility toward gender-nonconforming people, though it is a single dated case that does not establish a pattern of violence against visitors. For a transgender visitor who is outed or discovered — most plausibly in a police stop, clinic, or small guesthouse — the resulting exposure remains arrest, detention, harassment, extortion or assault, with documents that cannot match presentation and no effective recourse.

12702645B14713027314985.name: Vava'u
12702645B14713027314985.summary: Vava'u, the northern Tongan island group centred on Neiafu, operates entirely under Tonga's national framework, with no region-specific legal exception, protection, or documented local pattern of enforcement or targeting against transgender visitors. That inherited regime includes same-sex conduct that remains criminalised and unrepealed though recent enforcement is not documented, and a Criminal Offences Act provision covering a male who solicits in public with intent to deceive as to his true sex — a narrow but directly relevant limit on public gender presentation. There is no legal gender recognition, so no route to identity documents matching a visitor's gender (passports carry birth-sex markers), no statutory protection against gender-identity discrimination in services or employment, and no hate-crime coverage. The wider climate is conservative, church-centred and Christian — dominated locally by Wesleyan and other congregations, with rising fundamentalism, reported fear, discrimination and hostility toward LGBTQ people and fakaleiti, stigmatisation of fakaleiti, and the 2021 killing of an LGBTQ activist. Local conditions cut both ways: Vava'u's tourism, yachting, charter and whale-watching economy means foreign visitors are a constant, expected and generally tolerated presence, operators usually serve them courteously, morality policing against foreigners is rarely invoked, and foreign visitor status reduces scrutiny in casual encounters, while Tonga's visible, socially acknowledged fakaleiti community can soften everyday friction for gender-nonconforming foreigners. Against that, the islands are small and tightly knit, anonymity is essentially absent once word spreads, and discovery or a document mismatch is quickly noticed and passed through family and church networks, with no privacy, no trans-specific support, no shelter, only a small local police force and jail with no placement protocol (serious custody falling to Tongatapu), and thin consular infrastructure. On discovery or being outed, a transgender visitor can expect service refusal, outing, humiliation and possible police questioning under the deception provision rather than likely imprisonment, but with no legal recourse or local mechanism to prevent harassment, detention or denial of service; these uncertainties should not be read as evidence of safety.

12702645B6842520552302.name: 'Eua
12702645B6842520552302.summary: 'Eua is a small, rural island group of close-knit villages with a strong Methodist and broader church-centred tradition, few hotels, limited eco-tourism and a limited police presence; most visitors stay with families or in small guesthouses. Tonga's criminal law retains a sodomy provision carrying up to ten years' imprisonment that has rarely been enforced in recent years, alongside a public-solicitation offence covering a man soliciting in public for an immoral purpose with intent to deceive about his true sex, a provision bearing directly on visible gender presentation. Routine enforcement against visitors is not documented, and there are no enforcement records, prosecutions or protective practices specific to 'Eua either way, no visible LGBTQ or fakaleiti community infrastructure, and no documented trans-specific reception protections; the absence of such reporting is not evidence of safety. Anonymity is minimal compared with Tongatapu and Nuku'alofa, so a visitor's gender presentation or documents are likely to become known locally quickly, and disclosure to one person spreads through the community. Nationally, social attitudes are described as fearful and discriminatory, shaped by conservative religious values and rising religious fundamentalism following the 2021 murder of LGBTQ activist Polikalepo Kefu, and village-level hostility on 'Eua adds to this. For a discovered or outed trans visitor, consequences are chiefly community scrutiny, harassment, service denial, informal pressure and possible police leverage under the presentation offence rather than likely imprisonment, with outcomes depending heavily on the response of local families and community leaders; recourse is effectively nil, though there is no documented pattern of state-directed violence or custody harm against trans visitors.

17295835B48340970483027.name: Central Region
17295835B48340970483027.summary: The Central Region contains Kampala, the capital, along with Wakiso and Mukono districts, Entebbe airport, and the concentration of state institutions, police headquarters, embassies, clinics and LGBTQ support networks; the national Anti-Homosexuality Act 2023, upheld by the Constitutional Court in April 2024, is most actively enforced here, carrying a death penalty for 'aggravated homosexuality' and long prison terms for other offences, though the provision criminalising identification as gay or non-binary was dropped. Enforcement and documented harms cluster in this region: the June 2021 raid on the Happy Family youth shelter with 44 arrests and alleged invasive examinations, the January 2024 mob beating of a transgender woman following a TikTok allegation that left her in a coma, dating-app entrapment and doxxing, tabloid outing, the 2017 cancellation of Pride Uganda after arrest threats, and border screening at Entebbe that can expose mismatched documents; police, media and mobs nonetheless treat gender nonconformity as evidence of prohibited conduct. Kampala's relatively urban, cosmopolitan and international character — its anonymity, foreigner and tourist presence, embassies, NGOs, hotels, clinics, safe houses, shelters, LGBTQ organisations and an organised if hidden community, plus the country's only recorded legal gender-marker change — offers some mitigation unavailable elsewhere, but these spaces have themselves been raided, and authorities do not reliably protect gender-nonconforming or trans visitors; rural districts of the region are typically more conservative and offer little recourse, and no region-specific protection operates for visitors. Conditional on discovery or being outed, a transgender visitor here could face questioning, detention, arrest, extortion, forced outing, eviction, communal violence and prosecution under morality or sexuality provisions, with severe prison exposure and possible death-penalty categories, and no effective police recourse; local support infrastructure mitigates but does not offset national enforcement.

14850775B13681962240800.name: Volyn Oblast
14850775B13681962240800.summary: Volyn Oblast follows Ukraine's national framework: being transgender is not criminalised, courts can order legal gender recognition without surgery, and employment and media discrimination on grounds of gender identity are formally prohibited — though recognition remains gated by psychiatric diagnosis, gender identity is not a hate-crime aggravating ground, family recognition is contested, and equal-treatment rules are applied unevenly. The main traveller-facing exposures are national: holders of male gender markers have been stopped by border guards under martial law, with the consequences of such checks uncertain and any mobilisation exemption for trans status unresolved, and there is a documented past pattern of police tolerance of anti-LGBT violence whose most recent documented incident is over a decade old. No imprisonment or execution on account of trans status is documented. Locally, Volyn is a predominantly rural, socially and religiously conservative north-western border region centred on Lutsk, with small towns where anonymity is limited and a visibly transgender visitor attracts attention. It has less visible LGBT and trans community infrastructure and fewer documented services than Kyiv or Lviv, and specialist health services are sparse outside Lutsk, so diagnosis and care are harder outside major cities. The oblast has international land crossings into Poland and borders Poland and Belarus, making national checkpoint screening particularly relevant here; proximity to Poland also offers an exit route, though it brings checkpoints. No separate local law, protective regime, trans-specific protection, official targeting campaign, or documented local violence against trans visitors is known. If discovered or outed, a visitor is more likely to face document scrutiny by border or police officers, secondary interviews, delays, refusal of care, placement according to marked sex, social friction or service refusal, and police indifference or an unaided response than state-level penalties, with thin local recourse — although functioning national institutions remain in place. No organised campaigns or armed-group targeting are documented, and the limited local information does not by itself establish safety.

14850775B83802928232754.name: Rivne Oblast
14850775B83802928232754.summary: Rivne Oblast is governed by Ukraine's national framework: being transgender is not criminalised, legal gender recognition is available without surgery (though diagnosis involves psychiatric gatekeeping), and gender identity is protected in employment and media law, but hate-crime law does not treat gender identity as an aggravating ground, planned legal reforms have an uncertain status, and police responses to anti-LGBT violence have historically been weak, with documented NGO assistance (Gender Stream) available for document issues at the border. Wartime conditions add traveller-facing friction: border and checkpoint scrutiny of documents carrying male markers, an unresolved question about mobilisation exemptions, and military-medical assessments reported as difficult or humiliating. The border-stop practice for male-marker documents principally reaches Ukrainian document holders, so a foreign passport largely bypasses it, and the region's proximity to the Belarus border adds further checkpoints. Regional variation from the national picture is modest, and there is no local statute targeting gender identity or documented local pattern of organised targeting or severe violence against trans travellers. Locally, Rivne is a small, predominantly rural, Ukrainian-speaking western oblast centred on a mid-sized city, with a strongly church-attached, socially conservative and religiously observant society shaped by Orthodox influence — a more judgmental everyday climate than Kyiv or Odesa. LGBT visibility draws friction there, with western-region nationalist groups historically disrupting Pride and queer events, and the oblast has no record of a Pride, no established protective municipal machinery, minimal LGBT community infrastructure, and few specialised legal or medical services; trans-specific care generally means travelling to Kyiv or Lviv, leaving recourse thin for a visitor. A transgender visitor recognised or outed locally would more likely encounter curiosity, staring, misgendering, bureaucratic confusion and possible confrontation, along with prolonged questioning, suspicion, administrative delays and insensitive handling by police and officials, rather than state persecution — facing no local criminal penalty, but with fewer affirming services and legal-aid networks nearby than in the larger cities.

14850775B79197734087513.name: Zhytomyr Oblast
14850775B79197734087513.summary: Zhytomyr Oblast, a largely rural, predominantly Ukrainian-speaking region of northwestern Ukraine centred on the mid-size city of Zhytomyr, adds no documented local targeting, hostile ordinance or trans-specific campaign: no local punitive statutes, no recorded hostility incidents, and no local protections in either direction are known. 14850775B31033086218351.name: Luhansk Oblast
14850775B31033086218351.summary:
The occupied parts of the oblast run under Russian-appointed authorities applying Russian federal law — the all-audiences "propaganda" law, the 2023 transition ban, and the LGBT-movement "extremist" designation (participation punishable by up to 12 years) — plus wartime arbitrariness. The self-proclaimed LPR shared the DPR's original constitutional ban on same-sex unions and the same persecution pattern documented by ADC Memorial's interviews with displaced residents: targeted hunting of gay people, informal detention for ransom and forced labour, and violence with total impunity.

Freedom House (2022) records that discovery of LGBT identity by the military or occupation administration brings insults, violence, extortion, restriction of freedom and threats to life; the PROJECTOR project documented occupying forces specifically searching for LGBTIQ+ people (81 known victims). UN reporting (2025) finds LGBTQ+ persons at acute risk of sexual violence, particularly in detention. Arbitrary detention in unofficial sites without lawyers or family access is documented across the occupied areas (State Department 2024).

Transgender residents face appearance-document mismatch that blocks checkpoint passage and exit, plus discrimination in work, services and housing. Almost all openly LGBT residents have fled; no public expression of identity or support is possible, and no monitor or remedy operates.

sources.title: ADC Memorial & Center for Civil Liberties — Violation of LGBTI Rights in Crimea and Donbass (2016)
sources.summary: Interview-based report (Dec 2015–Mar 2016) with LGBTI people and experts from Crimea, Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts, many displaced. Documents physical attacks and targeted hunting of gay people, including a foreigner lured through a fake social-network date into an apartment where five men stripped him, beat him in a shower, forced him to lick a toilet and drink vodka, filmed the assault and posted the video online. In the self-proclaimed DPR and LPR, respondents report a gay man shot and buried behind the Yasynuvatskyi checkpoint near Donetsk, and people brought to "the Basement" for intimidation, ransom and forced labour. Transgender people face document-appearance mismatch that prevents them from leaving, and discrimination blocking work, services and housing. The first DPR constitution expressly provided that "perverted unions between people of the same sex are prosecuted by law"; the clause was later removed but persecution continued. Respondents who stayed in Crimea hoping to use Russian legal gender-change procedures found them unusable in practice under the occupation authorities.

sources.title: Hromadske / Krym.Realii — How LGBT People Are Treated in Russia-Occupied Territories
sources.summary: About 10,000 LGBT people lived in Crimea before annexation; the Simeiz drag bar scene ended as a public scene in 2014 when the Russian propaganda law was imposed and homophobic Russian nationalist movements arrived. Occupation head Sergey Aksenov threatened in September 2014 that "self-defense forces and police will react" if gays take to the streets; no public LGBT event has occurred in Crimea since. When activist Nikolay Alexeyev sent hate-crime alerts in 2016, deputy head Dmitry Polonsky told LGBT people to leave for "Gayrope", and the "Crimean self-defense" militia publicly threatened to "pack and post" proponents of same-sex relationships. International human-rights organisations and UN missions are barred from the peninsula. In the occupied east, support for LGBT people cannot be expressed publicly at all.

sources.title: Gwara Media / PROJECTOR — systemic violence against LGBTQ+ people in occupied regions
sources.summary: Documentation project on war crimes against LGBTQ+ people under occupation: Russian military specifically searched for people related to the LGBTIQ+ community; monitors know of 81 people who went through detention/violence, 20 interviewed. A 20-year-old endured a month and a half of detention and torture in occupied Kherson on suspicion of separatism. Cases include insults, violence, extortion, restriction of freedom and threats to life once the military or occupation administration learns a person belongs to the LGBT+ community.

sources.title: Freedom House — Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine, Freedom in the World 2025
sources.summary: Russian authorities disseminate anti-LGBT+ propaganda and regularly threaten LGBT+ people with aggressive rhetoric; violent attacks against LGBT+ people and people perceived as LGBT+ are reported. The November 2023 Russian Supreme Court designation of the "international LGBT public movement" as an extremist organisation applies in the occupied territories, with participation or financing punishable by up to 12 years in prison; LGBT+ organisations' human-rights work has become impossible. Russian law imposed in the occupied areas bans changing sex and gender in public records and via medical procedures (narrow congenital-anomaly exception) and recognises no same-sex unions. Hate crimes by private actors draw only small fines or short administrative detention. Rights groups report almost all LGBT+ individuals have long since fled the occupied areas; those who remain do not openly or visibly express their identity. Free movement is severely restricted; residents without a Russian passport are treated as stateless.

sources.title: UN Ukraine — LGBTQI+ survivors of conflict-related sexual violence in occupied Ukraine (2025)
sources.summary: UN account of conflict-related sexual violence against LGBTQI+ people under Russian occupation, citing the Secretary-General's 2025 annual report finding that LGBTQ+ persons were at acute risk of sexual violence, in particular in detention settings. Survivors describe rape, threats of rape, sexual torture, forced nudity and sexual humiliation committed in occupation and detention contexts, intersecting with discrimination based on actual or perceived sexual orientation or gender identity.

sources.title: US State Department — Ukraine, Russian-Occupied Areas 2024 Human Rights Report
sources.summary: Occupation authorities arbitrarily detain civilians without lawful grounds or procedural guarantees, hold people in unofficial detention sites (warehouses, barns) without access to relatives or lawyers, and commit torture and ill-treatment; the whereabouts of many detainees are unknown. Russian federal law, including the anti-LGBT propaganda and extremism framework, is applied throughout the occupied areas.

The oblast's position on the Slovak, Hungarian and Romanian borders — hosting Ukraine's busiest EU-bound crossings, where passport checks occur at every departure — concentrates that exposure, and documented stops of male-marker holders raise the odds of outing for a visitor whose markers do not match presentation. Locally it is more rural and religiously conservative than Kyiv or Odesa, with Greek-Catholic, Orthodox, Reformed and Hungarian-minority church influence, traditional attitudes in towns and villages, one of the country's smallest queer communities, and essentially no trans-specific services or broader LGBTQ infrastructure outside Uzhhorod; police responsiveness in towns and villages is uneven, and smaller local police and border units make enforcement less predictable outside Kyiv. The few public LGBT events in Uzhhorod have met counter-demonstrations and small attacks, while no region-specific incident record of transgender targeting, effective local protections, or distinct border practice has been identified — a genuine uncertainty rather than evidence of safety. For a visitor who is outed or discovered, the combination points to staring, refusal of service and other service friction, intrusive questioning, social hostility, and weak institutional recourse rather than routine arrest or severe custody; imprisonment for being transgender is not the regime, and emergency care or custody would follow Ukrainian rules and local biases rather than any protective subnational shield. Everyday life for a discreet visitor is mostly quiet, with Carpathian tourism resorts generally drawing less attention than villages, while border towns and checkpoints concentrate scrutiny; distance from the front lines reduces general risk but not the trans-specific concerns, and family- or minor-specific exposure in the oblast is not documented.

14850775B24260608407062.name: Autonomous Republic of Crimea
14850775B24260608407062.summary:
Under Russian occupation since 2014, the peninsula is governed by the full Russian legal regime: the "gay propaganda" law (extended to all audiences in 2022), the July 2023 ban on legal gender recognition and gender-affirming medical care, and the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, with participation or financing punishable by up to 12 years in prison. Crimean courts fine people tens of thousands of roubles for "propaganda" — books, images and social-media posts — with penalties exceeding the average local wage (Krym.Realii, June 2025).

The occupation leadership has openly threatened LGBT people: Aksenov promised in 2014 that "self-defense forces and police will react" to any gay street presence, and the "Crimean self-defense" militia threatened to "pack and post" LGBT people out of the peninsula. No public LGBT event has taken place since 2014. International monitors and UN missions are barred from entering.

ADC Memorial's interview-based report documents a foreigner lured via a fake dating profile into an apartment where five men stripped and beat him, forced him to lick a toilet, filmed the assault and published the video — a documented visitor-facing predation pattern with no police recourse. Freedom House (2025) reports violent attacks on LGBT people and those perceived as LGBT, almost all openly LGBT residents having fled, and those remaining not expressing identity visibly. Russian legal gender-change procedures that existed before 2023 were unusable in practice under the occupation authorities even when nominally available.

sources.title: Krym.Realii (RFE/RL) — prosecution for LGBT "propaganda" in Crimea (June 2025)
sources.summary: Crimean courts increasingly fine people tens of thousands of roubles for "propaganda of non-traditional values" — books, images and social-media posts are declared illegal, with penalties exceeding the average Crimean wage. Enforcement follows the Russian Supreme Court designation of the "international LGBT movement" as extremist; since no such organisation formally exists, any visible LGBT expression can be treated as participation.

sources.title: Freedom House — Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine, Freedom in the World 2025
sources.summary: Russian authorities disseminate anti-LGBT+ propaganda and regularly threaten LGBT+ people with aggressive rhetoric; violent attacks against LGBT+ people and people perceived as LGBT+ are reported. The November 2023 Russian Supreme Court designation of the "international LGBT public movement" as an extremist organisation applies in the occupied territories, with participation or financing punishable by up to 12 years in prison; LGBT+ organisations' human-rights work has become impossible. Russian law imposed in the occupied areas bans changing sex and gender in public records and via medical procedures (narrow congenital-anomaly exception) and recognises no same-sex unions. Hate crimes by private actors draw only small fines or short administrative detention. Rights groups report almost all LGBT+ individuals have long since fled the occupied areas; those who remain do not openly or visibly express their identity. Free movement is severely restricted; residents without a Russian passport are treated as stateless.

sources.title: Hromadske / Krym.Realii — How LGBT People Are Treated in Russia-Occupied Territories
sources.summary: About 10,000 LGBT people lived in Crimea before annexation; the Simeiz drag bar scene ended as a public scene in 2014 when the Russian propaganda law was imposed and homophobic Russian nationalist movements arrived. Occupation head Sergey Aksenov threatened in September 2014 that "self-defense forces and police will react" if gays take to the streets; no public LGBT event has occurred in Crimea since. When activist Nikolay Alexeyev sent hate-crime alerts in 2016, deputy head Dmitry Polonsky told LGBT people to leave for "Gayrope", and the "Crimean self-defense" militia publicly threatened to "pack and post" proponents of same-sex relationships. International human-rights organisations and UN missions are barred from the peninsula. In the occupied east, support for LGBT people cannot be expressed publicly at all.

sources.title: ADC Memorial & Center for Civil Liberties — Violation of LGBTI Rights in Crimea and Donbass (2016)
sources.summary: Interview-based report (Dec 2015–Mar 2016) with LGBTI people and experts from Crimea, Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts, many displaced. Documents physical attacks and targeted hunting of gay people, including a foreigner lured through a fake social-network date into an apartment where five men stripped him, beat him in a shower, forced him to lick a toilet and drink vodka, filmed the assault and posted the video online. In the self-proclaimed DPR and LPR, respondents report a gay man shot and buried behind the Yasynuvatskyi checkpoint near Donetsk, and people brought to "the Basement" for intimidation, ransom and forced labour. Transgender people face document-appearance mismatch that prevents them from leaving, and discrimination blocking work, services and housing. The first DPR constitution expressly provided that "perverted unions between people of the same sex are prosecuted by law"; the clause was later removed but persecution continued. Respondents who stayed in Crimea hoping to use Russian legal gender-change procedures found them unusable in practice under the occupation authorities.

14850775B93300237551625.name: Vinnytsia Oblast
14850775B93300237551625.summary: Vinnytsia Oblast lies in inland central Ukraine with no external border, so the wartime border stops and document checks applied to holders of male gender markers are encountered mainly through domestic travel and transit rather than at a regional frontier; under martial law those travellers also face mobilisation-related scrutiny, military medical commission procedures and uncertainty around military-service rules, alongside document-mismatch questioning at checkpoints. The oblast is a mid-sized central-western provincial centre, far from the front lines, with calmer wartime conditions, a functioning police and court presence, and a somewhat more western-oriented, Ukrainian-speaking social climate than eastern oblasts — yet it is more conservative and less urban than Kyiv, Odesa or Lviv, with no local Pride infrastructure, thinner LGBTI and trans support services, little dedicated trans-specific advocacy, limited urban anonymity, and local service providers who may misgender or deny care. No local ordinances, official hostility, raids or documented pattern of violence or organised targeting against trans visitors are recorded here, though variation in how local officials respond remains uncertain, and social friction is somewhat greater than in the capital, with no known offsetting local protections. Being transgender is not criminalised, and legal gender recognition is available without surgery, although diagnosis remains a gatekept and sometimes corruption-prone barrier and transsexuality is still classified as a psychiatric disorder. Employment and media discrimination bans cover gender identity, but there is no hate-crime provision covering gender identity, anti-discrimination recourse is uneven and the status of planned broader remedies is uncertain, courts and police have a documented history of tolerating anti-LGBT violence and failing to protect LGBTI victims, and family and custody recognition remains contested while no facility or custody exclusions specifically target trans visitors. For a visitor who is discovered or outed, these national conditions combine with the oblast's social conservatism to leave exposure that is chiefly administrative, border-adjacent and social rather than lethal, with weak recourse if attacked and uncertain local remedy quality, and with no local practice documented that is harsher or lighter than the national baseline.

14850775B95678810793770.summary: Cherkasy Oblast has no separate local rules for transgender visitors: it operates under Ukraine's national framework, in which being transgender is not criminalised and legal gender recognition is available without surgery, though a psychiatric diagnosis remains a gatekeeping pressure point, with reported barriers involving stereotypes, corruption and wartime military-commission processes. 27058087B19329078127106.name: Canelones
27058087B19329078127106.summary: Canelones is the department ringing Montevideo, taking in the commuter communities of Las Piedras and La Paz, Ciudad de la Costa, and the Costa de Oro beach resorts such as Atlántida, Marindia, Parque del Plata and Solís, along with Carrasco International Airport, plus wine towns and a rural north. It operates entirely under Uruguay's national framework with no departmental variation: the 2018 Comprehensive Law for Trans People remains in force after a failed 2019 repeal attempt, gender recognition is by self-declaration under Laws 19684 and 18.620 (with only female and male markers available), the Penal Code enhances penalties for identity-motivated crimes, the health system carries a non-discrimination obligation, marriage equality and equal age of consent apply, gender expression is not criminalised, and a trans prisoner may choose men's or women's placement. Courts, police and civil-registration institutions are national, and no local ordinance, police practice, facility exclusion or border-screening rule creating extra restrictions for trans visitors is documented here. conditions differ mainly in social familiarity rather than in law: the metropolitan and coastal belt adjoining Montevideo is largely suburban with steady domestic tourism, while smaller, more conservative towns and the rural interior are less accustomed to visible gender diversity and thinner on trans-specific community and health supports, so a visitor who is outed there may meet more curiosity, staring, misgendering, service hesitation, bureaucratic unfamiliarity, slower or uneven handling of complaints, and less institutional experience than in central Montevideo. Everyday exposure therefore depends chiefly on local attitudes and on access to supportive institutions outside the capital, while discovery itself brings no criminal exposure, no custody or facility restriction, and the same national anti-discrimination and health protections as elsewhere. Documented national shortcomings — uneven enforcement, gaps in implementation, hospital or service friction such as the 2024–2025 Maldonado hospital and BROU discrimination cases (which occurred outside this department and involved residents rather than visitors), recorded mistreatment in bureaucratic or hospital settings, national prison-placement practices, and a national record of substantial violence against trans residents — apply as countrywide conditions, and no Canelones-specific pattern of any of them affecting visitors is established; the absence of region-specific documentation reflects limited evidence rather than confirmed safety.

27058087B438131503863.name: Maldonado

There is no third gender marker for non-binary people. Locally, the department blends the international resort economy of Punta del Este — cosmopolitan, accustomed to foreign visitors including visibly gender-diverse ones, and host of Punta Pride each February, a public-acceptance signal unusual outside the capital — with the more ordinary urban and rural life of Maldonado and San Carlos and smaller inland towns that are more socially conservative. That tourist-facing character means foreign visitors routine attract less everyday scrutiny than in smaller inland settings, though enforcement remains uneven: in 2024 a trans health-service user, Andreina Stuart, denounced mistreatment at San Carlos hospital, with a criminal complaint pending before the courts, only an administrative investigation pledged (to follow the judicial stage), and local officials pressing for health-system updates, indicating discrimination can occur while recourse channels operate. No Maldonado-specific police targeting, organized targeting, facility exclusion, violence pattern, border or facility-access restriction, visitor-specific restriction, or additional document barrier is known. 4885205B10194269353937.name: Andijan Region
4885205B10194269353937.summary: Andijan Region falls wholly under Uzbekistan's national regime: Article 120 of the Criminal Code criminalises consensual sex between men, with up to three years' imprisonment and prosecutions recorded through 2023, and related morality provisions are used against trans women. Police are documented targeting gay men and trans women through arbitrary detention, prosecution, forced examinations amounting to torture, bribery and extortion demands, coercion to inform, blackmail and violence, with impunity for ill-treatment and no effective legal protection. The 2023 constitution omits sexual orientation from its protected characteristics, a proposed 'LGBT propaganda' ban remains in draft, and LGBTI organisations cannot register, leaving no registered protection and no trans-specific local advocacy, shelter or recourse. No local protective exception, no distinct Andijan enforcement pattern, and no regional record of relief or enforcement working for trans people is known, and no region-specific incidents involving transgender visitors have been identified — an absence that does not indicate safety. Regionally, Andijan sits in the Fergana Valley, described as the country's most socially and religiously conservative, densely settled and communally policed area, and is less cosmopolitan and more rural than Tashkent. Close-knit mahalla communities, strong family and honour norms, limited foreign tourism and support infrastructure, fewer tourist-facing venues and little independent oversight mean a visibly gender-nonconforming stranger is immediately conspicuous, with no large anonymous urban space in which to go unnoticed. A heavy security presence — heightened since 2005 and heavy near the Kyrgyz border — combined with little independent oversight and a limited international tourist profile means that discovery or being outed is more likely to reach community actors and police than in Tashkent, where it draws on the same documented detention, extortion and forced-examination practices rather than tolerance or remedy, with communal disapproval reinforcing rather than restraining official hostility. The degree of additional risk beyond the national baseline is uncertain, but local conditions plausibly worsen it rather than soften it.

4885205B77081451230863.name: Fergana Region
4885205B77081451230863.summary: Fergana Region has no separate local legal layer, but its conditions shape how Uzbekistan's national rules play out. The densely populated Fergana Valley is among the country's most socially conservative and religiously observant areas, with strong mahalla, neighbourhood and family oversight, a deep rural taboo around gender and sexuality, and little anonymity outside major hotels and transport hubs. The region is less cosmopolitan than Tashkent, with minimal tourism infrastructure, no visible queer community or safe venues, scarce tourist-facing LGBT spaces, and strong pressure toward family and community disclosure; no local protective infrastructure, advocacy or refuge is known, and LGBTI organisations cannot register, operating unofficially. Tourism-facing towns such as Kokand, Margilan and Rishton show some tolerance toward foreigners, but no tolerant enclave or regional safeguard has been established, and no region-specific case record beyond the national picture has been identified — the absence of such information is not evidence of safety. Policing outside the capital is reported as more arbitrary and corruption-prone, with social stigma and moral scrutiny running hotter than in Tashkent, and rural areas drawing more scrutiny than urban ones. Within that setting, Article 120 of the Criminal Code criminalises consensual sex between men, carrying imprisonment of up to three years, with documented prosecutions through 2023; there is no constitutional protection for sexual orientation or gender identity, proposed 'LGBT propaganda' legislation has been advanced, and official hostility is nationwide. Police documented nationally target gay men and especially trans women with arbitrary detention, threats, bribe extortion, coerced examinations amounting to torture, and impunity, leaving no effective legal recourse. A transgender visitor stopped at a routine document check, or whose documents or presentation attract attention, faces the same criminal-adjacent framing and extortion pathway; discovery or outing escalates through neighbourhood, family or police channels and can bring detention, humiliation, bribery or blackmail demands, prosecution, community hostility and mistreatment in custody, with no credible remedy. Execution for gender expression is not a credible documented outcome.

94954027B88448576527444.name: Charlotte
94954027B88448576527444.summary: Charlotte is a rural, agricultural parish on Saint Vincent's windward coast, including Georgetown and Colonarie and lying outside Kingstown's main urban and tourism centre, though it also serves as the capital and administrative parish with greater police, court, medical, consular and tourist-facing infrastructure. Tight-knit communities mean a visibly gender-nonconforming stranger draws immediate attention with little anonymity, and police and clinic staff in small district offices are likely to be personally known to those around them; no parish-specific legal exception, distinct enforcement practice, tolerance, or tourist-facing exception is documented, so the national regime applies in full. That regime criminalises consensual sex between men under sections 146 and 148, with penalties up to ten and five years, upheld by the High Court in February 2024; these laws do not criminalise trans identity itself, but no law protects against discrimination or harassment on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, same-sex unions are not recognised, and no LGBT organisation, helpline or dedicated support infrastructure operates locally or nationally. No visa or entry rule targets LGBT travellers, and no organised targeting or visitor-specific border restriction is documented in Charlotte. If a transgender visitor is discovered or outed, local conditions add visibility and isolation to the national picture: reported outcomes include harassment, intrusive questioning, denial of services, and police contact under public indecency, fraud or disorder provisions, as occurred in reported transphobic incidents. The record includes a 2018 attack on three cross-dressing men, met with only the Prime Minister's official condemnation, and a 2019 assault on a cross-dressing teenager who was then fraudulently charged with fraud before the charge was withdrawn; Human Rights Watch documents daily bias-motivated harassment under the title 'They Can Harass Us Because of the Laws'. Local institutions function enough to make immediate arbitrary violence less likely than in some Caribbean settings, but the absence of dedicated LGBT support, anti-discrimination rules or reliable protection means exposure after outing remains serious, and outcomes for trans visitors remain uncertain.

94954027B75488374461778.name: Saint David
94954027B75488374461778.summary: Saint David is a rural, windward mainland parish of Saint Vincent's main island, with less anonymity than the capital and less of a tourism enclave than the Grenadines resorts; it is less internationally serviced than Kingstown, with fewer private lodging or expatriate networks. No parish-specific legal regime, protections, enforcement practices, or entry, facility, or care restrictions are known beyond national law, so national conditions are experienced more directly, and rural visibility may increase social exposure — although distinct local targeting is not documented. Under that national regime, consensual sex between men remains criminalised under the buggery and gross-indecency provisions, which the High Court upheld in February 2024, and no law prohibits discrimination or harassment, or provides hate-crime protection, on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity; a 2023 Human Rights Watch study documents bias-motivated harassment against LGBT people enabled by those laws. Documented incidents include attacks on cross-dressing young men in 2018, which drew public condemnation from the Prime Minister though the available information does not show effective remedies for visitors, and an assault in April 2019 on a cross-dressing teenager who was then charged with fraud for allegedly pretending to be a woman, the charge being withdrawn without explanation — illustrating that fraud allegations can be deployed against gender-nonconforming people. Broader reporting describes discrimination and violence, including street assaults. If discovered or outed, a transgender visitor here may face hostile interpretation of conduct, harassment, possible detention if police are engaged, greater community scrutiny, and possible violence, extortion, or forced outing, with no LGBT organisation, helpline, or dedicated support service in the parish or the country, LGBT life remaining stigmatised and largely invisible, and little institutional recourse.

94954027B73683206567439.name: Grenadines

Local conditions differ mainly in emphasis: the islands are tourism- and yachting-dependent, with private-island resorts on Bequia, Mustique, Canouan and Union Island and a large transient expatriate presence, so foreign guests are handled by hospitality staff with a commercial incentive toward discretion and their private lives attract less scrutiny than those of residents. There is no documented entry screening or facility restriction targeting trans travellers, and no documented enforcement against visitors, but equally no documented local protection. Set against that, the communities are extremely small and close-knit, churches are conservative, and on Bequia, Canouan or Union Island there is no anonymity as gossip travels fast — so stigma, outing and harassment are realistic risks, while policing is minimal and medical or emergency services are thin, with serious cases referred to Saint Vincent. Gender nonconformity has drawn official attention elsewhere in the state: an assault on a cross-dressing teenager in 2019, and assaults on cross-dressing men in 2018 and 2019, were followed by a fraud charge against the victim that was withdrawn without explanation, indicating police willingness to frame gender nonconformity as deception. Conditional on discovery, a trans visitor therefore faces state-backed criminal law, social exposure and harassment with little formal recourse rather than a documented pattern of official targeting or any trans-specific border or accommodation rule; a trans traveller who is a minor encounters the same hostile legal and social setting.

42786344B73501178505024.name: Anzoátegui

Locally, the urban coastal corridor around Lechería, Puerto La Cruz and Barcelona is more cosmopolitan, service-oriented and accustomed to outsiders than the interior, and long-standing LGBT civil society centred there gives more visibility and community infrastructure than many interior areas — though this is not a formal shield or evidence that authorities reliably protect trans travellers. Rural and oil-town areas are more conservative. The coastal tourism economy also involves heavy passport-based hotel and SIM registration, which can expose mismatches between documents and presentation. For a trans visitor who is discovered or outed, weak rule of law means any police interaction carries extortion and arbitrary-detention risk, and consequences include humiliation, service denial, extortion or police harassment and questioning, with no reliable remedy; the documented national pattern is harassment and custody rather than lethal targeting, and because anti-trans violence is not treated as an aggravated offence, recourse after an attack is limited. 6923714B34072001548912.name: Southern
6923714B34072001548912.summary: Southern Province operates under Zambia's national regime with no known regional exception: consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised and enforced, gender-nonconforming presentation can be treated as evidence of immorality, and there is no legal gender recognition or broad anti-discrimination protection — only narrower health-care guidelines that may not reach visitors. The same churches, customary authorities and national anti-LGBTQI+ campaign structures function locally, and organised campaigning intensified after the president's 2022 statement against LGBT protections, with public advocacy not tolerated anywhere in the country. Choma, Mazabuka, Monze and the rural districts show pronounced conservative Christian norms, and much of the province is rural; police checkpoints, border crossings and hotel ID checks are routine discovery points. Legal aid and advocacy are concentrated in Lusaka, no local shelter, advocacy body or police accountability mechanism is known to operate here, health-care access is constrained, and reporting after an assault in smaller towns would be uncertain. Livingstone and the Victoria Falls corridor is the one local difference: a hospitality economy with steady foreign visitor numbers may make some service staff and officers more cautious and lower everyday friction, but this provides no protective infrastructure and does not alter police practice or custody exposure. Should a trans visitor be discovered or outed, the national exposures apply — stop-and-search, bribery and extortion demands, arrest under public-order or same-sex-conduct laws, prolonged detention, threatened charges, documented police violence and harassment, forced anal examinations in custody or used as court evidence, and mob violence including a documented attack involving police officers; a relationship read as same-sex can also trigger the law. Public advocacy remains impermissible, and no distinct local enforcement pattern or province-specific documentation is known to soften these consequences, which remain severe across the province with only marginal mitigation in tourist-facing areas.

6923714B71523451831393.name: Western
6923714B71523451831393.summary: Western Province sits under Zambia's national regime: consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised and the prohibition is enforced, with imprisonment documented, and police are a recorded source of harassment, violence, prolonged detention, bribery or extortion framed under other laws, and forced anal examinations used as evidence in related prosecutions. Public advocacy is restricted, no recognised LGBTQI+ organisation or trans-specific community infrastructure exists, and there is official rejection of LGBTQI+ protections alongside organised anti-LGBTQI+ campaigning, a hostile state-media climate and a documented spike in hate speech, with mob and police-involved assaults following political statements. Recourse is narrow, health-care protections are limited to specific professional and HIV-service instruments rather than broad coverage, and no legal exception, protective practice or distinct enforcement pattern in the province — including under customary Lozi authority centred on the Litunga and traditional courts in Barotseland — changes a transgender visitor's exposure if a relationship is read as same-sex or their identity is revealed. The province is predominantly rural, with Mongu as its main urban centre and small towns such as Zambezi plus remote safari areas, and it has thinner police, court and media presence than Lusaka; this may reduce routine paperwork-based or police encounters, and lower tourist visibility plus lodge hospitality may likewise limit routine contact, but it does not limit arrest, extortion, detention or community hostility once identity is revealed. The same thin institutional presence removes NGO, press and consular scrutiny of abuses, leaves little urban anonymity in a closely observant, tightly networked rural society — so a visibly trans or outed visitor may be known quickly and discovery through documents, policing or mob accusation can escalate faster than in the capital — and distances specialist support, discreet services and emergency healthcare. Local communal and chiefly conservatism, the absence of any documented local tolerance or shield, and the lack of a protective urban counterpart to Lusaka mean consequences after discovery remain broadly comparable to the national picture, with weakness of local recourse and distance from services potentially making them harsher, while reduced institutional touchpoints could make them marginally lower.

88200057B87996012089813.name: Harare
88200057B87996012089813.summary: Harare operates under Zimbabwe's national legal framework: same-sex sexual conduct and indecent acts between men are criminalised, legal gender-marker change is unavailable, and there is no general protection against discrimination or violence, alongside a documented history of police and state harassment, including state campaigns since 1995 that have involved infiltration, detention, beating and censorship of LGBTQ people and organisations. These offences are not trans-specific, yet discovery can still be consequential. The capital also concentrates police and intelligence services, protest restrictions and social hostility, so an outed visitor faces arrest, extortion, humiliation, ill-treatment and possible custody abuse; detention would likely place a trans visitor by birth sex, and complaints rarely produce effective recourse, with remedies slow, limited and unevenly enforced. A documented 2014 arrest over the use of a women's toilet, dismissed after a successful damages claim, occurred elsewhere in Zimbabwe rather than in Harare, and illustrates how facility access can become a criminal-nuisance matter. Countering these conditions, Harare concentrates GALZ's legal aid, counselling and resource centres and TREAT's legal aid, counselling and health referrals, alongside diplomatic missions, hotels, NGOs, urban courts and tourist infrastructure that improve access to support and healthcare, as well as the 2018 health ministry handbook requiring non-discriminatory, respectful care. Its large, comparatively diverse and cosmopolitan urban setting and anonymity reduce everyday friction for discreet visitors relative to rural provinces, but they do not shield visitors from police or official hostility, and urban courts and civil-society support do not offset national hostility. Visibility can still bring police stops, extortion and public-order enforcement against gender-nonconforming people, with arrest under indecency, sodomy or public-nuisance norms, detention, service denial and humiliation. No Harare-specific pattern of targeting or effective visitor remedy is established, and local violence and facility-placement practices are not documented — an uncertainty that is not evidence of safety.

88200057B49508968932773.name: Mashonaland East
88200057B49508968932773.summary: Mashonaland East introduces no local laws of its own: there is no province-specific hostile legislation, no local anti-trans ordinance, and no recorded local incident of arrest or violence targeting a transgender visitor — but equally there is no local protective machinery and no documented local tolerance. The province is largely rural and communal, centred on Marondera with towns such as Murehwa, Mutoko, Chikomba, Seke, Chivhu and the Harare-dormitory towns of Ruwa and Goromonzi, sees little foreign tourism, is more socially conservative than the capital, and has wide police discretion and no LGBTI organisation, resource centre or trans-specific support of its own, so a visibly trans visitor is conspicuous. Zimbabwe's national regime therefore governs: same-sex conduct and indecent same-sex contact remain criminal offences, with the 2006 Criminal Code provisions reaching physical contact between men even without a sexual act; gender markers cannot be changed in documents and the Registrar General may refuse name changes based on gender identity; and there are no general anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections. Trans identity or gender expression is not itself a criminal offence, but officials or others may read a trans visitor's circumstances through the hostile legal and social climate, and historical state campaigns against sexual minorities are documented.\n\nIf discovered or outed, a trans visitor here faces police discretion under morality and public-nuisance provisions, detention placed by birth sex, and questioning or harassment where documents mismatch presentation at public buildings, clinics, police stations or accommodation; family, church and community pressure may intensify the situation, and the absence of organised local enforcement does not neutralise inherited criminal law. Consequences are shaped by an unsympathetic, thinly resourced local environment rather than any province-specific targeting campaign, and fewer trained officials make remedies less predictable. A 2014 arrest of a trans woman for using a women's toilet, later overturned with damages awarded, shows both the risk and a possible remedy, though it is dated. Mitigating national measures exist — a 2018 Health Ministry handbook obliging public providers to serve transgender patients, and GALZ legal support and counselling — but both are Harare-centred and reached less readily from rural Mashonaland East, leaving thinner recourse than in the capital, with no region-specific offsets documented.

SYN-ABW.name: Aruba
SYN-ABW.summary:
Aruba is a constituent territory within the Kingdom of the Netherlands and stands under that framework; the island's own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, carries the anti-discrimination provisions in force here. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life, and Articles 2:61 and 2:62 set penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover heterosexual or homosexual orientation only. Gender identity and gender expression are not addressed, and no transgender-specific provision is cited in the sources.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. This is the only youth-specific legal threshold in the record; no findings on education, schools, or minors' access to services or documentation appear in the sources.

Partner recognition is established at two levels. On 8 September 2016 the Aruban Parliament voted 11 to 5, with four abstentions per the Associated Press account of 9 September 2016, to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered partnerships open to both opposite-sex and same-sex couples, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 12 July 2024, when the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba. Since the Dutch Supreme Court ruling of 13 April 2007, Aruba must recognize same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024, immediately before the July 2024 ruling. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship is dealing with a regime whose protections are written in terms of sexual orientation alone.

On 22 April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. Aruba's own representation at that meeting acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatized as disordered.

Harassment has been documented. Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge (2004–2007) that forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognize same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition to LGBT rights. The most recent documented incident of anti-LGBT harassment in this record is from that 2004–2007 period; no later instance is documented.

Several specific gay bars and clubs operate in the capital city of Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as 'LGBT-friendly'. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba. The last is quoted: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.'

sources.summary: Official Aruba tourism board page marketing the island as an established LGBT destination: positions feeling 'safe, secure, and welcome' as the foundation of the offering, and quotes a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. Self-description by the destination's own marketer, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

Aruba's own news site (Sep 9, 2016): parliament passed the civil-law amendment granting civil partnerships to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5 on Sep 8, 2016, making Aruba the first island in the Caribbean; the campaign ran 2.5 years, with openly-gay MP Desiree de Sousa-Croes as sponsor and an Igualdad Aruba petition at nearly 20,000 signatures.

GlobalGayz cultural report (edited Jan 2017): Aruba described as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curacao; notes the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands, and that same-sex adoption is legal; Catholic influence noted as the main brake.

Associated Press (Sep 9, 2016): parliament voted 11-5 with four abstentions to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered same-sex unions, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights; marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognized kingdom-wide, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route; religious and cultural opposition was strong, and neither Sint Maarten nor Curacao allowed unions at the time.

SYN-ABW.displaySummary: Aruba is a constituent territory within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The national record for Netherlands covers the federal layer in detail. The island's own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, carries the anti-discrimination provisions in force here. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life, and Articles 2:61 and 2:62 set penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover heterosexual or homosexual orientation only. Gender identity and gender expression are not addressed, and no transgender-specific provision is cited in the sources. Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. This is the only youth-specific legal threshold in the record, with no findings on education, schools, or minors' access to services or documentation. On 8 September 2016 the Aruban Parliament voted 11 to 5, with four abstentions per the Associated Press account of 9 September 2016, to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered partnerships open to both opposite-sex and same-sex couples, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 12 July 2024, when the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation. Since the Dutch Supreme Court ruling of 13 April 2007, Aruba must recognize same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024, immediately before the July 2024 ruling. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship is dealing with a regime whose protections are written in terms of sexual orientation alone. On 22 April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. Aruba's own representation acknowledged strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth, stigmatized as disordered. Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge (2004–2007) that forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognize same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition. The most recent documented harassment in this record is from that 2004–2007 period, with no later instance documented. Several gay bars and clubs operate in Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as 'LGBT-friendly'. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba, which stated: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.'.

SYN-AIA.name: Anguilla
SYN-AIA.summary:
Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory and the law that governs a visitor is local law; United Kingdom legislation reaches the island only where an Order in Council extends it, so no United Kingdom-level anti-discrimination floor applies of its own force.

Private consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised by order of the Privy Council on 5 January 2001, in a decision that also covered the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands. The order was issued unilaterally after the local legislatures refused to repeal their statutes, and religious leaders protested the decision. Anguilla had never carried the prohibition in exactly the same statutory form as those other territories.

Anguillian law provides no protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The Constitution's anti-discrimination clause reaches race, political opinions, colour, creed, sex and place of origin, so gender identity sits outside the protected categories and a trans visitor has no statutory non-discrimination footing in local law.

The age of consent is 18 for same-sex conduct and 16 for different-sex conduct. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore carries legal exposure that a different-sex couple does not face.

The Marriage Act defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman as husband and wife. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and Anguilla is among the British overseas territories that have not legislated for civil partnerships. A commercial destination-wedding service marketing ceremonies on the island states that same-sex marriage is not recognised under Anguillan law, so a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has access only to a symbolic, non-legal ceremony. Non-legal ceremonies of same-sex couples have taken place there.

Public LGBT life is highly constrained. A subdued and subtle climate of homophobia has pushed local LGBT people toward secrecy. The island has no pride events, gay organisations, venues, bars or clubs and no community infrastructure, which the source attributes to a population of about 15,000. The only recorded public event is a small protest on 17 May 2011 in The Valley marking the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia.

Visiting same-sex couples have described the island as gay-friendly and reported that nobody was discriminatory in any way, though the same source cautions that the position of local people may differ. A 2023 first-person account by a queer family found same-sex conduct legal under the British order but the scene muted rather than openly visible, an outcome that account attributes to decriminalisation imposed from outside rather than to local initiative.
