SYN-MYT.name: Mayotte
SYN-MYT.summary:
Mayotte is a French overseas department in the Indian Ocean and stands under the French national framework, including its places of deprivation of liberty.

Trans detainees in Mayotte's establishments are held according to the gender shown on their identity document under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code, which in practice places trans women in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them; placement follows the document marker rather than anatomy.

France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty, based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on-site inspections in which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse. The opinion extends to Mayotte's local jails as French establishments.

Legal gender change without surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatric certificates or proof of medical intervention was approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly on 24 May 2016, modified on 12 July 2016 to drop self-certification, re-approved on 12 October, ruled constitutional on 17 November, signed 18 November 2016 and effective 1 January 2017; a court appearance is still required to change the gender marker, while a first-name change can be done at the registry office. The National Assembly also voted the simplification of legal gender change. French law bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity: article 225-1 of the Penal Code was amended on 18 November 2016 to replace 'sexual identity' with 'gender identity', and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships or training and sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on that account. Since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison.

Formal entitlement and lived experience diverge. A teacher at the university centre of Mayotte and his Malagasy partner married at Sada town hall in 2023, after what reporting described as a long and complicated path, on a predominantly Muslim island where the written law is not the whole of what a couple faces. SYN-NCL.summary:
New Caledonia is a French collectivity. It stands under the French national framework: France retains responsibility for penal law, civil-status documents, the justice system and the prison service, while the collectivity legislates locally on many domestic matters. The protections a trans visitor would rely on are French national provisions, applying here because French law governs.

France's detention-places watchdog CGLPL reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty, a finding that by its terms covers establishments here. Its referrals since 2010 covered some forty transgender persons, and its on-site inspections at four establishments in France interviewed eight trans women and one trans man; no inspection of a New Caledonian establishment is documented.

Under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code, trans women in French prisons are placed according to their legal gender marker rather than anatomy, which in practice means all-male facilities where they face threats of assault by other detainees; a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 documented this pattern, and the French prison framework applies to this collectivity's establishments as French law.

Same-sex marriage has been available in New Caledonia since France's 2013 marriage-equality law, signed 18 May 2013, under which a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can marry here. CNN reported on 29 May 2013 on France's first same-sex wedding under that law; PinkNews reported on 26 August 2012 that the government would introduce its same-sex marriage and adoption bill into Parliament in October 2012.

The inventory records no New Caledonia-specific law, enforcement action, incident, institution or statistic bearing on trans visitors, and no local ordinance narrowing the national protections. No region-specific signal was identified beyond the extension of the French framework, and the national assessment for France applies.

SYN-PCN.name: Pitcairn Islands
SYN-PCN.summary:
The Pitcairn Islands are a British Overseas Territory. The United Kingdom reserves defence and external affairs, while local ordinance governs the constitutional, criminal and family law that a visitor would deal with on the island.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001, so a trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex faces no criminalisation exposure under local law.

The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 has prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2010. The guarantee is constitutional rather than an offence provision, and it names sexual orientation and not gender identity, so a trans visitor has no express constitutional protection on gender-identity grounds.

The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 made same-sex marriage legal on 14 May 2015 and defines marriage as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity. That definition is the only express reference to gender identity in the territory's legislation recorded in these sources. The ordinance was approved unanimously by the Island Council on 1 April 2015, signed by Governor Jonathan Sinclair on 5 May 2015 and published on 13 May 2015.

The same ordinance recognises civil partnerships performed outside the Pitcairn Islands, so a partnership or marriage entered abroad is recorded as recognised locally.

No incident of violence targeting a trans person is documented for the Pitcairn Islands in these sources, and no dated case of any kind appears in the record.

SYN-PYF.name: French Polynesia
SYN-PYF.summary:
French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France, and French law governs justice and civil status in the territory while territorial institutions in Papeete regulate much of daily life.

Gender-diverse healthcare in the territory is limited by the small number of specialists available locally. Under Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua, the territorial government tabled a social-security bill that would have fully reimbursed hormonal treatment with progesterone and testosterone, matching mainland France; after heated debate in the Territorial Assembly the bill did not obtain sufficient support and lapsed. For a trans visitor staying any length of time, the gap between the law on paper and the care actually reachable in the archipelago is the most concrete material constraint.

The mahu role, a traditional Polynesian recognition of gender diversity in which individuals embody both male and female qualities and hold recognised standing, predates colonisation, and mahu and rae-rae are visible across the islands in daily life. Reporting from OutTraveler in July 2025 described this openness as ingrained in the culture rather than secured by law, noting that a visiting gay couple checked online whether the destination was safe before travelling and found mainstream inclusivity and acceptance operating without pride flags or organised protest. The 118-island territory has no Pride movement to speak of, which visitors read either as reassurance or as evidence that visibility is tolerated rather than defended.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (Jan 2018): in France, detention follows the gender marked on an ID, and Article D248 requires separate men's and women's establishments, so trans women holding male markers are held with men. The article treats this as a legal grey area. France's framework governs French Polynesia as an overseas collectivity subject to French law.

CGLPL opinion (25 May 2021) on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: since France's Law 2016-1547 civil-status gender change no longer requires medical transition/surgery, yet no norms were added on how to house detainees accordingly - serious violations persist across French detention. French-framework treatment applicable in French Polynesia's prisons.

Grokipedia entry on trans rights in Tahiti: gender-diverse care is limited by local expertise, and some trans people (raerae) face family rejection and move to mainland France for specialised services. The mahu is a traditional Polynesian social role in which mahu embody both male and female qualities and hold cultural standing.

OutTraveler (4 Jul 2025): 'French Polynesia doesn't need Pride flags' describes openness as ingrained in the culture, with mahu and rae-rae visible in daily life across the 118 islands. A visiting gay couple reports first checking whether the destination is safe, and describes mainstream LGBTQ+ inclusivity and acceptance without Pride displays.

Concrete care-access reform failed.

Out Adventures presents Tahiti and Bora Bora across the 118 islands as a relaxed, gay-welcoming South Pacific culture. The assessment is travel-oriented and reports no trans-specific finding for French Polynesia.

sources.summary: French national law, drawn from Wikipedia country coverage, with no stated bearing on French Polynesia: sodomy provisions were repealed by the Penal Code of 1791 and the Penal Code of 1810 retained that silence; an indecent-exposure clause (article 330, 2nd alinea) inserted in 1960 by the Mirguet amendment doubled penalties where the act was homosexual and was repealed in 1980, and in March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under it, with the Senate yet to vote. A Vichy law of 6 August 1942 set consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 in 1982; LGBTQ people in Alsace and Lorraine were interned in Nazi camps after 1940. The law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, punishable by up to €45,000 and/or 12 months' imprisonment, criticised by Reporters Without Borders and defended by the Chirac government; Christian Vanneste was convicted under it in January 2006 and that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Sexual orientation became a protected ground in employment and services in 1985, 'sexual identity' was added in July 2012, and on 18 November 2016 'gender identity' replaced it in article 225-1 of the Penal Code, with the Labour Code covering sexual orientation and gender identity in recruitment and training. Assaults motivated by the victim's sexual orientation attract heavier penalties, and in 2017 transphobia became an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison. A report of 16 May 2020 recorded a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against roughly 1,380 in 2018. The conversion-therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and took effect on 1 February 2022; Le Refuge estimated 3-4% of its helpline calls concerned conversion therapy. The Académie Nationale de Médecine described the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem'; a March 2024 report commissioned from The Little Mermaid Observatory called gender-affirming care a 'health scandal' and youth transness a 'social contagion', and a bill banning medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 without National Assembly action since 23 July 2024. Late-2024 guidelines from the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommend puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) date from 1999; same-sex marriage passed the National Assembly 329-229 on 12 February 2013 and was signed on 18 May 2013, with joint adoption rare thereafter and assisted reproduction extended to lesbian couples from September 2021. Schools observe 17 May under the 2019 Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign, enrolment forms use 'parent 1' and 'parent 2', and since March 2019 higher education institutions should use trans students' preferred names. Mayotte reports frequent family rejection and discrimination, and in 2014 only about 20% of overseas residents viewed homosexuality as a sexuality like any other, against 77% in metropolitan France.

SYN-REU.name: Réunion
SYN-REU.summary: Réunion is a department of France and stands under French national law without local variation. No Réunion-specific signal on transgender visitors was identified in the source inventory: the criminal law, identity-document rules, anti-discrimination statute, marriage regime and custodial-placement rules that govern the island are the French national rules, and the national assessment applies here unchanged.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (12 Jan 2018): in France, where prisoners are placed by the sex on their ID under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code, transgender women held in male prisons fall into a legal grey area and are 'punished for a lot more than their alleged crimes' — the piece follows cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid inmate threats. French framework applying to Réunion as a department.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 of the French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL): finds 'the persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities, based on referrals since 2010 covering some forty transgender persons, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site/document inspections, with recommendations to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. National framework covering Réunion.

PinkNews (26 Aug 2012): PM Jean-Marc Ayrault announced the same-sex marriage and adoption bill would go to the National Assembly and Senate in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge; both houses had to approve, and the Catholic Bishops Conference came out against adoption. The marriage statute that subsequently applied to Réunion with the 2013 metropolitan law.

Yagg (25 Jul 2012, French): the harassment bill adopted by the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 to add 'identité sexuelle' as a discrimination ground, making transphobia prosecutable; deputies Sergio Coronado (EELV) and Elisabeth Pochon (PS) intervened in the debate. This is the discrimination-protection basis in force in Réunion.

Yagg (19 May 2016, French): the National Assembly adopted amendment 282 — tabled by about forty Socialist deputies — inserting a Civil Code section to facilitate legal gender change for trans people, though the government's three sub-amendments could limit its scope. The gender-change framework applying to Réunion as state law.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Réunion (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In 2010 France became the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness by decree, though transgender rights organizations stated nothing changed beyond the announcement, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale. Discrimination on the basis of "sexual identity" was banned in 2012, with the term replaced by "gender identity" in 2016 including amendment of article 225-1 of the Penal Code on 18 November 2016 and protection in the Labour Code, and since 2017 transgender people have been allowed to change legal gender without surgery or medical diagnosis. The legal gender-change regime took effect 1 January 2017 after Senate approval 6 November 2015, Assembly approvals 24 May 2016 and 12 July 2016 and 12 October 2016, Constitutional Council ruling of constitutionality 17 November 2016, signature 18 November 2016 and publication the next day, requiring application before a court without psychiatrist certificates or proof of reassignment surgery while first-name change can be done at the registry office. In 2017 transphobia became an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison, and a 16 May 2020 report recorded police identification of around 1,870 victims of transphobic and homophobic attacks in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Gender-affirming surgery within France was legalised in 1979, and a 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location and recommended informed consent and self-determination. The National Academy of Medicine has characterized increased treatment-seeking as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" and "primarily social problem" advising extreme caution without changing actual practice, while a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report led to a Senate-passed May 2024 bill to ban medical transition under 18 opposed by the Macron government and unlikely to pass the Assembly with no update since 23 July 2024, and in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommended puberty blockers from at least Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D supplements. Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces, conversion therapy was banned by a bill passed by the Senate 7 December 2020, concurred by the Assembly 25 January 2022 and published 1 February 2022 with proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and/or 30,000 euro fine, and in March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education announced institutions should use transgender people's preferred names including on student cards and exam forms. Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 with no mention of same-sex relations in private, retained in the Penal Code of 1810 and followed in French colonies adopting the Code, while a discriminatory age of consent of 21 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual introduced 6 August 1942 and lowered to 18 in 1974 was repealed 4 August 1982 to equalise at 15, and a 1960 provision doubling penalty for homosexual indecent exposure under article 330 alinea 2 was repealed in 1980. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) were enacted in 1999 for same-sex and unmarried opposite-sex couples affording most marriage protections, and France became the thirteenth country to legalise same-sex marriage through a bill approved by the Assembly 12 February 2013 by 329-229 and Senate 12 April 2013, ruled constitutional 17 May 2013, signed 18 May 2013 with first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier, with joint adoption legal since May 2013. National legislation prohibiting sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and goods/services was enacted in 1985 and incorporated in the Labour Code, and the law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic comments illegal punishable by up to 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment and amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred/violence or discrimination based on gender, sexual orientation or disability, while physical assault or murder motivated by sexual orientation carries increased penalties. The December 2004 law created the High Authority against Discrimination and for Equality, the Ministry of Education announced anti-discrimination including homophobia as a 2008-2009 priority and launched the January 2019 Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign with reporting services, helpline and LGBTQ guidance plus observance of 17 May, and lesbian, gay and bisexual individuals are allowed to serve openly in the Armed Forces. A ban on men who have sex with men donating blood dating to 20 June 1983 was recalled 12 January 2009, replaced by one-year abstinence effective 10 July 2016, reduced to four months from 2 April 2020, then removed 16 March 2022 applying the same policy regardless of sexual orientation, and in March 2024 the Assembly unanimously passed a bill for compensation to gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980 pending Senate vote.

SYN-SHN.name: Saint Helena
SYN-SHN.summary:
Saint Helena is a British Overseas Territory. United Kingdom legislation reaches it only where extended by order, so the territory's own ordinances and institutions, not United Kingdom law, determine what a visitor encounters. No transgender-specific criminal, documentation, screening, facilities, custody, care or violence provision is documented in territory law.

Consensual same-sex activity has been lawful since 2001, and the age of consent is equalised at 16 across Saint Helena, Ascension Island and Tristan da Cunha. No penalty provision specific to transgender people is documented.

The St Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha Constitution Order 2009 bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and has been in force since 2009. It defines "discriminatory" as affording different treatment to different persons on any ground such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, age, disability, birth or other status. The enumerated grounds do not include gender reassignment, and no extension of the ban to gender reassignment is documented.

The Commission for Equality and Human Rights Ordinance 2015 defines "gender reassignment" as an intended, current or past process, or part of such a process, for reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex, or the state of mind whereby a person psychologically identifies with a gender inconsistent with, or not culturally associated with, their assigned sex at birth. The same ordinance defines sexual orientation as a person's orientation towards persons of the same sex, the opposite sex, or either sex.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission in Saint Helena monitors human rights laws, promotes understanding of the importance of equality, and works towards the elimination of unlawful discrimination. It may conduct inquiries and investigations into persons suspected of having committed an unlawful act, including unlawful discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender reassignment.

Same-sex marriage is legal on Ascension Island under the Marriage (Ascension) Ordinance 2016, approved by the Ascension Island Council on 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0, signed and gazetted on 20 June 2016, and commenced on 1 January 2017. On Tristan da Cunha it has been legal since 4 August 2017 under the Marriages (Tristan da Cunha) Ordinance 2017, which defines marriage as the union of two persons regardless of sex and extends eligibility, formalities, rights and recognition to same-sex couples on equal terms with opposite-sex couples. On Saint Helena it has been legal since 20 December 2017 under the Marriage Ordinance 2017; the first same-sex marriage there took place on 31 December 2018. No marriage provision specific to transgender people is documented.

Adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since 2017. Under the Saint Helena Welfare of Children Ordinance 2010, covering Saint Helena and Tristan da Cunha, and the Ascension Island Child Welfare Ordinance 2011, single and married people may adopt regardless of sexual orientation. No adoption provision specific to transgender people is documented.

SYN-TCA.name: Turks and Caicos Islands
SYN-TCA.summary:
The Turks and Caicos Islands is a British Overseas Territory standing under the United Kingdom framework, and its own ordinances and courts govern immigration status, family recognition and non-discrimination. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal there since 2001, and the constitution prohibits discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation.

In a Court of Appeal ruling, the Director of Immigration was ordered to issue a residence permit to Timothy Haymon as the spouse of Richard Sankar. The court read "spouse" in the Immigration Ordinance to include a spouse lawfully married in another jurisdiction, and held that refusing the permit on sexual-orientation grounds contravened the constitution's equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees. The statutory definition of marriage was left untouched, so the decision creates no local right to marry. A trans visitor whose relationship local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status can rely on a marriage lawfully entered elsewhere to support residence in the territory, in the same way as the spouses of residents.

Document handling for trans people runs through United Kingdom channels. The HM Passport Office knowledge-base profile for the Turks and Caicos Islands, official operational guidance published in 2025, states that transgender citizens are recognised in the territory and that the passport office processes gender-recognised documents for this jurisdiction. A visitor presenting a United Kingdom passport with a changed gender marker can expect it to be treated as valid in the territory. No local statute or instrument giving effect to that recognition is identified in the available sources.

Visibility is low. A resident account published in 2009 described virtually no information about gay life in the territory and no visible social scene, with privacy as the everyday norm; the account attributed this partly to a population in which roughly two-thirds of residents are not originally from the islands, leaving full-citizen Belongers a demographic minority. That account is dated and impressionistic, and does not establish anything about current violence risk.

SYN-VAT.name: Holy See
SYN-VAT.summary:
No criminal provision in Vatican City law reaches consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults in private and non-commercial. The territory's legal code derives from the Italian Zanardelli Code of 1889 and has carried no such offence since 1890, including through the founding of the sovereign state in 1929. Nothing in the criminal law addresses being transgender.

The age of consent is 18 for all persons regardless of gender. A lower age of 14 applies to sexual relations within a marriage recognised as valid by the Catholic Church and by Vatican City law.

Vatican City has no legal mechanism for changing a gender marker on identity documents, and no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity applies in the territory. No rule governs access to single-sex facilities for a trans visitor, and no document-amendment route exists for a resident or a visitor.

Vatican City operates no prison system. It maintains a few cells for pre-trial detention, and a person sentenced to imprisonment by Vatican City serves the term in Italian prisons at Vatican expense. There is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy and no documented case of a trans prisoner held under Vatican City's authority.

The Congregation for Catholic Education's 2019 document 'Male and Female He Created Them' frames 'gender theory' as denying the difference and reciprocity of man and woman and as eliminating the anthropological basis of the family. It is an educational instruction addressed to Catholic institutions rather than a rule binding visitors, but it states the governing institution's position on gender identity.

A 2023 declaration by the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith permitted spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage. A January 2024 press release reiterated that blessings never extend to the unions themselves.

Vatican City has consistently rejected civil recognition of same-sex unions, same-sex marriage, and the granting of adoption rights to same-sex couples. Pope Francis in 2023 expressed support for same-sex civil unions outside the Catholic Church while maintaining that the Sacrament of Marriage is between a man and a woman as instituted by God.

SYN-VGB.name: British Virgin Islands
SYN-VGB.summary:
Same-sex intimacy has not been a criminal offence in the British Virgin Islands since January 2001, when the United Kingdom's Privy Council ordered the repeal of the sodomy laws across the territory and four other remaining British Caribbean territories after the local legislatures declined to act. The change came by order of the United Kingdom's highest court of appeal rather than by enactment of the local House of Assembly; local legislator Orlando Smith said at the time that "there is nothing we can do."

The British Virgin Islands stands under the United Kingdom's constitutional framework, and measures of the United Kingdom's Parliament extend to it only when brought into force by Order in Council. A trans visitor should not assume that United Kingdom discrimination and service-access protections, including the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code, are available in the territory by default; any such protection must be traced to British Virgin Islands legislation or to a specific extension order.

Whether a marriage between two people of the same sex validly contracted elsewhere is recognised under British Virgin Islands law remains contested rather than settled. The case testing whether the United Kingdom marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome is valid locally was still running when, on 29 July 2022, the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal the case-management orders of Justice Adrian Jack, as reported by BVI News. That refusal cleared a procedural obstacle and left the proceedings in place; it is not a ruling on recognition. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be classed locally as same-sex cannot rely on recognition being settled.

No criminalisation of trans people, and no trans-specific protection machinery, appears in the sources for the territory. The visitor-relevant legal questions are the framework relationship with the United Kingdom and the unsettled recognition of marriages contracted elsewhere.

SYN-WLF.name: Wallis and Futuna Islands
SYN-WLF.summary: Wallis and Futuna is a small, remote French overseas collectivity where French civil and criminal law applies: no law criminalises transgender identity or expression, gender-identity discrimination is prohibited, transphobia is an aggravating circumstance for offences, conversion therapy is banned, and same-sex marriage is recognised. A visitor's foreign documents and presentation are not subject to a local entry or facility ban, and no official campaign or criminal enforcement against transgender visitors is known — but region-specific documentation of enforcement or local recourse is thin, and the absence of recorded trans-specific targeting does not by itself establish safety. The French detention framework also applies, and national oversight has found recurring serious rights violations within it, including male-unit placement of some trans women whose legal marker is male, a consequential exposure if detained. France's proposed ban on care for minors remains stalled, though continuity of care on the islands is uncertain. Daily life is shaped by roughly 11,000 residents in tiny, close-knit Catholic Polynesian communities under customary authority, with almost no anonymity: a visibly trans visitor is quickly known across a small island. Traditional gender-variant roles comparable to fakafafine exist but coexist with stigma and concealment, and gender nonconformity is commonly met with curiosity, moral discomfort, staring, gossip, service friction and delayed care rather than arrest. Healthcare is thin — a small hospital at Mata-Utu, with serious cases evacuated to Nouméa or metropolitan France — so discovery in a medical or emergency setting is likely, ward placement follows French practice, and specialist or gender-affirming care may depend on travel abroad. There is no local trans or LGBT support infrastructure and little practical remedy for social hostility beyond appeal to distant French institutions, so isolation and weak local support leave everyday friction largely unmitigated, even though French institutions remain the formal recourse and foreignness can buffer some daily scrutiny.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News (Jan 2018): trans women in France whose legal gender is marked male — largely those without sex-reassignment surgery — are incarcerated in all-male establishments, a documented legal grey area; example of a trans woman transferred to Lille's men's facility in 2014. Relevant as the French prison framework Wallis and Futuna inherits (French law applies unless locally overridden).

CGLPL (French national preventive mechanism) opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: serious violations of fundamental rights persist in French detention, based on referrals about ~40 transgender detainees since 2010 and interviews with associations/experts; extends a 30 June 2010 opinion on trans prisoners. This French detention framework applies in Wallis and Futuna as a French collectivity.

Grokipedia compilation on transgender rights in Wallis and Futuna: French civil-law gender-marker recognition available without surgery or diagnosis since the 2016-17 French reforms; gender-identity discrimination protections since 2012 (employment, housing, services); but ~11,000 population, isolation and dominant Catholic/Polynesian norms leave practical healthcare and acceptance barriers, with fakafafine-type roles coexisting alongside stigma/concealment.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Wallis and Futuna (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Discrimination on the basis of 'sexual identity' has been banned since 2012, with the term replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016 amending article 225-1 of the Penal Code, and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships, sanctions, dismissal or discriminatory measures on account of gender identity. Effective 1 January 2017 after a Constitutional Council ruling on 17 November 2016, signature on 18 November 2016 and publication the next day, transgender people can legally change gender without sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or medical proof, but must go before a court, while first-name change can be done by registry office after the self-certification provision was dropped. Gender identity disorder was removed as a diagnosis by decree in 2010 with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender affirmative surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. Since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison, and police identified around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces, and in March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education sought use of transgender people's preferred names including on student cards and exam forms. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and location-dependent inequitable access to gender-affirming healthcare and recommended informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine characterized the rise as an epidemic-like and primarily social phenomenon urging extreme caution without changing practice. After a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report critical of youth gender-affirming care, a bill to ban medical transition under age 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 but is opposed by the Macron government and stalled since 23 July 2024, while late-2024 guidelines from the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommended puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2. Private same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 retained in the Penal Code of 1810 for colonies, while the 1960 Mirguet amendment doubling the penalty for homosexual indecent exposure under article 330 alinea 2 was repealed in 1980 and the discriminatory age of consent of 21 then 18 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual relations was equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980, still pending Senate vote. Sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public and private goods and services has been banned since 1985 with Labour Code protection, and same-sex marriage signed 18 May 2013 after Constitutional Council approval 17 May 2013 with first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier following PACS partnerships from 1999 and joint adoption since May 2013 is stated as legal in all overseas departments and territories. The law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic comments punishable by up to 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months imprisonment and amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination based on sexual orientation, with increased penalties when assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation, creating the High Authority against Discrimination and for Equality. Police identified around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019 versus around 1,380 in 2018, after President Macron in October 2018 denounced homophobic violence as unworthy of France. Conversion therapy was banned by law published 1 February 2022 after Senate passage 7 December 2020 and Assembly concurrence 25 January 2022 carrying two years imprisonment and/or 30,000 euro fine, and the MSM blood-donation ban from 20 June 1983 recalled in 2009 moved from one-year abstinence effective 10 July 2016 to four months from 2 April 2020 to removal on 16 March 2022 for all regardless of orientation, with lesbian, gay and bisexual individuals allowed to serve openly in the Armed Forces.

72843720B863019116732.summary:
Centro stands under Italy's national framework on legal gender recognition, discrimination and asylum. The findings specific to this region are judicial and documentary: a regional distribution of recorded anti-LGBT violence, an administrative ruling in Rome, and a homicide acquittal in Perugia.

Progetto Gionata's region-by-region study of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence, covering 2012 to 2025, ranks six Italian regions at the top by victim count. Lazio and Toscana, both within Centro, are two of the six, alongside Lombardia and Piemonte in the north-west and Campania and Puglia in the south. The ranking is by raw victim counts, which track population, and the study supplies no per-capita denominator, so it does not establish that any one of these regions carries a higher rate of violence than another.

In Rome, the municipal administration announced on 30 August 2025 that the Consiglio di Stato, the country's highest administrative court, had upheld the city's 2022 removal of Pro Vita & Famiglia posters attacking "gender" ideology in schools. The court found the images discriminatory, one of them showing a boy being handed a red hairbow, and held that public spaces may not be used for messages that generate alarmism, fear or serious disturbance, particularly where minors are concerned. The campaign behind the posters had collected 105,000 online signatures. The outcome confirms that anti-trans public messaging can be restricted in the region's largest city.

In Perugia, the Court of Cassation confirmed on 5 March 2026 the appeal acquittal of a trans woman, Pinheiro Reis Duarte Hudson, known as Patrizia, over the death of Samuele De Paoli on 27 April 2021. The court held that the death resulted from cardiac arrhythmia caused by accidental compression during a scuffle that De Paoli started, making the acquittal on the homicide charge final. The case was a national anti-trans media flashpoint, and the definitive judicial outcome favoured the trans defendant in the region's main university city.

sources.summary: On 24 January 2025 a Bologna first-instance court recognised a transphobic motive in the punitive rape of a trans sex worker, sentenced the perpetrator, awarded damages to the victim and to the trans-movement association that helps sex workers, and for the first time admitted the Movimento Identita Trans (MIT) as civil party. This is the strongest judicial recognition of transphobic aggravation recorded in Italy.

Progetto Gionata's region-by-region study of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence, covering 2012 to 2025, names the Italian regions with the highest victim counts, six regions ranking at the top. Lazio and Toscana, both in Centro, are two of the six highest-victim regions, alongside Lombardia, Piemonte (Nord-Ovest), Campania and Puglia (Sud). The study supplies the per-region distribution of violence.

72843720B99597932318450.name: Nord-Ovest
72843720B99597932318450.summary:
Nord-Ovest stands under the national framework of Italy; the findings below are specific to this region. Milan operates Italy's first gender registry, the registro di genere, which allows transgender people to use their chosen name on civic and municipal documents. LifeGate presents the registry as a milestone for transgender rights in the country and ties it to a 2022 council motion by the country's first elected transgender councillor. Turin runs a parallel practice, Identita Alias, at municipal offices and libraries. Both instruments are city-level, and the inventory documents no region-wide equivalent.

Progetto Gionata's breakdown of anti-LGBT aggressions by region and city for the period 2012–2025 places two of the region's constituent regions among Italy's six highest-victim regions for anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence. The ranking is by raw count of victims; the source supplies no population denominator, so it does not measure per-capita risk and does not show that a larger regional population is more dangerous than a smaller one.

sources.summary: LifeGate: Milan inaugurated Italy's first gender registry ('registro di genere'), letting transgender people use their chosen name on civic and municipal documents — presented as a milestone for transgender rights in the country; the record ties it to a 2022 council motion by the country's first elected transgender councillor, with Turin's parallel 'Identita Alias' practice at municipality and libraries.

Progetto Gionata's breakdown of aggressions by region and city, 2012-2025, shows that the region's two constituent regions rank among the country's six highest-victim regions for anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence.

sources.title: Italy 'to open first prison for transgender inmates' | BBC News
sources.summary: BBC News (12 Jan 2010): Italy announced plans for one of the world's first dedicated transgender prisons at Pozzale, near Florence - converting a nearly empty medium-security women's prison into a specially equipped detention centre for about 30 of Italy's roughly 60 transgender prisoners (mostly convicted of drug or prostitution offences); gay-rights groups welcomed the dedicated space and its psychological support. The report states that until then transgender prisoners had been located in women's prisons 'where they are often segregated for their own safety' - the documented 2010 baseline for placement practice in Italy. Repubblica (2013) later reported the Pozzale project was abandoned.

sources.title: La doppia sofferenza delle trans in carcere | La Repubblica (Inchieste)
sources.summary: La Repubblica investigative report 'La doppia sofferenza delle trans in carcere' (28 Aug 2013): at that date the prison administration counted 69 transsexual prisoners spread across ten Italian facilities, with placement tracking legal sex - female hormones could not be prescribed to prisoners who 'according to their identity card, count as men,' trans women were held in men's sections, and those who had already undergone sex-change surgery were 'destined for the women's sections.' Segregation practice: in some prisons trans prisoners were put in isolation when cells were lacking - described as the most inhumane way to preserve their safety - and protected sections such as the G8 section at Rebibbia (Rome) and the protected section at Poggioreale (Naples) imposed limitations, including on partner visits. Documented ruling: the 2011 Terni case in which the Spoleto surveillance magistrate ordered the local health authority to pay for the prisoner's hormone therapy 'to guarantee psychophysical integrity'; the ruling was appealed and followed by a July 2012 appellate decision. The dedicated Pozzale transgender prison project (2008-2010), which would have drawn trans women from the special wing of Sollicciano (Florence), was shelved.

72843720B59566147937015.summary:
Visitors to Nord-Est stand under the national framework of Italy. Entry rules, identity documents, legal gender recognition, criminal law and the national protection and health-care layers are set by Italy and are recorded in the country's own dossier. The material identified at region level concerns Veneto and, in narrower form, Emilia-Romagna.

The Veneto Regional Council passed motion n.340 at its 178th public session in Venice on 3 July. Deliberation n.92 of 14 October 2014 approved that motion, committing the regional government to a mandatory 'Natural Family Day' observance on the last school day before Christmas and rejecting the aims of gender-awareness content in schools. The official regional government bulletin carries the primary-source text of the deliberation. The most recent documented instance of this instrument in this record is 14 October 2014; no later amendment, repeal or successor measure is documented here.

The Veneto measure operates through the school calendar and regional policy statements. It creates no criminal offence, no penalty and no restriction on entry, documents or movement, and it does not alter the national rules on legal gender recognition or anti-discrimination protection.

72843720B88210905209841.name: Sud
72843720B88210905209841.summary:
Sud is a region of Italy and stands under the Italian national framework. No regional statute, court ruling or administrative measure specific to Sud addressing gender identity or sexual orientation was identified in this inventory, so the assessment rests on documented incidents within the region.

ILGA-Europe's annual country review for Italy, published in February 2025, records a troubling increase in the number and geographic spread of bias-motivated violence against LGBTI people in 2024, with incidents reported almost monthly. One such incident fell within this region: in March 2025 a young man was assaulted by attackers on a scooter in Scampia, a neighbourhood of Naples.

On 13 October 2025 a 63-year-old man was arrested in Torre Annunziata, in the province of Naples, after making stabbing threats against a young LGBTQIA+ activist; Il Gazzettino described it as a grave homophobic episode in the Naples area.

On detention, no dedicated transgender prison facility exists in Italy. A 2010 announcement that Pozzale, near Florence in Tuscany, would become one of the world's first prisons for transgender inmates was never realised; as of 2013 the facility had not been created, and trans detainees remain within the ordinary men's and women's prison circuit, including in this region.

82249235B5553315981608.name: Alberta
82249235B5553315981608.summary:
Alberta's trans-specific lawmaking is a package of three statutes that passed final legislative stage on 4 December 2024. The Education Amendment Act, 2024 introduced parental opt-in for classroom instruction on sexuality and rules governing students' preferred names and pronouns and their participation in school sport. The Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024 bars certain gender-affirming care for minors. The Fairness and Safety in Sport Act bars trans women from women's sport.

Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, passed at the tail of the fall sitting and invokes the Charter's notwithstanding clause to shield the three trans-youth laws from legal challenge for years. Egale Canada, the Skipping Stone Foundation and five families announced constitutional litigation, calling the package discriminatory, and state that their court challenge continues regardless; the laws are in force with constitutional litigation pending.

Premier Danielle Smith's 12 February 2024 announcement of the package stated the bans would not include a ban on women's shelters, women's prisons or women's changing rooms, and Alberta's statutory trans package deliberately excluded jail and prison settings. No provincial placement-by-birth-sex rule for trans prisoners was enacted, and no Alberta-specific trans-prisoner placement, special unit or segregation case is documented in this record.

Provincial correctional policies vary and no Alberta-specific rule is documented. Federal corrections operations inside Alberta accommodate offenders based on gender identity rather than sex assigned at birth: since 2018 the Correctional Service of Canada permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex/gender marker on identity documents, with requests refused only where CSC finds unresolvable overriding health or safety concerns. As of 2025 CSC reported 90 self-identified transgender women in federal institutions, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's. The Office of the Correctional Investigator called CSC's 2022 gender-diversity policy an important change but flagged the lack of clear parameters for what counts as an overriding health or safety concern and the absence of a dedicated mechanism for gender-diverse prisoners to report abuse.

Alberta's Human Rights Commission handles discrimination complaints in areas of provincial responsibility, and gender identity and gender expression are prohibited grounds in employment, housing and public and private accommodations across Canadian jurisdictions as of 2017. Section 15 of the Charter applies to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities, and Supreme Court jurisprudence has interpreted sex and physical disability in section 15 to include transsexuality. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in Alberta under provincial vital statistics rules governing identity documents such as birth certificates.

Since 2022 the Criminal Code statutorily bans conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults, making it a crime to subject anyone to it as defined by statutory law. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 20 July 2005 under the federal Civil Marriage Act; Alberta's 2000 Marriage Act defining marriage as between a man and a woman and invoking the notwithstanding clause was invalid because capacity to marry is exclusive federal jurisdiction and its five-year exemption expired in 2005.

In a poll commissioned for the Privy Council Office reported for 2020, 87.6% of those surveyed said they would be comfortable if a neighbour was a transgender person. This figure is a general-population attitude finding from 2020, not a measure of current risk or of violence.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Alberta (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal, provincial and territorial human rights acts prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations, with all jurisdictions explicitly including gender identity as a prohibited ground as of 2017. Supreme Court jurisprudence has interpreted the concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15 of the Charter to include transsexuality and HIV/STDs, and section 15 applies to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities, while private-sector complaints proceed under applicable federal or provincial human rights statutes. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules, with vital statistics including identity documents such as birth certificates falling under provincial jurisdiction. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause, which requires schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity and has prompted calls for repeal and legal action. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, the Education Amendment Act, 2024 and the Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges in Alberta courts, and in 2025 Alberta passed Bill 9: Protecting Alberta’s Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause to block those Charter challenges. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer Communities, acknowledged contribution to institutional bias, intolerance and violation of human rights and personal suffering, shame, trauma and distrust, stated “We must stand together against homophobia, transphobia, and any other kind of marginalization, shaming, disrespect or hate,” and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Since 2022 the Criminal Code statutorily bans conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults and makes it a crime to subject anyone to it as defined by statutory law. British Columbia, Ontario and Saskatchewan grant parental status to three or more intentional parents, allowing for a wider range of queer and trans families in addition to or in place of the birth parent. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized June 27, 1969 by the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968–69 (Bill C-150), and the remaining anal-intercourse offence in section 159 was repealed June 21, 2019 by Bill C-75 after courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta each declared it unconstitutional under Charter equality provisions, leaving a general age of consent of 16 since June 2019 and 18 where there is trust, authority, dependency or exploitation. In Egan v Canada (1995) the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under section 15 as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta (1998) held failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law itself violated section 15, with all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly including sexual orientation as a prohibited ground of discrimination in employment, housing and public and private accommodations as of 2017. Same-sex marriage became legal nationwide July 20, 2005 by the federal Civil Marriage Act, making Canada the fourth country worldwide and first in the Americas to do so with no residency requirement, following court rulings in several provinces and one territory between 2002-2005, while Alberta’s 2000 Marriage Act defining marriage as between a man and a woman and invoking the notwithstanding clause was invalid because capacity to marry is exclusive federal jurisdiction and its five-year exemption expired in 2005. Same-sex adoption was legalized province by province from British Columbia in 1996 to Nunavut in 2011 as the last jurisdiction, with Alberta legalizing stepchild adoption in 1999 and joint adoption in 2007. In 2022 Canada became the third country worldwide and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults, making it a crime under the Criminal Code to subject anyone to it as statutorily defined. On November 28, 2017 the Prime Minister issued a formal parliamentary apology for oppression of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and two-spirit communities, and on June 21, 2018 the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act received royal assent allowing RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records for pre-1969 homosexual acts or section 159 convictions, requiring notification to involved provincial or municipal police and courts, available to living and deceased persons and distinct from pardon or record suspension as recognition the act should never have been a crime. In December 2020 Canada’s police chiefs apologized for decades of oppression and opposition from the 1960s to the present, acknowledging institutional bias, intolerance and human rights violations. In a poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office reported for 2020, 91.8% of those surveyed said they would be “comfortable” if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual, a sexuality-tolerance finding distinct from transgender tolerance. In that same 2020 Privy Council Office poll, 87.6% said they would be “comfortable” if a neighbour was a transgender person, the article’s documented transgender-specific tolerance statement. 2020 Pew Research showed 85% of Canada’s general population (92% among Canadians aged 18-29) favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013, and June 2013 polls showed majority support for same-sex marriage available since 2005, with 70% agreeing same-sex couples should have same adoption rights and 76% agreeing they are just as likely to successfully raise children, all sexuality-specific findings. The article notes Canada was ranked first indicating least dangerous in Asher & Lyric’s LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024, general LGBTQ rankings not disaggregated for transgender people.

82249235B71336988791422.name: Saskatchewan
82249235B71336988791422.summary:
Saskatchewan's human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds of discrimination in employment, housing, and public and private accommodations, giving a visitor or resident a provincial complaints route.

Change of legal gender is a provincial function and is available in Saskatchewan under the province's own rules.

On 22 August 2023 the Saskatchewan education ministry announced parental inclusion and consent policies. Schools must seek parent or guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronouns of students under 16, parents must be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs were paused. That release initiated the court challenge.

The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 was passed with the province invoking the notwithstanding clause, a five-year override of the Charter. It requires schools to obtain parental consent for students under 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity. Human rights groups called for repeal, and the invocation of the clause may prevent legal action from succeeding on Charter grounds.

On 11 August 2025 the Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan (2025 SKCA 74) set aside the 2023 chambers decision, so the pronoun-notice policy stands. The appeal court held that Charter breaches under sections 1 and 15 cannot be tested where section 33 has been invoked. Reporting on the same judgment states that the appeal was granted in part, that a judge has jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights, and that UR Pride's litigation may continue in the Court of King's Bench.

Amnesty International Canada participated as an intervenor in the appeal and welcomed the 11 August 2025 decision as a meaningful victory for the protection of human rights in Canada. Amnesty argued that courts can still determine whether the province's anti-trans pronoun law violates the Charter and issue a declaration to that effect even where the notwithstanding clause shields the law from being struck down, and that use of the clause must align with Canada's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy.

Egale Canada co-counsel Bennett Jensen said UR Pride will continue the litigation, noting that students had been living under the reality of the law for two years.

On 6 November 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it will hear the appeals in the challenge to the school pronoun law. Both the province and UR Pride appealed the Court of Appeal decision and asked for the hearing to be expedited alongside the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21. No merits ruling has changed the policy, and the constitutionality of the shielded consent rule is now before Canada's highest court.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Saskatchewan (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The concepts of sex in section 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms have been interpreted to include transsexuality. As of 2017, all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly include gender identity as a prohibited ground of discrimination in their human rights acts, prohibiting discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations. Transgender people are now able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. In 2023, Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 while invoking the notwithstanding clause, requiring schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, and calls by human rights groups to repeal the law led to legal action that the clause may prevent from succeeding on Charter grounds. Saskatchewan is one of three provinces, with British Columbia and Ontario, that will grant parental status to three or more intentional parents, allowing for a wider range of queer and trans families. In December 2020, the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer communities, stated police must stand together against homophobia, transphobia and other marginalization, and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to address implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Bill C-150) was brought into force on royal assent. In 1995 in Egan v Canada the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under the equality clause of the Charter as an analogous ground under section 15, and in 1998 in Vriend v Alberta it found failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law violated section 15. Since June 2019 the general age of consent for all sexual activities is 16, and 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency or exploitation, with close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15, after former Criminal Code section 159 on anal intercourse was held unconstitutional by courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta and repealed by Bill C-75 receiving royal assent June 21, 2019. In 2005 Canada became the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to legalize same-sex marriage nationwide through the federal Civil Marriage Act on July 20, 2005, following 2002-2005 court decisions striking the opposite-sex-only common law definition. In 2022 Canada became the third country in the world and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for minors and adults and make subjecting anyone to it a crime under the Criminal Code. On November 28, 2017 the Prime Minister issued a formal apology for historical oppression related to criminalization, and on June 21, 2018 the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act received royal assent to require destruction or removal by the RCMP and federal departments of judicial records for pre-1969 homosexual acts and section 159 convictions, available to living and deceased persons and distinct from a pardon or record suspension. As of 2017 all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly include sexual orientation as a prohibited ground of discrimination, and same-sex adoption has been legalized in all provinces and territories, including Saskatchewan in 2001. 2020 Pew Research showed that 85% of Canada's general population, including 92% among Canadians aged 18 to 29, favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013. June 2013 polls showed a vast majority blessing same-sex marriage available since 2005, with 70% agreeing same-sex couples should have the same rights to adopt children as heterosexual couples and 76% agreeing same-sex couples are just as likely to successfully raise children. Canada was ranked first indicating least dangerous in Asher and Lyric's LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024. For sexuality-specific neighbour tolerance, a 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office found 91.8% said they would be comfortable if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual. For transgender-specific tolerance, the same poll documented that 87.6% said they would be comfortable if a neighbour was a transgender person.

82249235B4167839012994.name: New Brunswick
82249235B4167839012994.summary:
New Brunswick sets its own schools policy on sexual orientation and gender identity inside the Canadian legal framework. Policy 713, issued by the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development, has been in force since 17 August 2020 and was revised on 1 July 2023, 23 August 2023 and 1 January 2025.

In the version effective 1 January 2025, students of any age may choose the names and pronouns used for them in informal school settings; parental consent is encouraged but not required. Formal records for students under 16 still require parental consent. The revision went further than the recommendations of child advocate Kelly Lamrock.

The policy's application clause covers the school environment and names all students together with school personnel, contract and casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers and visitors, so its rules reach adults present in New Brunswick classrooms who do not live in the province.

From 1 July 2023 until the January 2025 revision, the policy barred teachers from using the chosen name and pronouns of a student under 16 without parental consent, reversing a three-year-old rule that required teachers to obtain the student's informed consent before discussing names and pronouns with parents. Correctional Service Canada's 2022 gender-diversity policy allows gender-diverse offenders to request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex marker on identification documents; each request is assessed individually and may be refused where an unresolved 'overriding health or safety concern' exists. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in New Brunswick (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is prohibited by all provinces and territories as well as the federal government, explicitly listed as a prohibited ground in human rights acts as of 2017. The concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms have been interpreted to include transsexuality, with section 15 applying to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities but requiring private complaints to be brought under federal or provincial human rights statutes. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause to require schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, prompting legal action by human rights groups. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024, and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges in Alberta courts but were shielded by Bill 9: Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for institutional bias, intolerance and violation of human rights against Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans, Transgender, and Queer communities, stating police must stand against transphobia and creating the Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Bill C-150) was brought into force upon royal assent. In Egan v Canada in 1995 the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under the equality clause in section 15 of the Charter as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta in 1998 found failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law violated section 15. Since June 2019 the general age of consent for all sexual activities has been 16, rising to 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency or exploitation, with limited close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15. Former Criminal Code section 159 criminalizing anal intercourse was held unconstitutional by courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta and was repealed on June 21, 2019 through Bill C-75. Same-sex marriage became legal nationwide on July 20, 2005 through the federal Civil Marriage Act, making Canada the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to legalize it. The Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act granted royal assent June 21, 2018 allows the RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records for pre-1969 homosexual acts or section 159 convictions, available to living and deceased persons and distinct from pardon or record suspension. In 2022 Canada became the third country in the world and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for minors and adults and make it a crime to subject anyone to it as defined in the Criminal Code. 2020 Pew Research showed that 85% of Canada's general population, including 92% among Canadians aged 18 to 29, favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013. June 2013 polls showed a vast majority blessed same-sex marriage available since 2005, with 70% agreeing same-sex couples should have the same rights to adopt and 76% agreeing same-sex couples are just as likely to successfully raise children. A poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office reported for 2020 found 91.8% would be "comfortable" if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual. That same Privy Council Office poll found that 87.6% said they would be "comfortable" if a neighbour was a transgender person.

14339913B23556801435424.summary:
Scotland is a constituent nation of the United Kingdom. Criminal law, policing, prisons and family law are devolved to the Scottish Parliament, while legal gender recognition and equality law are set at United Kingdom level; the findings below are those specific to Scotland.

Trans people in Scotland change their legal gender under the United Kingdom Gender Recognition Act 2004. A Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill was introduced to the Scottish Parliament in March 2022 and passed in December 2022 by 86 votes to 39, applying only to Scotland. The United Kingdom government blocked the Bill under section 35 of the Scotland Act 1998 while it awaited royal assent, the first time that power has been used to overturn Scottish legislation, so the reformed procedure the Scottish Parliament legislated for is not in force in Scotland.

Hate crime in Scotland is governed by the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021, passed by the Scottish Parliament in March 2021 by 82 votes to 32, given royal assent a month later and brought into force on 1 April 2024. It lists gender identity as a protected characteristic. Earlier Scottish legislation enacted in 2009 provides penalty enhancements where an offence is motivated by the victim's gender identity.

The Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service publication 'Hate crime in Scotland, 2025-26', issued 30 June 2026, records 7,115 hate-crime charges in total, up 17% on 2024-25 and the highest since 2003-04. Transgender-identity aggravation accounted for 104 charges, up 21% from 86 the previous year and the highest level since the 2021 Act took effect. Sexual-orientation aggravation accounted for 2,062 charges, the second commonest category.

Police Scotland recorded 8,538 hate crimes in 2024-25, according to the Scottish Government report published 17 February 2026, the first annual report under the 2021 Act. The highest rates per 10,000 residents were in Glasgow City and City of Edinburgh at about 32.25 each. Sixty-two per cent of recorded hate crimes carried a race aggravator and just over a quarter a sexual-orientation aggravator; the report gives no per-resident rate for the transgender-identity category.

Police Scotland published interim guidance on 25 June 2025 providing that searches involving the removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex, in both custody and stop-and-search contexts. Where a person's lived gender differs from their sex at birth, efforts will be made to provide an officer of that lived gender on request.

On 19 June 2026 in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Judge Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory guidance on trans custody as unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis. The guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in establishments matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The case was heard in February 2026, when the court was told that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as flexible; the claimant was challenging a policy of holding only biological females in the women's estate.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in Scotland since 16 December 2014 under legislation passed by the Scottish Parliament on 4 February 2014 by 108 votes to 15 and given royal assent on 12 March 2014, with the first ceremonies on 31 December 2014. No religious organisation or celebrant is obliged to perform such marriages.

A Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill to reform the 2004 Act was introduced in March 2022 and passed in December 2022 by 86-39, applying only to Scotland. The Bill was blocked by the UK government under section 35 of the Scotland Act 1998, the first use of that power to overturn Scottish legislation, while awaiting royal assent. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 16 December 2014 under the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Scotland) Act 2014, passed 4 February 2014 by 108-15 with royal assent 12 March 2014, with first ceremonies 31 December 2014 and no obligation on religious organisations or celebrants to perform them. Same-sex couples obtained joint and stepchild adoption rights from 28 September 2009, with the Looked After Children (Scotland) Regulations 2009 allowing consideration as foster parents on the same basis as others. The Equality Act 2010 outlaws discrimination, harassment and victimisation based on sexual orientation, and 2009 legislation provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by sexual orientation, with sexual orientation explicitly included in the 2021 hate-crime law effective 1 April 2024.

14339913B23556801435424.displaySummary: Scotland is a devolved nation of the United Kingdom. The national record for United Kingdom covers the federal layer in detail. A Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill was introduced in March 2022 and passed in December 2022 by 86 votes to 39, applying only to Scotland. It was blocked under section 35 of the Scotland Act 1998 while awaiting royal assent, the first time that power has been used to overturn Scottish legislation, so the reformed procedure is not in force in Scotland. Hate crime is governed by the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021, passed in March 2021 by 82 votes to 32, given royal assent a month later and in force on 1 April 2024, listing gender identity as a protected characteristic. Legislation enacted in 2009 provides penalty enhancements where an offence is motivated by the victim's gender identity. The Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service publication 'Hate crime in Scotland, 2025-26', issued 30 June 2026, records 7,115 hate-crime charges in total, up 17% on 2024-25 and the highest since 2003-04. Transgender-identity aggravation accounted for 104 charges, up 21% from 86 the previous year and the highest since the 2021 Act took effect. Sexual-orientation aggravation accounted for 2,062 charges, the second commonest category. Police Scotland recorded 8,538 hate crimes in 2024-25, per the Scottish Government report of 17 February 2026, the first annual report under the 2021 Act. The highest rates per 10,000 residents were in Glasgow City and City of Edinburgh at about 32.25 each. Sixty-two per cent carried a race aggravator and just over a quarter a sexual-orientation aggravator; the report gives no per-resident rate for the transgender-identity category. Police Scotland interim guidance of 25 June 2025 requires searches involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear to be on biological sex, in custody and stop-and-search. Where lived gender differs from sex at birth, efforts will be made to provide an officer of that lived gender on request. On 19 June 2026 in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Judge Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory trans custody guidance as unlawful, holding sex segregation must rest on a lawful basis. It had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in establishments matching gender identity rather than sex at birth. Heard in February 2026, the court was told housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as flexible; the claimant challenged a policy of holding only biological females in the women's estate. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Scotland since 16 December 2014 under legislation passed by the Scottish Parliament on 4 February 2014 by 108 votes to 15 and given royal assent on 12 March 2014, with first ceremonies on 31 December 2014. No religious organisation or celebrant is obliged to perform such marriages.
