sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mato Grosso (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: On 1 March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that a transgender person has the right to change official name and sex by self-declaration of psychosocial identity without surgery or professional evaluation. In 2019 discrimination based on gender identity was banned through a Supreme Federal Court decision. On 4 February 2025 Cuiabá Councilman Beal Ranalli introduced a bill to establish biological sex as the sole criterion for athlete participation in city competitions, stating that trans women should compete in men's sports. On 19 August 2025 the Cuiabá City Council passed a law banning trans athletes from competing in women's sports, signed by Mayor Abilio Brunini and published in the Official Gazette on 15 September 2025. The Mato Grosso LGBTQIA+ Pride Parade Association and the state Public Defender's Office filed a lawsuit seeking to overturn the law and obtain 600,000 reais in damages for moral harm, which was dismissed by the Court for Collective Actions on 30 October 2025, with the Association stating it would appeal to the Court of Justice of Mato Grosso. On 1 November 2025 a trans woman was expelled from a pizzeria in Feliz Natal after using the women's restroom, the owner was taken to the police station for gender identity discrimination and released on 2 November following a custody hearing, with the case under investigation by the Civil Police as of 16 September 2026. On 30 July 2025 Professor Maria Inês da Silva left the Municipal Conference of the Unified Health System in Cuiabá after being interrupted by Mayor Abilio Brunini for using gender-neutral language, an action condemned by health organizations, women's rights groups, and Black rights organizations. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Brazil since 1830 and homosexuality is legal in Mato Grosso. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Mato Grosso since 2013 via a National Council of Justice decision in compliance with a 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision. Same-sex adoption has been officially permitted in the state since 2015 through a Supreme Federal Court decision. The 1989 Constitution of Mato Grosso Article 10, item III prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and requires implementation of measures to ensure no one will be harmed or privileged on account of birth, race, color, sex, marital status, nature of work, age, religion, sexual orientation, political or philosophical beliefs, physical or mental disability, and any other particularity or condition. On 4 February 2025 Councilman Beal Ranalli introduced a bill to ban participation of minors in Cuiabá's Pride events.

25490228B14384488423733.name: Comunitat Valenciana
25490228B14384488423733.summary:
The Comunitat Valenciana has its own two-statute framework for trans and LGTBI people: Ley 8/2017 of 7 April, the integral law on the right to gender identity and expression, and Ley 23/2018 of 29 November on LGTBI equality. Both sit under the Spanish national framework on legal gender recognition carried by the national record; what follows is the regional layer.

Article 1 of Ley 8/2017 sets the law's purpose as guaranteeing an adequate normative framework for gender self-determination for people whose felt gender identity differs from that assigned at birth, and public bodies of the Comunitat Valenciana must treat people according to their felt gender identity. The duty reaches the regional administration, health and education services a visitor may deal with.

Ley 23/2018 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, provides access and admission rights (article 56), reverses the burden of proof (article 57), and establishes a Title V regime of administrative infringements and sanctions for discrimination against LGTBI people (articles 58 to 66). A complaint about being refused service or admission in the region can shift the evidential burden onto the respondent, and the regional administration can fine discriminators.

Regional courts have handled gender-identity-motivated offences. The Audiencia Provincial de Valencia, Section 5, convicted over a June 2022 incident in a Valencia park in Patraix, where an 18-year-old and several minors insulted, chased, filmed and mocked a trans woman solely because of her gender identity. The adult accepted six months' imprisonment, suspended for two years on condition of committing no offence, plus a 720-euro fine and 1,000 euros in moral damages to the victim; two minors had already been sentenced to supervision measures. The specialised hate-crime prosecutor (fiscal coordinadora de delitos de odio) handled the case.

19177384B97722443848736.name: Buenos Aires
19177384B97722443848736.summary:
Buenos Aires province stands under Argentina's national framework for gender recognition and implements that regime through its own civil registry. The provincial ombudsman published a guide in September 2024 setting out the steps for rectifying the gender marker of people born in the province, including provisions for people born in Buenos Aires province who now live elsewhere.

The provincial ombudsman's Gender Violence Office, created by Resolución Nº 100/10, submitted evidence to the UN Human Rights Committee for its June and July 2016 review documenting violence, persecution and harassment of trans and travesti people in Buenos Aires province by provincial police and by third parties acting under police cover. The submission carries a dedicated section on violence by judicial, state and police agents.

Academic and legal research records the criminalisation of trans and travesti women in the province through drug-offence prosecutions brought under microtrafficking enforcement, concentrated in La Plata's Zona Roja. After the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence, security-led street-offence policing became the operative instrument of indirect criminalisation in the province.

That instrument rests on a jurisdictional transfer: in 2005 Buenos Aires province assumed jurisdiction over drug sale and possession offences, the devolution that allowed provincial street-offence and drug-law prosecution to function as the enforcement route.

No trans-specific placement rule for prisoners is recorded for the province. Buenos Aires province operates no separate trans housing unit and no province-level rule on where trans women are held; placement is governed by the national prison-housing framework.

17162690B44985096553766.name: Subcarpathian Voivodeship
17162690B44985096553766.summary:
Subcarpathian Voivodeship stands under the national framework of Poland, which carries the country's entry rules, custody conditions, document and marker rules, and hate-crime measures; the findings below are those specific to the voivodeship.

On 20 September 2021 the Podkarpackie voivodeship council repealed its 'LGBT-free' resolution and replaced the ordinance with a generic anti-discrimination statement. The county-level layer ended later: on 27 April 2025 the county of Łańcut, in the voivodeship's southeast, repealed its anti-LGBT resolution at an extraordinary councillors' session, the last local authority in Poland to do so.

No region-specific enforcement action, prosecution, healthcare restriction, facility rule or trans-specific incident in Subcarpathian Voivodeship is documented in the available sources. For those matters the national assessment applies.

17162690B69262761487853.name: Lublin Voivodeship
17162690B69262761487853.summary:
Lublin Voivodeship, in south-eastern Poland, stands under the Polish national framework: passport and marker rules, conditions in custody, and hate-crime provisions are set nationally and are carried by the national assessment. What is specific to the voivodeship is its own record of official hostility.

Świdnik, a town in the voivodeship, was the first place in Poland to adopt an "LGBT-free" declaration. Its county council passed the resolution in March 2019, pledging to shield children from "homosexual propaganda" and to refrain from actions encouraging "tolerance of LGBT people". The text is non-binding; it does not itself restrict a visitor's movement or access to services, and it records the posture of a local authority rather than a rule enforceable against anyone.

The voivodeship legislature adopted a comparable declaration of its own and, when the matter was revisited, voted to keep it in place. It repealed the resolution on 20 September 2021, after the European Commission threatened to withhold funding from voivodeships that retained such declarations. The repeal changed the regional assembly's formal position. Whether the county-level declarations, including Świdnik's, were withdrawn is not established by these sources.

The region's own record in these sources consists of a municipal declaration of equality signed in the capital and a ruling by the province's administrative court that closed out the last local document of its kind in the country.

On 6 February 2024 the Voivodeship Administrative Court in Warsaw revoked the final document in Poland declaring a locality 'against LGBT ideology'. The ruling ended the sequence of local anti-LGBT resolutions. The sources do not name the municipality whose document was struck down, so these sources do not establish whether that last document sat inside Masovian Voivodeship or elsewhere; what is clear is that the administrative court sitting in Warsaw issued the decision.

In March 2019 the Mayor of Warsaw signed a declaration of equality and non-discrimination that includes commitments on responding to hate crime. The declaration stands and the sources record no repeal. It is an instrument of the capital's municipal authorities, not a province-wide provision, and it does not extend to the rest of the voivodeship.

27671186B7584771598694.name: Bauchi
27671186B7584771598694.summary:
Bauchi's Sharia Penal Code remains in force. The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 confirms it, and death by stoning is the penalty provided under Section 133 of the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 and Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001.

On 28 June 2022 a Sharia court sitting in Ningi local government area sentenced three men to death by stoning for homosexuality, among them 70-year-old Malam Haruna. The prosecution was brought by members of the Hisbah Vanguard through Adamu Dan Kafi, who told the court the three were arrested at Gwada village, Ningi LGA, on 14 June 2022. Presiding judge Munka'ilu Sabo-Ningi held that they had violated Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001 and granted a 30-day appeal window. Relatives of the convicted men said the judgment had not been carried out at the time of reporting. Reuters described the sentence as the first time the death penalty had actually been imposed for homosexuality in Nigeria.

The UK Home Office note records that the 2022 Bauchi sentence could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor, and that a further report placed a death-by-stoning sentence for homosexuality from a Sharia court in Bauchi in May 2024.

Earlier convictions in the state were reversed on appeal. Jubrin Babaji was convicted on 25 September 2003 under Section 133 of the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 and sentenced to death by stoning; the Upper Sharia Court of Bauchi State quashed the sentence for denial of counsel and a defective confession. Yunusa Rafin Chiyawa's conviction was quashed on 14 November 2003. Amnesty International recorded a number of cases in which convictions and sentences to death were quashed on appeal.

In 2007 Bauchi state police arrested eighteen men and charged them with sodomy for dressing as women, an offence under the Shari'a penal code. The charges were later reduced to vagrancy, and the men were held in jail for several years awaiting trial; the pre-trial detention dissolved by the end of 2011.

Persons perceived as trans-feminine in Bauchi have been arrested and held in custody under Shari'a charges for years.

27671186B50148357657004.name: Kano
27671186B50148357657004.summary:
Kano stands under Nigeria's national legal framework and operates its own Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, in force since 26 November 2000. Consensual same-sex activity under that code carries 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment where the person is unmarried, and stoning to death (rajm) where the person is or has been married.

The capital maximum is not confined to men. The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 records Kano's maximum penalty for what the note terms lesbianism as death, and records the Sharia codes as remaining in force.

27671186B99510750195830.name: Sokoto
27671186B99510750195830.summary:
Sokoto State stands under Nigeria's national legal framework and layers its own religious penal code on top of it. The Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code Laws took effect across the state on 31 January 2001. Under the code, male same-sex activity is punished by stoning to death where the offender is or has been married, and by 100 lashes where he is not. Sexual acts between women, recorded in the code as wsafa, draw ta'azir punishment of up to 100 lashes and imprisonment.

Sokoto's Shari'a criminal code applies to Muslims in the state, one of twelve northern states whose codes carry a maximum penalty of death for men and whipping or imprisonment for women for same-sex acts.

Sokoto's Sharia courts apply the code in practice, including its capital provisions. On 9 October 2001 the Upper Sharia Court at Gwadabawa convicted Safiyatu Hussaini Tungar Tudu of zina under sections 128 and 129 of the Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code and sentenced her to death by stoning; the co-accused was discharged and acquitted. She filed an appeal on 26 October 2001, and the Sharia Court of Appeal of Sokoto State quashed the conviction and discharged and acquitted her on 25 March 2002. The conviction was for zina rather than same-sex conduct, but it establishes that the state's religious courts impose the code's capital sentences and that an appellate tier reviews them.

The groundwork for the code within the state is documented. An interim committee report was submitted to Sokoto Governor Attahiru Dalhatu Bafarawa on 13 October 1999, and a final report followed on 16 December 1999 with an annexe draft bill to establish Sharia courts applying Sharia law in the state.

27671186B69054806776702.name: Yobe
27671186B69054806776702.summary:
Yobe adopted Shari'a into its criminal legislation in 2000 under Governor Bukar Abba Ibrahim, as part of the 1999-2002 wave of northern states that created a parallel religious-criminal jurisdiction. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report lists Yobe among the twelve states that had done so by 2002, the only states whose Shari'a courts try Muslim criminal cases beyond federal law.

The state's inhabitants are mainly Muslims, so the Shari'a penal code's personal scope covers most people in the state, residents and visitors alike. A visitor who is not Muslim falls outside that code's application to persons, but the practical exposure in Yobe is shaped by a security environment in which identification as LGBTQ+ has been used as grounds for detention regardless of the formal personal scope of the code.

The UK Home Office Country Policy and Information Note on SOGIESC in Nigeria (Version 4.0, June 2025) records that Shari'a penal codes in the twelve northern states apply to Muslims, with death the maximum penalty for men in all twelve and penalties for acts between women ranging from death in a minority of states to flogging and imprisonment. The same note records public flogging of persons cross-dressing in 2023, and observes that few secular cases reach court.

The federal criminal code, which also applies in Yobe, penalises same-sex male conduct with up to 14 years' imprisonment (3 years for attempts) and is silent on women. A trans visitor therefore faces exposure under both the federal layer and, if Muslim or identified as such, the state Shari'a layer.

27671186B21163522287660.name: Zamfara
27671186B21163522287660.summary:
Zamfara operates its own Sharia criminal-law layer in addition to Nigeria's national framework. 27671186B753479316714.name: Borno
27671186B753479316714.summary:
Borno State stands under Nigeria's national framework, and its criminalisation of same-sex conduct rests independently on Borno's own legislation. The state's statute on prostitution, homosexuality, brothels and other sexual immoralities was signed by Governor Kachalla on 10 December 2000 and gazetted in Borno State Gazette No. 42 Vol. 26 on 18 October 2001. Section 3 makes engaging in prostitution, lesbianism, a homosexual act or pimping an offence in the state. Section 7 provides that any person who 'engages in sexual intercourse with another person of the same gender shall upon conviction be punished with death'. Section 4 deems all brothels closed on commencement, and Section 9 assigns jurisdiction over the statute's offences to the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts.

Borno enacted a second, parallel layer of its own. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report lists Borno among the twelve northern Nigerian states that had adopted Shari'a into their criminal legislation by 2002, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law. The sourcebook of enacted Shari'a Penal Codes records a Borno State Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 3 March 2003, with no operation date or gazette identified; the Borno text was obtained only in May 2006, after the volume's annotation had been completed, which is why Borno is not among the individually annotated codes. The parallel Shari'a layer for Borno therefore rests on a Borno-specific enactment rather than on federal or umbrella coverage.

The UK Home Office country-of-origin information note of June 2025 states that Islamic law applies to Muslims in the twelve northern states and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women; the maximum penalty for 'sodomy' for men is death in all twelve states, and penalties for 'lesbianism' range from death to flogging and imprisonment. The note carries a dedicated section on enforcement of Shari'a provisions and on the attitude of the hisbah, the morality police. A visitor to Borno therefore faces two state-level regimes, one secular and one Shari'a-based, each of which independently reaches same-sex conduct, and the secular statute's own jurisdiction clause routes those cases to Shari'a and Area Courts as well as to Magistrate Courts.

27671186B90305463766462.name: Gombe
27671186B90305463766462.summary:
Gombe State criminalises same-sex conduct under its own Shari'a Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 23 November 2001. The enacted statutory text covers conduct by men and women and reaches beyond Nigeria's federal criminal code. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report on Shari'a implementation lists Gombe among the twelve northern states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond the federal code.

The penalties set by the state statute are severe and gendered. Unmarried men convicted of sodomy face caning of 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment, and married men face stoning to death (rajm). The lesbianism offence carries up to 50 lashes plus imprisonment of up to six months. Gombe's own formulation defines gross indecency as any sexual offence against the normal or usual standards of behaviour.

The UK Home Office country-of-origin information note of June 2025 states that Islamic law applies to Muslims in the twelve northern states, which include Gombe, and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women. It records the maximum penalty for 'sodomy' between men as death in all twelve states, with penalties for 'lesbianism' ranging from death to flogging and imprisonment. The note carries a dedicated section on enforcement of Shari'a provisions and on the attitude of the hisbah, the morality police.

Enforcement in Gombe is documented through a single mass operation. In October 2023 the Gombe State Command of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps raided a gathering at Duwa Plaza along the Bauchi-Gombe Expressway that was preparing a same-sex wedding, arresting 76 people. State spokesperson Buhari Sa'ad told reporters that 59 males were detained, 21 of whom wilfully confessed to being homosexuals, and that 17 females were present at the scene; the command stated that the detainees would be charged in court for a crime of social vice in Gombe State.

The Guardian of 23 October 2023, byline James Agberebi, independently confirmed the operation from Lagos press, reporting that the arrests followed a tip-off about a same-sex birthday party and planned marriage. Gombe NSCDC Commandant Mohammed Muazu confirmed the arrests; the spokesperson said the remaining males and the 17 females were invited guests and onlookers, and officers voiced concern over the participants' ages. Detention therefore reached people present at a gathering rather than only those alleged to have engaged in conduct. The most recent documented enforcement action in this record is this October 2023 raid; no later instance is documented.

27671186B1226853346294.name: Jigawa
27671186B1226853346294.summary:
Jigawa State's own criminal layer is the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, Law No. 12 of 2000, signed into law on 18 December 2000 and brought into operation on 27 December 2000 (Jigawa State Gazette Vol. 1 No. 12). It stands under Nigeria's national framework rather than replacing it, and it adds offences the national code does not reach.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025) lists Jigawa in a twelve-state table of Sharia penalties: for male same-sex conduct, married men face death by stoning, while unmarried men face 100 lashes and imprisonment of up to one year; same-sex acts between women carry up to 50 lashes and imprisonment of up to six months. The June 2025 note confirms that the Sharia penal layer remains the operative criminal frame for Muslims in Jigawa.

The sourcebook places Jigawa among four states, with Gombe, Kano and Zamfara, whose sodomy offence punishes unmarried men with 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment and married men with stoning to death (rajm); lesbianism carries up to 50 lashes plus up to six months' imprisonment, and Jigawa's code includes the 'unnatural fusion of the female sexual organs' explanation of the offence. The code criminalises conduct the federal code does not reach, including women's same-sex conduct.

Human Rights Watch (2004) records Zamfara's governor as the first to extend Sharia to criminal law, introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000. By 2002 twelve northern states, Jigawa among them, had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation, to date the only states where Sharia courts have jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

27671186B54051914323789.name: Kaduna
27671186B54051914323789.summary:
Kaduna State stands under Nigeria's national framework, and its own criminal law adds two layers that a visitor has to read together. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity (June 2025) records that Kaduna separately adopted its own secular Penal Code in 2017, whose Section 259 punishes 'unnatural offences' (sodomy, lesbianism and bestiality) with up to 21 years' imprisonment and a fine, a ceiling above the federal 14-year maximum.

Running in parallel, the Kaduna Sharia Penal Code Law 2002 (Law No. 4 of 2002) applies to Muslims. It was signed into law and came into operation on 21 June 2002, published in Kaduna State Gazette No. 17 Vol. 36 of 4 July 2002, and bound with the Sharia Criminal Procedure Code. Human Rights Watch (2004) traces the wave of adoption back to Zamfara's Sharia Establishment Law of 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000, after which twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation by 2002; those twelve remain the only states where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases, Kaduna among them.

The Home Office's June 2025 note carries Kaduna's own row in its twelve-state Sharia penalties table (section 8.4.3, ILGA-derived): death by stoning as the maximum for liwat (sodomy), and same-sex acts between women punishable 'at the discretion of the qadi (Sharia court judge)'. Ostien's annotated volume of Kaduna's enacted text records that Kaduna is one of only three states whose statute states without qualification that 'Whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm)', with no unmarried/married graduation, while the lesbianism offence is left to ta'azir, discretionary punishment. A trans visitor read as Muslim therefore faces a capital ceiling on men's same-sex acts under Kaduna's own promulgated code, alongside the 21-year secular ceiling that applies regardless of faith.

27671186B99661334382691.name: Katsina
27671186B99661334382691.summary:
Katsina stands under Nigeria's national framework and additionally operates its own Sharia criminal layer. Katsina is among the northern states that adopted Sharia criminal codes from 1999 onward, and the provisions cited remain in force.

Katsina's own statute is the Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, Law No. 2 of 2001, which came into operation on 20 June 2001 and was gazetted in Katsina State Gazette Vol. 12 No. 23 on 27 August 2001.

The code's sodomy provision reads: "Whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm)". Katsina is one of three states, with Kaduna and Kebbi, whose sodomy text carries that wording.

Katsina's lesbianism provision is among the harshest in the northern block. Only Kano and Katsina reach stoning to death as the maximum for the lesbianism offence, against the harmonised code's base penalty of 50 lashes and up to six months. Katsina is one of only two states whose law carries death as the maximum for same-sex acts between women as well as men.

For a trans person held in Katsina, the penalty structure runs from lashing or caning to capital punishment. Lesbianism, defined as carnal acts or stimulation between women, is punishable by imprisonment or caning in most northern states, with death penalties applied in Kano and Katsina.

The Sharia layer in Katsina reaches women as well as men. Arrest data for these offences is limited, so the recorded enforcement picture is incomplete.

Presentation is separately exposed. Sources describe a cross-dressing layer in the northern states under which men who dress or behave as women face prison or a fine.

27671186B53868438251790.name: Kebbi
27671186B53868438251790.summary:
Kebbi is one of twelve northern Nigerian states that adopted criminal Shari'a during the wave that ran from 1999 to 2002, and it stands under Nigeria's national framework on sexual-orientation and gender-identity law, which the national record carries. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report on the extension of Shari'a to criminal law records that by 2002 twelve northern states, Kebbi among them, had Shari'a criminal legislation and Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, the only states in the country with such jurisdiction.

Kebbi's own penal layer is the Penal Code (Amendment) Law, Law No. 21 of 2000, signed into law and brought into operation on 1 December 2000 and published in Kebbi State Gazette Vol. 2 No. 1, Supplement, 31 December 2000. The enacted text states that whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm), a capital ceiling for men's same-sex acts. Kebbi is one of only three states, with Kaduna and Katsina, whose enacted statutory text carries this stoning provision.

Women's same-sex conduct is also criminalised under Kebbi's own statute: lesbianism carries 50 lashes and up to six months' imprisonment, the harmonised bloc penalty for women's conduct rather than the Kano/Katsina capital maximum. The UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note carries Kebbi's own row in its twelve-state Shari'a penalties table (section 8.4.3), confirming that Kebbi's Shari'a layer extends criminalisation to acts between women, leaving the state's code broader in scope and harsher than the federal statute for Muslim defendants.

Wikipedia's overview of LGBTQ rights in Nigeria places Kebbi inside the northern Shari'a block, where same-sex acts carry penalties ranging from imprisonment to capital punishment and where lesbianism is punishable by imprisonment or caning in most states, with death penalties applied only in Kano and Katsina. On that account Kebbi falls in the lashing and imprisonment tier for women's conduct rather than the capital tier, consistent with Kebbi's own statute, while its sodomy provision for men remains capital. The same source records a cross-dressing layer in the northern block: prison or a fine for men who dress or behave as women, illustrated by a Kano court's 2025 one-year imprisonment sentence. No housing, segregation or placement rule for trans prisoners is documented for Kebbi or elsewhere in Nigeria.

27671186B79778155682183.name: Niger
27671186B79778155682183.summary:
Niger is an independent country with its own criminal law; the assessment below is national.

Article 25 of the Refoundation Charter, adopted in March 2025, criminalises all lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex and asexual acts or practices, expressly including transgender acts or practices. The February 2026 penal code punishes LGBTQIA+ acts or practices with 5 to 10 years' imprisonment and a fine of up to 100 million CFA francs, and the punishable practices expressly include changing or attempting to change one's birth sex. Same-sex sexual relations carry the same 5 to 10 year term and fine, covering same-sex sexual activity and public announcement of a romantic relationship with a person of the same sex.

Creating, managing, financing or participating in LGBTQIA+ organisations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, is punished with 10 to 20 years' imprisonment and a fine of up to 500 million CFA francs. Mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences cannot be applied to these penalties.

Since March 2025, Article 24 defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman. Since June 2026, marrying a person of the same sex and officiating, organising or bearing official witness to a same-sex wedding is punished with 10 to 20 years' imprisonment.

There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on gender identity or sexual orientation. Article 95 of Law 2022-59 punishes collecting and processing data revealing sexual life or sexual orientation with three months to five years' imprisonment and a fine of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs; Law 2015-36, which had prohibited discrimination including on grounds of sexual orientation, was repealed in 2023 with convictions expunged.

Same-sex sexual activity was explicitly outlawed in 2025 and penalised in 2026. Before that change the age of consent stood at 13 for heterosexual acts and 21 for homosexual acts.

After the 2026 code took effect, dozens of people were arrested across the country and some imprisoned, including military officials, and LGBTQ people went into hiding. Organisations providing HIV prevention services to men who have sex with men stopped working, ending access to condoms, HIV testing and PrEP.

Documented enforcement includes two men caught naked in a parked car arrested for public indecency and fined; two young women in Maradi in 2022 prosecuted for lesbianism and acquitted for lack of legislation but imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos allegedly portraying a lesbian act; and two young women reported as lesbians in Niamey in 2025 prosecuted for public indecency but acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere, with the judge allegedly sanctioned for leniency. As of 8-9 December 2022 Niger had no specific law criminalising same-sex relationships, and Maradi lawmaker Nana Djibou Harouna had presented to the Speaker of Parliament a proposal backed by nearly all MPs to criminalise same-sex relationships, with punishment unspecified and no debate scheduled.

No violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity was reported and no documented cases of discrimination in employment, housing, education, health care or statelessness on those grounds were recorded, though stigma or intimidation probably prevented incidents from being reported. Two gay rights organisations operated in secret, partly because they were not formally registered.

Asylum seekers from Cameroon, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire who held LGBTQ public demonstrations in Niamey in 2022 were denied refugee recognition, hindering relocation, and faced shops refusing to serve them and verbal or physical violence from strangers.

Gay men and lesbians face strong pressure to conform to societal norms, leading many to lead socially acceptable lives in public while seeking LGBT relationships privately. The 2025 acquittal of two women prosecuted for public indecency caused widespread debate ranging from approval to outrage. The only official cultural-values statement in the record concerns LGBTQ practices generally: "all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be (...) are not in line with our social and cultural values". The record contains no statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Niger (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Article 25 of the Refoundation Charter, adopted in March 2025, criminalizes all lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, asexual acts or practices, expressly including transgender acts or practices. The February 2026 penal code punishes LGBTQIA+ acts or practices with 5 to 10 years in prison and a fine up to 100 million CFA francs (€152,448.94; US$176,604.56). The punishable practices expressly include changing or attempting to change one's birth sex. Creating, managing, financing, or participating in LGBTQIA+ organizations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, is punished with 10 to 20 years in prison and a fine up to 500 million CFA francs (€762,244.71; US$882,829). Mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences cannot be applied to these penalties. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on gender identity. After the 2026 code took effect, dozens of people were arrested across the country and some imprisoned, including military officials, and LGBTQ people went into hiding. Same-sex sexual activity was explicitly outlawed in 2025 and penalized in 2026, and before that change the age of consent was 13 for heterosexual acts and 21 for homosexual acts. Article 25 of the March 2025 Refoundation Charter criminalizes same-sex sexual relations and LGBTQIA+ acts or practices. The February 2026 penal code punishes same-sex sexual relations with 5 to 10 years in prison and a fine up to 100 million CFA francs, covering same-sex sexual activity and public announcement of one's romantic relationship with a person of the same sex. Creating, managing, financing, or participating in LGBTQIA+ organizations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, is punished with 10 to 20 years in prison and a fine up to 500 million CFA francs, with no mitigating circumstances or suspended sentences allowed. Since March 2025 under Article 24 marriage is defined as a union between a man and a woman, and since June 2026 getting married to a person of the same sex and officiating, organizing or bearing official witness to same-sex weddings is punished with 10 to 20 years in prison. There are no broad protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation, but Article 95 of Law 2022-59 punishes collecting and processing data revealing sexual life or sexual orientation with three months to five years imprisonment and a fine of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs, while Law 2015-36 which had prohibited discrimination including sexual orientation was repealed in 2023 with convictions expunged. Enforcement included two men caught naked in a parked car arrested for public indecency and fined a small fee, two young women in Maradi in 2022 prosecuted for lesbianism and acquitted for lack of legislation but imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos allegedly portraying a lesbian act, and two young women reported as lesbians in Niamey in 2025 prosecuted for public indecency but acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere with the judge allegedly sanctioned for leniency. After the 2026 code, dozens were arrested across the country and some imprisoned, LGBTQ people went into hiding, and organizations providing HIV prevention services to MSM stopped working, ending access to condoms, HIV testing and PrEP. Gay men and lesbians experienced societal discrimination with strong pressure to conform to societal norms, leading many to lead socially acceptable lives in public while seeking LGBT relationships privately. No violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity was reported and no documented cases of discrimination in employment, housing, education, health care or statelessness based on sexual orientation were recorded, though stigma or intimidation probably prevented incidents from being reported. Two gay rights organizations operated in secret partly because they were not formally registered. Asylum seekers from Cameroon, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire who held LGBTQ public demonstrations in Niamey in 2022 were denied refugee recognition hindering relocation and faced shops refusing to serve them and verbal or physical violence from strangers. Niger's attitude toward LGBTQ issues is described as usually discreet, even though male prostitution was prevalent in Niamey and effeminate men were known for having always been part of Niger's culture by organizing traditional wedding ceremonies and supporting themselves that way. The 2025 acquittal of two women prosecuted for public indecency caused widespread debate ranging from approval to outrage. The article documents no statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically; the only official cultural-values statement concerns LGBTQ practices generally: "all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be (...) are not in line with our social and cultural values".

27671186B8148656125930.name: Imo
27671186B8148656125930.summary:
Imo is a state in south-eastern Nigeria and stands under the national legal framework. Its own record covers enforcement action taken inside the state against private gatherings and against people accused of same-sex conduct in public.

On 26 April 2018 two men in Imo State were stripped, beaten and paraded through the streets after being accused of gay sex. An inquiry by NoStringsNG found that the victims were then arrested by the police themselves, and that they might need legal support. The state's role in the episode was to detain the people who had been attacked, not the crowd that attacked them.

Enforcement continued into 2025. On 19 February the Imo Police Command broke up a party at Graziella Hotels in Orogwe, Owerri West, arrested many of those present, described as gay and lesbian suspects, and placed attendees who fled on a police search list. The event was a private hotel gathering, and the police treated it as an operation with names attached to people who were not detained.

Seven years separate the two documented episodes, and they occurred in different parts of the state: a street in 2018, a hotel in Owerri West in 2025. Police action in Imo is therefore not confined to a single locality, and it has not been limited to public conduct. Both a public street and a closed private venue appear in the record as points of exposure, and leaving before an arrest did not remove people from the search.

27671186B63712480376187.name: Edo
27671186B63712480376187.summary:
Edo State stands under Nigeria's national legal framework. Its own documented record is one of mob violence against people accused of same-sex conduct, and it contains no instance in which police protected the person accused.

In February 2008, in a remote community in Edo State, police declared Ugbogbo Ovbukhan wanted over 'gay practice' after he and his partner Jerry were found together. A mob beat both men for desecrating the community; Ovbukhan escaped before police arrived and police arrested Jerry for interrogation. The Nigerian Observer reported the wanted declaration on 15 August 2008.

On 10 June 2010, The Nigerian Observer reported from Benin City, in Oredo local government area, that Mark Osato Edomwonyi narrowly escaped being killed by a mob after he was found with his partner Paddy in Paddy's rented apartment. A neighbour raised the alarm; Edomwonyi fled through the backyard before the mob arrived, and the crowd then, in the newspaper's words, 'unleashed terror' on Paddy. No police intervention, arrest or prosecution appears in the report, and Edomwonyi's whereabouts were still unknown when it was filed.

In May 2018, at Ekpoma, a mob lynched one of two men found together while the other escaped. The report presented the killing as an 'abominable act' against traditional heritage, treating it as community redress.

For a visitor, the documented exposure in Edo comes from community perception rather than from a prosecution: in these accounts it is neighbours, not patrols, who raise the alarm, and the single police action documented across the three cases was taken against the couple rather than against those who beat them. The cases reported involve men accused of same-sex conduct, and the inventory holds no Edo case in which a report identifies the victim of violence as a transgender person. Risk to a trans visitor therefore has to be read from the way accusations of sexual and gender nonconformity mobilise a crowd, not from a documented attack on a trans person in the state.

sources.summary: Nigerian Observer (May 2018): in Ekpoma a mob lynched one of two men caught together and the other escaped, framed as an 'abominable act' under traditional heritage. Documents fatal community violence in Edo State.

The Initiative for Equal Rights (TIERs) '2024 Human Rights Violations Report', published January 2025, records 556 violations affecting 850 victims based on real or perceived SOGIESC across Nigeria during the reporting period. 65028918B93184959873838.name: Aceh
65028918B93184959873838.summary:
Aceh stands under Indonesia's national legal framework; the national layer is carried by the parent record. The region-specific layer is a provincial sharia criminal code. Special autonomy granted in 2005 authorised the introduction of Islamic criminal law for Muslim residents, and Qanun Aceh Nomor 6 Tahun 2014 tentang Hukum Jinayat, enacted in 2014, has been enforced since 23 October 2015. Aceh is Indonesia's only province that criminalises same-sex relations and enforces Islamic law in addition to the national criminal code.

Article 63 of the Qanun defines liwath as sexual acts between males and Article 64 defines musahaqah as sexual acts between females, each determined by sex at birth. Each offence carries up to 100 lashes, up to 100 months' imprisonment, or a fine of up to 1,000 grams of gold. Because the definitions turn on birth sex rather than presentation or legal gender marker, a trans visitor whose documents, presentation or partner's sex are read as same-sex conduct falls within the provision and faces caning, imprisonment or a fine.

Public caning is the province's standing punishment for sharia offences. On 23 May 2017 an Islamic court in Banda Aceh applied the 2014 provisions for the first time, ordering two men caned 82 times each before hundreds of spectators outside a mosque; in 2017 two further men, aged 20 and 23, were sentenced to public caning for same-sex relations.

The most recent documented enforcement in this record is from 2025. Two men aged 20 and 21 were sentenced on 11 August 2025 to public caning for kissing, after an April 2025 arrest in which police broke into a toilet; CBS News and the Associated Press reported on 26 August 2025 that two men were publicly caned in the province after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing. No later Aceh enforcement incident is documented in this record.

Trans people in Aceh have faced targeted enforcement. In January 2018 police in North Aceh arrested twelve transgender women, forcibly cut their hair, compelled them to wear men's clothing and closed their beauty salons. In a separate parlour raid in Aceh in January 2018 police tortured detainees, shaved the heads of transgender women, removed their shirts and bras, and paraded them through the street forcing them to shout that they were to become men.

Aceh legal scholarship analysing the rise of waria cases through a sharia-law-enforcement lens.

CBS News/AP (26 Aug 2025): two men were publicly caned in conservative Aceh province after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing. Public caning is the province's standing punishment for sharia offences.

iNews Aceh (undated local report, Feb-2025 round-up context): Satpol PP and Wilayatul Hisbah Banda Aceh secured an alleged gay couple in a boarding house; a local advocate urged police to investigate and boarding-house owners to monitor tenants. The report concerns a gay couple, and no trans person is identified in it.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Aceh (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Cross-dressing is not per se illegal in Indonesia, and transgender identity (also called waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture and society. Transgender people are allowed to change their legal gender on official documents after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and receiving a judge's approval, after which they can marry a person of the opposite legal gender, exemplified by Vivian Rubiyanti Iskandar as the first trans Indonesian legally recognized as female and by Aprilio Manganang in 2021 as the first service member to legally change gender from female to male although his case was intersex assigned female at birth. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with identification papers including Kartu Tanda Penduduk for residents of Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua, recognizing only male and female descriptors with no third gender/X option and printing gender at birth unless court recognition was already obtained, on the stated reasoning that many were undocumented where families did not approve. Indonesian law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment, and transgender people who do not hide their gender identity often find it challenging to maintain legitimate employment and are thus often forced into prostitution and other illegal activities to survive. In Aceh transgender people have faced targeted enforcement: in January 2018 police in North Aceh arrested twelve transgender women, forcibly cut their hair, compelled them to wear men's clothing, and closed their beauty salons, and in a January 2018 parlour raid in Aceh police tortured LGBTQ citizens, shaved the heads of transgender women, stripped their shirts and bras, and paraded them in the street forcing them to shout "to become men". In Jakarta the Social Agency declared waria to be socially dysfunctional and regularly conducts raids against transgender women, taking detained individuals to city-owned rehabilitation centres where they are incarcerated with homeless people, beggars and street buskers and only released upon documentation of lack of homelessness and a signed promise not to repeat the offence, with officials stating this is to create a deterrent against being transgender and continued violations will result in jail time. The Indonesian Ulama Council ruled transgender persons must live in the gender they were born with, stating if not willing to cure themselves medically and religiously they must accept their fate to be ridiculed and harassed, while the judicial system takes the contrary position recognizing actual genders and authorities have in some cases arrested and prosecuted perpetrators of hate crimes against the transgender community. Aceh has special autonomous status implementing Islamic Sharia-based criminal law (Qanun Jinayat), with authority granted in 2005 to introduce Sharia law for Muslim residents and the 2014 Qanun Jinayat providing that consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults are punishable by up to 100 lashes or up to 100 months (8 years) imprisonment, set for enforcement by the end of 2015. Enforcement outcomes in Aceh include the 2017 sentencing of two young gay men aged 20 and 23 to public caning, several high-profile cases of men publicly caned after guilty findings for same-sex relations, and the 11 August 2025 sentencing of two men aged 20 and 21 to public caning for kissing after April arrest when police broke into a toilet. Nationally Indonesia has allowed private consensual same-sex activity since 1993 at age 18, has no explicit sodomy law unlike Malaysia, and the Penal Code does not prohibit non-commercial private consensual activity between consenting same-sex adults. In December 2022 Parliament passed a Penal Code criminalizing sex outside marriage upon complaint by immediate family, set to take force on 2 January 2026 with up to one year imprisonment for unmarried partners, with the spokesperson stating the draft will not criminalize private sexual orientation including LGBTQ persons and Coordinating Minister Mahfud MD stating it did not criminalize an LGBTQ person and only targets adults committing sexual violence or rape of underage same-sex children and immoral acts in public, while Article 421(1) punishes obscene acts against a same-sex person in public with maximum 1 year and six months imprisonment or maximum fine category III. Indonesian law does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, households headed by same-sex couples lack the same legal protections as opposite-sex couples, and same-sex couples are ineligible to adopt as only married husband-wife couples can adopt. As of 2019 no specific law protects from discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity nor prohibits hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity, though a 2015 police circular states processing of hate speech related to sexual orientations and gender identity and Head of National Police Regulation No. 8 of 2009 stipulates the duty to protect special rights of minority groups including sexual orientation. Police have conducted repeated raids and detentions for gay parties and saunas under pornography-related offences, including the November 2016 Jakarta raid after an Islamic Defenders Front tip-off, May 2017 arrest of 141 men for a gay sex party with ten charged and detention of 144 in the Atlantis Gym raid, October 2017 arrest of 51 in a Central Jakarta sauna with six charged including the owner, and 2025 raids detaining 56 on 1 February, nine on 24 May, and arresting 75 on 22 June near Jakarta. The article states: "While transgender people in Indonesia are generally more accepted than gays, lesbians and bisexuals, they have, in recent years, faced growing discrimination and rejection, mostly from sharia-supporting Muslim groups, which have become more and more popular in Indonesia." The article states "some public tolerance is given to some transgender people working in beauty salons or the entertainment industry, most notably the celebrity talk show host Dorce Gamalama." The article states transgender identity (also called waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture and society. The article states discrimination and harassments directed at transgender people is not uncommon, though violence is quite rare, and transgender people who do not hide their gender identity often face employment exclusion forcing reliance on prostitution and other illegal activities. The article reports officials justify rehabilitation detention as creating a deterrent against being transgender and cites the Ulama Council position that those unwilling to cure themselves medically and religiously must accept their fate to be ridiculed and harassed, evidencing institutional rejection despite noted cultural presence.

65028918B84835514626455.name: West Papua
65028918B84835514626455.summary:
West Papua operates no provincial criminal law reaching sexual conduct or gender expression. The province stands under Indonesia's national framework without local additions, and no regency-level regulation on dress, public morality or gender presentation is documented in this inventory.

Security-force conduct is the province's defining documented risk. A report published on 22 July 2025 by the Asia-Pacific Solidarity Network recorded 138 acts of torture or other ill-treatment by police and military against people in detention in Maybrat and the Central Highlands through early 2025, with most victims male and under 24, seven female, and seven minors aged 15 to 17; the report's framing is 'impunity, secrecy and silence', indicating near-total absence of accountability. Any visitor to the province, including a visibly gender-nonconforming one, stands in this security-force environment.

The Papua human-rights monitor's Q3 2025 quarterly records a notable increase in military deployments and operations in West Papua's highland regions since August 2025. In Sorong, police arrested over a dozen protest participants in August 2025. On 27 September 2025 a military task force opened fire on civilians in Agats, Asmat Regency, alongside ongoing displacement and racial tension affecting indigenous Papuans. No trans-specific finding accompanies this pattern, but it amplifies exposure for a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor.

Provincial document practice follows the national pattern: since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with Kartu Tanda Penduduk, including residents of Papua, but the card recognises only 'male' and 'female' with no third gender or X designator, and prints gender at birth unless a court recognition is obtained. Families' disapproval can block the documentation process, which officials cite as leaving some residents undocumented and unable to access work or social services.

Legal gender recognition is available nationally after sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, after which the person may marry someone of the opposite legal gender. The judicial system has recognised trans status: Vivian Rubiyanti Iskandar was the first trans Indonesian legally recognised as female, and there are documented cases where perpetrators of hate crimes against the transgender community were arrested and prosecuted.

Indonesian law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment. The Indonesian Ulama Council ruled that transgender persons must live in the gender they were born with, stating that if they are 'not willing to cure themselves medically and religiously' they must be willing 'to accept their fate to be ridiculed and harassed'. This religious-body position sits alongside the judicial system's contrary practice.

Targeted enforcement documented against trans people includes the January 2018 North Aceh police arrest of twelve transgender women, during which their hair was forcibly cut, they were compelled into men's clothing, and beauty salons were closed. The Jakarta Social Agency declared waria socially dysfunctional and conducted regular raids and incarceration in city-owned 'rehabilitation' centres alongside homeless people, beggars and buskers, requiring documentation and a signed pledge before release; officials stated this was intended as a deterrent against being transgender and warned that continued violations would result in jail time. These are national-level actions, not West Papua ones, but they set the enforcement backdrop.

Discrimination in employment is documented: transgender people who do not hide their gender identity often find it challenging to maintain legitimate employment and are frequently pushed into prostitution and other informal or illegal activity to survive, with discrimination and harassment described as not uncommon though violence as quite rare. The article also notes that gays in jails are often sexually abused because of their orientation and do not report it, due to trauma and fear of return.

The control environment includes the 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction, which prohibits presentations suggesting same-sex relations and carries a fine or up to seven years' imprisonment; a March 2016 broadcasting commission policy banning programmes that make LGBTQ behaviour appear 'normal' and discouraging effeminate, transgender or cross-dressing figures; bans on sites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ terms including Grindr; and widely practiced, openly advertised conversion therapy, including rehabilitation-centre treatment with de facto legalisation by some city governments after the 'RUU Ketahanan Keluarga' Family Resilience draft was rejected by 5 of 9 factions.

Care context: a 2012 Health Ministry estimate put the number of transgender women at around 31 thousand. Yayasan Srikandi Sejati, founded 1998, focuses on transgender health, providing HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers at a free health clinic, operating amid a lack of school sex education and a historical movement focus that led the public to believe AIDS was a 'gay disease'.

Cultural context: transgender identity, also called waria, has long been part of Indonesian culture and society, and some public tolerance is given to transgender people working in beauty salons or the entertainment industry. The article states that while transgender people in Indonesia are generally more accepted than gays, lesbians and bisexuals, they have in recent years faced growing discrimination and rejection, mostly from sharia-supporting Muslim groups, which have become more popular in Indonesia.

Military service context: in 2021 Aprilio Manganang became the first service member to legally change gender from female to male, though his case involved an intersex person assigned female at birth and raised as a girl.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in West Papua (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Cross-dressing is not, per se, illegal in Indonesia, and transgender people are allowed to change legal gender on official documents after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and receiving a judge's approval, after which they can marry people of the opposite legal gender. Indonesian law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment, and the Indonesian Ulama Council ruled transgender persons must live in the gender they were born with, stating if they are "not willing to cure themselves medically and religiously" they must be willing "to accept their fate to be ridiculed and harassed." The judicial system takes the contrary position, with Vivian Rubiyanti Iskandar as the first trans Indonesian legally recognized as female, and there have been cases where perpetrators of hate crimes against the transgender community were arrested and prosecuted. Targeted enforcement includes January 2018 North Aceh police arrest of twelve transgender women with forcibly cut hair, compelled men's clothing and closed beauty salons, and Jakarta Social Agency declaration of waria as socially dysfunctional with regular raids and incarceration in city-owned "rehabilitation" centres with homeless people, beggars and buskers until documentation and signed pledge, with officials stating this creates deterrent against being transgender and continued violations will result in jail time. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with Kartu Tanda Penduduk including residents of Papua, but recognizes only "male" and "female" with no third gender/X designator and prints gender at birth unless court recognition obtained, citing undocumentation where families disapprove blocking work or social services. Transgender people who do not hide gender identity often find it challenging to maintain legitimate employment and are thus often forced into prostitution and other illegal activities to survive, with discrimination and harassments not uncommon though violence quite rare. In the military, Aprilio Manganang in 2021 became the first service member to legally change gender from female to male, although his case was intersex assigned female at birth and raised as a girl. Private, non-commercial consensual sexual activity between consenting adults of the same sex has been allowed nationally since 1993 at 18 years of age, with no explicit sodomy law unlike Malaysia, and a 2003 national bill to criminalize same-sex activity with cohabitation, adultery and witchcraft failed with no subsequent reintroduction. In December 2022 Parliament passed a Penal Code criminalizing sex outside marriage upon complaint by immediate family, set to take force on 2 January 2026 with up to one year in prison for unmarried partners, while the draft spokesperson stated it will not criminalize private sexual orientation including LGBTQ persons and Coordinating Minister Mahfud MD said it only targets adults who commit "sexual violence" or rape of underage same-sex children and public immoral acts, though same-sex marriage is not legally recognized effectively placing all same-sex sexual activity outside legal recognition. Aceh, allowed special autonomous Sharia law under 2014 Qanun Jinayat, punishes consensual adult same-sex acts by up to 100 lashes or up to 100 months (8 years) imprisonment, with public caning imposed including two young gay men aged 20 and 23 in 2017 and two men aged 20 and 21 sentenced 11 August 2025 for kissing after April arrest when police broke into toilet. Police have repeatedly raided private "gay parties" and gay saunas under national pornography law in the 2010s-2020s, including November 2016 Jakarta raid, May 2017 arrest of 141 men with ten charged and detention of 144 at Atlantis Gym Jakarta, October 2017 arrest of 51 with six charged, February/May/June 2025 South Jakarta hotel/villa raids detaining 56, nine and 75, August 2025 arrest of three for creating LGBTQ Facebook page facing up to 12 years and 6 billion rupiah fines, and 22 May 2026 sentencing of 25 to prison for violating anti-pornography law. Indonesian law does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships or adoption by same-sex couples, limiting adoption to husband-wife married couples, and as of 2019 provides no specific anti-discrimination protection nor hate-crime prohibition based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Limited protection machinery cited is a 2015 police circular to process hate speech related to sexual orientations and gender identity, Regulation of Head of National Police No. 8 of 2009 duty to protect special rights of minority groups including sexual orientation, and theoretical constitutional and Human Rights Law No. 39/1999 guarantee against employment discrimination on any ground. The article states "While transgender people in Indonesia are generally more accepted than gays, lesbians and bisexuals, they have, in recent years, faced growing discrimination and rejection, mostly from sharia-supporting Muslim groups, which have become more and more popular in Indonesia." It further states "some public tolerance is given to some transgender people working in beauty salons or the entertainment industry, most notably the celebrity talk show host Dorce Gamalama," noting transgender identity (also called waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture and society. For trans visitors, the article reports discrimination and harassments directed at transgender people is not uncommon though violence is quite rare, but those not hiding gender identity often cannot maintain legitimate employment and are forced into prostitution and other illegal activities, while gays in jails are often sexually abused due to orientation and do not report due to trauma and fear of return. Documented violence includes the January 2018 Aceh parlour ransacking where police tortured all LGBTQ citizens, shaved transgender women's heads, stripped shirts and bras and paraded them forcing them to shout "to become men," criticised by human rights organisations. Care context notes the 2012 Health Ministry estimate of around 31 thousand transgender women and Yayasan Srikandi Sejati founded 1998 focusing on transgender health providing HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers at a free health clinic, amid lack of school sex education and early movement focus leading public to believe AIDS was a "gay disease." Control environment includes the 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction prohibiting presentations suggesting same-sex relations punishable by fine or up to seven years, March 2016 broadcasting commission policy banning programs making LGBTQ behaviour appear "normal" discouraging effeminate, transgender or cross-dressing figures, bans on sites/apps with "gay" or LGBTQ terms including Grindr, and widely practiced openly advertised conversion therapy including rehabilitation centre treatment with de facto legalization by some city governments after the "RUU Ketahanan Keluarga" Family Resilience draft was rejected by 5 of 9 factions.

65028918B37605681672150.name: North Sumatra
65028918B37605681672150.summary:
North Sumatra is a province of Indonesia and stands under the national legal framework, which applies here as it does nationwide.

North Sumatra is one of eight provinces covered by OutRight Action International's mapping of national laws and discriminatory regional regulations. That mapping documents regional rules imposing dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, with significant variation between regions; the report states its findings hold for areas beyond the provinces it examined directly.

Medan, the provincial capital, is the site of the only documented legal-process case for a transgender person in North Sumatra. Dimas Cahya became the first transgender man in the city to change his name legally to match his identity, and the Medan District Court granted the application after a six-week process. The judge warned that the change would 'erase my identity' but declined to engage with LGBTI issues, and no enforcement action against the couple is recorded.

UNAIDS reporting describes Medan as conservative, with LGBTI people regarded locally as 'immoral'.

sources.summary: OutRight Action International's 'Creeping Criminalisation: Mapping of Indonesia's National Laws and Regional Regulations That Violate Human Rights of Women and LGBTIQ People' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; 2022 file copy) maps national laws and discriminatory regional regulations across eight focus provinces: Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta. It finds much overlap but significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

sources.title: The first but not the last: Indonesian transgender man fights for recognition | UNAIDS
sources.summary: Dimas Cahya, a transgender man from Medan, North Sumatra's capital, told UNAIDS how he became the first transgender man in Medan to legally change his name to match his identity. After a six-week process the Medan District Court granted the application; the judge warned that the change would 'erase my identity' but stayed out of LGBTI issues completely. The article frames Medan as conservative, with LGBTI people deemed 'immoral', and reports that a Medan legal-aid organisation asked the couple invasive questions before the case. This is the only documented legal-process case for North Sumatra: a local court handled a trans person's application neutrally, and the article records no enforcement action against the couple.

65028918B26897900130576.name: North Sulawesi
65028918B26897900130576.summary:
North Sulawesi stands under Indonesia's national framework, and the national laws described in the Indonesia record apply to visitors to this province. The sources reviewed contain no North Sulawesi-specific provincial regulation on gender identity or sexual orientation.

OutRight Action International's mapping of Indonesia's national laws and discriminatory regional regulations (Katjasungkana and Wieringa, 2022) examined regional regulations in eight focus provinces: Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta. North Sulawesi was not among them. The study documented significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set, but no such provincial restriction is documented for North Sulawesi itself.

Police conduct in Manado is documented through a local account. On 11 June 2016 LGBT groups joined the city's women's movement in a street action against sexual violence at Bundaran Zero Point, running from 08.00 to 10.00 WITA, with SALUT (Sanubari Sulawesi Utara), the local LGBT organisation, taking part. The same reporting records that police raids in Manado have included harassment of LGBT people: SALUT's director Coco Jericho reported that a butch lesbian was groped during a raid. Victims often do not report such conduct because they fear their families will not accept their orientation. No arrests or prosecutions are reported in that account.

Public visibility by trans people in the province is documented at official level. On Saturday 10 November 2012 a waria beach-queen pageant was held at Malalayang beach in Manado, organised by Indonesian parliament member Paula Sinjal together with the National Narcotics Agency of North Sulawesi as an outreach event on the dangers of drugs and HIV/AIDS. Sinjal was quoted saying that waria are among local people and deserve attention. No adverse official action is recorded in connection with the event.

Media stigma following public visibility is documented in a 2024 Konde.co interview with Alexa, elected Ratu Waria Sulawesi Utara for 2016 to 2018 at the Sahid Kawanua Hotel in Manado. She states that after her title she suffered discrimination from sensationalist media and from the public, with her personal crisis peaking around 25 March 2019. No legal or police action appears anywhere in her account. The most recent incident documented in these sources dates from 2019 and was published in February 2024; no later instance is documented.

65028918B6070530336190.name: Special Region of Yogyakarta
65028918B6070530336190.summary:
The Special Region of Yogyakarta carries its own layer of discriminatory regional regulation. A 2022 mapping of Indonesia's national laws and regional regulations that violate the rights of women and LGBTIQ people examined eight focus provinces, Yogyakarta among them, and found substantial overlap alongside significant regional variation. The regulations it documents include dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear. The mapping states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the eight it examined, so the categories it identifies are not confined to the provinces it names.

The most fully documented enforcement action against a trans institution in Yogyakarta is the February 2016 closure of Pondok Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah, a religious school where trans women study Islam. The hardline Front Jihad Islam threatened to seal the school, and on the night of 24 February 2016 a two-hour meeting at the Jagalan ward office in Yogyakarta ended with an agreement to shut it. Those present included ward and residents' officials, the lurah and the local military district commander; an earlier session on 19 February was attended by the Banguntapan camat and the local police sector chief. The district head justified the closure on the grounds that the pesantren lacked a permit, conflicted with Islamic values and had once had alcohol found on site. Its founder, Shinta Ratri, said about 20 waria attended the weekly weekend classes, which taught ordinary Islamic instruction.

A waria witness at the meeting said a Front Jihad Islam leader delivered anti-LGBT remarks to shouts of "Allahu Akbar" and vowed the group would keep hunting LGBTI people wherever they gather. The Governor of the Special Region of Yogyakarta, Sultan Hamengku Buwono X, publicly urged restraint on both sides, called LGBT people "sama-sama anak bangsa" (fellow children of the nation) and said the regional government would study the issue. The shutdown concluded on administrative and community grounds; no provincial anti-trans statute was cited.

The pesantren and the Yogyakarta waria community were operating again years after the closure, and economic and social marginalisation of trans people in the province persists.

76434192B26311534340602.name: KwaZulu-Natal
76434192B26311534340602.summary:
KwaZulu-Natal is a province of South Africa and stands under the national framework: the constitutional equality guarantee, the Equality Court under the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act, legal gender recognition, the 2024 hate-crime statute and the national correctional rules for transgender inmates apply here as they do elsewhere in the country. No provincial law, by-law or provincial institution departing from that layer is documented in the sources.

The provincial evidence on violence and victimisation is a 2024 masters thesis in criminology at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in Durban. It interviewed 15 self-identifying queer participants recruited through the Imvelo Yesizwe Organisation in KwaMashu township and reports substantial queerphobic violence and victimisation in that township setting. The study also examines whether the support and interventions available to those residents were adequate, and what safety strategies they used.

The study is small and its participants were purposively recruited, so it records the experiences of that group rather than a measured rate of violence. It does not disaggregate transgender participants from other sexual minorities, and no source gives a KwaZulu-Natal figure for violence against transgender people. A trans visitor to the province has no validated local victimisation figure to work from.

PinkNews (26 Jan 2012): Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini's anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival prompted demands for apology; police opened investigation, with the KwaZulu-Natal Premier and Contralesa weighing in on the royal family's account. Region-specific evidence of top traditional authority hostility toward gay people in the province.

sources.title: Transgender prisoners challenge prison authorities (GroundUp)
sources.summary: GroundUp news feature (6 Aug 2025, Elna Schutz) documenting where transgender prisoners are held in South Africa: Jade September, a transgender woman, was imprisoned in the male section of Pollsmoor and won her 2019 Equality Court case against the Minister of Correctional Services, which ruled that not allowing her to express her gender identity was unfair discrimination. Reports that the resulting Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedure (SOP) for LGBT+ prisoners requires a safety-risk assessment within the first six hours of admission and stipulates that transgender men and transgender women are to be detained or transported only with other transgender men or transgender women respectively, alongside respectful-search and communication rules. Also notes Lawyers for Human Rights representation of 'NM', a transgender woman serving a long-term sentence at Johannesburg Correctional Centre, in litigation against DCS over gender-affirming healthcare, and rights organisations' concern about implementation of the SOP.

sources.title: Nthabiseng Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre - Lawyers for Human Rights
sources.summary: Lawyers for Human Rights case page (14 Nov 2025): the South African High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, ruled in favour of transgender inmate Nthabiseng Mokoena against the Department of Correctional Services (DCS), finding unfair discrimination and harassment because DCS refused to allow her to express her gender identity (feminizing attire, she/her pronouns) and failed to provide appropriate accommodation. The court held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at State expense, rejected DCS's contrary argument, and ordered DCS to immediately implement accommodations, enforce its own SOPs relating to transgender inmates, and provide the prescribed medical care. Subject-verified: documents that trans inmates are accommodated inside the standard national corrections system (here Johannesburg Correctional Centre) and that placement/accommodation obligations rest on DCS SOPs enforced through litigation.

sources.summary: South African Human Rights Commission, acting as the National Preventive Mechanism under OPCAT (designated 4 Dec 2024), media statement (14 Nov 2025) welcoming the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, judgment (delivered 10 Nov 2025) in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075). Describes Mokoena, assigned male at birth and identifying as female from early childhood, being restricted from wearing feminine clothing and makeup and misgendered while in a correctional facility. Subject-verified: an official state human-rights body confirming that transgender persons are held in the ordinary correctional system and that the 2025 ruling affirms their rights in correctional facilities, including accommodation.
