31927357B81008000569871.name: Tabasco
31927357B81008000569871.summary:
Tabasco is a state of Mexico. It has not reformed its legislation and operates no legal gender recognition procedure; Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that the state is one of eight in Mexico with no such procedure.

Without a procedure, a trans person's identity documents never match their gender. Mismatched documents invite police stops and institutional mistreatment.

Human Rights Watch's Tabasco-dedicated report, published on 6 March 2024 and produced with a local community centre for inclusion, documents that the documentary mismatch curtails rights across four socio-economic areas.

The report sets those findings against the August 2023 murder of Karina Gómez, a trans woman killed in Tabasco.

31927357B88239390016047.name: Tamaulipas
31927357B88239390016047.summary:
Tamaulipas has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people, according to Human Rights Watch's state-by-state table dated 31 March 2025. The table places the state among eight Mexican states with no procedure at all. A trans person whose identity documents are issued in Tamaulipas therefore has no administrative route to change those documents to match their gender identity. Tamaulipas stands under Mexico's national framework, which governs passports, entry and federal enforcement.

On 18 June 2025 the Tamaulipas Congress unanimously approved reforms to the state Penal Code adding a chapter on crimes against sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression. The reforms explicitly ban conversion therapies, with prison terms of two to six years and fines of up to 2,000 UMA. Penalties rise by half where victims are minors, disabled or elderly, or where the offence occurs in a subordinate setting such as the family, a medical context or the workplace. The state's criminal law thus protects gender identity even though no administrative gender-recognition procedure exists.

On 4 February 2026 deputies of Tamaulipas's 66th legislature and LGBT+ civil-society groups agreed a joint agenda to press for a Gender Identity Law and for anti-discrimination and health reforms. The initiatives have been pending since June 2025. The absent law continues to limit trans people's access to health care, education and employment. As of early 2026 no legal gender-recognition procedure exists in Tamaulipas and the Gender Identity Law remains unpassed.

31927357B35199150741361.name: Yucatan
31927357B35199150741361.summary:
Yucatán is one of Mexico's 32 states and stands under the national framework; the federal layer of law and enforcement is carried by the national record. The rules that govern a visitor's documents, marriage and access to conversion therapy inside the state are the state's own.

Legal gender recognition in Yucatán is administrative. In 2024 the state congress passed a reform to the Civil Registry Law creating a procedure through which transgender people can update the legal gender recorded on their documents without a court order. The reform was published in the state's official gazette, the Diario Oficial, on 26 April 2024. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state rundown of 11 March 2025 carries Yucatán on that basis. The operative fact for a visitor is that a Mexican identity document issued through Yucatán's registry can be corrected by application rather than litigation.

Marriage is open to same-sex couples in Yucatán, first through the courts and then by statute. On 1 July 2013 the Third District Court of the State of Yucatán ruled that two petitioners could marry, and the first same-sex marriage in the state was registered on 8 August 2013. The Yucatán Constitutional Court dismissed a challenge to the Civil Code's marriage provisions on 2 March 2015, and the federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2015. The Congress of Yucatán passed a constitutional amendment allowing same-sex marriage on 7 September 2021 and amended secondary legislation to permit it on 1 March 2022. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classed as same-sex under local law can marry here.

Yucatán enacted a conversion-therapy (ECOSIG) ban on 25 August 2021, making the practice unlawful for those who carry it out in the state.

31927357B22408340646138.name: Zacatecas
31927357B22408340646138.summary:
Zacatecas is a state of Mexico and stands under the national framework for passports, federal identity documents and federal criminal jurisdiction. The findings below are those specific to the state.

Zacatecas has a legislated administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. Deputies of the state's 64th Legislature approved a reform of the Family Code on gender identity on 23 December 2022 by 14 votes in favour to 7 against, after the Justice Committee issued a positive opinion on the measure. The reform establishes the possibility of issuing a new birth certificate recognising an applicant's gender identity, principally for the trans community. Zacatecas is not among the states identified as having no legislated gender-recognition procedure.

Implementation followed at the administrative level. In 2023 the director of the state Civil Registry issued guidelines giving effect to the law. Human Rights Watch's March 2025 state-by-state feature on legal gender recognition records both the 2022 Family Code reform and the 2023 Civil Registry guidelines for Zacatecas.

The state's criminal law carries its own protections. On 25 August 2021 the Congress of Zacatecas approved a prohibition and sanction on conversion therapies, known locally as ECOSIG, by adding fraction VI to article 182 Bis of the state Penal Code. Anyone who incites hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or who promotes such practices, faces one to three years' imprisonment or up to 300 days of community work. The same session typified hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity in the state Penal Code.

Recognition came later than those protections. A gender-identity initiative debated in the same 2021 session, alongside a constitutional and family-code reform, failed to obtain enough votes and remained pending; the gender-identity reform passed in December 2022.

82249235B96958463903898.name: Newfoundland and Labrador
82249235B96958463903898.summary:
Newfoundland and Labrador stands under Canada's national framework on gender identity and gender expression; that national layer is carried on the country's own record and is not restated here. The findings below concern provincial documents, provincial services and enforcement of provincial responsibility.

Provincial law has not required sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing the gender marker on a birth or marriage registration since an amendment to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009 received Royal Assent on 13 April 2016. The amendment brought the statute into compliance with an order of a Board of Inquiry under the provincial Human Rights Commission, issued in December 2015 on complaints brought by two trans women.

Since 23 June 2021, when further amendments to the same act received Royal Assent, a person born outside Newfoundland and Labrador who has lived in the province for at least three months has been able to obtain a change of sex designation there. The change certificate costs $25, counts as official provincial identification, and is described by the government as a document that can be leveraged to update records in other jurisdictions. The amendments align with the earlier addition of a non-binary option on provincial birth certificates; the bill received second reading on 17 June 2021.

Under the current application rules, applicants must be 16 or older, or be represented by a parent or legal guardian, with the consent of the other parent or guardian and the written consent of applicants aged 12 to 15. Applicants must be born in the province or have resided there at least three months. The application itself carries no fee; charges apply only to official copies of the updated documents, at $35 for a new birth certificate or $30 online.

The province states that it cannot guarantee a birth certificate bearing an 'X' gender marker will be accepted by authorities in other organisations. That is the documented cross-border caveat for carrying provincial records outside Newfoundland and Labrador.

Police-reported hate crime in the province was recorded at 5.3 per 100,000 for 2024, the joint-lowest provincial rate in Canada alongside Manitoba. The figure rests on 29 incidents, up from 19 in 2023, which makes the 51 per cent rise statistically fragile at that volume. Police counts capture only incidents reported to and recorded by police. Statistics Canada published the data on 30 March 2026.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Newfoundland and Labrador (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Gender identity is explicitly included as a prohibited ground of discrimination in human rights acts in all provinces and territories and by the federal government as of 2017, prohibiting discrimination in employment, housing and public and private accommodations. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. The concepts of sex under section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms have been interpreted to include transsexuality, providing equality protection applicable to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities. In Saskatchewan, The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoked the notwithstanding clause to require schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity. In Alberta, the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024, and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act were met with legal challenges, after which Bill 9: Protecting Alberta’s Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 invoked the notwithstanding clause. British Columbia, Ontario and Saskatchewan grant parental status to three or more intentional parents, allowing for a wider range of queer and trans families. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 by the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968–69, with the general age of consent for all sexual activities 16 since June 2019, or 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency. Section 159 of the Criminal Code on anal intercourse was declared unconstitutional by courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta, with repeal pursued through Bill C-32 incorporated into Bill C-75 receiving royal assent on June 21, 2019. The Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act received royal assent on June 21, 2018, allowing the RCMP and federal departments or agencies to destroy or remove any judicial record of conviction for homosexual acts prior to being lawful in 1969 or anal intercourse under section 159. Sexual orientation was held constitutionally protected under section 15 in Egan v Canada in 1995, and failure to include it in human rights law was held a violation in Vriend v Alberta in 1998. Same-sex marriage was legalized nationwide on July 20, 2005 by the federal Civil Marriage Act, making Canada the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to do so. Same-sex adoption was legalized in Newfoundland and Labrador in 2002, with joint adoption legalized in all provinces and territories by 2011, and conversion therapy was statutorily banned nationwide for minors and adults in 2022 and made a crime under the Criminal Code. A 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office found that 87.6% said they would be "comfortable" if a neighbour was a transgender person. The same poll separately measured sexuality tolerance, finding 91.8% said they would be "comfortable" if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual, preserving a distinct result for transgender acceptance. Historical record states many transgender people in traditional Indigenous roles were in positions of reverence, where they acted as caretakers of children who had lost their families, spiritual healers and warriors in battle, with terms including Cree napêw iskwêwisêhot, Ktunaxa titqattek, Blackfoot aakíí'skassi, and Ojibwe ikwekaazo and ininiikaazo. Following colonisation and spread of Christianity by missionaries many traditions died out and transgender individuals were forced and assimilated, with Indigenous groups in the early 1990s reclaiming customs and proposing "two-spirit" to refer to a traditional and cultural "third gender," with LGBT2S or LGBTQ2S increasingly used. Formal state apologies acknowledged past harm, with the Prime Minister on November 28, 2017 apologizing "For the oppression of the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and two-spirit communities," and the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police in December 2020 apologizing for harm to Two-spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, and Queer Communities and stating "We must stand together against homophobia, transphobia, and any other kind of marginalization."

82249235B3191732862561.summary:
Prince Edward Island stands under the national framework of Canada. The province's own instruments govern gender-marker changes on provincial documents and driver's licences.

In April 2016 the MacLauchlan government tabled a bill amending the Vital Statistics Act so that an Islander can change the gender recorded on official provincial documents by declaring the gender they identify with and providing a letter from a doctor. Sex-reassignment surgery ceased to be required, and the province's gender-marker change has operated without a surgery requirement since that amendment.

Since 4 December 2018 Islanders identifying gender on a driver's licence may select 'gender not listed', shown on the licence as X, or 'prefer not to say', shown as a blank, alongside male and female. The Government of Prince Edward Island states this made the province the first jurisdiction in Canada to offer the 'prefer not to say' blank option; provincial photo ID issued at Access PEI locations can therefore carry an X or a blank gender marker.

Under the province's published process, an adult may apply for a change of gender designation if born in Prince Edward Island and resident in the province for at least three months and not in the lawful custody of another person. The application requires completed forms including a physician statement and a written statement by the applicant, with signatures arranged before a commissioner of oaths at Vital Statistics.

82249235B69645938038492.summary:
Nova Scotia stands under the Canadian national framework, which the parent record carries. Within provincial competence, the province operates no restrictive trans-specific legislation and instead maintains an explicit inclusion framework.

The Government of Nova Scotia released the province's first 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan on 8 January 2026, developed under the Dismantling Racism and Hate Act passed in 2022, described by the province as the first Canadian law of its kind to explicitly acknowledge 2SLGBTQIA+ people. The plan was informed by more than 600 community members through surveys, virtual meetings and consultations, and maps actions to improve programs and policies supporting full inclusion of 2SLGBTQIA+ people.

On 10 June 2026 the province announced more than $176,000 through the first round of its 2SLGBTQIA+ Community Impact Grant program, including $12,067 to SeaHorse Sexual Health Centre for queer and trans outreach on the Eastern Shore, $25,000 to LakeCity Works' Queer Careers program in Dartmouth, $25,000 to Pictou County Pride, and $50,000 to Truro Pride to host the province's first provincial 2SLGBTQIA+ conference. Per-project grants are capped at $25,000 from the 2025-26 fiscal year.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and accommodation is prohibited in Nova Scotia as in all Canadian provinces, territories and the federal government; as of 2017 all Canadian jurisdictions explicitly include gender identity as a prohibited ground in their human rights acts. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in Nova Scotia under provincial rules.

The documented Nova Scotia correctional case concerns a transgender woman from the Halifax region held in a men's prison while serving a two-year robbery sentence. On 18 March 2025 a federal judge granted her more time to file her application for judicial review of that placement, citing a lack of transparency and clear, timely communication in the institutional decision-making and systemic barriers restricting her access to her lawyer. No later instance of this case is documented in the record.

Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that 4,882 police-reported hate crimes were recorded nationally in 2024, a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000, down 2% in 2024 and up 142% since 2018; eight provinces recorded stable or declining rates. The release carries no Nova Scotia-specific rate or incident count. The underlying analysis of sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations comes from Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report.

In the 2024 Spartacus Gay Travel Index, Canada including Nova Scotia shared first place with Malta, New Zealand, Spain and Portugal among 213 countries and regions as a travel destination covering lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex people.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Nova Scotia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is prohibited by all provinces and territories as well as the federal government. As of 2017, all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly include gender identity as a prohibited ground of discrimination in their human rights acts. The concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15 of the Charter have been interpreted to include transsexuality and HIV/STDs, with sexual orientation added as an analogous ground in Egan v Canada in 1995. Transgender people are now able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. Saskatchewan's The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 requires schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, passed while invoking the notwithstanding clause. Alberta in 2024 passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024, and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges that the Alberta government sought to block by passing Bill 9: Protecting Alberta’s Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm to Two-spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, and Queer Communities, stated police must stand together against homophobia, transphobia and other marginalization, and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 was brought into force upon royal assent. The general age of consent for all sexual activities has been 16 since June 2019, rising to 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency, with close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15 absent trust or exploitation. Section 159 of the Criminal Code criminalizing anal intercourse was declared unconstitutional by courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta and was repealed effective June 21, 2019 through Bill C-75, setting the age of consent for anal intercourse at 16. In Egan v Canada in 1995 the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under section 15 of the Charter, and in Vriend v Alberta in 1998 held failure to include it in human rights law violated section 15. Parliament enacted the Civil Marriage Act on July 20, 2005, making Canada the fourth country and first in the Americas to legalize same-sex marriage nationwide. In 2022 Canada statutorily banned conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults and made subjecting anyone to it a crime under the Criminal Code. On June 21, 2018 royal assent was granted to the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act allowing RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records for certain homosexual acts and section 159 convictions, available to living and deceased, distinct from pardon or record suspension. In a poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office reported by 2020, 87.6% of those surveyed said they would be "comfortable" if a neighbour was a transgender person. The same poll found 91.8% said they would be "comfortable" if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual, preserving a distinction between sexuality acceptance and transgender acceptance. The article presents the transgender figure as a comfort-with-neighbour measure, not as a measure of law, enforcement, or protection outcomes. The article states no additional transgender-specific tolerance figures, enforcement data, or facility-access survey results beyond that poll result.

82249235B52639524229375.name: Quebec
82249235B52639524229375.summary:
Quebec is a province of Canada and stands under Canada's national framework: federal criminal law and the federal human-rights regime apply in Quebec as in every other province. Provincially, the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms has prohibited discrimination because of gender identity and gender expression since 2016, reaching employment, housing, and public and private accommodation.

Provincial enforcement machinery has produced a documented win for a trans visitor or resident. On 10 June 2024 the Quebec Human Rights Tribunal found that a Montreal bar had discriminated against a trans woman in hiring because of her gender identity, ordering the employer to pay $10,000 in moral damages, $4,000 in punitive damages and $118.40 for unpaid training.

Quebec's rules on sex designation and identity documents were reshaped by litigation. After a two-month trial with 29 witnesses, the Quebec Superior Court (2021 QCCS 191) declared provisions of the Civil Code of Quebec invalid because they violated the fundamental rights of trans, intersex and non-binary people; the Quebec Court of Appeal largely upheld that decision (2024 QCCA 348), and the ruling led to legislative reform of the Civil Code.

Correctional placement in Quebec now turns on anatomy rather than gender identity. On 19 June 2025 Quebec's public security minister announced that transgender inmates in the province will be incarcerated according to their anatomical sex rather than their gender identity, citing fairness and safety priorities; the directive was issued just after trans woman Levana Ballouz, convicted of murdering her partner and children, sought a transfer to a women's prison. Advocates say the policy violates the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms. This is a dated, province-specific reversal of the previous practice of considering gender identity in correctional placement.

Statistics Canada's police-reported hate crime release of 30 March 2026 reports 4,882 hate crimes nationally in 2024, a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000, with provincial rates ranging from 5.3 per 100,000 (Manitoba, Newfoundland and Labrador) to 16.0 (Ontario). No Quebec-specific rate figure appears in that release, so the record's assessment of Quebec at national parity rests on the absence of a divergent provincial figure rather than on a measured Quebec number. The underlying analysis of national police hate-crime data, including sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations, was published by Egale Canada, an LGBTIQ+ organisation.

Consensual sexual activity between adults was decriminalised nationally in 1969, and effective 21 June 2019 (S.C. 2019, c. 25) Criminal Code section 159 was repealed, barring conviction for any historical sexual offence unless the act would constitute an offence if committed on the day the charge was laid; that repeal removed that consensual-sex criminal liability in Quebec.

Quebec created civil unions by amending the Civil Code in 2002, giving couples regardless of gender or sexual orientation the same effects as marriage in respect of family direction, parental authority, expenses, family residence, family patrimony and compensatory allowance, valid only within Quebec. Same-sex adoption was legalised in Quebec in 2002.

2021 census data cited by Éducaloi indicates that 0.14% of Quebecers aged 15 and older, and 0.27% of those aged 15 to 34, identify as transgender.

Provincially, this division's charter of human rights and freedoms has prohibited discrimination because of gender identity and gender expression since 2016, reaching employment, housing, and public and private accommodation.

Provincial enforcement machinery has produced a documented win for a trans visitor or resident. On 10 June 2024 the divisional human-rights tribunal found that a bar in the division's largest city had discriminated against a trans woman in hiring because of her gender identity, ordering the employer to pay $10,000 in moral damages, $4,000 in punitive damages and $118.40 for unpaid training.

Rules on sex designation and identity documents in this division were reshaped by litigation. After a two-month trial with 29 witnesses, the division's superior trial court (2021, first-instance decision 191) declared provisions of this division's civil code invalid because they violated the fundamental rights of trans, intersex and non-binary people; the divisional court of appeal largely upheld that decision (2024, appellate decision 348), and the ruling led to legislative reform of the civil code.

Correctional placement in this division now turns on anatomy rather than gender identity. On 19 June 2025 the division's minister for public safety announced that transgender inmates in the province will be incarcerated according to their anatomical sex rather than their gender identity, citing fairness and safety priorities; the directive was issued just after a trans woman inmate, convicted of murdering her partner and children, sought a transfer to a women's prison. Advocates say the policy violates this division's charter of human rights and freedoms. This is a dated, province-specific reversal of the previous practice of considering gender identity in correctional placement.

The national statistics agency's police-reported hate crime release of 30 March 2026 reports 4,882 hate crimes nationally in 2024, a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000, with rates by province ranging from 5.3 per 100,000 (recorded jointly by two provinces) to 16.0 (recorded by another province). No rate figure specific to this division appears in that release, so the record's assessment of this division at national parity rests on the absence of a divergent provincial figure rather than on a measured figure for this division. The underlying analysis of national police hate-crime data, including sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations, was published by a national LGBTIQ+ organisation.

Consensual sexual activity between adults was decriminalised nationally in 1969, and effective 21 June 2019 (national legislation, 2019, c. 25) section 159 of the national criminal code was repealed, barring conviction for any historical sexual offence unless the act would constitute an offence if committed on the day the charge was laid; that repeal removed that consensual-sex criminal liability in this division.

This division created civil unions by amending its civil code in 2002, giving couples regardless of gender or sexual orientation the same effects as marriage in respect of family direction, parental authority, expenses, family residence, family patrimony and compensatory allowance, valid only within this division. Same-sex adoption was legalised in this division in 2002.

2021 census data cited by a public legal-information body indicates that 0.14% of residents aged 15 and older, and 0.27% of those aged 15 to 34, identify as transgender.

82249235B66370767641120.name: Ontario
82249235B66370767641120.summary:
Ontario stands under the national framework of Canada; this assessment covers Ontario's own layer: its human rights code, the commission that administers it, the province's published policy, and Ontario's recorded hate-crime figures.

The Ontario Human Rights Commission's policy on gender identity and gender expression states that under the Ontario Human Rights Code people are protected from discrimination and harassment on those grounds in employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts, and membership in unions, trade or professional associations. The policy defines gender identity as a person's internal and individual experience of gender and notes that a chosen name and pronoun are common ways of expressing gender. It is the official provincial statement of the human-rights protections a trans person holds in Ontario's workplaces, housing and services.

Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that police recorded 4,882 hate crimes in Canada in 2024, 1% more than in 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Ontario recorded the highest provincial rate at 16.0 incidents per 100,000 population. The figure covers all reported motivations and does not isolate gender-identity motivation. Police figures capture only reported incidents, and reporting levels are shaped by awareness and community trust.

On 28 August 2023 Ontario education minister Stephen Lecce said parents 'must be fully involved and fully aware' of a child's decision to use a different name or pronoun at school. He said teachers and school boards already weigh 'exceptional circumstances' and potential harm to the child. Ontario had not adopted parental-consent legislation of the kind other provinces were enacting at that time, and no later Ontario legislative instance on this question is documented in this record.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Ontario (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: All federal, provincial and territorial human rights acts explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity, including in employment, housing and public and private accommodations as of 2017. Section 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms has been interpreted so that the concepts of sex and physical disability include transsexuality, providing equal protection guidance for courts interpreting human rights laws. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause to require schools to obtain parental consent for students under 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, which drew calls for repeal and legal action. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024 and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges in Alberta courts, and in 2025 the government passed Bill 9: Protecting Alberta’s Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause to prevent the challenges. On November 28, 2017 the Prime Minister issued a formal parliamentary apology for the oppression of the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and two-spirit communities. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm from not fully supporting Two-spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer Communities, acknowledged institutional bias, intolerance and human rights violations causing suffering, shame, trauma and distrust, pledged to stand against homophobia, transphobia and other marginalization, and created the Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968–69 (Bill C-150) received royal assent. Since June 2019 the general age of consent for all sexual activities is 16, rising to 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency or exploitation, with limited close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15. Former Criminal Code section 159 criminalizing anal intercourse was declared unconstitutional by courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta as violating Charter equality, and was repealed through Bill C-75 which received royal assent on June 21, 2019 setting the age at 16. In Egan v Canada (1995) the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is protected under section 15 of the Charter as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta (1998) it held failure to include sexual orientation in Alberta human rights law violated section 15. Parliament enacted the federal Civil Marriage Act on July 20, 2005 making Canada the fourth country worldwide and first in the Americas to legalize same-sex marriage nationwide, after court rulings required it in most provinces and territories by July 2005. Same-sex adoption was legalized province by province from British Columbia in 1996 to Nunavut in 2011, with stepchild adoption in Alberta from 1999 and joint adoption from 2007. In 2022 Canada became the third country worldwide and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults and make subjecting anyone to it a crime as defined in the Criminal Code. On June 21, 2018 the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act received royal assent allowing RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records for pre-1969 homosexual acts and section 159 convictions, available to living and deceased persons as recognition of historical injustice distinct from pardon or record suspension. In a poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office reported for 2020, 87.6% said they would be "comfortable" if a neighbour was a transgender person. In the same poll, 91.8% said they would be "comfortable" if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual, preserving a distinction between sexuality tolerance and transgender tolerance. The article documents that different Indigenous groups had traditions referring to transgender, gender variance or sexual identity in which many transgender people in traditional roles were in positions of reverence as caretakers of children who had lost families, spiritual healers and warriors in battle. It states that following colonisation and the spread of Christianity by missionaries many of these traditions began to die out, transgender individuals were forced and assimilated into Europe-centric culture and perceptions changed even among Indigenous peoples, before Indigenous groups in the early 1990s sought to reclaim customs including proposing the term "two-spirit" for a traditional and cultural "third gender."

82249235B50381585000441.name: Manitoba
82249235B50381585000441.summary:
The Manitoba Human Rights Code prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and accommodation. On 18 March 2025 the provincial government introduced a bill to add gender expression as a protected ground; Justice Minister Matt Wiebe stated the change would bring Manitoba into line with most other provinces and would cover preferred pronouns and outward appearance such as clothing. The bill was before the Legislative Assembly for debate later in 2025, and Trans Manitoba executive director Charlie Eau welcomed it.

Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that police in Canada recorded 4,882 hate crimes in 2024, a 1% increase over 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Manitoba recorded the joint-lowest provincial rate at 5.3 per 100,000, alongside Newfoundland and Labrador, with no increase in 2024; it was one of eight provinces whose rates were stable or declining. The underlying analysis of sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations in that data was published by Egale Canada, an LGBTIQ+ organisation. Police-reported figures capture only incidents reported to police.

On 30 May 2024 the Manitoba legislature passed a bill recognising 31 March as Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility, brought forward by Logan Oxenham, a backbench New Democrat MLA for Kirkfield Park who is transgender. Oxenham said the day would show transgender, two-spirit and non-binary Manitobans that they are supported.

On 20 November 2023 the province raised the transgender flag in Winnipeg's Memorial Park for the Transgender Day of Remembrance, an observance first marked eight years earlier. The flag was raised by Logan Oxenham, the first openly trans man elected to the Manitoba legislature. Families minister Nahanni Fontaine and health minister Uzoma Asagwara stated that the government supports and upholds the life-saving work of trans, two-spirit and gender-diverse Manitobans. Brandon advocate Anastasia Gibson said the day memorialises people murdered as a result of transphobia, violence she said shows no sign of slowing.

sources.summary: Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is prohibited by all provinces and territories as well as the federal government, with explicit inclusion as a prohibited ground completed as of 2017. Transgender people are now able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules, while vital statistics including identity documents such as birth certificates fall under provincial jurisdiction. The concepts of sex under section 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms have been interpreted to include transsexuality, and section 15 applies to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities, with courts required to interpret human rights statutes consistently with the Charter. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause, requiring schools to obtain parental consent for students under 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, prompting human rights calls for repeal and legal action. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024, and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, then prevented Alberta court challenges by passing Bill 9: Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025, which used the notwithstanding clause. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, and Queer Communities, stated police must stand together against homophobia, transphobia and marginalization, and created the Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and discrimination in practices and policies. Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private was decriminalized June 27, 1969 by the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Bill C-150), and the former section 159 anal-intercourse offence was declared unconstitutional by courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta and repealed by Bill C-75 receiving royal assent June 21, 2019, leaving a general age of consent of 16 since June 2019, 18 where there is trust, authority, dependency or exploitation, with close-in-age exceptions for ages 12-15. In Egan v Canada (1995) the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under section 15 as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta (1998) failure to include sexual orientation in a human rights law violated section 15; section 15 binds laws and government including law enforcement subject to section 1 reasonable limits under the Oakes Test and section 33 notwithstanding clause, which has never been used by federal Parliament. Same-sex marriage became legal nationwide July 20, 2005 by the federal Civil Marriage Act after 2002-2005 court rulings, making Canada the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas, while Alberta's 2000 Marriage Act opposite-sex definition invoking section 33 was invalid because capacity to marry is exclusive federal jurisdiction and the exemption expired in 2005. Adoption by same-sex couples was legalized in all provinces and territories between 1996 and 2011, from British Columbia in 1996 to Nunavut in 2011, with stepchild adoption in Alberta in 1999 and joint adoption in 2007. Discrimination on sexual orientation in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is now prohibited federally and in all provinces and territories. In 2022 Canada statutorily banned conversion therapy nationwide for minors and adults and made it a crime to subject anyone to it as defined in the Criminal Code. On November 28, 2017 the Prime Minister apologized for oppression of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and two-spirit communities, followed June 21, 2018 by the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act requiring RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records for pre-1969 homosexual acts and section 159 convictions for living and deceased persons, and in December 2020 police chiefs apologized for decades of oppression from the 1960s onward. Transgender-specific tolerance finding: in a poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office reported for 2020, 87.6% said they would be "comfortable" if a neighbour was a transgender person. Broader sexuality-acceptance trend: 2020 Pew Research showed 85% of Canada's general population, 92% among ages 18-29, favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013. 82249235B9619254975586.name: Yukon
82249235B9619254975586.summary:
Yukon is a territory of Canada. Its human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression among prohibited grounds of discrimination, covering employment, housing, and public and private accommodation.

Legal change of gender is available in Yukon. Vital statistics and identity documents such as birth certificates fall under territorial jurisdiction; the sources reviewed do not set out Yukon's own requirements for amending a marker.

On 30 March 2026 the Yukon Legislature marked International Transgender Day of Visibility, with members rising to speak across party lines. Yukon Party MLA Wade Istchenko (Kluane) praised the courage, resilience, contributions and accomplishments of transgender, two-spirited and gender-diverse Yukoners, acknowledged that too many people have experienced discrimination, harassment and hate for far too long, and cited a national study showing transgender 15-17-year-olds face 7.6 times the risk of suicide attempt. This is the territory's own cross-party, in-legislature acknowledgement of trans residents on record.

On 13 June 2024 Yukon News reported that a Pride flag was allegedly vandalized and stolen from Holy Family Elementary School in Whitehorse's Porter Creek neighbourhood over a weekend in June 2024, with a replacement flag promptly put up. In a statement issued 12 June, Yukon Education Minister Jeanie McLean reaffirmed her commitment to the territory's sexual orientation and gender identity policy (SOGI 123).

Statistics Canada's release 'Police-reported hate crime in Canada, 2024' (published 30 March 2026) reports that police reported 4,882 hate crimes in 2024, up 1% on 2023 and up 169% since 2018, at a rate of 11.9 per 100,000. Hate crimes targeting gender identity or expression rose 8% to 139, a fourth consecutive yearly increase and up 184% since 2020. These are national figures; the release does not report Yukon-level victimisation. Police-reported hate crime rates are about 2.5 times higher in large metropolitan areas (13.9 per 100,000) than in smaller towns (5.5), which bears on sparsely-populated territories where reporting infrastructure is thinner.

Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis examines police-reported hate-crime data with gender identity or expression and sexual-orientation motivations; its figures are national and do not report Yukon-level victimisation.

82249235B82395866892480.summary:
The Northwest Territories is a territory of Canada. Criminal law, human rights protections and entry rules are set nationally rather than by the territory, and the territory's own legislative activity on transgender issues concerns vital statistics and name change.

In June 2026 the Legislative Assembly was taking feedback from police and from the Northern Mosaic Network on proposed amendments to the Vital Statistics Act and the Change of Name Act intended to make the legislation more inclusive for transgender, non-binary, gender-diverse and two-spirit people. The proposals include an option for trans and non-binary people to request that a name change not be published in the NWT Gazette. This is the first on-record territorial legislation in the Northwest Territories specifically addressing transgender and non-binary people. The amendments were under consultation and had not been enacted.

The RCMP has taken a position against part of the proposal. Chief Superintendent Dyson Smith asked MLAs to remove or amend the registrar general's option not to notify authorities, arguing that criminal records are tied to a person's legal name and that officers may put themselves in danger if records are not transferred to a new name. Yellowknife North MLA Shauna Morgan pressed the RCMP on how officers would verify legal names without identification. The police service is therefore on record opposing a measure designed to keep a trans person's former name out of public view.

Organised community support for trans and Two-Spirit young people is documented in the territory. In June 2023 the Beaufort Delta Education Council bused seventeen regional students into Inuvik for pride events centred on feeling comfortable in one's own gender and sexuality, with workshops led by Two-Spirit Anishinaabe/Metis musician G.R. Gritt, a screening of 'Small Town Pride' and a pride parade. The gathering included a moment of silence at the Inuvik Community Greenhouse for Frank Gruben, an LGBTQ2S community member from Aklavik missing since 2023.

Tulita, a small hamlet on the Mackenzie River in the Sahtu region, held its first Pride celebration on 28 June 2025, organised jointly by Chief Albert Wright School, the hamlet administration and the local RCMP detachment. Const. Matt Ryan counted more than 50 attendees and described the day as creating a safe and welcoming space for the 2SLGBTQI+ community. The RCMP covered food and paint while the hamlet and school supplied volunteers, firewood and the venue.

82249235B23927232378620.summary:
Nunavut is a territory of Canada and stands under the national human-rights and criminal law framework of the country, supplemented by territorial statute. The Nunavut Human Rights Act prohibits discrimination on the grounds of gender identity and gender expression: members of the Legislative Assembly voted unanimously on third and final reading of Bill 31 on 13 March 2017, and Justice Minister Keith Peterson stated that the amendment would make clear that discrimination against transgender people is prohibited. At the time of that vote Nunavut was the first Canadian territory to list gender identity or expression among the protected grounds in its human-rights law.

Nunavut birth certificates carry a third, non-binary sex designation. On 18 September 2025 members of the Legislative Assembly voted 12-8 in committee of the whole to restore that option through amendments to the Vital Statistics Act, after the standing committee had struck it from Health Minister John Main's May 2025 bill, and the bill was then approved on third reading. Bill sponsor Adam Arreak Lightstone said the Government of Nunavut now joins the rest of Canada in recognising non-binary and transgender individuals.

The territorial government funds transition-related care for transgender and non-binary residents. Reporting of 22 March 2022 records that the Nunavut Health Department began funding such care, with breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty named among the procedures, under a partnership with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal. The local LGBTQ group Positive Space called the funding overdue while flagging information gaps for residents living outside the capital.

No trans-specific violent incident, hate-crime count or victimisation figure for Nunavut itself is documented in this record, and no dated instance of anti-trans violence in the territory appears in it.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Nunavut (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: As of 2017, all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly include gender identity as a prohibited ground of discrimination in their human rights acts, prohibiting discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations. The Supreme Court has interpreted the concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15(1) of the Charter to include transsexuality, and section 15 applies to all laws and government institutions in Canada including law enforcement authorities. Transgender people are now able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause, with controversy over its requirement that schools obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request the use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, prompting calls for repeal and legal action. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024 and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges in Alberta courts, but the government shielded them by passing Bill 9: Protecting Alberta’s Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm, institutional bias and rights violations toward Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer communities, stated police must stand together against transphobia and other marginalization, and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968–69 (Bill C-150) was brought into force upon royal assent. Since June 2019 the general age of consent for all sexual activities has been 16, with age 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency and close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15, after former section 159 criminalizing anal intercourse was repealed by Bill C-75 receiving royal assent on June 21, 2019. In Egan v Canada in 1995 the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under the equality clause of the Charter as an analogous ground under section 15, and in Vriend v Alberta in 1998 it found failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law itself violated section 15. Same-sex marriage became legal nationwide on July 20, 2005 with the federal Civil Marriage Act, making Canada the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to legalize it, following court rulings between 2002 and 2005, while same-sex adoption was legalized in all provinces and territories with Nunavut last in 2011. In 2022 Canada statutorily banned conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults and made it a crime to subject anyone to it as defined in the Criminal Code, the third country in the world and first in North America to do so. On June 21, 2018 royal assent was granted to the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act allowing the RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records of pre-1969 homosexual convictions and section 159 convictions, available to living and deceased persons and distinct from a pardon or record suspension, following the Prime Minister’s formal apology on November 28, 2017. On sexuality-specific tolerance, 2020 Pew Research showed that 85% of Canada’s general population (92% among Canadians aged 18 to 29) favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013. June 2013 polls showed a vast majority blessing same-sex marriage available since 2005, with 70% agreeing that “same-sex couples should have the same rights to adopt children as heterosexual couples do” and 76% agreeing that “same-sex couples are just as likely as other parents to successfully raise children”. Canada was referred to as the most gay-friendly country when ranked first for least dangerous in Asher & Lyric’s LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024. The largest cities feature gay areas including Toronto’s Church and Wellesley, Montreal’s Gay Village, Vancouver’s Davie Village and Ottawa’s Bank Street Gay Village, with Pride celebrated every summer in major cities with federal, provincial and municipal political figures. Distinct from sexuality tolerance, on transgender-specific tolerance the article documents that “87.6% said they would be ‘comfortable’ if a neighbour was a transgender person” in a 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office, compared to 91.8% saying they would be “comfortable” if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual.

sources.title: Criminal Code s.159 repeal via Bill C-32 / Bill C-75
sources.summary: Assented 2019-06-21, S.C. 2019, c. 25 repealed Criminal Code section 159 criminalizing anal intercourse and barred conviction for any historical sexual offence unless the act would constitute an offence if committed on the day the charge was laid, eliminating criminal liability in Nunavut for consensual conduct previously captured by the repealed provision.

The territorial human-rights act prohibits discrimination on the grounds of gender identity and gender expression: members of the legislature voted unanimously on third and final reading of a bill on 13 March 2017, and the justice minister stated at the time that the amendment would make clear that discrimination against transgender people is prohibited. At the time of that vote this territory was the first territory within this country to list gender identity or expression among the protected grounds in its human-rights law.

Birth certificates issued here carry a third, non-binary sex designation. On 18 September 2025 members of the legislature voted 12-8 in committee of the whole to restore that option through amendments to the vital statistics statute, after the standing committee had struck it from the health minister's May 2025 bill, and the bill was then approved on third reading. The bill's sponsor said the territorial government now joins the rest of this country in recognising non-binary and transgender individuals.

The territorial government funds transition-related care for transgender and non-binary residents. Reporting of 22 March 2022 records that the territorial health department began funding such care, with breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty named among the procedures, under a partnership with a surgical centre in a major city of a neighbouring jurisdiction. The local LGBTQ group called the funding overdue while flagging information gaps for residents living outside the capital.

14339913B95766344400054.summary:
England stands under the United Kingdom's national framework, which the national record carries.

The definitions that govern services, searches and detention allocation in England were fixed by the UK Supreme Court's unanimous judgment in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers, handed down 16 April 2025. "Woman" and "sex" in the Equality Act 2010 mean biological woman and biological sex, so a gender recognition certificate does not entitle a trans woman to the Act's sex-based protections. Lord Hodge stated that the ruling should not be read as reducing the Act's protection against discrimination for transgender people.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission, the body enforcing the Equality Act 2010 in England and Wales, updated its code of practice on 20 May 2025 in response to that judgment. The code advises that services and businesses may ask a person for a birth certificate where there is "genuine concern" about biological sex, and that trans people may be excluded from single-sex sport "when necessary" for safety. This is the operative guidance a trans visitor encounters at venues, transport and services.

Prison and custody decisions in England are governed by the same UK-wide ruling, under which Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights confers no automatic right to accommodation with the opposite biological sex. In argument on 5 February 2026 in a judicial review testing how far that ruling reaches into prison accommodation, government lawyers said a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while For Women Scotland called the identity-based policy "Orwellian".

The Home Office statistics for England and Wales, published 9 October 2025, record 115,990 police-recorded hate crimes in the year ending March 2025. The transgender strand fell 11% and the sexual-orientation strand 2% against the previous year. The bulletin cautions that recorded figures understate prevalence, giving a Crime Survey estimate of about 176,000 hate-crime incidents a year, and that a February 2024 Metropolitan Police recording-system change means earlier years over-counted.

The Supreme Court had already held that Article 8 confers no automatic right to accommodation with the opposite biological sex, and that UK-wide ruling governs England's prison and custody decisions. The first minister said the government will consider the judgment.

The UK Supreme Court's April 2025 ruling is the predicate for England's EHRC code and BTP strip-search policy, and a judicial review reported by BBC News on 5 February 2026 tests how far it reaches into prison accommodation UK-wide. In argument, government lawyers said a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while For Women Scotland called the identity-based policy 'Orwellian'.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in England (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In 1970 Corbett v Corbett barred transgender people from changing the sex marker on their birth certificate, which also prevented legal marriage to a person of the other gender as it would have been treated as an unrecognised same-sex marriage. In 1996 P v S and Cornwall County Council held that European anti-gender discrimination law applied to trans people, and in 2002 Goodwin v United Kingdom found the UK in breach of Articles 8 and 12 of the European Convention on Human Rights for maintaining that status quo, leading to the Gender Recognition Act 2004. A December 2002 Lord Chancellor's policy document categorically stated that transsexualism "is not a mental illness." Since 4 April 2005 the Gender Recognition Act 2004 has allowed transgender people to change legal gender and obtain a new birth certificate giving full recognition of acquired sex for all purposes. Applicants must present evidence to a Gender Recognition Panel for a Gender Recognition Certificate, must have transitioned for two years before issuance, and are not required to have undergone sex reassignment surgery though such surgery counts as supporting evidence, with formal approval for medical gender reassignment available on the NHS or privately. Under the Act as originally framed, a married transgender applicant was required to divorce or annul the marriage before issuance of a certificate, and a married couple including a transgender partner could not directly re-register but had to dissolve the marriage, obtain gender recognition, then register for civil partnership with associated paperwork and costs. ILGA-Europe's executive in 2020 expressed concern about a "hostile climate on trans rights fuelled by opposition groups" as the UK fell to ninth place with 66%, dropping further to 22nd place with 45% by 2025. The 1533 Buggery Act made male anal sex a civil offence punishable by death in England and Wales, later removed as capital by section 61 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 while male homosexual acts remained imprisonable, and lesbian acts were never criminalised as civilian offences. The Sexual Offences Act 1967, receiving royal assent 27 July 1967, provided limited decriminalisation in England and Wales only where the act was consensual, in private limited to two persons, and both were aged 21, a higher threshold than 16 for heterosexual acts and strictly interpreted to exclude hotel rooms or homes with a third person present. Equalisation came through the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2000, in force 8 January 2001, lowering the age of consent to 16 throughout the UK and for the first time creating an age of consent for lesbian acts, followed by the Sexual Offences Act 2003 in force 1 May 2004 which removed privacy conditions and created sex-neutral offences. Section 28, introduced in the 1980s to prohibit "promotion of homosexuality" by schools and local authorities, was repealed in 2003, while discrimination protections in place since 1999 were extended to all areas by the Equality Act 2010 and the ban on open service by LGBT personnel was officially lifted in 2016 after non-enforcement since 2000. The Merchant Shipping (Homosexual Conduct) Act 2017 repealed sections 146(4) and 147(3) of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, and the Policing and Crime Act 2017 in effect 31 January 2017 provided posthumous pardons and a disregard application process for historic convictions, with "disregards" available since 2012 under the Protection of Freedoms Act. Civil partnerships with most rights of marriage were legalised by the Civil Partnership Act 2004 effective 5 December 2005, adoption by same-sex couples in England and Wales took effect 30 December 2005 under the Adoption and Children Act 2002, and same-sex marriage in England and Wales was allowed by the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 in force 13 March 2014 with first marriages 29 March 2014. ILGA-Europe gave the UK the highest score in Europe in 2015 with 86% progress toward "respect of human rights and full equality" for LGBT people, but the score fell to 66% and ninth place by 2020.

82085004B13995298844162.name: Queensland
82085004B13995298844162.summary:
Queensland is a state of Australia and stands under the national framework; the national record carries the federal law, and this record covers the state layer.

Gender identity has been a protected attribute under Queensland's Anti-Discrimination Act since 2002. Amendments that commenced on 29 April 2024 moved serious vilification out of that Act and into the Criminal Code, with a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment, raised from six months. The same amendments explicitly extend protection to non-binary and gender-diverse people and broaden the definition of gender identity. The Queensland Human Rights Commission described the Anti-Discrimination Bill 2024 as a rewrite that modernised the gender identity attribute and revised the vilification provisions.

Queensland was the first Australian state to criminalise conversion practices. The Health Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 passed the parliament on 13 August 2020, making practices including electro-shock, drug and hypnotherapy aimed at changing a person's sexuality or gender identity offences carrying fines and imprisonment for practitioners, with a maximum of 18 months. Survivors report that the ban does not reach conversion practices in informal, non-healthcare settings.

Access to gender-affirming care for minors has been restricted since January 2025. The health minister, Tim Nicholls, halted puberty blockers and hormone therapy for new public-system patients under 18 with gender dysphoria, formalised by a Queensland Health directive of 28 January 2025. The restriction remains in force and is legally contested. Patients already enrolled with the Queensland Children's Gender Service are exempt, so the practical effect falls on new patients and their families.

Queensland documents have carried an X non-binary option alongside male and female since 1 September 2021, including marriage certificates and official forms. Transgender and intersex residents can update government records and their birth certificate; the requirement to divorce before changing a record was repealed in 2018 and the surgery requirement was repealed in 2024.

State law recognises relationships through civil partnership registration or an unregistered de facto relationship, recognised since 2002. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can register a civil partnership or rely on de facto recognition in the same way as any other couple.

The state's criminal-law regime has been progressively liberalised. Private consensual sex between men has been legal since 1991, and lesbian sexual acts were never criminalised. The age of consent was equalised at 16 for all sexual acts in 2016, Queensland being the last Australian jurisdiction to do so; the former section 208 carried up to 14 years' imprisonment for anal sex involving a person under 18. The gay panic defence was abolished from the criminal law in 2017.

82085004B14973555098025.summary:
South Australia stands under the Australian national framework: federal law, federal courts and national entry rules apply here and are carried by the national assessment. The findings below are the state's own.

State anti-discrimination law protects gender identity and sexual orientation. The Equal Opportunity Act 1984 was amended in 2016 to add both grounds, giving trans residents and visitors a state-level remedy alongside the federal one.

Hate-crime sentencing laws that explicitly cover sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex characteristics passed and were implemented in November 2021, so offences motivated by a victim's gender identity fall within the state's sentencing aggravation provisions.

The gay-panic defence was abolished on 1 December 2020 and ceased to operate on 1 April 2021. A defendant can no longer rely on a claimed non-heterosexual advance by the victim as a partial defence.

The Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2024 is in legal effect from 1 April 2025, prohibiting conversion practices in the state.

Birth certificate changes have been available since 23 May 2017 under the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration (Gender Identity) Amendment Act 2016, which received royal assent on 15 December 2016. A change of sex descriptor requires appropriate clinical treatment but not sex-reassignment surgery, and a marriage does not have to be ended first. Non-binary and indeterminate sex descriptors are also available on state birth certificates.

Registered domestic relationships have been available since 1 August 2017. Marriage is recognised under the federal Act that took effect in December 2017; 62.5% of South Australian respondents voted Yes in the 2017 postal survey.

82085004B70793016411369.name: Tasmania
82085004B70793016411369.summary:
Tasmania is an Australian state and stands under the national framework carried by the parent record. Within Tasmania, the Anti-Discrimination Act 1998 prohibits discrimination on the grounds of gender identity, gender expression, sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics. A September 2013 amendment extended the Act's reach to transgender and intersex people and made it unlawful to offend, humiliate, intimidate, insult or ridicule a person on the basis of actual or perceived gender, sexual orientation or gender identity. The 2019 amendments to the same Act added gender expression, an express definition of gender identity covering being transgender or transsexual and identifying or living as another gender, and sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics, including as grounds for the prohibition on incitement of hatred.

Gender registration on a Tasmanian-registered birth is self-declared. Act 2019 No. 7, amending the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act 1999, received royal assent on 8 May 2019 and took effect on 5 September 2019: no medical certificate or other medical document is required, and a person aged 16 or over may register male, female, indeterminate gender, non-binary or another self-described gender without parental approval. Parents or guardians may register a gender for a child under 16, supported by the child's own gender declaration where the child is able to give it. Birth sex registration remains male-or-female only and cannot be changed except to correct an initial error, but it ceases upon gender registration. The same laws let parents choose whether a child's gender is recorded, allow a person to remove a gender descriptor entirely, permit parents to change a child's legal gender, and extend the registration period for parents of intersex children to 120 days after birth. Tasmania issues 'X' sex descriptors on birth certificates as of 2019.

The 2019 reforms passed the Tasmanian House of Assembly on 10 April 2019 after Liberal Speaker Sue Hickey crossed the floor to vote with the Opposition, the bill having already passed the Legislative Council. They made gender on birth certificates optional and removed the requirement that transgender people undergo surgery for their gender to be recognised. The Tasmanian Government opposed the amendments and declined to rule out later repeal; no repeal is recorded in the sources reviewed.

The age of consent in Tasmania is 17 years, equal for all forms of sexual activity, a figure shared only with South Australia.

A hate crimes bill passed the lower house in September 2025 and explicitly includes gender identity within the 1997 sentencing act. The upper house had not voted on it in the sources reviewed.

Cross-dressing was an offence under section 8(1)(d) of the Police Offences Act 1935 until its repeal on 12 April 2001, Tasmania having been the only Australian state to criminalise it. Charges and convictions under that provision as in force before 12 April 2001, including attempts and inciting, instigating, aiding or abetting, are eligible for expungement on application under the Expungement of Historical Offences Act 2017, which received royal assent on 21 November 2017, with expungement available from 9 April 2018 and compensation of up to $75,000 available from 2 August 2026. The expungement scheme followed a parliamentary apology on 13 April 2017.

As of September 2026 conversion therapy practices remain legally permitted within Tasmania.

Same-sex couples can enter registered domestic partnerships in Tasmania with an optional official ceremony.

No state-specific incident series, enforcement pattern or trans-specific violence figure for Tasmania appears in the sources reviewed.

Norfolk Island, Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands and Jervis Bay Territory have no territory-specific law on gender identity, sexual orientation or intersex status. Each stands under Australia's national framework, which the national record carries; the territory-specific question is which body of law attaches to each.

Norfolk Island was incorporated into New South Wales legislation from 1 July 2016 under the Norfolk Island Legislation Amendment Act 2015 and the Territories Legislation Amendment Act 2016. A visitor there meets New South Wales law rather than a Norfolk Island enactment.

Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, administered together as the Australian Indian Ocean Territories, are jurisdictions in which Western Australian law applies.

Jervis Bay Territory is governed directly under Commonwealth law, and the Commonwealth Sex Discrimination Act 1984, as amended in 2013, applies throughout Australia including the external territories governed directly by Commonwealth law. That statute is the anti-discrimination framework a visitor to Jervis Bay stands under.

Availability of the 'X' sex descriptor and anti-discrimination protection on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity or expression extend across the states and territories alongside concurrent federal protection. sources.summary: Brazil's national framework: same-sex marriage legal nationwide via CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), adoption since 2010 (full rights 2015), and gender-marker change without surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option nationwide, though civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020 and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. First transgender federal legislators (Salabert, Hilton) were elected in 2022.

OutRight International reports that Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination, and trans voters may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections.

An OAB/SP guide for expatriates states that Brazil has among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America on paper: same-sex marriage (CNJ Resolution 175/2013), joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia and transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism (ADO 26 and MI 4733, 13 June 2019, imprisonment 1-5 years). Enforcement is uneven in practice. Major cities including Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasilia, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianopolis are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

On 19 February 2022 the Public Defender's Office of Amapá filed the state's first request for name and gender rectification on behalf of a non-binary person, treating the request as legally viable on the same self-determination basis as for transgender people and arguing that the registry should reflect social presentation.
