14911670B46798344041190.name: Amazonas
14911670B46798344041190.summary:
Amazonas stands under Brazil's national framework, and adds its own layer of protection. State Ordinary Law No. 3079 of 12 September 2006 prohibits discrimination on grounds of gender identity across employment, housing and other areas, and a provision in force since 2 August 2006 prohibits the manufacture, sale and distribution of symbols inciting discrimination, prejudice, hatred or violence on gender-identity grounds.

Non-binary recognition is not available in practice through Amazonas registries. In 2022 Alex Souza de Sa became the first non-binary person in the state to obtain recognition, doing so only after a rectification in Rio de Janeiro and an intervention by the Amazonas Public Defenders Office in Manaus, where no gender-neutral marker existed. Non-binary recognition in the state remains decided case by case.

Facilities are a live exposure in the state capital. On 18 October 2022 the mayor of Manaus signed a municipal law prohibiting unisex or multigender restrooms, and Equaldex records that bathroom access in Amazonas carries no explicit legal protection.

Access to gender-affirming care is contested on two fronts. On 10 June 2025 the governor of Amazonas signed Law 7552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under 18. In the opposite direction, in November 2023 the State Public Defenders Office opened a collective procedure to monitor public health services for trans and travesti people, covering hormone treatment, outpatient services and the refusal of authorisation for transsexualising surgeries including sexual reassignment surgery; after an October 2023 meeting, Manaus municipal health officials committed to dispensing standardised medications on Ambulatório Codajás prescriptions for hormone therapy and to designating reference primary-care units in each zone of the city, and the state health secretariat was required to report on gaps in equitable care and hormone therapy. In August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutors Office recommended that Amazonas formally enable outpatient and hospital transsexualisation services, including sexual reassignment surgeries, with deadlines for approval and for presentation to the Ministry of Health.

Recorded violence against LGBTQ people in Amazonas is thin and structurally undercounted. Research published in the Brazilian Journal of Public Security finds that cases of violence against LGBTQ people in the state are underreported, and the Brazilian Public Security Forum has registered 43 cases. For 2021-2022, crimes reported in Manaus and the interior involving homosexual, lesbian, bisexual and transsexual persons accounted for 0.36% of all reports, with homophobia and transphobia motives and the categories of gender, sexuality, race and intersectionality absent from the records; LGBT victim data were few and poorly structured, victims were not infrequently recorded as perpetrators because of failures in police occurrence reports, and public agents were unprepared to handle these demands. On 5 July 2025 Fernando Vilaca de Souza was beaten and killed in Manaus after reacting to homophobic insults, with residents reporting that he had been bullied by other young people in the region.

State and municipal law also restricts LGBTQ expression and public presence. Amazonas Ordinary Law No. 6463, enacted 10 October 2023, expressly prohibits the use of neutral language, non-binary dialect or any expression departing from standard Portuguese in curricula and teaching materials of public and private educational institutions and in official documents of educational institutions and public agencies across the state. State Law 6469 of 2023 prohibits the participation of children and adolescents in pride parades, with fines of up to 10,000 reais for non-compliance. On 17 October 2024 the Legislative Assembly enacted a law prohibiting reproduction of digital media using children linked to homosexuality; it was amended on 13 December 2025 to remove the term homosexuality and instead prohibit reproduction of sexual content linked to children in cultural and artistic media.

Protection machinery exists at state level alongside those restrictions. In 2021 the State Public Defenders Office created the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group, focused on human rights violations and on training security agents. In August 2024 the Amazonas State Court of Justice released the booklet Home is a Right, aimed at LGBTQ youth expelled from their homes, which states that conversion therapies are prohibited and ineffective and points readers to the Specialized Human Rights Public Defender's Office. In November 2012 a judge of the Amazonas Court of Justice authorised the state's first adoption by a same-sex couple.

14911670B32365136910534.name: Piaui
14911670B32365136910534.summary:
Piauí sits within Brazil's national framework for LGBTI people; national rules on marriage, legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination and custody placement apply in the state. The findings below are those specific to Piauí.

The state's own statutory layer is Ordinary Law No. 5,431, signed by the Governor on 29 December 2004, which bans discrimination based on sexual orientation. The source does not record gender identity among the grounds it covers.

Ordinary Law No. 5,916, enacted on 10 November 2009 and published on 12 November 2009, guarantees travestis and transexuais the right to be identified by their social name on registrations, forms, medical records and related documents when using the services of all direct and indirect state public administration bodies. The law defines the social name as the name by which they recognise themselves and are recognised socially, requires it to appear first and prominently with civil identification below, directs the Executive to designate within 60 days the body responsible for registration and issuance of social-name identification, and retains use of the civil name where public interest or third-party rights require.

On 20 July 2021 the Piauí judiciary granted civil registration as a non-binary person to a young person, the first recognition of a non-binary gender marker in the state.

On 14 December 2012 the Court of Justice of Piauí began granting marriage licences to same-sex couples through all notaries statewide, without the need for a judge's approval; the change was published in the Diário de Justiça on 17 December 2012. In 2012 Judge Maria Luiza de Moura de Melo e Freitas of the 1st Children and Youth Court granted adoption rights to a lesbian couple living together in a stable union since 2007.

Teresina restricts facilities. On 17 June 2026 the city council approved by 12 votes to 5, with one abstention, a bill prohibiting transgender women and travestis from using women's public restrooms, and on 30 July 2026 Mayor Sílvio Mendes signed it into law after LGBTQ rights activists protested that it is unconstitutional. The measure governs the capital only; no statewide facilities law is recorded.

Violence risk in the state is documented only in aggregate. A 2015 Grupo Gay da Bahia report listed Piauí as the second Brazilian state with the highest risk of LGBTQ people being murdered. That ranking is LGBTQ-wide rather than transgender-specific, and the source supplies no per-capita rate and no transgender-specific breakdown, so it does not establish a separate trans-specific risk level.

14911670B96632893955983.name: Acre
14911670B96632893955983.summary:
Acre is a state of Brazil and stands under the national framework carried in the Brazil record: nationwide marriage, gender-marker self-declaration and the 2019 criminalisation of transphobia on the same footing as racism apply here as elsewhere in the country. What Acre adds is a state and municipal layer of anti-discrimination, social-name and document-rectification instruments, and a documented pattern of social friction outside the capital.

Assessments of Brazil describe enforcement as uneven in practice. Smaller cities and rural areas, including those in Acre, may present more social friction than the major cities despite identical legal rights.

Violence data for the state is thin. The Associação de Homossexuais do Acre recorded 18 murders of homosexual people in the state between 2007 and 2018, 14 of them in Rio Branco. That is a raw count over eleven years with no per-capita denominator published, so it does not by itself establish Acre as more dangerous than a larger or smaller state. State government and Public Prosecutor's Office material issued in January 2025 states that no trans deaths were recorded in Acre in 2024.

Rio Branco Law 2389, enacted 30 December 2020 and in force from 5 January 2021, prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in the municipality and reaches conduct a visitor is likely to meet: refusing entry or stay in any public or private establishment open to the public, selective service not required by law, denying or surcharging hotel, motel or pension lodging, denying or surcharging the rental, purchase or lending of property, restricting access to buses and taxis, refusing school enrolment, and inciting discrimination or violence through any medium. Individuals and legal entities are liable. Penalties run from a warning and a fine set by municipal regulation to suspension of activities or operating licence for up to 30 days and interdiction or loss of licence, graded by gravity, recidivism and economic capacity. Any resident may complain, with confidentiality on request.

State Law 3,355 of 18 December 2017 guarantees the nome social in all acts, registrations, records and forms of the state's direct and indirect public administration. Registration and attendance must record both the civil-registry first name and the chosen social name; state servants must address the person by the indicated name in written acts, with the civil-registry name confined to internal use alongside the social name; pejorative expressions are prohibited; official letters, summons and notifications must carry both names; servant training is mandated; and non-compliance is a functional infraction carrying administrative liability and sanction. Dissemination is assigned to the State Secretariat of Justice and Human Rights.

State Decree 7311 of 3 August 2017 created the State Council for Combating Discrimination and Promoting the Rights of Lesbians, Gays, Bisexuals, Travestis and Transsexuals, charged with proposing public policy for the state's LGBTQ population.

Document rectification is free for those who cannot afford it. On 15 October 2024 the Court of Justice of Acre published Order 15/2024 requiring that legal change of name and gender on documents carry no charge for people without financial means.

Non-binary recognition is newer and slower. In 2025 a 46-year-old Sena Madureira resident became the first person in Acre to obtain a document marked with gender X, after a two-year process through the state public defender's office and a judicial grant by judge Luana Cláudia de Albuquerque Campos. The 48-hour compliance order to the Sena Madureira registry office was still pending transfer in late June 2025 and no physical rectified documents had been issued at that point. Non-binary document changes in Acre otherwise still require judicial action.

The public defender's office and the State Secretariat for Women ran a "Viver com meu nome" name-and-gender rectification mutirão on 28 June, with certificate issuance on 24-26 June, requiring RG and CPF, passport if held, voter title, proof of address, and negative state, federal, electoral, labour and, where registered male, military certificates, alongside health, social and electoral services.

On 29 January 2025 the State Secretariat for Social Assistance and Human Rights and the Public Prosecutor's Office of Acre signed a technical cooperation agreement on LGBTQIAPN+ rights and issued a booklet, "O que você precisa saber sobre os direitos da população LGBTQIAPN+: Mudança de nome e gênero de pessoas Trans e Travestis", covering rectification documents and steps and access to health, education and employment, with distribution through public bodies and civil society and prosecutor oversight of public policies including the trans outpatient clinic.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020 and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. First transgender federal legislators (Salabert, Hilton) were elected in 2022.

On 1 March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that a transgender person has the right to change official name and sex by self-declaration of psychosocial identity without surgery or professional evaluation. On 15 October 2024 the Court of Justice of Acre published Order 15/2024 establishing that legal change of name and gender on documents must be free of charge for individuals lacking financial means. In 2025 Ariel Sebastos became the first person in the state to obtain a document marked with gender X, while non-binary document changes still require judicial actions. On 29 January 2025 the State Secretariat for Social Assistance and Human Rights and the Public Prosecutor's Office of Acre signed a cooperation agreement to promote LGBTQ rights and launched a booklet guiding Trans and Travesti people on rectifying name and gender on documents. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the 1830 Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Acre since 2013 via a National Council of Justice decision implementing a 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision. Same-sex adoption has been legal nationwide since 2015 through a Supreme Federal Court decision, following a 30 May 2008 ruling in Senador Guiomard allowing a gay couple in an eight-year stable relationship to adopt. Discrimination based on sexual orientation became explicitly illegal through a 2019 Supreme Federal Court decision equating it to the crime of racism and through Rio Branco Law 2389 enacted 30 December 2020 prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation in the city. On 13 November 2024 the Rio Branco City Council approved Bill 14/2024 by 10 votes to 1 to prohibit participation of children and adolescents in LGBTQ pride parades, which was criticized by the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office for perpetuating stereotypes about homosexual people and was vetoed by Mayor Tião Bocalom as unconstitutional. Between 2007 and 2018 the Associação de Homossexuais do Acre recorded 18 murders of homosexual people in the state, with 14 occurring in Rio Branco.

sources.title: Acre Law No. 3,355 (19 December 2017, Governor Tião Viana)
sources.summary: Acre Law No. 3,355 of 18 December 2017, published 19 December 2017 with entry into force 60 days after publication, guarantees all natural persons use of their nome social — the name by which they recognize themselves and are recognized socially — in all acts, registrations, records and forms of the state's direct and indirect public administration, requires indication of civil-registry first name and chosen social name at registration or attendance, obliges state servants to address the person by the indicated name in written acts while restricting civil-registry name to internal use accompanied by the social name and prohibiting pejorative expressions, requires both names on formal documents such as official letters, summons and notifications, mandates servant training, treats non-compliance as a functional infraction subject to administrative liability and sanction, and assigns dissemination to the State Secretariat of Justice and Human Rights.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018
sources.summary: On 1 March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court in ADI 4275 held that the right to equality without discrimination encompasses gender identity and expression and permitted alteration of name and gender in the civil registry without sex-reassignment surgery or judicial authorization, requiring the State to recognize self-declared gender identity as a manifestation of personality.

sources.title: 2025 first 'X' gender marker case - Ariel Sebastos
sources.summary: After a 2-year process via the Defensoria Pública do Estado do Acre initiated circa 2023, judge Luana Cláudia de Albuquerque Campos granted 46-year-old Sena Madureira native Ariel Sebastos Nascimento Silva the first Acre civil-registry rectification to "sexo não binário" with a 48-hour compliance order to the Sena Madureira cartório still pending transfer in late June 2025 and no physical rectified documents yet issued, while DPE/AC with the Secretaria de Estado da Mulher scheduled the "Viver com meu nome" name-and-gender rectification mutirão for 28 June 8h-13h at the Defensoria with OCA certificate issuance 24-26 June requiring RG/CPF, passport if any, voter title, proof of address and negative state, federal, electoral, labor and military if registered male certificates plus health, social and electoral services.

sources.title: SEASDH-MPAC cooperation agreement and booklet (29 January 2025)
sources.summary: On 29 January 2025 Acre's SEASDH and MPAC signed a Technical Cooperation Agreement to protect LGBTQIAPN+ dignity and launched the booklet 'O que voce precisa saber sobre os direitos da populacao LGBTQIAPN+: Mudanca de nome e genero de pessoas Trans e Travestis' guiding trans and travesti people through legal name and gender rectification with required documents and steps and through access to health services, education, employment and humanized non-discriminatory care with planned wide distribution via public bodies and civil society and MPAC oversight to enforce public policies and maintain essential services including the trans outpatient clinic; 2024 saw no recorded trans deaths in Acre, while prejudice-driven exclusion from dignified work with many without fixed income dependent on social programs and school evasion limiting progression to higher education remain identified challenges.

sources.title: Rio Branco Law No. 2389 (30 December 2020, Mayor Socorro Neri)
sources.summary: Enacted 30 December 2020 and in force on publication (5 January 2021), Rio Branco prohibits any discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity and punishes violent acts and discriminatory acts against homosexuals, bisexuals, travestis or transexuals including prohibiting entry or stay in any public or private establishment open to the public, selective service not required by law, denying or surcharging hotel/motel/pension lodging, denying or surcharging rental/purchase/lending of movable or immovable property, restricting access to public transport such as buses and taxis, denying school enrollment, and inciting discrimination/violence via any media/publication, with liability for individuals and for-profit or non-profit legal entities in the municipality and penalties of warning, fine set by municipal regulation, suspension of activities/operating license up to 30 days, and interdiction/cassation graded by gravity and recidivism and economic capacity, open to complaint by any resident with guaranteed confidentiality if requested.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court 2019 criminalization decision
sources.summary: On 23 May 2019 six of eleven Supreme Federal Tribunal justices voted to frame homophobia and transphobia as crimes under Brazil's 1989 racism law punishable by up to five years' imprisonment until Congress enacts specific sexual-orientation and gender-identity discrimination legislation, with the measure to take effect after the remaining votes on 5 June 2019.

sources.title: Rio Branco Bill No. 14/2024, Federal Public Prosecutor's Office criticism and mayoral veto
sources.summary: Rio Branco Bill No. 14/2024 proposed prohibiting minors from participating in the LGBT+ Parade, and the municipal government vetoed the bill following controversy including criticism from the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office.

14911670B1613159902410.name: Rondonia
14911670B1613159902410.summary:
Rondônia is a state of Brazil and stands under the national framework; the state has no statute of its own prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so protection for trans visitors and residents rests on national law rather than on state legislation.

An ordinance signed on 28 August 2025 by appellate judge Daniel Ribeiro Lagos guarantees transgender people the use of their social name and the use of bathrooms and locker rooms in accordance with gender identity. It is the clearest region-specific rule on gendered facilities in the state.

In 2022 Hanier Miranda became the first person in Rondônia to obtain a birth certificate carrying an X sex marker. The civil registry had refused the entry for lack of a regulated third-gender procedure, and the marker was secured through a year-long lawsuit brought by the Center for Legal Practices, Research and Extensions at the Catholic Faculty of Porto Velho.

On 5 May 2025 the state prosecution service, the federal prosecution service, the labour prosecution service, the federal public defender's office and the state public defender's office jointly recommended that the state security secretariat and the state justice secretariat provide regular training for military police, civil police, firefighters, penitentiary and socio-educational agents on respect for LGBTQIA+ rights and improved service. The recommendation set a response deadline of 20 business days and required a training plan within 60 days covering 2025 and later years. It also requires gender identity, sexual orientation and social name to be recorded in police occurrence reports and prison records, with data protection and privacy safeguards, so that violence against transsexual women and travestis, including domestic and family violence, can be monitored.

Police records in the state logged 240 occurrences of anti-LGBTQIA+ violence across 2020 and 2021.

sources.summary: Same-sex marriage is legal nationwide under the CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), with adoption permitted since 2010 and full rights since 2015. Gender-marker change requires no surgery, hormones or diagnosis under the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option exists nationwide, but civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020, and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. The first transgender federal legislators, Salabert and Hilton, were elected in 2022.

Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. The country retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination, and trans voters may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, evidencing local political visibility.

Brazil has among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America: same-sex marriage (CNJ Resolution 175/2013), joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia and transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism (ADO 26 and MI 4733, 13 June 2019, imprisonment of 1-5 years). Enforcement is uneven in practice. Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasilia, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianopolis are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure. Smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Rondonia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Rondonia has no state law prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity, but since 2019 such discrimination is criminalized nationally by a Supreme Federal Court ruling equating it with the crime of racism. In July 2022 Hanier Miranda became the first person in the state to obtain a birth certificate with sex marker X after initial denial at the registry for lack of a regulated third-gender procedure and a year-long lawsuit by the Center for Legal Practices, Research and Extensions at the Catholic Faculty of Porto Velho. On 28 August 2025 an ordinance signed by Appellate Judge Daniel Ribeiro Lagos guarantees transgender people the use of their social name and the use of bathrooms and locker rooms in accordance with gender identity. Between 2017 and 2021 there were 12 murders of transgender people in the state, with Rondonia ranked as the 3rd state with the highest homicide rate in the North Region of Brazil. In 2025 federal and state prosecution and defender bodies recommended training on gender identity for police officers and firefighters and inclusion of LGBTQ population data in official reports. State Law no. 5123 banning gender-neutral language in schools, approved in October 2021 and signed on the 19th by Governor Marcos Rocha, was blocked in November 2021 by preliminary injunction and struck down on 10 February 2023, while a law passed on 10 July 2026 requiring parental authorization for classes on gender identity was struck down on 17 August by the Court of Justice of Rondonia. Homosexuality has been legal in Rondonia and throughout Brazil since 1830 when the Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. On 26 April 2013 the General Inspectorate of Justice published Provision 008/2013-CG providing for direct same-sex marriage and conversion of stable union into marriage in civil registration records. sources.title: Brazilian Supreme Federal Court (STF) 2019 ruling on homophobia/transphobia
sources.summary: On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court criminalized transphobia throughout Brazil including Rondônia by applying Law 7.716/1989 Article 20 to anti-LGBTI discrimination and offenses, punishable by 1 to 3 years' imprisonment as a non-bailable and imprescriptible crime.

sources.title: 2025 Joint Recommendation - MPF, MPRO, MPT, DPU, DPE-RO

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court ruling 1 March 2018 on gender identity

sources.title: ADI by National Confederation of Workers in Educational Establishments / STF decision 10 February 2023 (Justice Edson Fachin injunction November 2021)

Sergipe's own constitutional layer is older than most in Brazil: in 1989 the state, alongside Mato Grosso do Sul, was among the first to write a ban on sexual-orientation discrimination into its constitution. On 17 December 2025 Constitutional Amendment No. 59, proposed by state deputy Linda Brasil (PSOL), amended article 3(II) of the State Constitution to guarantee protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, with violators subject to punishment by law, effective on promulgation. Sergipe is the first Brazilian state to write gender-identity protection into its constitution.

The state judiciary has its own marriage provision. On 5 July 2012 the State Judiciary Power issued Provimento nº 06/2012, which regulated same-sex marriage throughout Sergipe. Since 2025 the state has allowed individuals to change their gender marker on documents to non-binary.

Court facilities in the state capital are explicitly gender-neutral. From 28 August 2025 the Court of Justice of Sergipe provides operating gender-neutral bathrooms on the ground, first and eighth floors of the Palácio da Justiça in Aracaju, usable by any person regardless of gender identity. The same measure directs that in all Sergipe judiciary units male and female bathrooms be used respecting each person's gender identity, under human-rights and non-discrimination principles, and requires that all new constructions and renovations be planned with gender-equity demands.

Institutional access has widened at the state's federal university. On 17 November 2025 the Federal University of Sergipe approved affirmative-action quotas for trans people in undergraduate courses.

A counter-current sits in the state legislature. On 1 December 2020 state deputy Rodrigo Valadares (UNIÃO) tabled a bill to prohibit the use and teaching of gender-neutral language in Sergipe's public and private schools and in state public offices, requiring traditional Portuguese in schools, official notices and public offices.

sources.summary: Same-sex marriage is legal nationwide via CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), with joint adoption since 2010 (full rights 2015) and gender-marker change without surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option exists nationwide, but civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020, and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. Salabert and Hilton, the first transgender federal legislators, were elected in 2022.

OutRight International country report, 12 March 2026: Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. The country retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination, and trans voters may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, evidencing local political visibility.

Brazilian law-firm guide for expatriates (OAB/SP, updated April 2026): Brazil has among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America on paper - same-sex marriage (CNJ Resolution 175/2013), joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia/transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism (ADO 26 and MI 4733, 13 June 2019, imprisonment 1-5 years). Enforcement is uneven in practice: major cities (Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasilia, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba, Florianopolis) are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

14911670B72497658138655.name: Tocantins
14911670B72497658138655.summary:
Tocantins has no state law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, a gap recorded by the state's own Public Defender's Office. A trans visitor in Palmas or in the interior depends on Brazil's national framework, which applies here without state-level variation, and on national enforcement machinery rather than any state statute.

The state bodies that have acted on trans documentation are the Public Defender's Office of Tocantins (Defensoria Pública do Estado do Tocantins) and the state judicial inspectorate, the Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça. On 29 January 2026 the Public Defender's Office published an article explaining how trans people change names and gender markers on documents.

Rectification in Tocantins is administrative and rests on self-declaration. A trans man, trans woman, travesti, non-binary or queer person may apply at the civil registry where the birth was recorded, with effect on the birth certificate and on all official documents, without medical or psychological reports and without proof of surgery or hormone treatment. The service is free where the applicant proves inability to pay, and a court is involved only if the registry refuses the request.

The exception is a change to a non-binary or unspecified marker, which the Public Defender's Office states requires a judicial decision. In August 2022 that office asked the Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça to allow "non-binary" entries in civil registry records, and in 2023 the inspectorate published a resolution authorising non-binary individuals to change their documents to include a third gender option. Whether an administrative route to a non-binary marker is open in practice is unresolved.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court of Brazil - 1 March 2018 ruling on gender identity
sources.summary: On 1 March 2018 in ADI 4275 the Plenary of the Supreme Federal Court held that the right to equality without discrimination encompasses gender identity and expression and that travestis, transexual and transgender persons may obtain alteration of name and gender on the civil registry without sex-reassignment surgery or judicial authorization, because gender identity is a manifestation of personality that the State must recognize.

sources.title: Public Defender's Office of Tocantins - August 2022 request to General Inspectorate of Justice
sources.summary: In August 2022 the Tocantins Public Defender's Office requested the state General Inspectorate of Justice to allow inclusion of non-binary gender in civil registry records.

sources.title: General Inspectorate of Justice of Tocantins - 2023 resolution on non-binary gender marker
sources.summary: On 31 January 2023 the Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça of Tocantins issued Provimento No. 3 consolidating extrajudicial service norms, providing civil-registry procedures for birth registration with a transgender parent and for averbação of altered prenome and sex for transgender and non-binary persons.

sources.title: Public Defender's Office of Tocantins - 29 January 2026 article on National Trans Visibility Day
sources.summary: In Tocantins, trans men, trans women, non-binary, queer and travesti persons may request administrative rectification of name and/or gender marker at the civil registry where birth was registered with full legal effect in birth certificate and all official documents based solely on gender self-determination without medical or psychological reports or proof of surgery or hormonal treatment under the Federal Supreme Court understanding since 2018 and National Council of Justice norms, free upon proof of inability to pay with judicial recourse only if denied, except rectification to non-binary or unspecified gender which requires a judicial decision.

sources.title: Supreme Court Justice Luís Roberto Barroso - injunction of 27 August 2018
sources.summary: On 27 August 2018 STF Justice Luís Roberto Barroso suspended the Palmas municipal-law article prohibiting teaching about gender and sexuality in schools, allowing such teaching.

14911670B28216513632935.name: Espirito Santo
14911670B28216513632935.summary:
Espirito Santo sits within Brazil's national framework for LGBTI rights; the national record carries the marriage, identity-marker and hate-crime provisions that apply here, and what follows is the state's own layer of law, institutions and enforcement.

Facilities are contested at municipal level. On 6 June 2022 the Vitoria City Council approved a bill banning the installation of unisex restrooms in the city. The source records the council vote but not whether the mayor signed or vetoed the measure, so its current legal force is unresolved.

On 14 April 2024 the Legislative Assembly of Espirito Santo approved a bill restricting athletes' participation in competitions according to biological sex. Governor Renato Casagrande vetoed it on 28 April 2024.

On 21 June 2025 the Legislative Assembly approved a law allowing parents to prohibit their children from participating in classes dealing with LGBTQ topics. LGBTQ rights organisations challenged it at the Supreme Federal Court, which began hearing the case on 21 November 2025 and struck the law down in May 2026 by 8 votes to 2; Justice Carmen Lucia stated that it violated the Brazilian Constitution.

Partner recognition was addressed in Espirito Santo before the national framework was settled. On 3 August 2012 a judge in Colatina authorised registration of the marriage of Ediana Calixto and Kamila Roccon, the first same-sex marriage recognised in the state. The State Public Prosecutor's Office appealed and the recognition was revoked on 15 August; on 20 September the state Court of Justice reversed that decision and authorised recognition. On 15 August 2012 the General Inspectorate of Justice issued a Circular Letter requiring all civil registries to treat same-sex marriages on the same terms as opposite-sex couples, making Espirito Santo the third Brazilian state to address the question statewide.

State institutions have also acted on document recognition. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Espirito Santo (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: On 1 March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that a transgender person may change official name and sex by self-declaration of psychosocial identity without surgery or professional evaluation. On 22 January 2025 the Public Defender's Office of Espirito Santo filed suit to secure name and gender rectification for a non-binary person from Vitoria, and the court granted the request and authorized rectification. On 27 June 2025 the Legislative Assembly with the Public Defender's Office held a free event to facilitate name and gender changes on official documents for trans, non-binary and travesti individuals. On 6 June 2022 the Vitoria City Council approved a bill to ban installation of unisex restrooms in the city, which had not yet been vetoed or signed by the mayor. On 14 April 2024 the Legislative Assembly approved a bill to restrict athletes' participation in competitions based on biological sex, which Governor Renato Casagrande vetoed on 28 April. On 3 August 2012 a judge in Colatina authorized registration of the marriage of lesbian couple Ediana Calixto and Kamila Roccon as the first same-sex marriage recognized in the state. The State Public Prosecutor's Office appealed and the recognition was revoked on 15 August, then on 20 September the state Court of Justice reversed and authorized recognition. On 15 August 2012 the General Inspectorate of Justice issued a Circular Letter requiring all Civil Registries to treat same-sex marriage the same as opposite-sex couples, making Espirito Santo the third Brazilian state to address the subject statewide. In 2015 the city of Cachoeiro de Itapemirim passed a law prohibiting "ideological indoctrination" in city schools. On 21 June 2025 the Legislative Assembly approved a law allowing parents to prohibit their children from participating in classes on LGBTQ topics. LGBTQ rights organizations sued in the Supreme Federal Court, which began hearing the case on 21 November 2025 and struck down the law in May 2026 by an 8-2 vote with Justice Carmen Lucia stating it violated the Brazilian Constitution.

The reported risk attaches to venues and nightlife rather than to street crime generally.

14911670B30315977547221.name: Parana
14911670B30315977547221.summary:
Paraná is a state of Brazil and stands under the national framework carried by the parent record; the findings below are specific to the state and its municipalities.

Access to sex-separated facilities has been contested in Paraná's own legislature and in municipal councils. In 2021 state representative Mara Lima introduced a bill prohibiting unisex bathrooms statewide and requiring separate male and female facilities. On 16 November 2021 the Curitiba City Council approved a municipal bill of the same kind, introduced by councilman Ezequias Barros. The inventory does not record whether either measure was enacted.

On 4 October 2023 the Curitiba City Council approved, by symbolic vote, a motion of protest against Resolution 2/2023 of the federal Ministry of Human Rights and Citizenship, issued on 19 September 2023, which provided that educational institutions must guarantee use of bathrooms, changing rooms and other gender-segregated spaces according to each student's gender identity and expression, while recommending additional individual-use bathrooms in public spaces. The Ministry stated that the resolution has no binding effect and that no school is obliged to adopt it. The Curitiba motion was to be converted into an official letter to the federal government.

Gender markers on documents issued in the state are governed by the Court of Justice of the State of Paraná. In 2023 that court published a provision guaranteeing inclusion of a non-binary option in the Civil Registry gender marker, then revoked it in November 2023, limiting administrative replacement of first name and sex to male and female only. In 2025 the Court of Justice of the State of Paraná authorized a third gender option on documents.

Trans participation in sport has produced conflicting rulings between a municipality and the national courts. On 26 April 2024 Londrina enacted a law banning transgender people from competing in sports according to gender identity, with a R$10,000 fine for non-compliance. On 26 February 2026 the Londrina City Council approved a motion to bar transgender athlete Tiffanny Abreu from the Brazilian Women's Volleyball Cup; the Brazilian Volleyball Confederation filed suit in the Supreme Federal Court and Justice Cármen Lúcia issued a preliminary injunction the same day allowing her to compete. In March 2026 LGBTQ rights organizations filed suit against the Londrina law in the Supreme Federal Court, and on 7 August 2026 rapporteur Justice Cristiano Zanin voted to strike the law down. The inventory does not record a final judgment.

Relationship recognition in Paraná was established before the national rule took effect. On 26 March 2013 the General Inspector of Justice of Paraná ruled that same-sex marriage and the conversion of stable unions to marriage must use normal marriage procedures, and same-sex civil marriage was authorized in all cartórios statewide under the same procedure and documentation as heterosexual marriage, with conversion of a stable union into marriage permitted without judicial authorization. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Rio Grande do Sul (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2019, discrimination based on gender identity has been prohibited nationwide in Brazil through a Supreme Federal Court decision. On 1 March 2018, the Supreme Federal Court ruled that a transgender person may change official name and sex by self-declaration of psychosocial identity without surgery or professional evaluation. On 27 January 2020, the Rio Grande do Sul government installed signs in women's restrooms of state government offices stating use in accordance with gender identity and installed unisex restrooms. In August 2021, Special Secretary of Culture Mário Frias criticized those restroom measures as posing risks to children. On 22 April 2022, Rio Grande do Sul Justice allowed non-binary people to change first name and sex in the birth record to include 'non-binary' upon request to a notary without judicial authorization, but in December 2023 the Court of Justice revoked that provision. On 28 September 2025, a Porto Alegre court ordered a bar to pay 10,000 reais compensation for denying a trans man access to the men's restroom, and on 28 May 2026 an appellate court overturned that decision. Homosexuality is legal in Rio Grande do Sul. On 19 December 2002, the Legislative Assembly enacted State Law No. 14,896 prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation. On 29 May 2012, four of six notaries in Porto Alegre agreed to convert civil unions into marriages. On 11 November 2005, a Bagé judge permitted adoption of two brothers by a lesbian couple in a seven-year stable union, described as Brazil's first LGBTQ adoption. On 6 April 2006, same-sex couples in committed relationships were allowed to register at any notary office with rights to jointly own property, establish custody of children, and claim pensions and property on a partner's death. On 27 April 2010, the Superior Court of Justice recognized shared adoption of two sons by Bagé lesbian couple Lídia Brignol Guterres and Luciana Reis Maidana to secure pension, separation and inheritance rights. On 3 June 2011, Pelotas justice authorized adoption of a four-year-old by a gay couple with the biological mother's consent.

1811400B81659894240990.name: Puducherry
1811400B81659894240990.summary: Puducherry is a small coastal union territory built around Pondicherry town and Auroville, a former French enclave with a cosmopolitan, tourism-oriented economy of cafes and guesthouses accustomed to foreign visitors. Its urban towns are high-literacy and tourist-facing, where visible gender nonconformity tends to draw curiosity, staring and awkward bureaucracy rather than confrontation, and routine policing is generally less overtly anti-trans than in some conservative South Indian districts, with police abuse judged likelier in pockets away from the seafront. Sitting within the Madras High Court's jurisdiction, the territory is covered by that court's 2021 guidelines on police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy and protection from police harassment; same-sex conduct is decriminalised and courts remain accessible. Puducherry runs its own transgender welfare board alongside a culturally visible Tamil Aravani community and local advocacy, within a Tamil culture with longstanding recognition of aravani communities and a transgender welfare board in neighbouring Tamil Nadu, and it is viewed as somewhat more tolerant than the neighbouring Tamil Nadu interior and conservative rural areas. These conditions may ease ordinary social friction in central tourist areas, but they do not establish trans-specific acceptance or a working remedy: there is no documented local campaign or organised targeting of trans visitors, no recorded local criminalisation, and no documented facility restrictions, while local Tamil conservatism, limited transgender infrastructure, the absence of territory-specific protections, and uncertainty about how consistently local police and facilities apply protections to visitors keep everyday friction elevated; constitutional and court protections remain available but are unevenly enforced. Because it is a union territory with no separate entry, custody, bathroom or care regime, the full national framework applies on discovery or being outed. The 2026 amendment narrowing official recognition to hijra, kinner and intersex categories is principally resident-facing rather than a process visitors must use, but it signals the climate; document and presentation mismatches at airports, railway stations, hotels, checkpoints, hospitals and police contact can out a traveller and prompt questioning, and reported police mistreatment raises concern about protection if an incident occurs. Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita's removal of gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences, uncertainty over legal recognition and sexual-violence protections persists, and visitors can expect staring, misgendering, ward placement by documented sex, and bureaucratic friction.

1811400B74762431478096.name: Nāgāland
1811400B74762431478096.summary: Nāgāland sits within India's national framework, which carries no criminal penalty for being transgender and provides constitutional gender-identity protection, national police guidelines on handling trans people, and health-cover provisions for transition care — but a 2026 amendment narrows legal recognition largely to hijra, kinner and intersex people, removes gender-identity-specific sexual-offence protections, and leaves many self-identified trans people without a recognition pathway or a route to local marital recognition. Those recognition rules do not themselves govern a visitor's home-issued documents. Nationally documented concerns include passport and checkpoint document mismatches leading to questioning and intrusive checks, and police abuse reported as limited and mostly non-systemic: the known situation is far from routine presentation-based arrests or abusive detention, though it lacks the documented, effective visitor protections found in more protective jurisdictions. Locally, conditions push a transgender visitor's exposure above the metropolitan Indian norm: the state is predominantly Baptist and largely rural, with Article 371A insulating Naga customary law and church, village and tribal bodies shaping public morality; binary gender norms and the absence of any hijra or third-gender tradition leave gender diversity unfamiliar, and the church vocally condemns homosexuality. Close-knit towns and villages make an outed visitor highly visible, while trans visibility and support infrastructure are very low outside Kohima and Dimapur, so discovery raises everyday social exposure — staring, curious attention, disapproval, moral pressure, exclusion, extortion or informal punishment — more than the prospect of state punishment; the typical responses are curious attention, disapproval and moral pressure rather than violence, and there is no region-specific record of trans violence, policing or facility targeting, nor evidence of routine arrest solely for being transgender, though reporting is thin. Foreigners need a Protected Area Permit, with checks at Dimapur airport and railway station and on state highways, and parts of the state remain under AFSPA, adding routine scrutiny of identity papers at frequent checkpoints with military immunity — increasing the chance of being questioned and of being outed at a counter. Remoteness from courts and legal-aid services, scarce gender-affirming care and thin local legal and health infrastructure weaken practical recourse, although the Gauhati High Court's Kohima bench offers formal recourse; tourist-facing settings such as the Hornbill Festival and Kohima and Dimapur hotels may be more tolerant in practice.

1811400B55669546485086.name: Lakshadweep
1811400B55669546485086.summary: Lakshadweep is a small Union Territory of India of roughly 65,000 people, overwhelmingly Muslim, socially conservative and socially insular, with close-knit communities that leave almost no anonymity — a visitor's presence and any outing can spread quickly. Tourism is restricted and heavily administered, entry generally requires a permit, and identity documents are scrutinised at the permit and ferry or flight stage, adding a document-mismatch exposure specific to the territory. There is no documented transgender community infrastructure, no visible queer venues, and no record of local sensitisation programmes or enforcement of protective guidelines, while medical and legal services are thin, with serious incidents or care usually handled through Kavaratti or referred to Kochi; local police capacity and the handling of complaints are not well documented, and police responses may reflect local conservatism. No territory-specific hostile legislation, organised targeting, trans-specific violence or criminal prosecution, or local regime of imprisonment or execution for being transgender is documented — but neither are local protections or specialised recourse, and absence of such records is not evidence of safety. India's national framework still applies: same-sex conduct is decriminalised, constitutional anti-discrimination protection covers gender identity, courts function, and Supreme Court rulings against harassment stand, alongside 2021 Madras High Court police and conversion-therapy guidelines and expanded healthcare coverage. Offsetting these, a 2026 change narrows formal legal recognition to hijra, kinner and intersex people, excluding many trans men, trans women and non-binary people (that domestic pathway does not govern a visitor's home-issued documents), gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences have been removed, and document and security frictions are documented — passport medical-examination demands, invasive questioning at airports and stations, security stops of openly trans travellers, and reported police groping. For a trans visitor who is outed, or visibly gender-nonconforming, these combine: high visibility in a small population with limited privacy raises the likelihood of discovery, and local disapproval may translate into staring, intrusive questioning, harassment, refusal of services, social confrontation, pressure to leave, coercive policing or hospital ward-placement problems — resolved slowly and informally against thin, distant recourse, with national constitutional protections still formally operating.

1811400B49281905528064.name: Mizoram
1811400B49281905528064.summary: Mizoram follows India's national framework, under which transgender identity is not criminalised, same-sex conduct is decriminalised, and the constitution bars sex discrimination as interpreted to cover gender identity, backed by Madras High Court directions on police sensitisation, police protection and conversion therapy. In practice, the 2026 recognition regime is narrowed to specified socio-cultural groups and intersex people, leaving self-identified visitors without clear local status, and identity checks remain a live friction point — passport medical-examination demands, airport and railway stops, reported custody abuse by railway protection personnel, and the loss of gender-identity-specific sexual-offence provisions. Mizoram itself documents no visitor-facing restrictions, no Mizo-specific bans on presentation, facilities or care, and no Mizoram-specific trans-facing law; but Inner Line Permit and Protected Area Permit checks, together with border and internal travel controls, add repeated document scrutiny, which is the main formal exposure. The state is small, predominantly Christian and socially conservative, with high literacy, functioning courts and low violent crime — yet church authority shapes public attitudes, church bodies have publicly condemned homosexuality, the legislature formally opposed same-sex marriage, and there is no entrenched third-gender social tradition comparable to parts of mainland India. Mizo Local Councils and customary norms have enforced community morality, and with low inbound tourism and tight community surveillance there is little urban anonymity, so discovery by family or neighbours becomes social quickly. An out or outed visitor is more likely to face gossip, church or family pressure, staring, moral disapproval, misgendering, persistent curiosity and intrusive questioning by staff, police and healthcare workers, service hesitation or refusal of lodging, possible confrontation in towns and villages, bureaucratic scrutiny over IDs or hospital placement, unsympathetic or mocking treatment from local police and uneven complaint handling, with less ready recourse than in larger metropolitan centres. No organised state targeting, raids, imprisonment or lethal violence aimed at transgender travellers is documented, though local data is thin and such absence is not evidence of safety; legal recourse exists on paper but is limited locally by low trans awareness, minimal queer visibility and weak support infrastructure.

1811400B16134215155042.name: Arunāchal Pradesh
1811400B16134215155042.summary: Arunāchal Pradesh applies India's national framework, under which same-sex conduct is decriminalised, gender expression is not criminalised, constitutional Article 15 protection and Supreme Court recognition of gender identity bar discrimination, and courts function — but the March 2026 amendment narrows legal recognition to specified socio-cultural groups and intersex people, leaving many self-identifying trans and non-binary people outside the pathway, and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences. Document-and-presentation mismatches have caused airport stops (including a 2024 Chennai stop), a 2026 Allahabad medical-examination order and railway/custody abuse, with such friction also reported in the region; police-harassment guidelines issued in Madras in 2021 and constitutional recourse function only intermittently, and healthcare under Ayushman Bharat is mixed. Locally, entry itself is gated: foreign nationals in many districts need a Protected Area Permit and other visitors an Inner Line Permit, requiring registration and identity-document checks repeated at district and police checkpoints, so mismatches between documents and presentation are examined more often than in most of India. Parts of the state have been subject to Armed Forces Special Powers Act coverage. The state is sparsely populated, overwhelmingly rural and socially conservative, with strong customary and church influence and mission-driven Christian conservatism growing in some districts, limited LGBTQ visibility, and attitudes that vary across tribal, Christian and urban communities, while some tribal traditions retain recognised gender-diverse roles. Trans-specific services, sensitised clinics and community infrastructure are almost absent outside Itanagar, and medical, police-oversight and legal-aid capacity is thin, unlike metropolitan centres such as Kolkata or Chennai; no local trans-specific protections, documented targeted enforcement, facility bans or state hostility beyond deeper conservatism are known. UK travel advice from 2025 warns that police-abuse risk is higher in conservative rural areas, which describes much of this state, and remote terrain means hospitals, police oversight and legal aid are distant. Deeper social conservatism and limited visibility raise the likelihood of friction on discovery, while no region-specific pattern of organised trans-targeted enforcement has been documented.

1811400B97532436596698.name: Manipur
1811400B97532436596698.summary: Manipur follows India's national framework: constitutional protection against discrimination, no criminalisation of gender expression, and 2026 changes to the transgender recognition law that confine legal recognition largely to hijra, kinner and intersex categories, leaving other trans, non-binary and gender-fluid visitors dependent on foreign documents that authorities may challenge through medical examination or intrusive questioning, including at airports, railway stations and police stops; police abuse in custody is reported nationally, and gender-specific sexual-violence offences were removed from the criminal code. Local conditions differ in both directions: Manipur has one of India's most visible indigenous trans communities (Nupi Maanbi), a historic Maibi priestess tradition, a state transgender welfare board and organised advocacy, giving everyday familiarity with gender diversity that is uncommon nationally — though this does not amount to broad acceptance or reliable protection. Entry also requires Inner Line or Protected Area permits, specialist care is concentrated in Imphal, and the healthcare framework is mixed, with hill areas largely Christian and socially conservative and conservative rural districts less familiar with trans people than the capital. Since 2023, severe Meitei-Kuki ethnic conflict has displaced large numbers, disrupted movement and emergency care, and produced documented mass sexual violence with little accountability, alongside extended military and paramilitary deployment, armed barricades, curfews, checkpoints run by security and insurgent groups, armed groups and civil-defence militias operating where state authority is contested in the hills, and a police force stretched thin and divided along community lines; long-standing armed-forces powers give immunity that makes complaints against security personnel harder to pursue. Identity documents are examined frequently, by judicial and non-judicial actors alike, raising the chance of being outed, and both the Meitei valley and the tribal hill districts hold strongly gender-binary norms with vigilant moral policing. If a trans visitor is outed, documented police failures and impunity in the 2023 violence weaken recourse: remedy outside Imphal and in custody is unreliable, and visible gender nonconformity may invite harassment, extortion, detention or sexualised violence, with police mistreatment in conservative rural areas applying with extra force given strained institutions. No Manipur-specific statute or campaign targeting transgender visitors is documented, and the conflict is not itself evidence of anti-trans targeting, but undocumented border practices, facility rules and absent remedies cannot be treated as safety, and assistance is less predictable.

1811400B56841107211215.name: Karnātaka
1811400B56841107211215.summary: Karnataka follows India's national framework, under which no law criminalises transgender identity and constitutional gender-identity protections apply, but the 2026 amendment narrowed legal recognition to hijra, kinner and intersex people, the criminal code removed gender-identity-specific sexual-offence provisions, and courts have ordered police sensitisation without marital recognition. Locally, Bengaluru stands out as a large technology and university hub with one of India's largest visible trans and hijra communities, an annual Namma Pride march, queer venues, a dense civil-society network including organisations associated with Sangama, Jeeva and Akkai Padmashali, a state transgender welfare board and policy, third-gender employment and welfare measures, and periodic police sensitisation; Mysuru and other urban centres are also comparatively tolerant, and hijra communities are a historically embedded, visible presence across the state, which generally lowers everyday street exposure. There is no state-level facility ban or additional criminalisation, and no documented state campaign of organised targeting or custody abuse of visitors; the Karnataka High Court functions as an available forum. Coastal and rural districts (the Mangaluru belt, Uttar Kannada and other smaller towns) are markedly more conservative, with weaker recourse, while state-level protections are principally resident-facing and do not establish a remedy for visitors, and no region-specific record of how airport, railway-police or custody practice treats trans visitors exists. For a visitor who is discovered or outed, the national document and detention risks remain the main exposure combined with these local conditions: passport or ID mismatches and document screening at airports and stations including Kempegowda International, hotel or station checks, hospital ward or custody placement, and moralised public harassment, alongside the March 2026 recognition amendment excluding people outside recognised categories. In Bengaluru the outcome is mainly social friction, occasional ID-check friction at transit hubs, inconsistent service treatment and common everyday misgendering, with police conduct inconsistent but no documented targeted enforcement of the kind seen in more conservative regions; documented incidents of groping and degrading custody exist but are not shown to be systemic, and national safeguards plus Bengaluru's civic infrastructure give partial remedy. 1811400B6111924962807.name: Goa
1811400B6111924962807.summary:
Goa is a state of India and stands under the national framework on transgender recognition, identity documents and criminal law. No Goan statute diverging from that national position is on file.

Marriage and partnership recognition in Goa is set by the Goa Civil Code, a state-level instrument that defines marriage as between a man and a woman and gives no legal recognition to same-sex marriage or civil union. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status cannot have that relationship recognised in Goa, and the code applies in this state rather than the personal-law system used elsewhere in India.

Goa has no state-level anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation. Protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity in Goa rests on the national Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, which applies in the state.

On 7 May 2025 the state government constituted a 14-member Model Transgender Welfare Board, chaired by the Chief Secretary, under the 2019 Act and the 2020 Rules, with a mandate covering implementation of welfare schemes and safeguarding transgender persons' rights in healthcare, education, employment and housing.

Administrative recognition in Goa lags the resident population. The 2011 census recorded 398 transgender people in Goa; by 2024 only 12 transgender people were registered on the state's electoral rolls, the first registrations having taken place in 2022. A trans visitor dealing with state offices should expect registration and documentation processes that have only recently begun to include transgender residents.

Harassment of transgender people in Goan institutions is documented. A 2018 study by the Goa Livelihoods Forum found that 87 per cent of transgender respondents had dropped out of school because of harassment. The figure describes the state's social climate for transgender residents rather than a specific risk to short-stay visitors, but it records a local pattern of harassment in schools and comparable settings.

No bill on relationship recognition has been introduced in the Goa legislature.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Goa (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal law has recognized transgender identity since NALSA v. Union of India in 2014. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 prohibits discrimination based on gender identity. In 2025 Goa formed the Model Transgender Welfare Board under the provisions of that Act to facilitate welfare schemes for transgender people. The 2011 census counted 398 transgender people in Goa, but as of 2024 only 12 transgender people were registered in electoral rolls, with the first registrations occurring in 2022. A 2018 Goa Livelihoods Forum study found 87% of transgender respondents had dropped out of school due to harassment. Same-sex activity was decriminalized at federal level in 2018 by Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India. In 16th century Goa, the Goa Inquisition criminalized same-sex activity with death penalty by burning to ashes and confiscation of property to the Crown, as applied in 1528 to a Muslim man and later to 16-year-old Portuguese army soldier Alberto Homem. Under the 1568 Constitutions of the Archbishopric of Goa, same-sex activity was classified as a serious sin punishable by deposition from office and lifelong penance in a religious institution for a clergyman and excommunication until repentance and required penance for a layman. In 1644 the Tribunal of Goa sought clarification on female same-sex acts and the majority concluded such acts generally did not constitute sodomy but sexual immorality rather than the crime of sodomy. Goa applies the Goa Civil Code defining marriage as between a man and a woman with no legal recognition for same-sex marriages or civil unions, though in 2023 the Supreme Court noted same-sex couples have the right to cohabit and enjoy some protections under law. Following the Supreme Court's 2023 decision not to legalize same-sex marriage, activists in Goa urged legislative steps but no bills have been introduced. There are currently no state-level anti-discrimination laws protecting sexual orientation in Goa.

10402087B60055985875400.name: Baden-Württemberg
10402087B60055985875400.summary:
Baden-Württemberg stands under Germany's national framework, and no region-specific signal on trans visitor risk was identified in the source inventory; the national assessment applies.

Custody placement remains the sharpest documented exposure. Baden-Württemberg's own prison law retains the unrevised 1970s-era placement rules, which operate on a binary men and women housing model. A Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 reports that placement rules in most Länder have stood unchanged since the 1970s and are now being revised: since 1 March 2026 a new Art. 17 of Rhineland-Palatinate's prison law is in force, and Bavarian, Saxon and Hamburg rules have also recently entered into force, giving a majority of Länder revised rules. Baden-Württemberg is not named among them.

The same analysis argues that no constitutional duty exists to anchor placement to the registered gender entry, since a prisoner self-declaration would intrude less on the right to gender self-determination. Only Bremen's law explicitly references the gender entry; other Länder, implicitly or not at all, do so.

How placement is applied in practice has gone both ways. A July 2026 report concerns a convicted far-right extremist holding a legally recognised female gender entry who was transferred from a women's prison to a men's prison after public outcry. The transfer indicates that placement follows the civil-registry entry and that exceptions permitting placement contrary to that entry are invoked inconsistently.

10402087B44391416804171.name: Bremen
10402087B44391416804171.summary:
Bremen, as a German city-state, stands under the national framework set by the Self-Determination Act (Selbstbestimmungsgesetz). It has enacted no trans-specific statute of its own and no prison-placement rule of its own. Prison administration and the civil-registry offices are competences of the city-state, so the layer a trans person actually deals with in Bremen is run by Bremen authorities, applying the federal framework without local amendment.

Under the Self-Determination Act the legal gender entered in the civil registry is the reference point for prison placement in every Land, and § 6(1) SBGG permits Land law to override that entry. Bremen has not passed such an override. The placement of a trans person held in a Bremen facility therefore turns on the registered entry rather than on a Bremen exception clause; how intake review is conducted in Bremen's prisons is not documented in the available sources.

Legal gender changes for Bremen residents are processed through the city-state's own registry offices. Bremen maintains no separate rule on bathrooms, changing or leisure facilities, or identity documents of its own, so a visitor meets the national framework rather than a local variant.

sources.summary: A 16 July 2026 France24/wire report covers the neo-Nazi prisoner in the 'Liebich' case, placed in a men's prison despite a legal gender change. The case drove Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia to launch a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act. The issue is framework-level for every Land, since prison administration and registry offices are Land competences.

Framework analysis (Verfassungsblog, 18 Mar 2026) of German state prison-placement rules under the Self-Determination Act: all Länder tie placement to the prisoner's legal gender; § 6(1) SBGG lets state law override the entry, and many Länder have enacted exception clauses — some abstract (all inmates), some criticised as trans-targeted. Bremen has no placement statute of its own, so this national framework is the operative standard for inmate-placement questions.

sources.summary: Germany's federal Self-Determination Act, the framework a trans visitor to Bremen stands under, passed parliament by 374-251 and took effect on 1 November 2024: adults over 18 can change their legal gender by self-determination, and the change is entered in the civil registry, i.e. handled through offices including Bremen's own. The article records that years of self-identification apply to adults without requiring the previous medical/court pathway, and that same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 October 2017. It confirms no Bremen-specific deviation: the city-state operates the unchanged federal act as of the article's coverage.

No Bremen-specific statute or enforcement appears in the overview. Bremen relies on the federal framework.

Placement decisions for transgender people held in Hamburg's correctional facilities therefore rest with the Hamburg justice administration rather than with a federal authority. Documentary matters for a trans visitor or resident in Hamburg stand under the national framework of Germany. Legal gender and first-name changes are made by self-declaration at Hamburg's registry offices under the Self-Determination Act, in force since 1 November 2024, with three months' notice and without a psychological evaluation or a court order. Hamburg's own procedural handling of those declarations is not documented in the sources reviewed.

Hamburg has a long-established gay commercial quarter in the St. Georg district, where bars, cafés and clubs operate in the streets adjoining the Reeperbahn entertainment area; German-language reference material describes the city as the principal centre of the gay scene in the north of the country. 10402087B86022102756745.name: Nordrhein-Westfalen
10402087B86022102756745.summary:
North Rhine-Westphalia has enacted no trans-specific legislation of its own. A trans visitor's legal position in the state is set by the German national framework, and the state's correctional law contains no trans-specific placement provision, so a detained trans person in a North Rhine-Westphalia prison is placed under the national default rule that the legal gender entry governs, with no state exception clause to override it.

The closest thing to a regional assessment of trans people's situation is the study "Queer durch NRW – Lebenslagen und Erfahrungen von LSBTIQ*", published on 25 April 2025, the first comprehensive dataset on the living situations of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, inter, queer and non-binary people in the state. It combined quantitative online surveys of more than 5,000 LSBTIQ* respondents, 775 relatives and over 5,000 professionals with qualitative focus groups and expert interviews. Three thematic areas structure it: discrimination, violence and safety; health, care and ageing; and integration, migration and flight.

The study was commissioned under a Landtag resolution, Drucksache 18/6360, to give the state's "Aktionsplan für Vielfalt und gegen Homo- und Transfeindlichkeit" a broader data basis. The action plan is a policy programme of the state government rather than a statute, and it creates no rights a visitor can invoke. That discrimination, violence and safety are among the domains the state government measures indicates a recognised problem, but the figures for trans respondents are not in the reviewed sources, so no risk magnitude can be stated for the state.

sources.summary: A 16 July 2026 France24/wire report documents the 'Liebich' case, in which a neo-Nazi prisoner who had undergone a legal gender change was held in a men's prison. Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia responded by launching a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act. That federal framework applies to NRW as to every other Land.

Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 examines Länder placement of trans prisoners under the Self-Determination Act (SBGG). Legal gender entry governs placement unless state law provides otherwise (§ 6(1)). Several states' exception clauses are criticised for singling out trans inmates, while abstract clauses such as RLP's § 17 are defended. No NRW-specific trans placement statute is on file, so the 2026 case framework is the operative standard for this Land.

10402087B42728698084544.name: Rheinland-Pfalz
10402087B42728698084544.summary:
Prison placement for people held in Rheinland-Pfalz is set by the state rather than the federal government: prison administration is a competence of the German Länder, so the placement rule for Rheinland-Pfalz prisoners sits in the state's own correctional act, while legal gender recognition and anti-discrimination law sit in the federal framework. Section 17 of the Landesjustizvollzugsgesetz Rheinland-Pfalz took effect on 1 March 2026 and anchors inmate placement to the legally recorded gender entry. The accompanying exception clause is drafted in general and abstract terms and is available to all prisoners; it is not written specifically for transgender prisoners. A trans visitor detained in Rheinland-Pfalz therefore has the placement decision taken at intake against the gender entry on their legal record, with the exception clause as the only route away from it.

A constitutional-law analysis published on 18 March 2026 reads the Rheinland-Pfalz drafting as the model preferable to the alternative used in other states, where exception clauses are written to target transgender prisoners specifically, and raises constitutional doubts about that alternative approach. The analysis is legal commentary on the statute and on the drafting choice; it is not a record of how the Rheinland-Pfalz clause has been applied.

sources.summary: France24/wire report of 16 July 2026 covers the 'Liebich' case, in which a neo-Nazi prisoner was held in a men's prison despite a legal gender change. The case drove the eastern Länder to launch a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act. Prison administration is a Land competence in Germany.

Verfassungsblog analysis (18 Mar 2026) of the new § 17 Landesjustizvollzugsgesetz Rheinland-Pfalz, in force 1 March 2026, which anchors inmate placement to the legally recorded gender entry with a general, abstract exception clause open to all prisoners (not targeted at trans people as such). RLP is the Land that took the (now absolute) majority of states past the point of modernising placement rules unchanged since the 1970s. The piece raises constitutional doubts about the alternative, trans-targeted exception clauses used by other states; direct relevance for RLP visitors facing detention placement decisions.
