10402087B83775792336645.name: Saarland
10402087B83775792336645.summary:
Saarland has no trans-specific statute of its own. Its state constitution was amended in 2011 so that its anti-discrimination provisions explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity, one of five Länder constitutions to carry such a clause. The consequence for a visitor is that transphobic hate speech is prohibited under Saarland's constitution, while hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned nationwide.

Prison placement in Saarland is governed by the national framework because the state has enacted no placement statute of its own; the legal gender entry is the default basis for placement unless a state law provides otherwise. A constitutional-law analysis published on 18 March 2026 cites Saarland's single-cell accommodation with en-suite shower as a positive practice model for trans inmates. The same analysis records that constitutional law does not oblige authorities to follow the legal gender entry, so the default in Saarland is a practice rather than an enforceable guarantee.

sources.summary: A 16 July 2026 live-news report covers a German court sending a person convicted of neo-Nazi incitement, whose legal gender was changed to female under the Self-Determination Act, to a men's prison amid public outcry over women's-prison safety. The case sits behind the state-level prison-placement law debate addressed in the accompanying analyses.

Verfassungsblog framework analysis (18 Mar 2026) of how German Länder place trans prisoners under the Self-Determination Act (SBGG, in force 1 Nov 2024): placement follows the legal gender entry unless a state law provides otherwise (§ 6(1) SBGG); no constitutional obligation to follow the entry. Cites Saarland's single-cell-with-en-suite-shower accommodation as a positive practice model for trans inmates; framework-relevant to Saarland, which has no separate placement statute.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Germany (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The page records that Saarland's state constitution was amended in 2011 so that its anti-discrimination provisions explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity, one of only five Lander constitutions to carry such a clause (Berlin since 1995, Brandenburg since 1992, Bremen since 2001, Saarland since 2011, Thuringia since 1993; Saxony-Anhalt in the public sector since 1997). It further records that Saarland, with Hesse, Berlin, Bremen and Schleswig-Holstein, tabled a joint Bundesrat motion for a ban on conversion therapy, presented in plenary on 12 April 2019, with Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia agreeing and Bavaria offering modified support. Gives the state-constitutional protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity that a trans visitor stands under within Saarland.

sources.title: Transgender rights in Germany (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The page states that hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned nationwide in Germany, but that some states have laws banning all forms of discrimination in their constitutions - Berlin, Brandenburg, Bremen, Saarland and Thuringia - and that in those states hate speech based on both sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited. For Saarland this is a jurisdiction-specific enforcement difference: transphobic hate speech is prohibited under the state constitution, unlike in most of Germany, and the federal General Act on Equal Treatment (in force since 18 August 2006) bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, education, health services and the provision of goods and services.

sources.title: Jens Spahn will Pseudotherapien gegen Homosexualität verbieten
sources.summary: Zeit Online (10 April 2019) reports that, parallel to Federal Health Minister Jens Spahn's announced plan to ban so-called conversion therapies, Hesse, Berlin, Bremen, Saarland and Schleswig-Holstein planned to present a joint Bundesrat motion (Entschließungsantrag) for a ban that same week. Saarland is one of the five tabling states in the run-up to the 12 April 2019 Bundesrat plenary presentation recorded on Wikipedia's LGBTQ rights in Germany page; the federal ban was subsequently approved by the Bundestag on 7 May 2020.

25490228B84620027724461.name: Canarias
25490228B84620027724461.summary:
Canarias is an autonomous community of Spain and stands under the national framework on legal gender recognition and LGTBI rights; its own statutory layer is a regional non-discrimination and self-identification regime.

Ley 8/2014 of 28 October 2014, on non-discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognition of trans persons' rights (BOE-A-2014-11995), gives a trans visitor to the islands a region-specific statutory basis against discriminatory treatment.

Canarias has allowed trans people to self-declare their legal gender since 2021, one of 14 autonomous communities to do so before the national statute of 28 February 2023 took effect.

The community is listed among those that ban conversion therapies, and it created a registry for same-sex couples in 2003, giving partners a regional recognition instrument.

sources.summary: The Basque Parliament passed a law against discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognising the rights of trans people, dated 2013, which for the first time incorporated an LGTBI perspective into gender-violence prevention in the Basque education system. Institutional markers predating it include the first Basque Pride march in Bilbao in 1978, the legalisation of the activist collective EHGAM in 1983, and the creation of Emakunde, the Basque Women's Institute, in 1988. A 2017 survey by the Basque Youth Observatory reported that 9 in 10 Basque young people favour same-sex marriage and legal change of sex. Osakidetza, the Basque health service, provided assisted reproduction regardless of sexual orientation and reaffirmed that position in 2013. The Basque Country operates its own non-discrimination legal instruments and equality institutions, including Emakunde, within the national framework.

25490228B27950689864224.name: Región de Murcia
25490228B27950689864224.summary:
Región de Murcia stands under Spain's national framework. The region's own layer is Ley 8/2016 of 27 May 2016 (BOE-A-2016-6170), which prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and sex characteristics across public and private activity in the region. Within its scope the statute bars any requirement that a person prove a declared gender identity by psychological or medical report, so a regional service, clinic or venue cannot demand documentation of a visitor's gender as a condition of service.

Article 5 creates the Observatorio regional contra la discriminación por orientación sexual e identidad de género, a participation and consultation body on which LGTBI entities are represented.

Title IV sets the sanctioning ladder. Minor breaches draw a warning or a fine of up to EUR 3,000. Serious breaches run EUR 3,001 to EUR 20,000 and cover degrading remarks or incitement to violence against LGBTI people or their families in the provision of services. Very serious breaches run EUR 20,001 to EUR 45,000, with accessory penalties that include exclusion from regional public aid for up to one year. Multiple discrimination raises the grade of the infraction.

Murcia was among eight autonomous regions that approved LGBTI and trans equality laws in the 2010s, and Ley 8/2016 remains the operative regional instrument. Implementation of the national trans-equality law falls to the regional government.

25490228B94236519555378.name: Galicia
25490228B94236519555378.summary:
Galicia is an autonomous community of Spain, and the national framework set by Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the organic law on real and effective equality for trans persons and the guarantee of LGBTI rights, governs legal gender recognition and protection against LGBTIphobic discrimination in the region as it does in the rest of the country.

The statute assigns implementation of its education-facing and administrative provisions to the autonomous communities. The Xunta de Galicia is one of the regional governments charged with carrying them out, and public authorities in Galicia act within their own competences when they do so. How the region's schools, administrative services and public bodies apply those provisions determines what trans residents and visitors meet in practice, and the sources reviewed do not describe Galicia's implementation record.

Galicia's courts have produced the first application of the discrimination aggravating circumstance for transfobia recorded in the country. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo fined the author of WhatsApp messages that threatened a trans woman EUR 300. The conviction was a misdemeanour, and it is the only documented regional enforcement of that aggravating circumstance in the sources reviewed.

Nothing in the sources reviewed documents region-specific legislation or practice in Galicia that restricts trans visitors. Recognition, document markers, facility access and healthcare access are governed by the national law, and no Galicia-level measure narrowing them appears.

sources.summary: Official gazette text (BOE-A-2023-5366) of State Law 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of LGBTI rights. Title II regulates rectification of the registered sex entry by the person's freely expressed will, depathologizes the procedure (no medical diagnosis or treatment requirement) and removes the former age-majority requirement for requesting it, with corresponding document adaptation; Title III provides protection and reparation against LGBTIphobic discrimination and violence. The law mandates measures across administrative, workplace, health and education fields, with public authorities acting within their competences; the education-facing and administrative provisions are implemented by the autonomous communities, this region's government among them.

Human Rights Watch, 16 February 2023, reporting the Spanish Congress of Deputies' passage of the comprehensive LGBTI law known as the 'Trans Law': legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the prior requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment aligned to the sought marker. The law strengthens sexuality education, bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before their consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing; children from age 12 may obtain recognition under certain conditions, a provision that provoked political conflict. HRW assesses the reform as upholding European and international standards against abusive, disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.

25490228B80227492032103.name: Cataluña/Catalunya
25490228B80227492032103.summary:
Catalunya stands under the national framework of Spain; the region-specific layer is set by Ley 11/2014 of 10 October 2014, published in the Diari Oficial de la Generalitat de Catalunya (DOGC núm. 6730) on 17 October 2014.

Ley 11/2014 defines direct discrimination, indirect discrimination and discrimination by association on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics.

The statute obliges Catalan public administrations to establish mechanisms so that administrative documentation reflects a person's gender identity.

Its protections extend across education, health, employment and sport, and it broadens the mandate of the Observatori Català de l'Esport to act against violence and discrimination in sport.

On partnership, the statute guarantees participation in death procedures, specifically identification of the body, burial and the handling of personal effects, to a surviving partner whose relationship is classed as same-sex under the law.

Article 35 sanctions minor breaches by reference to the indicador de renda de suficiència de Catalunya, at between seven days' and three months' worth of that indicator. Article 38 places the sanctioning regime under the department competent for LGBTI non-discrimination, and the Síndic de Greuges may instigate proceedings.

Implementation of the national framework in the region falls to the Generalitat de Catalunya.

sources.summary: The Spanish Congress of Deputies approved the Trans Law: legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the previous requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment, Human Rights Watch reported on 16 February 2023. The same law expands access to assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. Children from age 12 can obtain recognition under conditions, a provision that proved contentious. HRW places the reform within European and international standards against disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.

19177384B69455221212116.name: Chubut
19177384B69455221212116.summary: Chubut has no documented local legislation restricting transgender visitors and inherits Argentina's national framework: transgender identity and expression are not criminalised; adults may change legal gender and name without surgery, hormones, diagnosis or judicial approval; national identity documents offer an X marker; marriage equality applies; and gender-affirming care is available through public and private plans, with a February 2025 decree banning care for under-18s ruled unconstitutional and access restored nationwide in April 2025. Federal law carries life imprisonment for killings motivated by gender identity, though the aggravator was not applied in the Diana Sacayán case, and there is no national anti-discrimination statute covering gender identity, the anti-discrimination agency having been abolished in 2024, while national prison-housing decrees remain contested. Reported 2025 hate-crime totals are record highs but carry no trans-specific breakdown or denominator, and the Gender Identity Law functions as an institutional signal rather than a process a foreign visitor would use to change documents. Provincially, Chubut is a sparsely settled Patagonian region whose economy runs on foreign tourism in places such as Puerto Madryn, Península Valdés, Esquel and Comodoro Rivadavia, where visitors are routine and visible difference is somewhat less remarkable; the realistic local difference is visibility rather than severity, since small oil and valley towns such as Trelew offer limited everyday anonymity and may draw attention to a visibly gender-nonconforming outsider, raising the chance of being outed. Inland and rural areas are described as more socially conservative, with fewer trans organizations than Buenos Aires, little trans-specific legal aid or community infrastructure, and more discretionary services; police and courts function, but recourse for a trans visitor rests on national rather than documented provincial protections, and a mismatched document at a hotel, clinic or checkpoint can bring friction or humiliation without a reliable local remedy. No local hostility pattern, trans-specific visitor restrictions, or specific border, facility, police and visitor-service practices are documented, so consequences center on misrecognition, harassment and delayed remedies rather than certain severe punishment.

19177384B39000171219781.name: Córdoba
19177384B39000171219781.summary:
Córdoba is a province of Argentina. Legal gender recognition, access to gender-affirming care and recognition of relationships that local law would class as same-sex are set by the national framework described in the Argentina record, and the sources reviewed here record no provincial statute or provincial administrative rule departing from it. Provincial machinery that would matter to a visitor or a resident — a provincial anti-discrimination statute, provincial hate-crime reporting, provincial health-plan coverage rules, provincial custodial arrangements — does not appear in the available sources.

The one Córdoba-specific enforcement fact in the inventory concerns a cluster of deaths. Between 18 and 26 November 2025, police forces in three Argentine provinces, Córdoba among them, intervened in the deaths of three LGBT+ people over eight days. The source does not disaggregate the cluster by province, by victim group, or by whether any of the deceased was transgender, and it does not state whether police involvement was investigative or otherwise. Three deaths across three provinces in eight days is a raw count with no population denominator; no per-capita rate can be derived from it, and it cannot be read as a measure of risk in Córdoba specifically.

sources.summary: Agencia Presentes (19 Mar 2026) on the national hate-crime observatory: 227 hate crimes against LGBT+ people in Argentina in 2025 (up 62%, one every 38 hours), 64 security-force institutional-violence cases vs 17 in 2024, 32% of incidents in stations/prisons, 43% of perpetrators unknown to victims. Directly relevant to this province: between 18 and 26 November 2025 police of Salta, Córdoba and Buenos Aires provinces intervened in the deaths of three LGBT+ people in eight days - this province's forces explicitly named in that documented pattern.

Agencia Presentes (6 Feb 2025): Emergency Decree 62/2025 amends the national Gender Identity Law (26.743) to bar under-18s from gender-affirming surgeries and comprehensive hormonal treatment; Decree 61/2025 changes placement of trans people in the prison system. Both bind every province including this one; FALGBT announced legal action and constitutional experts call the decrees unlawful.

19177384B45303095947895.name: Formosa
19177384B45303095947895.summary: Formosa, a poor and largely rural northeastern province on the Paraguayan border, applies Argentina's national framework: legal gender recognition without surgery or judicial approval under the 2012 Gender Identity Law, an X marker on passports and identity documents, legal recognition of same-sex relationships, and no criminalisation of gender identity or expression. Gender-affirming care, including for minors, was restored nationwide after the 2025 under-18 restriction was ruled unconstitutional in April 2025, and gender-motivated killing carries life imprisonment, though the aggravator was not applied in a 2025 Supreme Court decision and is rarely used. No Formosa-specific rule barring trans visitors from facilities, entry, care or documents is known, and no documented local campaign targeting trans visitors has been recorded. National gaps carry into the province as well: there is no anti-discrimination statute, the national anti-discrimination agency closed in 2024, 2025 saw a record year of recorded hate crimes, reported totals do not establish a trans-specific rate, and recent care and prison decrees signal instability. The national recognition process also does not protect a visitor's own foreign documents. Locally, Formosa is more socially conservative, more rural and economically peripheral than Buenos Aires, with fewer visible trans organisations, fewer trans-specific and specialist services, thinner legal-aid resources, greater distance from Buenos Aires institutions, less-trained police, health and lodging staff, less independent provincial oversight under a long-serving and highly centralized administration, and denser community scrutiny with limited anonymity. No local protection beyond national law was confirmed, and police and service responses remain uncertain. A trans visitor who is outed or discovered should therefore expect curiosity, social disapproval, misgendering, intrusive questioning, service friction and uneven official handling rather than criminal sanction, with recourse slow, uneven and further away.

The judgment binds Poland and governs trans people's healthcare in Polish prisons and detention in every voivodeship, including this one.

17162690B77437931625010.name: Pomeranian Voivodeship
17162690B77437931625010.summary: Pomeranian Voivodeship adds no local layer of risk: Poland does not criminalise same-sex conduct or gender expression, imposes no facility ban and allows visa-free tourist entry, and no region-specific pattern of anti-trans enforcement or violence is documented here. The voivodeship's Tricity — Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot — along with other coastal resort areas, is a Baltic university and tourism centre with a visibly more liberal, internationally exposed population, LGBTQ venues and events, active NGOs, municipal equality initiatives, regular Equality Marches held without the large-scale counter-protest violence seen elsewhere (Białystok, 2019), courts accustomed to rights claims, an anti-discrimination resolution covering gender identity and sexual orientation, and no anti-LGBT resolution among the handful still in force nationally; Gdańsk policing and services are comparatively cosmopolitan, and visible gender-nonconforming visitors are more likely to encounter tolerant hospitality. Rural and smaller-town Pomerania remains socially conservative and may generate staring, questioning or local hostility, and 2019-era survey hostility signals apply nationally. Local tolerance eases street-level exposure but adds no traveller-facing legal protection, and no local detail contradicts the inherited national picture. A transgender visitor who is outed or discovered inherits Poland's national framework unchanged: gender identity remains outside hate-crime and hate-speech coverage after the 2025 amendments were struck down following presidential referral and a Constitutional Tribunal ruling (earlier efforts were vetoed), legal gender recognition remains demanding, document mismatch and secondary inspection remain possible at Gdańsk airport, and conservative national attitudes persist. If detained, placement by birth sex and interruption of hormone therapy are documented exposures (2024 cases, including a European Court of Human Rights ruling awarding damages for hormone denial in prisons), although legal recourse exists. Region-specific trans visitor treatment at borders, in hospitals or in custody, and outcomes for travelling minors, are not documented; overall the exposure is friction, service uncertainty and occasional institutional failure rather than imprisonment or lethal punishment.

17162690B34878575347312.name: West Pomeranian Voivodeship
17162690B34878575347312.summary: West Pomeranian Voivodeship runs on Poland's national rules, with no known region-specific deviation in border, custody, health-care or policing practice and no documented local protective machinery. Consensual same-sex conduct and transgender identity are not criminalised, so discovery carries no trans-specific criminal penalty and no credible pathway to imprisonment, but legal gender recognition remains a burdensome, resident-only process that visitors do not use, and gender identity is not covered by hate-crime or hate-speech protections following the 2025 constitutional ruling and failed legislative amendments, leaving bias-motivated harassment with limited recourse. Documented national conditions include demanding document and gender-marker checks, misgendered custody and interruption of a trans detainee's hormone treatment, a European Court of Human Rights finding on denial of hormone therapy, hostility from senior officials, counter-protests and violence at Equality Marches, and mass arrests at a 2020 Warsaw protest; offsetting developments include a 2024 ruling on prisoners' hormone access and a 2025 Supreme Court ruling on non-binary discrimination. Locally, Szczecin — a border, university and port city with an established LGBTQ community, recurring Equality Marches and a secular, outward-facing culture — and the tourist-facing coast at Świnoujście and Kołobrzeg are generally welcoming, and the voivodeship is not among the regions known to retain 'LGBT-free zone' or Family Rights Charters resolutions, although one review could not confirm whether any such resolutions fall within it; recent administrative-court practice against local anti-LGBT acts also supports rule of law at this level. These are social signals rather than enforceable protections, and attitudes are more mixed in smaller towns, rural counties and conservative venues, where risk rises, particularly late-night, while local services and transport are otherwise ordinary. Discovery at borders or hotels can still prompt document questions and awkward or hostile reactions, but there is no documented pattern of police targeting or imprisonment of trans visitors, no distinct region-specific restriction, no separate regional age-dependent rule for travelling families, and local violence rates are not established. Overall, a trans visitor who is outed faces the national exposure — bureaucratic gender checks, possible misgendered detention if arrested, no hate-crime recourse and variable public tolerance — with modest local social mitigation but no custodial or execution risk.

17162690B16879770934003.name: Silesian Voivodeship
17162690B16879770934003.summary: Silesian Voivodeship follows Polish national law: a transgender visitor is not criminalised for their identity or gender expression, and same-sex conduct is not criminalised, but gender identity is not covered by hate-crime or hate-speech protections after the presidential veto and Constitutional Tribunal ruling (with 2025 amendments blocked), legal gender recognition remains demanding, police treatment is uneven, and documented detention failures — including a 2024 placement of a trans detainee in a male-guarded centre with interrupted hormone therapy — show that institutional encounters can be harmful, though courts and the European Court of Human Rights have provided recourse when medication is denied. No Silesian rule creates a separate traveller-facing regime or a worse facility-exposure position than the national one, and remedies remain national; no region-specific pattern of police targeting or serious state violence is documented, though serious violence remains possible rather than part of a local campaign. Locally the picture is uneven. The Katowice conurbation — dense, urban-industrial, multicultural and secular, with universities, transport hubs, recurring equality marches, visible LGBT organisations and relatively moderate civic authorities — offers community infrastructure and reduces everyday scrutiny, though this does not amount to broad social acceptance or guarantee protection, and local tolerance is moderate rather than protective. By contrast, smaller towns, mining towns, rural communes, the Beskid districts and other conservative Catholic communities can be harsher on gender-nonconforming visitors, and some municipalities have kept family-rights declarations or anti-LGBT resolutions. For a trans visitor who is discovered or outed, the likely harms are misgendering, service refusal, public harassment, bureaucratic friction and document checks, plus — if detained or hospitalised — medication interruption or placement problems. Conditions differ between Katowice and smaller communities, but the available local distinctions do not support assuming either uniformly greater safety or a distinct regional enforcement pattern.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria — Wikipedia
sources.summary: Cross River falls under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 makes same-sex marriage or civil union, and registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or publicly showing same-sex affection, punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment nationwide. The Criminal Code separately criminalises sex between men (14 years) and gross indecency between men (3 years). The twelve northern states under Shari'a law carry up to a death-penalty maximum: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. Cross River is not among them. The source documents the nationwide 'kito' entrapment-and-blackmail scheme targeting gay men and trans women, police profiling and extortion of people perceived as gay, and mass arrests (42 men in Lagos, August 2017; 53 charged in Kaduna, April 2017; 100+ detained after a Delta hotel raid, June 2018; 67 in Warri, August 2023; 76 in Gombe, October 2023). No anti-discrimination protections exist for LGBTQ people.

sources.title: "Everyone's on the Game": Corruption and Human Rights Abuses by the Nigeria Police Force (Human Rights Watch)
sources.summary: Human Rights Watch's 17 August 2010 report on the Nigeria Police Force documents arbitrary arrests, mass 'raid' arrests, prolonged unlawful detention used as a 'cash cow', and extortion using threats and acts of physical abuse, with bribery the standard price of release. Research was conducted in June and July 2010 in Lagos, Anambra and Kaduna states and the federal capital as case studies of three of Nigeria's six geopolitical zones. The report is national in scope and does not name Cross River. It substantiates the national baseline that police treat suspected same-sex conduct and perceived 'gayness' as an extortion opportunity, with release on payment of a bribe as the documented outcome.

sources.summary: Oyo is a southern state outside the Shari'a regime. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 punishes same-sex marriage or civil union, and the registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or public show of same-sex affection, with up to 14 years' imprisonment. The Criminal Code criminalises sex between men (up to 14 years) and gross indecency (up to 3 years). Twelve states apply Shari'a law: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara, where male same-sex conduct carries a maximum of death. Police profile, entrap and extort people perceived as gay ('kito'), and mass arrests recur: 42 men arrested in Lagos in August 2017, 53 charged in Kaduna in April 2017, more than 100 detained after a Delta hotel raid in June 2018, 67 in Warri and 76 in Gombe in 2023. No anti-discrimination protections exist. The 2014 statute reaches LGBTI organisations, and LGBTI people face arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation under a framework that applies in full to Oyo.

27671186B41407594687181.summary:
Ondo is a state in south-western Nigeria and stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and the secular criminal provisions covering same-sex conduct extend to Ondo in full. The sources record no Ondo statute, protective measure or enforcement divergence of the state's own, and Wikipedia's overview of LGBT rights in Nigeria does not name Ondo at all.

The Shari'a penalty layer does not reach Ondo. The twelve northern states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, where male sodomy can carry death by stoning, are separate jurisdictions; as a southern state Ondo stands under the secular framework, where the maximum penalty recorded is a life sentence.

Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act was passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, criminalising all forms of same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 quotes Section 217 of the Criminal Code, under which any male who commits or procures an act of gross indecency with another male, in public or in private, is guilty of a felony liable to three years' imprisonment. That offence applies in southern states such as Ondo. Victor Oluwasina Ayeni, senior lecturer in law at Adekunle Ajasin University in Ondo state, observed in a January 2017 book chapter that the Code fails to define what constitutes an act of gross indecency.

The same Home Office note documents the national criminal framework applying across all states, including the 2014 statute, and records countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people. It confirms that the twelve northern states' Shari'a penal codes, with penalties up to death by stoning, remain in force, so that penalty layer does not extend to Ondo.

Wikipedia records no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protections and no recognition of same-sex relationships anywhere in the country, and Ondo supplies none of these itself.

27671186B69086015704361.name: Delta
27671186B69086015704361.summary:
Delta State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies in the state, as does section 217 of the Criminal Code, which makes male gross indecency a felony carrying three years' imprisonment; the maximum exposure under the 2014 Act is 14 years' imprisonment. Delta has enacted no protective statute of its own. The death penalty attached to same-sex conduct under Shari'a provisions operates only in the twelve northern states and has no application in Delta.

Enforcement in Delta has taken the form of raids on private hotel gatherings. In June 2018 police in Asaba arrested more than 100 people attending a party at a hotel on charges that they were gay and lesbian, and by July 2018 the group was facing homosexuality-related charges in court.

The Warri raid of 27 August 2023 is the most detailed Delta incident in this inventory. At around 9 pm, officers from the Ekpan Division of the Delta State Police Command raided Teebolus Hotel on Refinery Road, Ekpan, in Uvwie Local Government Area and arrested 67 people at what police described as a same-sex wedding between a 22-year-old groom and a 20-year-old bride. The command spokesman, DSP Bright Edafe, said the operation followed a confession by a male cross-dresser that he belonged to a gay club travelling to a marriage ceremony, that the suspects fled on the officers' arrival, that 67 were chased and arrested, and that drugs and 'gay marriage ceremonial dresses' were recovered. The 67, publicly known as the 'Warri 67', were charged to court, and the spokesman said efforts continued to arrest those who fled.

Accounts of that night differ. The USSD 2023 human rights report records that police raided a 'white party' organised by the LGBTQI+ community in Delta State on 27 August 2023 and detained more than 200 individuals, that police alleged the event was a same-sex wedding, and that some civil society representatives disputed that description. One of the 67 arrested at the Warri hotel alleged that he was sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated.

Reporting from Delta indicates that the law suppresses complaints as well as enabling arrests. A human rights lawyer based in Warri told the UK Home Office that victims of 'kito' — predatory same-sex assault and extortion — under-report for fear of prosecution under the same statute. A visitor who uses dating or hook-up applications in the state faces the same luring and blackmail pattern documented nationally, in which the threat of disclosure is the leverage.

Delta has enacted no protective statute of its own. Section 217 of the Criminal Code applies in the state, making male gross indecency a felony carrying three years' imprisonment; the maximum exposure under the 2014 Act is 14 years. The death penalty attached to same-sex conduct under Shari'a provisions operates only in the twelve northern states and has no application in Delta. Enforcement in Delta has taken the form of raids on private hotel gatherings. In June 2018 police in Asaba arrested more than 100 people attending a party at a hotel on charges that they were gay and lesbian, and by July 2018 the group was facing homosexuality-related charges in court. The Warri raid of 27 August 2023 is the most detailed Delta incident in this inventory. At around 9 pm, officers from the Ekpan Division of the Delta State Police Command raided Teebolus Hotel on Refinery Road, Ekpan, in Uvwie Local Government Area and arrested 67 people at what police described as a same-sex wedding between a 22-year-old groom and a 20-year-old bride. The command spokesman, DSP Bright Edafe, said the operation followed a confession by a male cross-dresser that he belonged to a gay club travelling to a marriage ceremony, that the suspects fled on the officers' arrival, that 67 were chased and arrested, and that drugs and 'gay marriage ceremonial dresses' were recovered. The 67, publicly known as the 'Warri 67', were charged to court, and the spokesman said efforts continued to arrest those who fled. Accounts of that night differ. The USSD 2023 human rights report records that police raided a 'white party' organised by the LGBTQI+ community in Delta State on 27 August 2023 and detained more than 200 individuals, that police alleged the event was a same-sex wedding, and that some civil society representatives disputed that description. One of the 67 arrested at the Warri hotel alleged that he was sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated. Reporting from Delta indicates that the law suppresses complaints as well as enabling arrests. A human rights lawyer based in Warri told the UK Home Office that victims of 'kito' — predatory same-sex assault and extortion — under-report for fear of prosecution under the same statute. A visitor who uses dating or hook-up applications in the state faces the same luring and blackmail pattern documented nationally, in which the threat of disclosure is the leverage.

27671186B95832466049157.name: Rivers
27671186B95832466049157.summary:
Rivers State has no statute, policy or enforcement practice of its own on same-sex conduct or gender expression in the sources reviewed. The state stands under Nigeria's national framework, which applies nationwide; its provisions and penalties are set out in the national assessment. The layer that varies by geography is the criminal code in force across southern Nigeria, and it applies in Rivers: sex between men carries up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency up to 3 years. Rivers is not among the northern states where Sharia provisions apply, so the death-penalty exposure those states attach to same-sex conduct does not arise for a visitor to Port Harcourt or elsewhere in the state.

The sources place one documented incident inside Rivers. In January 2015 a 21-year-old man from Lagos travelled to Port Harcourt to meet a person he had contacted on Facebook and was attacked and sexually abused there. He did not report the attack to the police. The sources record no arrest, charge or official response in connection with it.

Beyond that case, the sources identify no Rivers prosecution, arrest, police operation or state-government statement on same-sex conduct or gender expression, and no enforcement pattern specific to the state. No Rivers institution appears in the sources as either hostile or protective, and no trans-specific incident, facility rule or care restriction particular to Rivers is recorded.

sources.summary: The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, signed by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, makes same-sex marriage and civil unions invalid and illegal and criminalises registering, operating or supporting gay organisations. 27671186B96047513549152.name: Kogi
27671186B96047513549152.summary:
Kogi State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2013 and the Criminal Code provisions on sexual conduct apply in full on its territory, and the ceiling on a visitor's exposure is the national 14-year maximum rather than any Kogi-specific statute.

Kogi is not one of the twelve Nigerian states that administer Shari'a criminal law. The death-penalty Zina provisions applied to same-sex acts in Kano and Katsina do not operate here, so the exposure in Kogi is imprisonment under secular provisions, not corporal or capital punishment.

The 2013 act, passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, makes entering a same-sex marriage or civil union liable to 14 years' imprisonment, and makes registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or making a public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, liable to 10 years. The Criminal Code separately criminalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years.

In 2022 a coalition of Nigerian human rights organisations won a court ruling that Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 act breached the Constitution and could not be enforced anywhere in the country. Those provisions therefore do not operate in Kogi either, and the ruling effectively allows LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and organise there. The same source records no comparable ruling for the conduct provisions or the marriage-prohibition provisions, which remain the operative exposure in Kogi.

BBC News reported on 9 August 2024 that mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people take place across Nigeria, including in Kogi, and are especially frequent in northern states.

27671186B51792679167430.name: Plateau
27671186B51792679167430.summary:
Plateau State is a North Central state in Nigeria with its capital at Jos and a population of around 4.7 million. It stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 criminalises same-sex conduct, bans same-sex cohabitation and public shows of a same-sex amorous relationship, and carries penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment.

Shari'a criminal law does not apply in Plateau State, so the death-penalty exposure that applies in Nigeria's twelve northern states does not apply here; criminal liability rests on national statutory law alone.

Plateau State is not recorded as showing the concentration of arrests and communal tension attributed to the North Central zone.

Nigeria has no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and violence against them is documented as frequent.

A 2022 court challenge ruled Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act unconstitutional and unenforceable anywhere in the country.

LGBTQ+ people in Anambra have no legal protections under Nigerian law and face violence; the national record documents police torture, arbitrary arrests, mass arrests at private gatherings and hotels, and unprosecuted killings of transgender women.

27671186B91150779192485.name: Ekiti
27671186B91150779192485.summary:
Ekiti State operates under Nigeria's national legal framework; the provisions and penalties of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act are carried by the national assessment. What is specific to Ekiti is the documented enforcement and violence inside the state, and it is concentrated in Ado Ekiti, the capital.

On 21 January 2014, days after the SSMPA was passed, Debbie, a 26-year-old transgender woman, was beaten in Ado Ekiti by six men who told her, 'You will get 14 years in prison.' Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report states she was beaten at least twice over the period. The assault carried the statute's maximum penalty as its threat, naming the term she faced.

Health care inside Ekiti was not usable for her. Unable to attend the state's health services safely, she travelled three hours each way to Ibadan for HIV treatment, a round trip of roughly six hours to obtain care she could not safely reach closer to home.

Police enforcement in the capital appears in the same reporting. In September 2014 a man was arrested at Faguyi bar in Ado Ekiti, his third arrest, and released after two days in detention after 2,000 naira was paid for him and 10,000 naira for a friend. In a separate 2014 case, a 25-year-old man in Ado Ekiti was extorted by a state investigator.

The two documented enforcement cases involve men pursued over same-sex conduct rather than trans identity; the trans-specific incident is the January 2014 assault. The state-level material shows police and a state investigator in the capital extracting payments from men perceived as gay, and a trans woman who could not obtain HIV treatment within Ekiti without risk.

27671186B90910891533368.name: Enugu
27671186B90910891533368.summary:
Enugu State stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies in full across the state. Enugu-specific documentation comes from Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report, which records the statute's effects through testimony gathered in the state.

An Enugu-based activist told Human Rights Watch that there are no clinics in Enugu State where gay men and men who have sex with men can obtain services without fear of harassment. For a trans visitor who needs medical care while in the state, that leaves no documented service point where disclosure of gender or sexual identity is not itself a risk.

Human Rights Watch also records the account of Sharon, a bisexual woman from Enugu State, who married a male friend from high school in July 2015 under family and social pressure and said, "For as long as I am in Nigeria, I will stay married." The account documents the law operating as social pressure toward heterosexual marriage in the state.

sources.title: Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act | Human Rights Watch
sources.summary: Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report documents the SSMPA's impact in Enugu State. Sharon, a bisexual woman from Enugu State, told HRW she married a male friend from high school in July 2015 under family and social pressure, saying 'For as long as I am in Nigeria, I will stay married.' An Enugu-based activist told HRW that 'the major challenge in Enugu State is the rate of HIV and STIs among members of the community' and that there are no clinics where gay men and men who have sex with men can access services without fear of harassment, forcing many to travel to Lagos and other states.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch's report of 20 October 2016, 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act', records that the SSMPA, signed into law on 7 January 2014, imposes prison terms of 10 to 14 years on anyone who operates, participates in or supports gay clubs, societies or organisations, and finds that its passage was immediately followed by mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detention of LGBT people across the country, including the arrest without charge of 21 young men at a birthday gathering in Ibadan and repeated police detentions reported by interviewees elsewhere. Since June 2021 the Indonesian Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue identity papers, including the electronic identity card (e-KTP), to transgender Indonesians, and Banten is named among the nine provinces where this has operated, alongside West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua.

It records that the 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising sexual activity outside marriage is set to take effect on 2 January 2026, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison, and that because same-sex marriage is not legally recognised, all sexual activity between same-sex couples falls under that outside-marriage restriction. It further notes that transgender identity (waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture, alongside documented repressive incidents including raids on transgender women by the Jakarta Social Agency and the January 2021 flogging of two men in Aceh province (BBC/Reuters). A visitor in this province therefore stands under Indonesia's national position: no criminalisation of gender identity itself, no X-marker, and no legal recognition of same-sex marriage.

65028918B10722647473585.name: Bangka-Belitung Islands
65028918B10722647473585.summary:
Bangka-Belitung Islands stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is assessed as a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to one year's imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The provision applies in Bangka-Belitung Islands as throughout Indonesia.

No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and Indonesia has no anti-discrimination or hate-crime provisions for LGBT people. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unrecognised, so no same-sex relationship carries legal recognition anywhere in the country.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, a process that shapes what documents a trans visitor or resident can present at airports, hotels and police checks.

Physical risk is rising across Indonesia. Reporting by The Diplomat in August 2026 describes a transgender community facing growing repression, with vigilante mobs attacking trans people as the government moves to codify anti-LGBT provisions. Reporting in the same period ties the surge in attacks to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them inside national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. A visitor travelling onward from Bangka-Belitung Islands to either province carries the national exposure plus that provincial layer.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Social and institutional hostility is documented at national level. A 2025 Pew figure found 93% of Indonesians rating homosexuality 'morally unacceptable'. The Constitutional Court rejected a petition to criminalise gay sex on 14 December 2017 by 5-4, and Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025. No deviation from this national position has been documented in Bangka-Belitung Islands.

15666254B97003483933575.summary:
Kuala Lumpur is a federal territory of Malaysia. It stands under the national framework: Malaysia's Penal Code applies directly in the territory, with Sections 377A and 377B punishing "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" by up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping and Section 377D covering "gross indecency" with up to two years, and the Federal Territories Sharia criminal enactment operates alongside it. The Sharia offences bind Muslims only; non-Muslim visitors are exposed to the Penal Code alone.

Enforcement in Kuala Lumpur is carried out jointly. On 28 November 2025 an operation by the Kuala Lumpur police, Kuala Lumpur City Hall and the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) arrested over 200 people at an all-male health centre in the territory. The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Malaysia, last updated 16 December 2025, records that enforcement since the 2018 election has included arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment, and that the Federal Court has struck down some state Sharia criminal-code provisions as beyond state power.

Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, reporting on 10 August 2022, interviewed 73 LGBT people between 2018 and 2021, including people living in Kuala Lumpur, and documented state-sponsored discrimination against them. The report states that each state and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintain Sharia codes that typically criminalise same-sex conduct, quotes a Kuala Lumpur activist describing regression as a conservative strand of Islam gains ground, and calls on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity. The sample was LGBT people broadly rather than trans people specifically, and the interview window closed in 2021.

15666254B60207109163985.name: Negeri Sembilan
15666254B60207109163985.summary:
Negeri Sembilan stands under the national framework of Malaysia, which carries the federal Penal Code offences, the identity-document rules and the entry position; those apply here as they do nationwide and are set out in the national record. The state's own layer is its Sharia criminal law.

In November 2014 the Court of Appeal declared section 66 of the Syariah Criminal Enactment 1992 (Negeri Sembilan), which criminalised cross-dressing, unconstitutional for breaching rights guaranteed by the Federal Constitution. The Federal Court has more recently struck down Sharia criminal-code provisions in Selangor and Kelantan on the ground that state legislatures lack criminal-law power; those rulings concern other states, not Negeri Sembilan's section 66.

Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, reporting on 10 August 2022, documented state-sponsored discrimination and criminalisation of LGBT people in Malaysia through interviews with 73 people conducted between 2018 and 2021, including people living in Negeri Sembilan. The report states that every state and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintain Sharia codes that typically criminalise same-sex conduct, and calls on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity and to abandon 'rehabilitation' programs and rhetoric.

Enforcement against trans and gender-nonconforming people in Negeri Sembilan is carried out by the state Islamic religious department under Sharia provisions that apply to Muslims. The Human Dignity Trust profile of Malaysia, last updated 16 December 2025, records a national crackdown involving arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment since the 2018 election, alongside the persistence of federal criminalisation under Sections 377A and 377B of the Penal Code 1936, which carry up to 20 years' imprisonment with whipping.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, and the profile reports that discrimination and violence against LGBT people occur regularly, with transgender people particularly vulnerable.

Documented enforcement since the 2018 election includes an October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur with at least 20 LGBT people arrested, an August raid on an LGBT venue with twenty men arrested, a Terengganu Sharia court ordering a lesbian couple caned, and November 2023 Johor plans for conversion-therapy centres. 28173009B80457268982215.name: Altai Krai
28173009B80457268982215.summary:
No law, enforcement action or incident specific to Altai Krai appears in the sources. The national framework of Russia applies in full, and the national assessment of risk to a trans visitor carries over to this region without regional deviation.

No case under the propaganda statutes or the extremism provisions is documented in Altai Krai. The sources covering the region, among them the US State Department travel advisory and the UK Home Office country policy and information note, are national in scope and do not disaggregate enforcement by region.

sources.summary: UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity (June 2025, assessment updated 11 Jun 2025): same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, trans people cannot adopt or foster, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and no legislation prohibits SOGI-based discrimination in housing, healthcare or employment. Publicly 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is an administrative offence (fines or detention up to 15 days; repeat offences can become criminal, up to 4 years), the 2023 'extremist' designation of the international LGBT+ movement criminalises support/activity, and at least 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws 2022-2024. Assesses LGB people generally face no real risk of state persecution on orientation alone, except in the North Caucasus — a zone that does not include Altai Krai; this is the national baseline the record stands assessed at.

US State Department travel advisory for Russia, which covers Altai Krai: foreigners found guilty of violating the 'propaganda' law may be arrested and detained for up to 15 days and then deported, displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is a crime, and the advisory advises against all travel to Russia.

Human Rights Watch (30 Jun 2025): Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions over alleged participation in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols, about 98 of them administrative. Since January 2024, 81 people in 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying symbols such as the rainbow flag. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges for alleged participation; one died by suicide in pretrial detention, two were sentenced to prison, and 17 cases remain pending or unknown. On 15 May 2025, investigators charged three staff of two publishing houses under article 282.2 with running an 'extremist organisation' over selling fiction exploring LGBT themes; they face up to 12 years in prison. These national figures apply equally in Altai Krai, where no specific case is documented.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Khakassia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, after April-May 2023 proposals to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents and to ban reassignment without surgery. The propaganda law as expanded in 2022 applies to anyone regardless of age group and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and single-person foreign adoption is allowed only where the country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor allows gender transition. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on gender identity. In a 30 September 2022 speech President Putin said teaching children about other genders and offering sex-change surgeries is unacceptable, linking opposition to transgender rights to willingness to use all means against Ukraine. Officials cited protection of family values and draft evasion, claiming about 2,700 recent legal-gender changes and that many young men turned to private clinics for sex change to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation. Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after 1993 re-legalisation removing Article 121 from the RSFSR Penal Code, which had punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment under Article 154-a and later Article 121, with age of consent at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, with a July 2020 constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage, and same-sex couples are ineligible for legal protections available to opposite-sex couples with no legal recognition offered despite the 2021 Fedotova and Others v. Russia ruling. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation, and refuses to register LGBTQ organisations. A 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors, expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age group. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement includes arrests of gay bar owners, fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag, a 2010 European Court of Human Rights fine for systemic refusal of pride parade permits and an August 2012 Moscow City Court decision upholding a ban on Moscow Pride through 2012, and Chechnya detentions, torture and killings targeting persons based on perceived sexual orientation since February 2017 with over 100 men detained and OSCE confirmation in December 2018. Adoption is limited domestically to single persons regardless of sexual orientation and jointly only to married heterosexual couples, with foreign single-person adoption barred where the country recognises same-sex marriage.

sources.title: Supreme Court of Russia ruling designating 'international LGBT public movement' as extremist - November 2023
sources.summary: On 30 November 2023 the Supreme Court of Russia designated the 'international LGBT public movement' as extremist and banned it throughout Russia including Khakassia, making organizing, participation, funding, public display of LGBT symbols including trans-related expression, and advocacy punishable as extremist activity with fines, administrative detention and imprisonment.

sources.title: ILGA-Europe ranking - 2024
sources.summary: In 2026 Russia, including Khakassia, scored 2% on the 0-100% European LGBTI legal-policy scale and maintains explicit bans/legal limitations that make legal gender recognition practically impossible.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Tatarstan (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Transgender people are not allowed to change legal gender and gender-affirming care is banned under a bill passed in 2023 and a July 2023 law prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law applies to anyone regardless of age and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. Russian children cannot be adopted by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions under a 2024 law, and a single foreign adopter is permitted only if their country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. The military medical expertise statute provides that people 'who have problems with their identity and sexual preferences' can only be drafted during wartime, while authorities claimed about 2,700 legal gender-change decisions in recent times were sought to avoid conscription amid the special operation. On 30 September 2022 President Putin stated 'Do we want them to be taught that instead of men and women, there are supposedly some other genders and to be offered sex-change surgeries? This is unacceptable to us.' Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after homosexual acts between consenting males were re-legalised in 1993 with removal of Article 121, which had punished consensual sex between men with three to five years' imprisonment with an estimated 800 to 1000 men imprisoned per year in the Soviet era. The age of consent is 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation, and homosexuality was removed from the list of mental illnesses in 1999 with ICD-10, though new laws introduced 1 July 2023 effectively reinstate the classification. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, with a July 2020 constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage and no legal recognition available despite the 2021 Fedotova and Others v. Russia ruling finding a human-rights violation. The 2013 law criminalising distribution of 'propaganda' promoting 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors was expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated 'the international LGBT public movement' as an extremist organisation, formally listed 22 March 2024, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols including the rainbow flag a criminal offense punishable by prison time, leading to arrests of gay club owners with at least one dying in custody as of April 2025 and fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawed nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections, has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation, refuses to register LGBTQ organisations which are prohibited as extremist, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. Anti-gay purges in Chechnya since February 2017 involved forced disappearances, secret abductions, imprisonment, torture and extrajudicial killings with over 100 men detained and tortured and at least three dead, a further purge from December 2018 with around 40 detained and two killed, confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report and followed by EU economic sanctions on two Chechen officials in March 2021, while nationally an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals with 365 fatalities occurred between 2010 and 2020, tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015 with hate groups using dating apps to hunt homosexuals.

28173009B91429860602147.name: Chuvashia
28173009B91429860602147.summary: Chuvashia, a largely rural Volga republic centred on Cheboksary, inherits Russia's national framework: there is no legal gender recognition, and the 2023 law bars both medical transition and changes to official gender markers, so a visitor's passport and visa remain as issued and any mismatch with presentation is a standing exposure at document checks. Nationwide propaganda statutes were expanded in 2022, and the designation of the "international LGBT movement" as extremist has produced more than 100 convictions by mid-2025 and has been used to justify arrests and venue raids; police raids, arrests and detention connected to LGBTQ expression and venues are documented nationally, with lethal risk in detention, and there are no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections. Locally the republic is ethnically Chuvash and socially conservative — more so in rural areas and small towns — with a small and largely invisible trans community, no visible LGBT infrastructure, advocacy or queer-friendly venues, no sanctuary-type support, and no documented local tolerance policies or protective exceptions; regional authorities have historically aligned with Moscow's social policy, and provincial police can apply federal morality and extremism powers with little local restraint or oversight. Cheboksary offers some urban anonymity, but a visibly trans foreign visitor still attracts attention, and the documented concentration of enforcement in larger cities means the republic's lower visibility of LGBTQ life does not reduce what a visitor carries. Anyone outed here faces administrative and criminal proceedings, hostile policing and isolation from support networks, with greater exposure to rural scrutiny and less anonymity than in Moscow or St Petersburg but the same severity of consequences. The frequency of raids within Chuvashia specifically is not established, and that uncertainty does not indicate safety.

28173009B77673499236961.name: Tyumen Oblast
28173009B77673499236961.summary: Tyumen Oblast operates entirely under Russia's national framework, with no region-specific law, tolerance practice, protective exception, sanctuary provision or trans-specific visitor resource documented. The 2023 law bars gender reassignment and changes to Russian gender markers, so a visitor's foreign-issued documents remain as issued with no legal route to align them, making any passport or ID check a moment of possible discovery, even though those marker rules do not themselves alter a foreign document. The Supreme Court's designation of the 'international LGBT movement' as extremist has produced over 100 convictions along with raids, arrests, searches, photography, fines and criminal proceedings; propaganda statutes amended in 2022 are actively enforced and reach expression and identity at all ages. There is no anti-discrimination protection or hate-crime recognition, and public attitudes are documented as hostile, with about three-quarters expressing non-acceptance. Locally, the oblast is a conservative oil-and-gas province and Tyumen a prosperous Siberian administrative city with conventional conservative politics and a sizable security- and church-influenced public climate; its oil-industrial character brings some stability and monitoring but no trans-specific safeguards. Local authorities align with federal enforcement, no known regional rule or practice materially changes a visitor's national exposure, and enforcement geography is ordinary with minimal discretion. At the same time, compared with Moscow and St Petersburg, social attitudes are more conservative, trans visibility is lower and organised LGBTQ venues or advocacy networks are limited, reducing practical recourse; Tyumen's university population may offer some urban anonymity. The oblast's large, partly rural geography and distance from major legal-aid centres in Moscow and St Petersburg increase isolation if police intervene, and federal security and local police retain discretion. A visitor discovered as transgender faces police attention, arrest, extremism or propaganda charges, raid exposure and detention under conditions that have proved lethal, including a 2024 pretrial death linked to an LGBTQ-related extremism charge, with no established remedy.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mari El (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, following April-May 2023 State Duma proposals to prevent trans women from changing legal gender from male to female without surgery and to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law applies to anyone regardless of age group and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and foreign single-person adoption is permitted only where the country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. The article links legal gender change to conscription avoidance, stating that many young men have turned to private clinics to provide a sex change to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation and that Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin claimed 2,700 such decisions in recent times. On 30 September 2022 President Putin stated "Do we want them to be taught that instead of men and women, there are supposedly some other genders and to be offered sex-change surgeries? This is unacceptable to us." while invoking transgender rights in justification for action against Ukraine and willingness to use all means at disposal. Consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal after re-legalisation in 1993 removing Article 121, which had previously punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment under 1934 Article 154-a and up to five years under 1961 Article 121, with age of consent at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, voters approved a constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage in July 2020, no legal recognition is offered despite the 2021 Fedotova and Others v. Russia ruling finding a human rights violation, and only married heterosexual couples may adopt jointly though single persons regardless of sexual orientation may adopt domestically. The 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors and was expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement includes arrests of gay bar owners, fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings, at least one death in custody as of April 2025, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawing nine organisations including Centre T, Coming Out, Russian LGBT Network and others with convictions of founders for leading an extremist organisation. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation and gender identity and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community, with estimates of 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 with 365 fatalities, annual crimes tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015, and group-organised hunting via dating apps including Occupy Pedophilia active in 40 regions. In Chechnya, authorities targeted persons based on perceived sexual orientation with forced disappearances, secret abductions, imprisonment, torture and extrajudicial killing, with over 100 men detained and tortured and at least three dead from February 2017 and around 40 detained and two killed from December 2018, confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report and followed by March 2021 EU sanctions on two officials.

28173009B3082792446388.name: Nenets Autonomous Okrug
28173009B3082792446388.summary: Nenets Autonomous Okrug is a sparsely populated Arctic district of roughly 44,000 people centred on Naryan-Mar and scattered oil and gas settlements, with traditional hunting and reindeer-herding communities and a large indigenous Nenets population; it is reachable mainly by air. There are no LGBTQ venues, no visible queer community infrastructure, and no known local trans-specific protections, sanctuary, complaint mechanism or support organisations, and local legal aid, healthcare and police services are limited. The okrug's own enforcement practice, venue presence and police conduct are not documented in the record, and there is no basis to infer either milder or harsher local enforcement than the national picture; no documented local protection exists in either direction. Federal Russian law applies directly through local police, courts and federal security services: gender recognition and the 2023 ban on transition-related surgery and marker changes do not affect a visitor's foreign-issued documents, which remain as issued at home; the 'international LGBT movement' is designated extremist, with over a hundred convictions, documented raids involving searches and photographs, extremism arrests and a death in pretrial detention in 2024; and propaganda statutes reach ordinary expression across all ages. There is no anti-discrimination protection on gender identity and no recording or aggravation of bias-motivated violence, so such violence carries no added legal consequence. If discovered or outed, a visitor faces this same national exposure — official hostility, possible extremism or propaganda charges, and detention carrying documented lethal risk — with no local mitigation. Small, close-knit settlements sharply reduce anonymity: a visibly transgender outsider is highly noticeable, draws attention rather than finding cover, and has less community support than in Moscow or St Petersburg. Public attitudes are conservative and broadly hostile, unlikely to be more accepting than the national baseline, while remote placement provides no independent remedy; the practical local difference is a lower likelihood of safe public life and less formal recourse rather than any reduction in severity.

28173009B27844369294009.name: Novosibirsk Oblast
