Novosibirsk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia. The federal ban on legal gender recognition, the expanded propaganda statutes and the November 2023 extremism designation of the "international LGBT movement" are carried by the national record; what follows is what is documented in the oblast itself.

A court in Novosibirsk fined the Elton John Bar 500,000 rubles (about £4,598) for "promoting LGBTI propaganda" through a rainbow flag. The case followed the venue's appearance in a video by the LGBT+ activist blogger Karen Shainyan. The fine shows the propaganda statutes reaching a commercial venue in the oblast, a step beyond enforcement against individuals posting online.

Coercive conversion practice has been documented in the oblast. A transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour. She escaped only after police responded to a phone she had found.

A priest in a village in the Novosibirsk region told The Moscow Times that religion can correct "deviations", indicating that local religious authority frames gender variance as a defect to be corrected.

Human Rights Watch's tally of 101 extremism-related convictions nationally since the November 2023 designation records no case specific to Novosibirsk Oblast. The absence of a documented oblast case does not establish that none has been brought.

sources.title: Vitaly Milonov - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's biography of Vitaly Milonov documents the city-level origin of the anti-LGBT law a trans visitor to Saint Petersburg stands under. As a member of the Saint Petersburg Legislative Assembly (2007-2016), he is recorded as the principal sponsor of the legislation criminalising 'homosexual propaganda directed toward minors', the city ban enacted in 2012 that the New York Times report 'Anti-Gay Law Stirs Fears in Russia' (29 February 2012) covered. The page quotes his statement that he fully intended to catch Madonna committing a possible offence under it when she visited the city. It also records Milonov stating in 2013 that gay athletes could be arrested at the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics if they promoted homosexuality to minors, and his protests against the city's Side by Side LGBT film festival in November 2013.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Russia - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's country overview of LGBTQ rights in Russia supplies the federal framework Saint Petersburg is assessed under: a 2013 law criminalises distributing 'propaganda' of 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors, with fines up to 5,000 roubles for citizens, 50,000 for officials, and 1 million roubles plus up to 90 days' suspension for organisations, while foreigners face up to 15 days' detention, a fine up to 100,000 roubles and deportation. Ten regions including Saint Petersburg (2012) enacted regional versions of the ban before the federal law, and Saint Petersburg removed its regional law in 2014, leaving the federal statute in force there. A July 2023 law bans gender transition outright, prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition. A 2010 European Court of Human Rights ruling fined Russia over the systematic refusal of pride-event permits.

28173009B36269087375583.name: Sakhalin Oblast
28173009B36269087375583.summary: Sakhalin Oblast operates under Russia's national regime: since 2023 gender-marker changes and transition-related care are barred, so foreign-issued documents remain as issued; the 'international LGBT movement' is designated extremist, with related convictions, raids, searches, arrests and prosecutions at LGBTQ venues; and federal propaganda statutes covering non-traditional relationships and changing sex apply to all ages, alongside a regional-level propaganda ban adopted in 2013. There is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection based on gender identity and no recognition of same-sex partnerships, and pretrial detention carries documented lethal risk. Local conditions add to rather than soften that framework: the oblast is remote, sparsely populated and island-based, with no visible trans or LGBT infrastructure, so a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor is more conspicuous than in a large metropolis; it contains border-zone districts where foreign nationals face additional document controls and police contact, increasing the chance a passport mismatch escalates to official scrutiny; and limited nightlife in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk plus ferry and air links to the mainland and Japan add exposure at ports and checkpoints. Social attitudes track the national pattern of strong public hostility toward gender diversity, and federal courts, security agencies and registration systems operate throughout the oblast. No local protective exception, official tolerance or distinct enforcement practice is documented, and this absence of local information is not evidence of safety. Should a transgender visitor be discovered or outed, the same consequences as elsewhere in Russia apply — document mismatch, refusal of services, police scrutiny, detention, and prosecution for perceived association with LGBTQ expression — including where a minor's transition-related needs or expression draw official attention for adult visitors and travelling families alike.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Sakha Republic (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender and gender-affirming care is banned. In 2022 the 'propaganda' law was expanded to apply to anyone regardless of age group and to prohibit distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, following April-May 2023 State Duma proposals to 'rule out the possibility of changing a person's gender purely by changing the documents' and to ban reassignment without surgery on 'family values' grounds. In 2024 Russia passed a law banning adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions; inside Russia single persons regardless of sexual orientation can adopt but a couple can adopt jointly only if a married heterosexual couple, and a foreign single adopter must live in a country that neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. In the draft-evasion context, authorities claimed many young men turned to private clinics for sex change to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation, with the Duma Speaker claiming some '2,700' such decisions, and Russian men were described as considering changing legal gender to avoid being drafted. On 30 September 2022 President Vladimir Putin said teaching children that 'instead of men and women, there are supposedly some other genders and to be offered sex-change surgeries' is 'unacceptable to us' while stating Russia would use 'all means at our disposal' against Ukraine. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on gender identity, and authorities refuse to register LGBTQ organisations while pro-LGBTQ advocacy groups have been declared extremist and prohibited from operating. Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after re-legalisation in 1993 removing Article 121, which under Stalin from March 1934 as Article 154-a and from 1961 as Article 121 punished consensual sex between men with three to five years' imprisonment with a maximum of five years, with an estimated 800 to 1000 men imprisoned per year in the Soviet era; the age of consent is 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation, and homosexuality was removed from the mental-illness list in 1999 with ICD-10 but new laws on 1 July 2023 effectively reinstated classification as mental illness. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, the 2020 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage, marriage is defined as between a man and a woman, same-sex couples are ineligible for legal protections available to opposite-sex couples, and Russia did not implement the 2021 European Court of Human Rights Fedotova ruling requiring legal recognition after leaving the court in 2022. The 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of 'propaganda' promoting 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors and was expanded in 2022 to anyone regardless of age; in November 2023 the Supreme Court designated 'the international LGBT public movement' as extremist, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, where leading, participating in, financially supporting or repeatedly displaying symbols is a criminal offense punishable by prison time, leading to arrests of gay bar owners with at least one dying in custody as of April 2025 and fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings. Enforcement includes refusal to register LGBTQ organisations, prohibition of advocacy groups as extremist and 'foreign agents,' systemic refusal of pride parade permits with Moscow never approving a request and Moscow City Court upholding a yearly ban through 2012 despite a 2010 European Court fine for discrimination, and Defence Ministry guidance recommending asking recruits about sexual history and examining genital or buttocks tattoos allegedly indicating homosexual orientation while openly gay men are formally not excluded from service but warned not to reveal orientation to avoid beating. Violence and custody include Chechen forced disappearances, secret abductions, imprisonment, torture and extrajudicial killings targeting perceived sexual orientation, with over 100 men detained and tortured since February 2017 and at least three dead, a December 2018 OSCE report confirming persecution ignored by authorities, another purge from December 2018 with around 40 detained and two killed, and March 2021 EU economic sanctions on two Chechen officials; nationally the government does not officially record hate crimes, with an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 including 365 fatalities, annual crimes tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015, increased premeditated group attacks in 2017-2019 using dating apps to 'hunt' homosexuals, and 205 cases by homophobic hate groups including Occupy Pedophilia active in 40 regions. Protection machinery is absent with no anti-discrimination protections based on sexual orientation and no hate-crime designation, illustrated by the January 2013 firing of television anchor Anton Krasovsky after announcing he was gay and the September 2013 firing of Khabarovsk teacher Alexander Yermoshkin after attack by neo-Nazi group 'Shtolz Khabarovsk' amid a campaign by 'Movement against the propaganda of sexual perversions.'

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Tuva (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In 2022 the propaganda law was expanded to apply to anyone regardless of age group and to prohibit distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. In April and May 2023 the State Duma considered laws to prevent trans women from changing legal gender from male to female without surgery to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents, amid claims that men sought gender change to avoid conscription with Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin citing 2,700 such decisions. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright. In 2024 Russia passed a law banning adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and single persons living abroad may adopt Russian children only if that country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. On 30 September 2022 President Vladimir Putin said teaching children that instead of men and women there are supposedly other genders and offering sex-change surgeries is unacceptable to Russia. Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after re-legalisation in 1993 removing Article 121 from the RSFSR Penal Code, which had punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment under Article 154-a from 1934 and Article 121 from 1961 with an estimated 800 to 1000 men imprisoned per year, with age of consent at 16 since 2003 regardless of orientation and homosexuality removed from mental illness list in 1999 under ICD-10 though new laws on 1 July 2023 effectively reinstated the classification. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, with a July 2020 constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage, same-sex couples ineligible for protections available to opposite-sex couples, couples allowed to adopt only if married heterosexual, and no anti-discrimination protections or hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation and gender identity. In 2013 Russia passed a federal law criminalising distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors, expanded in 2022 to anyone regardless of age. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, where leading, participating in, financially supporting or repeatedly displaying symbols is a criminal offense punishable by prison time, leading to arrests of gay bar owners and fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawed nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist. Authorities in Moscow have never approved a gay pride rally, and in 2010 the European Court of Human Rights fined Russia for discriminating by refusing permits, while in 2012 the Moscow City Court upheld blocking permits yearly through 2012 citing public disorder. In Chechnya since February 2017 over 100 men were detained and tortured with at least three dead in extrajudicial killings in what witnesses called concentration camps, confirmed by a December 2018 Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe report as ignored by authorities, with another purge reported in December 2018 with around 40 detained and two killed, and European Union sanctions imposed in March 2021 on two officials. The government does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community, with an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 with 365 fatalities, annual crimes tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015 with increased premeditated group-organised crimes using dating apps to hunt homosexuals between 2017 and 2019, including 205 cases by homophobic hate groups such as Occupy Pedophilia present in 40 regions.

28173009B63182593849600.summary: Tver Oblast offers no exception to Russia's national regime. 28173009B42697300509311.name: Ulyanovsk Oblast
28173009B42697300509311.summary:
Ulyanovsk Oblast stands under the Russian national framework, which applies in full. No regional law or policy deviates from it, and no regional authority is recorded as moderating enforcement.

Two prosecutions document how that framework operates locally. In August 2024 Ilya Zhuravlev, former head of the dialysis centre in Inza, was detained on charges of participating in the activities of the designated "international LGBT movement" under Part 2 of Article 282.2, alongside a charge of coercion of a person to act of a sexual nature under Part 1 of Article 133. The case is recorded in an October 2024 OVD-Info report cited in the UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025).

In March 2025 a doctor in the region, already facing a maximum of one year's imprisonment over an allegation of sexual coercion, was additionally prosecuted for "involving" another man in the designated movement. He received a three-year sentence, as recorded by Human Rights Watch. The sentence exceeded the maximum available on the original allegation, so the extremism count drove its length.

A trans visitor to the region faces the national legal position without local relief, and the documented local cases show charges being brought against men in professional positions, a dialysis centre director and a doctor, rather than against people with any prior profile.

Since the November 2023 Supreme Court 'extremist' designation of the international LGBT+ movement, participation carries 2-6 years and organising 6-10 years' imprisonment (Article 282.2). The note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, the state able but not willing to provide protection. Region-specific: in March, a Ulyanovsk-region doctor who faced a maximum of one year's imprisonment for alleged sexual coercion was also prosecuted for 'involving' another man in the 'LGBT movement' and received a three-year sentence, the federal enforcement pattern operating inside this region.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Kalmykia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition that prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, after April-May 2023 proposals to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents and to ban reassignment without surgery. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions and applies to anyone regardless of age group. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and a single person living abroad may adopt only if their country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor allows gender transition. A 1 July 2003 military medical expertise statute provided that people "who have problems with their identity and sexual preferences" can only be drafted during war times, while Major-General Valery Kulikov stated the statute does not forbid people of non-standard sexual orientation from serving. Amid draft-avoidance claims, Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin claimed some "2,700" gender-change decisions had been made in recent times, with reports that young men turned to private clinics for sex changes to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on gender identity. Sexual activity between consenting adults of the same sex is legal, after re-legalisation in 1993 removing Article 121; prior law punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment under 1934 Article 154-a and up to five years under 1961 Article 121, and the age of consent stands at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are ineligible for legal protections available to opposite-sex couples, and July 2020 voters approved a constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage after the 2021 Fedotova ruling found failure to offer any recognition violated human rights, though Russia left the court in 2022. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation, and authorities refuse to register LGBTQ organisations while pro-LGBTQ advocacy groups have been declared extremist and prohibited. A 2013 law criminalised distribution of "propaganda" promoting "non-traditional sexual relationships" among minors, expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age group. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated "the international LGBT public movement" as extremist, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations and persons, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement has included arrests of gay bar owners, fines or jailing for displaying the rainbow flag designated as the movement's symbol, at least one death in custody as of April 2025, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawing nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist including Centre T, Coming Out, LGBT Resource Centre, Irida, Kallisto movement, Moscow Community Center for LGBT+ Initiatives, Parni Plus, Russian LGBT Network and T9 NSK with founders convicted for leading an extremist organisation. Authorities have never approved Moscow pride requests, and in 2010 the European Court of Human Rights fined Russia for discriminating by refusing permits, while in August 2012 Moscow City Court upheld blocking yearly permits through 2012 citing public disorder. Documented violence includes Chechnya detentions since February 2017 of over 100 men with torture and at least three extrajudicial killings, a further purge from December 2018 with around 40 detained and two killed, and an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 with 365 fatalities rising from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015, including 205 cases by homophobic hate groups such as Occupy Pedophilia using dating apps to hunt homosexuals.

sources.title: Supreme Court of Russia ruling, November 2023 - 'international LGBT public movement' as extremist

Public expression 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the 'gay propaganda' law by fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025) reports that Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participating in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison. Kamchatka Krai is assessed at the national level on this enforcement baseline.

Kemerovo Oblast has no separate legal regime governing gender identity. No oblast-level statute, decree or regional protection mechanism addressing trans residents or visitors appears in the sources; the national framework of the Russian Federation applies in the oblast without regional amendment.

The documented region-specific enforcement event is a prosecution inside the penal system. In February, a person already serving a prison sentence in Kemerovo region received an additional six-year sentence for participating in the "LGBT movement" and for "involving" other prisoners in its activities. RIA Novosti reported the sentence citing the Federal Security Service, and Human Rights Watch recorded it in reporting published on 30 June 2025. The case shows the extremism designation being applied by regional courts to conduct occurring in custody, and that a prisoner already sentenced faces further prosecution for contact with other inmates.

For a trans visitor the oblast presents the national enforcement regime with no regional variation: no regional advisory, exemption or protection modifies what applies elsewhere in the country. 28173009B57295377776076.name: Khabarovsk Krai
28173009B57295377776076.summary:
Khabarovsk Krai is a krai within the Russian Federation and has no regional law or institution of its own on gender identity or expression. The national framework applies in full, and the national assessment of visitor risk governs here.

The region's documented enforcement event concerns a biology and chemistry teacher in Khabarovsk who was forced to resign in September after video of him dancing in high heels surfaced amid public controversy. He filed suit against the Khabarovsk education department in October seeking reinstatement, and the case was still pending when the UK Home Office country policy and information note was published in June 2025. The episode shows that gender-nonconforming presentation can carry employment consequences in the krai, pursued through public controversy and an employer rather than through a criminal charge.

sources.summary: The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity for Russia (June 2025) sets out the national position: consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the 'gay propaganda' law by fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.

Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025) reports that Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participating in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison. HRW also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences (article 20.3) for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media, and 257 'gay propaganda' penalties imposed in 2023-24 versus 22 in 2021-22.

28173009B46831765844996.name: Primorsky Krai
28173009B46831765844996.summary: Primorsky Krai inherits Russia's national framework: legal gender recognition does not exist, a 2023 law bars gender transition and changes to official gender markers, and there is no anti-discrimination protection or official recording of hate crimes against LGBTQ people. Extremism and propaganda laws are enforced through venue raids with mass searches and photographing, arrests and convictions for displaying LGBTQ symbols, an extremist designation of the "international LGBT movement" with over 101 convictions and the 2025 outlawing of major groups, propaganda fines that have escalated eighteenfold and now reach all age groups, and a documented 2024 pretrial detention death following an extremism-related arrest. Visitors keep their home-issued documents, so any mismatch between papers and presentation remains a route to scrutiny, and families travelling with minors face added sensitivity around discussion or material concerning gender transition. Public attitudes are broadly hostile. No local protective practice is documented in the krai: there is no regional shield, sanctuary, exemption, or identity-respecting facility, health, or police protocol to offset federal rules, and limited local reporting does not establish that enforcement is absent or safer. Vladivostok's tourist core is somewhat more cosmopolitan than the interior, with historic cross-border tourism, foreign visitors and a small underground queer venue scene, but it operates under the same national raids and extremism prosecutions within a socially conservative, militarised border region with conservative authorities, limited queer infrastructure, weaker police oversight in the Far East, and a record of nationalist violence against gender-nonconforming people; the port city's security-sensitive character adds no protective layer. Heightened document scrutiny at ports and checkpoints, hotel registration or police stops raises discovery risk for someone whose documents, visa and appearance conflict, while Vladivostok's distance from Moscow and St. Petersburg means less visible trans support infrastructure or consistent institutional recourse. For a trans visitor who is discovered or outed, these conditions combine with the federal framework to expose them to detention, custody or housing assigned by birth sex, exposure under extremism or propaganda statutes, violence in custody, discrimination, and a documented lethal risk in detention; outcomes follow the harsh national rules, with no documented local remedy.

28173009B30250450380208.name: Bashkortostan
28173009B30250450380208.summary:
The Republic of Bashkortostan stands under Russia's national legal framework. No source in this inventory contains information specific to Bashkortostan, so a trans visitor should expect the national regime to apply unchanged.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (version 2.0, June 2025; page updated 12 August 2026) is the assessment framework for this division. It records that same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.

Under the 'gay propaganda' law, public expression 'promising' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition, including displaying rainbow symbols, is punishable by fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) for individuals or detention of up to 15 days. A repeated offence can bring up to four years' imprisonment.

The Supreme Court designated the international LGBT+ movement an 'extremist' organisation in November 2023. Between 2022 and 2024, at least 139 individuals were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participating in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols since that designation, with penalties of up to 12 years in prison. HRW also identified 81 people in 98 cases found guilty since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. The 2013 'gay propaganda' law already made any positive or neutral depiction of non-heterosexual relations an administrative offence.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia advises against all travel regardless of personal characteristics. It warns that foreigners found guilty under the 'propaganda' law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and deported, and that displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is a crime.

76434192B57942368908249.name: Free State
76434192B57942368908249.summary:
Gender-affirming care in South Africa is concentrated in the major metropolitan centres, and the Free State has no documented concentration of its own. A trans visitor who needs hormone therapy or surgery while in the province should expect to travel outside it, paying private prices in the hundreds of thousands of rands or waiting on a long public list. No Free State-specific provider, waiting-time or funding data was identified.

No Free State-specific statute, provincial enforcement record, prosecution or documented incident involving a transgender person was identified. Policing, provincial hospitals, municipal facilities and the province's correctional centres operate under the national framework carried by the South Africa record, and for those matters the national assessment is the one a visitor should rely on.

sources.summary: Court record (High Court of South Africa, Gauteng Local Division sitting as an Equality Court, case 2024/070075, judgment 10 November 2025) in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (Medium B): the landmark ruling for a trans inmate against the Department of Correctional Services - refusal of gender expression (feminine attire, she/her pronouns), inadequate accommodation and denial of state-funded gender-affirming hormone therapy held to be unfair discrimination; hormone therapy recognised as part of the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e).

Human-rights commission / National Preventive Mechanism media statement (14 November 2025): welcomes the 10 November 2025 High Court ruling in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075); describes the OPCAT monitoring mandate over places of deprivation of liberty, the inmate's account (initially allowed to express her gender, later restricted from feminine clothing and make-up, misgendered, denied prescribed hormone therapy, DCS arguing it was cosmetic), and the court's finding that gender-affirming healthcare forms part of adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e) of the Constitution.

sources.title: LGBT rights in South Africa - Wikipedia
sources.summary: National framework applicable in the Free State: the 1996 Constitution was the world's first to expressly bar sexual-orientation discrimination, and the Constitutional Court's December 2005 judgment compelled Parliament to legalise same-sex marriage (Civil Union Act, National Assembly vote 229-41, November 2006). The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act 2003 allows a person to change sex status in the population registry, and therefore on identity documents and passports, on proof of medical treatment such as hormone therapy, without requiring surgery. Gender-affirming care is concentrated in the main cities, so transgender people in provinces like the Free State must travel long distances to reach it; private treatment costs hundreds of thousands of rands and public waiting lists are long. The Justice Department's National Task Team (2011) and 2014 National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities address hate crimes against LGBT people.

19338628B5758982491638.name: Centre-Val de Loire
19338628B5758982491638.summary: Centre-Val de Loire has no trans-specific legislation, ban or protection of its own: gender identity, facilities and discrimination law are national, police and courts operate on the national system, and no local sweeps, border practices or facility bans differ from the French pattern. The region is largely rural and small-to-mid-sized — Orléans, Tours, Blois, Chartres and Bourges, with château and Loire Valley tourism — and is less cosmopolitan and more socially centre-right than Paris and Île-de-France, with trans community infrastructure and trans-affirming clinicians thin outside Tours; Orléans and Tours do provide institutional recourse and visibility. A visibly trans visitor in small towns or rural château country should expect staring, curiosity and ordinary day-to-day friction, along with more misgendering and administrative scrutiny where specialist services are scarce, rather than organised hostility, and tourist-facing hospitality in the Loire Valley marginally softens that picture; compared with France's lower-acceptance overseas departments, the region offers a more urban, tourist-oriented rule-of-law setting. Overall practical exposure therefore remains close to the national picture. If discovery or being outing occurs, national conditions apply unchanged: gender expression is not criminalised, transphobia has been a statutory aggravating factor since 2017, conversion therapy is banned, and anti-discrimination and hate-speech law sit alongside a functioning rights ombudsman and prosecutorial machinery. Against these protections stand documented exposures — documents are checked at entry and in everyday services, with border-police document friction; in custody, placement follows the gender or birth sex recorded on identity papers, with isolation, improvised units and strip-search exposure reported by custodial oversight as unremedied since 2010; and discrimination persists in services and healthcare, with a 2023 EU survey recording 64% reporting identity-related discrimination.

blindSourceSummaries: News feature (January 2018) on transgender women in national prisons: under the criminal-procedure code men and women are held in separate establishments, so trans women whose legal gender is marked male (the vast majority, without surgery) are placed in men's facilities; a detainee recalled hostile shouts and threats of violence; the national controller of places of deprivation of liberty says transgender detainees — overwhelmingly women — are the group that suffers the most in prison, illustrated by a trans woman held in 'worrying' conditions. National prison-placement framework; no division-specific detail for this region.

National preventive mechanism opinion (May 2021) on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty (follow-up to its June 2010 opinion): records the persistence of serious violations of trans detainees' rights in adult prisons, while none were noted in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres; the review covered the situations of some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man. National custodial-inspection framework; no division-specific finding for this region.

19338628B74392602121343.name: Grand Est
19338628B74392602121343.summary: Grand Est applies France's national framework unchanged: trans identity is not criminalised, there is no trans-specific entry ban, transphobia has been a statutory aggravating factor since 2017, and equality and anti-discrimination protections are in force. The national exposures remain: border officers may publicly question a mismatch between a traveller's documents and presentation, with a documented case of a trans traveller questioned at an airport; periodic security and immigration controls at the Schengen crossings — Mulhouse-Basel and the German, Belgian and Luxembourg borders — apply the same French document checks and can raise routine scrutiny; and in custody, placement follows either the sex shown on identity documents or birth sex (accounts differ), with isolation and, as reported by inspectors, strip-search exposure. Ombudsman findings record persistent discrimination in services and accommodation. Within the region, Strasbourg — home to the Council of Europe and the European Court of Human Rights — along with Metz, Nancy and Reims have larger LGBTQ communities, visible Pride events, LGBT associations, university hospitals and cosmopolitan settings, and cross-border traffic with Germany, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland makes official and service-provider encounters there comparatively routine; the visitor-facing tourism economy of Alsace Christmas markets, Reims and Colmar is habituated to outsiders. Rural and small-town areas — the Vosges, Ardennes, parts of Champagne, former industrial areas, and Alsace-Moselle with its retained local law and practising Catholic milieu — are more socially conservative, with thinner recourse in practice. No region-specific punitive measures, hostile legislation, enforcement pattern, protective regime or documented exception to national border, facility or custody practice is known here; the difference from the national picture is one of degree rather than kind.

19338628B73800214047876.name: Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes
19338628B73800214047876.summary:
Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes stands under the French national framework. No region-specific signal was identified: the region's own page carries no trans-specific content, and no regional deviation from the national position was located in the source inventory.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Article D248 of the criminal procedure code assigns detainees according to the sex inscribed on their identity documents, and each facility improvises around that rule. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018, 'The Plight Of Trans Women In Prison', reports first-person accounts of placement in all-male facilities, including a three-day stay in Lille's men's prison in 2014 marked by detainee and staff hostility, and the story of an Argentinian trans woman's incarceration. The feature also covers the well-publicised case of a US trans woman detained in poor conditions after a 2016 Paris protest case.

The controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty states that transgender detainees are the group that suffers the most in prison.

The CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021, issued by the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté, examines the treatment of transgender persons in all places of deprivation of liberty. It rests on about forty referrals received since 2010, interviews with trans associations and European experts, and five on-site inspections covering Fleury-Mérogis men's and women's prisons, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse-Seysses and the Toulouse central police station, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. The opinion finds persistent serious violations of the fundamental rights of trans detainees, including isolation and overcrowding risks, and recommends that the 2016 depathologising law, which removed the surgery requirement for civil-status change, be translated into prison regulations. Its scope explicitly extends to intersex and non-binary people.

For partner recognition, France legalised same-sex marriage and full adoption in 2013, and civil solidarity pacts have existed since 1999. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore encounters a recognised legal baseline.

Penal Code article 225-1 has covered gender identity since an 18 November 2016 amendment that replaced 'sexual identity', protected since 2012. Homophobic hate speech has carried penalties of up to EUR 45,000 and/or one year's imprisonment since a 31 December 2004 amendment.

On legal gender recognition, a bill approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and by the National Assembly on 24 May 2016 was signed into law on 18 November 2016 and took effect on 1 January 2017. It abolished the sex-reassignment-surgery and forced-sterilisation requirements, rejected a Senate amendment that would have demanded proof of medical treatment, and requires going before a court rather than any medical intervention.

Transsexualism is classed under long-term-illness ALD 31, so gender-affirming treatment is funded by the Sécurité Sociale.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed feature (Rozenn Le Carboulec) on trans women in French prisons: Article D248 of the Criminal Procedure Code mandates separate establishments for men and women, so placement follows the sex on identity documents and trans women are typically held in men's facilities - as of 1 Nov 2016 there were 13 transgender detainees held across eight establishments, most at Fleury-Mérogis. Profiles Paola, an Argentine trans woman transferred to a men's facility in 2014 and met with shouts of 'We don't want any women here', despite a passport listing her as female, because French law does not recognise her Argentine legal gender for placement purposes. Documents inconsistent access to treatment and a 2,000-euro symbolic damages award over detention conditions, with the justice minister pressed to amend D248.

Opinion of the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté (CGLPL), France's national preventive mechanism, dated 25 May 2021, on the care of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: building on referrals received since 2010 and a 2010 opinion on transsexual prisoners, it covers all places of deprivation of liberty. Inspections cited include Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station, with evidence from eight transgender women; it documents discrimination, stigmatisation and health and social-care blind spots and recommends policies to combat the discrimination and exclusion they face, referencing law n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016 on justice modernisation and prison transfers and the 'racism, antisemitism, LGBT and discrimination' referents appointed since 2018. The CGLPL reports persistent serious violations of trans detainees' rights across the prisons it inspected.

sources.summary: Outright International (IGLHRC) Philippines country overview (updated 2025): same-sex relations are legal and acceptance indices rank the country among the most accepting in Asia, but trans people cannot access legal gender recognition - the 2001 Clerical Error Law (RA 9048) blocks gender-marker correction - and national non-discrimination bills filed since 1999 remain unenacted, with two civil-union bills filed since 2022 facing religious-conservative opposition; non-discrimination ordinances exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels. A 2018 SWS survey found only 22% of Filipinos supported same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets. The Safe Spaces Act criminalises homophobic and transphobic slurs; the Anti-Bullying Act and the Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy (reiterated 2022, June designated Pride Month) cover sexual orientation and gender identity in schools; Executive Orders No. 100 (2019) and No. 51 (2023) creating the national Diversity and Inclusion Program remain unimplemented as of 2025.

Bulatlat (26 Jun 2025): 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol, a Cagayan State University business-management student, was found dead in a Cagayan province river on 23 June 2025, days after being reported missing, with signs of physical assault. A criminology student who admitted driving her surrendered to police while denying involvement. On the same day, trans woman and former activist-journalist Ali Macalintal was shot by an unidentified gunman inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos. Bahaghari and other groups cite the cases in calling for passage of the SOGIESC Equality Bill, stuck in Congress for 25 years (latest version Senate Bill 1600), which would prohibit admission denial, denial of public and health services, and infliction of physical harm or verbal abuse based on SOGIE.

36201628B90061603712355.name: Davao Region
36201628B90061603712355.summary:
Davao Region has no regional statute or regional ordinance of its own governing sexual orientation or gender identity. A trans visitor to the region stands under the national framework of the Philippines, together with the municipal law of the particular city or municipality visited.

Davao City, the region's administrative center, is recorded among the Philippine localities that have a non-discrimination ordinance. Its council passed the measure in December 2012, banning discrimination against gays (LGBT people), minorities and differently-abled persons. Within Davao City, that ordinance is the only documented local layer of protection available beyond the national position.

Custody practice specific to the region is documented. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology in Davao moves LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex, holding them alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens as a stated measure to prevent abuse. Placement of trans detainees in Davao thus takes the form of administrative segregation rather than gender-matched accommodation.

The two legal standards it documents, the restroom-access damages ruling and the removal of the surgical prerequisite for a registered sex change, are national in scope and are recorded as applying in the province with no Gangwon-specific case attached to either. A trans visitor to Gangwon therefore faces the national legal position with no documented province-level variation.

sources.summary: Korea Times (22 July 2024): the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a 3 million won claim, ruling that police advice to a person transitioning from male to female, who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights. The appellate court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink and 36% forwent restroom use. A 2021 Daegu District Court (Pohang branch) award of 7 million won against a beauty academy that prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom forms part of the national standard applied in Gangwon, where no specific incident is documented.

Yonhap wire (8 May 2024): a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that court guidelines requiring surgery are now only reference, not criteria. The court said every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. The ruling removed the surgical prerequisite for registered-sex change and is the standard applied in Gangwon, where no province-specific case is documented.

1875124B58976419670313.name: Tacna
1875124B58976419670313.summary:
Tacna stands under Peru's national framework; national law on criminalisation, anti-discrimination protection, identity documents and public-facility access applies here as it does across the country and is set out under Peru.

On 19 April 2025 Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a room of the Los 5 Titos hostel on Arias y Aragüez street in central Tacna. The autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the airways. She had entered the hostel with a man who registered under a false identity and who left alone roughly two hours later carrying a white bag. Staff found the body when the rental time expired.

Tacna authorities are investigating the death as a possible hate crime, an offence motivated by prejudice and discrimination on grounds of the victim's sexual orientation or gender identity. No suspect had been identified in the reporting of 21 and 27 May 2025. The victim was initially processed as an unidentified body and was named through the hostel's cameras; police were analysing surveillance footage from inside and outside the premises to trace the suspect's escape route.

Family members and local LGTBIQ+ collectives held a vigil on Friday 23 May 2025 demanding justice, describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence that silences trans lives. Relatives publicly denounced the killing and pressed for police action.

13589884B77991835419453.name: Atlántico
13589884B77991835419453.summary:
Atlántico department stands under Colombia's national framework. The department's own signal comes from the 2025 report "Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia", published by the regional LGBTI+ rights organisation Caribe Afirmativo and covered by Publimetro Colombia.

For Atlántico the report counts 54 cases of intrafamily violence, 41 sexual offences, 69 threats, 12 discrimination cases, 8 cases of digital violence, 8 cases of lethal violence, and 2 killings of LGBTIQ+ human-rights defenders during 2025. These are raw departmental totals; the report supplies no population or per-capita denominator, so they cannot be read as a ranking against other Colombian departments and no conclusion about relative danger follows from the counts alone.

The report designates Barranquilla and Soledad as territories carrying a "high" threat level for this population. Violence is described as expanding into territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, with the state response judged insufficient.

Threat cases recorded in the report show near-total impunity: 99.8% never advance past the investigation stage. Whether that percentage is calculated for the department or for the country as a whole is not stated in the material available here.

The department's development plan and Barranquilla's development plan commit the local authorities to coordinated action with the prosecutor's office, the police and the judiciary to strengthen reporting, investigation and prosecution of violence against LGBTIQ+ people.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Amazonas (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2006 Amazonas state policies include discrimination based on gender identity, and since 2019 transphobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to racism. Since the March 2018 unanimous Supreme Federal Court ruling, transgender people may change legal gender at a registry post without surgery, hormonal therapy, judicial authorization or medical report, with registry-office gender changes reported up 59% by 2024. Amazonas has no specific law recognizing non-binary gender; in 2022 Álex Souza de Sá became the first non-binary person recognized, requiring rectification in Rio de Janeiro and six months of insistence plus intervention by the Public Defender's Office to obtain recognition in Manaus where the registry lacked a gender-neutral marker. For facilities, on 18 October 2022 the mayor of Manaus signed a law banning unisex restrooms in the city. For care, in November 2023 the State Public Defender's Office opened monitoring of public health services for transgender and travesti people including hormones and surgeries, in August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended the state formally enable outpatient and hospital transsexualization services including sexual reassignment surgeries with deadlines for submission to the Ministry of Health, and on 10 June 2025 Governor Wilson Lima signed Law No. 7,552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under 18. For protection machinery, in 2021 the State Public Defender's Office created the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group focused on human rights violations and training security agents, and in August 2024 the State Court of Justice released the booklet Home is a Right! for LGBTQ youth expelled from homes stating conversion therapies are "prohibited and ineffective." Cases of violence against LGBTQ people in the state are described as underreported, with 43 cases registered according to Brazilian Public Security Forum data cited in research. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1830 when the Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Amazonas since 2013 via National Council of Justice decision following the 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision, with a 328% increase between 2020 and 2025, 287 unions registered in 2024 and 98 in the first five months of 2025. Same-sex adoption was first authorized in Amazonas in November 2012 by a state court judge, with nationwide legalization by the Supreme Federal Court in 2015. Since 2006 state policies include discrimination based on sexual orientation, and since 2019 homophobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to racism. Assembly and expression restrictions include State Law 6,469/2023 prohibiting participation of children and adolescents in pride parades with fines up to R$10,000, and the 17 October 2024 law prohibiting reproduction of digital media using children linked to homosexuality, amended on 13 December 2025 to remove the term homosexuality and prohibit reproduction of sexual content linked to children in cultural and artistic media. On 5 July 2025 Fernando Vilaça de Souza was beaten and killed in Manaus after reacting to homophobic insults, with prior bullying reported by area residents.

sources.title: Brazilian Supreme Federal Court ruling, March 2018 - legal gender change
sources.summary: In March 2018 Brazil's Supreme Federal Court ruled that transgender people may change their legal name and gender marker on civil records without sex-reassignment surgery, hormonal treatment, or judicial authorization.

sources.title: Manaus municipal law banning unisex restrooms - 18 October 2022
sources.summary: On 18 October 2022 Manaus sanctioned a municipal law prohibiting multigender/unisex restrooms.

sources.title: Federal Public Prosecutor's Office (MPF) Recommendation - August 2024
sources.summary: In August 2024, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended that the state of Amazonas guarantee integral health care to the LGBTQIAPN+ population, including trans people.

sources.title: Amazonas Public Defender's Office (DPE-AM) monitoring process - November 2023
sources.summary: In Amazonas as of 1 November 2023 the State Public Defender's health unit opened a collective procedure to audit SUS care for trans people covering access to hormonization, outpatient services, and lack of accreditation for gender-affirming surgeries including sexual reassignment, and in October 2023 the Manaus Municipal Health Secretariat committed to dispense standardized medications to trans people on prescription from the Codajás Outpatient Clinic that handles hormonization and to designate reference UBS primary-care units in each city zone, while the State Health Secretariat was ordered to report on equitable integral care including remedying hormoniotherapy gaps guaranteed under Federal Council of Medicine Resolution No. 2,265 of 2019.

sources.title: Amazonas State Law No. 6,463/2023 - gender-neutral language ban in schools
sources.summary: On 10 October 2023 Amazonas State Law No. 6,463 expressly prohibited use of neutral language, non-binary dialect, or any expression departing from standard Portuguese in curricula and teaching materials of public and private educational institutions and in official documents of schools and public agencies statewide.

sources.title: Amazonas State Court of Justice (TJAM) booklet Lar e Direito! / Home is a Right! - August 2024
sources.summary: In Amazonas as of August 2024, LGBTQIAPN+ adolescents facing family discrimination and expulsion are guaranteed under ECA Article 17 physical, psychological and moral integrity including identity and autonomy and under Constitution/ECA duties of family, society and State to ensure health, food, education and protection from negligence and discrimination with equal treatment of children regardless of sexual orientation, with bullying criminalized under Law 14.811/2024 by fine to 4 years' imprisonment, homophobia criminalized per 2019 STF ruling as imprescriptible and non-bailable, conversion/"gay cure" therapy prohibited as illegal and ineffective, and legal support available through the Defensoria Especializada em Direitos Humanos.

sources.title: DPE-AM Working Group on Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship - 2021
sources.summary: On 28 June 2021 the Amazonas Public Defender's Office created the permanent Working Group on Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship to identify LGBTQIA+ human-rights violations in public security, train public-security agents for service to LGBTQIA+ people, and issue recommendations and extrajudicial measures, while LGBTQIA+ victims in Manaus can obtain assistance via Disk 129 Monday-Friday 8am-2pm through the Specialized Human Rights unit, in a context where Amazonas led North and Central-West states with 4.66 LGBTQIA+ persons murdered per million inhabitants in 2018.

sources.title: Nationwide criminalization of homophobia and transphobia - 2019
sources.summary: On 23 May 2019 a majority of Brazil's Supreme Federal Tribunal (6 of 11 justices) voted to criminalize transphobia under Brazil's 1989 racism law punishable by up to five years' imprisonment until Congress enacts specific LGBT-discrimination legislation, to take effect after all justices voted on 5 June 2019.

sources.title: Brazilian Public Security Forum / Brazilian Journal of Public Security data + Fernando Vilaca de Souza homicide 5 July 2025
sources.summary: In Amazonas during 2021-2022, crimes involving transsexual persons formed part of only 0.36% of total reported crimes in the capital and interior, police occurrence reports did not identify transfobia or gender, sexuality, race and intersectionality markers, trans victim data were few and badly structured with victims not infrequently inverted to accused through faulty BOs, and unprepared public agents and defective registration mechanisms left trans subjects invisibilized and without protection.

sources.summary: Colombia decriminalised homosexuality in 1981, and in 2011 Congress passed a law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation. The Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in a 6-3 ruling of 28 April 2016, with the first wedding in Cali on 24 May 2016. Three rulings between February 2007 and April 2008 had granted same-sex couples property, social-security and pension rights, and a November 2015 ruling granted full adoption rights with dual-parent birth registration. Since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options: male, female and X. Adults can change legal gender before a notary without surgery, with a free simultaneous name change on first request. Gays, lesbians and bisexuals have served openly in the armed forces since a 1999 court ruling. Casanare adds no separate legal regime, so these national provisions define the formal legal exposure of a trans visitor to the department.

13589884B16144547040567.name: Caquetá
13589884B16144547040567.summary:
Caquetá is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework: legal gender recognition, identification markers, entry rules, marriage and partner recognition, and the national protection machinery are carried by the national record and are not restated here. The department-specific signal concerns organised armed-group targeting rather than statute.

Reporting dated 30 July 2024 documented armed groups in Caquetá running a 'social cleansing' campaign, distributing flyers on the streets and through WhatsApp that named 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets.

The campaign has produced displacement. A trans woman who was a local election candidate was told by three armed men that she had one week to leave town; she hid for a week and then fled at night. A second trans woman in the department said a friend had been killed.

For a trans visitor, the exposure in Caquetá is not the statute book but the presence of armed groups that have publicly designated trans people as targets and have acted on that designation by driving residents out. The campaign's categories are social rather than documentary: the flyers name people by perceived sexual orientation and gender expression, not by any official record.

sources.summary: On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia. The assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April; she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents, and no one had been arrested even after the president ordered an urgent investigation. EL PAÍS English (14 April 2025) reports 13 trans people killed by hate in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, alongside earlier killings of gay men and the stabbing death of a trans rough-sleeper. Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina has no recorded incident, law or enforcement finding on this point. What bears on a visitor to the islands is the national pattern of lethal anti-trans violence.

The Guardian (30 July 2024) documented armed groups in Caquetá department running a 'social cleansing' campaign: flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp named 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets. Three armed men told a trans woman and local election candidate she had one week to leave town; she hid for a week, then fled at night. A second trans woman said a friend was killed. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina has no specific finding here; the national kill figures and the armed-group 'social-cleansing' pattern are what bear on a visitor.

1875124B3772980127380.name: Puno
1875124B3772980127380.summary:
No region-specific finding on trans visitor safety was identified for the department of Puno. The sources record no Puno ordinance, exemption, enforcement practice or regional institution of its own on trans matters.

The national framework that governs Puno includes a public-restroom restriction. On 2 April 2025 the Peruvian congressional Plenary approved, exempt from a second vote, a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', with narrow listed exceptions; IDEHPUCP's legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025 states this violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors argue the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

An earlier committee-stage measure of the same family, reported by Infobae Perú on 20 February 2025, was approved unanimously by the congressional Women and Family Commission as a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and noted there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. As national law this binds Puno.

The authors say the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. The analysis addresses the national framework that governs Puno and records no Puno-specific finding.

1875124B82769317880582.name: Tumbes
1875124B82769317880582.summary:
Tumbes stands under Peru's national framework. No region-specific signal was identified: the sources addressing this department do so only through national legislation and national legal analysis, and none records a Tumbes ordinance, enforcement action, incident or institution. The national assessment applies.

Under the national framework binding Tumbes, Law 32331 of 13 May 2025 restricts trans people's use of public restrooms. The congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, required medical attention, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and noting there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions. IDEHPUCP legal analysts Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte argue this violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. They state that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

Separately, the April 2025 'Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents' mandates that public-restroom entry be restricted by 'biological sex', barring trans people including trans youth from facilities matching their identity; its vague child-protection articles enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational content, and the obscenity minimum sentence rises from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states child protection is a pretext for repression and trans scapegoating. The IDEHPUCP states the restriction openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing trans people as harassment risks; the institute cites Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

1875124B82769317880582.tangentialFactors:
The bathroom-restriction measures stand alongside other national turbulence affecting LGBTIQ organising: April 2025's NGO foreign-funding law lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order' or 'security' grounds, risking weaponisation against queer organising, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional. Public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination.

A report of 22 July 2024 by Agencia Presentes finds hate crimes rose in Peru with trans women most affected; co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender and journalist, stresses that recorded numbers are only a sub-registry. The report cites a 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study finding that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work.

On 19 December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the torture and sexual abuse of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. The judgment, issued after years of litigation, is Peru's first conviction in a sexual-discrimination-motivated case and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court via the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Opinion polls show age-based variation: 18 to 24-year-olds (66%) were markedly more favourable toward homosexuals than the population overall (49%), and younger people showed higher approval of same-sex marriage (8.3% approval among Peruvians in 2010, higher among younger respondents).

1875124B82769317880582.localsOnly:
Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November 2016, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem to cover trans healthcare; after protests, in June 2024 the Ministry of Health (MINSA) revised the term to 'gender discordance' for health-insurance classification purposes. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities also removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases. Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, a protection with specific relevance to trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

The 2016 national education curriculum includes information on sexual orientation, sex and gender issues, describing sexual orientation as the result of complex biological, cognitive and environmental circumstances and not a voluntary choice. Pride marches have been held annually since 2002, with the oldest recorded march in 1984.

sources.summary: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports that the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex. Exceptions cover custody, cases where medical attention is required, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities; the draft also bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and states there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The measure stood at committee stage in February 2025 and binds Piura as national legislation.

IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) states that on 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', with narrow listed exceptions. The authors argue this violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. They hold that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. The framework governs Piura as national law.

sources.summary: Infobae Peru (20 Feb 2025): the congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457 (sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante) that would prohibit any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions (custody, and cases where required, including accompanying minors, the elderly or people with disabilities), and would oblige venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs; the article notes the text still needed plenary backing and reports the trigger as the July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho is quoted arguing the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender. This is the national framework this department is scored against; the article contains no Lambayeque-specific content.

IDEHPUCP legal analysis (15 April 2025, Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte): on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the 'Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes', whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The institute reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination (Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights), resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, and recalls documented cases of trans people barred from public restrooms - including SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissing a trans woman's discrimination complaint against SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI - and the fact that gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive. This is the national framework this department is scored against; the article contains no Lambayeque-specific content.

Agencia Presentes (22 July 2024), drawing on the annual report of the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia: Peru recorded 54 assassinations of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in 2020-2023, the homicide victims being 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian; 19 killings occurred in 2023 alone (12 of them trans women), and killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides (13 of 19 in 2023). The piece recounts the February 2023 murder of trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano (31), kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots (Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot days earlier), with two killers arrested in March 2023, and notes the state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such. This is the national violence baseline this department is scored against; the article contains no Lambayeque-specific content.
