sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Amazonas (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2006 Amazonas state policies prohibit discrimination based on gender identity, and since 2019 transphobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to the crime of racism. In 2021 the Amazonas State Public Defender's Office created the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group to address human rights violations and train security agents, and in November 2023 it opened a process to monitor public health services for transgender and travesti people including provision of hormones and surgeries. In March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court unanimously ruled transgender people may change legal gender at a registry post without surgery, hormonal therapy, judicial document or medical report, with registry gender changes reported up 59% by 2024. On 18 October 2022 the mayor of Manaus signed a law banning unisex restrooms in the city. In August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended Amazonas formally enable outpatient and hospital services for the transsexualization process including sexual reassignment surgeries, with deadlines for approval and presentation to the Ministry of Health. On 10 June 2025 Governor Wilson Lima signed Law No. 7,552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under age 18. Amazonas has no specific law recognizing non-binary gender, and in 2022 Alex Souza de Sa became the first non-binary person recognized in the state after rectification in Rio de Janeiro and intervention by the Public Defender's Office to secure recognition in Manaus after six months when the local notary lacked a gender-neutral marker. Homosexuality has been legal in Amazonas and Brazil since 1830 when the Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 via National Council of Justice decision following the 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision, and same-sex adoption was first allowed in Amazonas in November 2012 by an Amazonas Court of Justice judge before nationwide legalization by the Supreme Federal Court in 2015. Since 2006 Amazonas state policies prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation, and since 2019 homophobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to the crime of racism. The August 2024 Amazonas Court of Justice booklet Home is a Right! for LGBTQ youth expelled from homes states that conversion therapies are "prohibited and ineffective." Research from the Brazilian Journal of Public Security states that cases of violence against LGBTQ people in Amazonas are underreported. Data from the Brazilian Public Security Forum indicates cases of violence against LGBTQ people have increased, with 43 cases registered. On 5 July 2025 Fernando Vilaca de Souza was beaten and killed in Manaus after reacting to homophobic insults, and residents reported he had previously been bullied by other young people in the region. The Ministry of Human Rights and Citizenship, the Order of Attorneys of Brazil and federal deputy Erika Hilton expressed regret over the incident. The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically so no such quote can be reproduced, and the above violence figures refer to LGBTQ people generally not to transgender people specifically.

sources.title: Federal Public Prosecutor's Office (MPF) recommendation - August 2024
sources.summary: In August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended that the state of Amazonas guarantee comprehensive health care for the LGBTQIAPN+ population, including trans people.

sources.title: Public Defender's Office of the State of Amazonas (DPE-AM) monitoring process - November 2023
sources.summary: In Amazonas in October-November 2023, trans access to SUS was under enforcement review for primary care, outpatient services, hormonization, and lack of local authorization for transexualizing surgeries including sexual reassignment, with the municipal health authority committing to dispense standardized hormone medications on Ambulatório Codajás prescriptions and to designate a reference UBS in each city zone and the state health authority required to report on equitable integral care and hormoniotherapy gaps guaranteed under CFM Resolution No. 2.265/2019.

sources.title: Manaus municipal law banning unisex restrooms - 18 October 2022
sources.summary: On 18 October 2022 the municipality of Manaus sanctioned a law prohibiting multigender/unisex bathrooms.

sources.title: Amazonas State Law No. 6,463/2023 on gender-neutral language ban
sources.summary: On 10 October 2023 Amazonas Law No. 6,463 prohibited the use of gender-neutral language, non-binary dialect, or any expression deviating from standard Portuguese in the curricula and teaching materials of public and private educational institutions and in official documents of educational institutions and public offices throughout the state of Amazonas.

sources.title: Amazonas State Court of Justice (TJAM) booklet Lar e Direito! / Home is a Right! - August 2024
sources.summary: In Amazonas since August 2024, LGBTQIAPN+ adolescents facing family discrimination and expulsion from home are affirmed as protected by ECA Article 17 guaranteeing physical, psychological and moral integrity including identity, autonomy and beliefs, by Constitutional/ECA duties of family, society and State to ensure health, food, education and protection against negligence and discrimination with equal treatment of all children regardless of sexual orientation, by Law No. 14.811/2024 criminalizing bullying with penalties ranging from fine to 4 years' imprisonment, by the 2019 STF recognition of homophobia as an imprescriptible and unbailable crime, and by the prohibition of conversion/"cura gay" therapies as illegal and ineffective, with legal support available from the Defensoria Especializada em Direitos Humanos.

sources.title: Amazonas State Public Defender's Office (DPE-AM) Working Group - 2021
sources.summary: On 28 June 2021 the Amazonas Public Defender's Office (DPE-AM) created the permanent Working Group "Diversidade Sexual, Identidade de Gênero e Cidadania" to defend LGBTQIA+ rights and identify human rights violations in the area of public security. Its mandate includes training public security agents for service to LGBTQIA+ persons and issuing recommendations and other extrajudicial referrals. Victims of LGBTphobia are served by the Specialized Human Rights Defensoria via Disk 129 in Manaus Monday to Friday 8h-14h, in a context where Amazonas led North and Center-West states with an average of 4.66 LGBTQIA+ persons murdered per million inhabitants in 2018.

sources.title: Brazilian Public Security Forum / Brazilian Journal of Public Security + 5 July 2025 homicide case
sources.summary: In Amazonas during 2021-2022 trans persons faced persistent diverse violence intensifying each year while only 0.36% of crimes reported in the capital and interior involved homosexual, lesbian, bisexual and transsexual victims, police occurrence reports did not identify homophobia and transfobia motives or gender, sexuality, race and intersectionality markers, victim data were few and poorly structured with victims at times inverted to accused through faulty reports, and unprepared public agents and defective registration mechanisms produced invisibilization and lack of protection for trans victims.

sources.summary: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports that Congress' Commission on Women and Family unanimously approved a dictamen covering bills 6506 and 8457 that would bar entry to public sanitary facilities destined to the sex opposite to one's birth sex, with exceptions for custody, medical care, or accompanying an adult, a child under 12 or a disabled person, and would require unambiguous signage; as of publication it still awaited plenary backing. Trans-rights activist Gianna Camacho is quoted calling the measure discriminatory and warning that security staff would effectively judge people by personal criteria, such as requesting their DNI. The bills contain no Arequipa-specific provision, and as national law they bind the department.

IDEHPUCP analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) reports that the Congress plenary on 2 April 2025 approved, exempt from second vote, the dictamen of the law 'fortaleciendo el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los niños y adolescentes'. Its article 5 bars anyone whose biological sex does not match the facility's intended sex from public sanitary facilities, with exceptions limited to accompanying or assisting minors, patients or people with specific needs. The authors argue the measure implicitly brands trans people as more prone to entering bathrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, conditions basic rights on verifiable 'biological sex', and violates equality, non-discrimination and gender self-determination; they note that Congress had already banned inclusive language and again rejected equal marriage. The analysis makes no Arequipa-specific finding.

Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024) reports the TLGBI Rights Observatory's annual report: 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru between 2020 and 2023, with trans women the most affected and hate crimes rising. It recounts the February 2023 kidnapping of trans woman Rubí Torres Silvano (31) in central Lima and her murder in Carabayllo with approximately 30 gunshots at the hands of the 'Los Gallegos' gang, the bodies showing gunshots, stab wounds and throat-slitting that indicate extreme hate. No Arequipa-specific finding appears; the national figures describe the risk environment the department shares.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025) reports a leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus 11th Judicial Package that would open the way to criminal charges against LGBT people, described as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades. Conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, including its so-called promotion, would bring up to three years in prison. Participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies would bring up to four years; since same-sex marriage is not legal, such ceremonies are by definition symbolic. Gender-affirming care would be restricted, with the surgery age raised from 18 to 25 and permanent infertility made mandatory. Hostility is presented as institutionalised under 'Year of the Family' instructions to public institutions, with hate speech from senior officials, censored broadcasts and cancelled artistic events. The report describes national practice rather than provincial choice, and no Ağrı-specific finding appears in it.

25984515B97476213604692.name: Antalya
25984515B97476213604692.summary: Antalya is a large Mediterranean resort province centred on Antalya city, Alanya, Side and Kaş, with a major foreign-visitor economy, a relatively secular urban culture and Kaş's long-established gay-friendly community. Resort businesses and foreign status generally buy more discretion than in Istanbul or Ankara, police priorities lean toward tourist security, public venues tend to treat foreign guests with pragmatic indifference, there is less visible street-level policing of gender nonconformity than in Istanbul's Beyoğlu, and local authorities and businesses have economic incentives to avoid public scandal involving foreign visitors. A historically visible, though periodically banned, LGBTQ venue and Pride scene exists. These advantages are everyday ones only: hotel and police document checks can still out a visitor, trans community infrastructure and LGBT venues are scarce and trans-specific advocacy is much thinner than in Istanbul, conservative attitudes are stronger outside central tourist zones and hotel and beach enclaves, provincial authorities have banned LGBTI+ events in the past, and local enforcement tends to follow national policy. No region-specific record of prosecutions, lethal violence or targeted raids against trans visitors, no Antalya-specific trans-targeting pattern, and no effective local safeguard are documented, and specific local rules affecting facilities, care, document checks, or travelling families and minors are not documented.

25984515B1602304411378.name: Artvin
25984515B1602304411378.summary: Artvin is a small, mountainous, lightly visited Black Sea province on the Georgian border, with small towns, limited tourist infrastructure, ethnic homogeneity, low visibility of transgender people and a close-knit social environment that offers far less anonymity than Istanbul or Ankara. It has no documented LGBT or trans organisations, pride events or visible community infrastructure, no recorded local protections or Artvin-specific statute, no documented local tolerance, protective practice or organised anti-trans campaign, and no recorded region-specific incidents involving foreign visitors or local enforcement pattern — and equally no local remedy or shield. Legal aid and support networks are concentrated far away in Istanbul and Ankara, specialised healthcare is limited so hormone therapy would depend on private arrangements, and the more organised police apparatus documented for Istanbul appears thinner locally, although social stigma in this conservative rural setting may exceed the national average. Discovery or outing would still trigger Turkey's national regime: no entry restrictions target LGBTQ visitors, but carried-ID checks at transit and border points are the main outing mechanism and can lead to police stops, GBT background checks and documented detentions (including a 2025 Istanbul round-up and street detentions and "documentation" of trans women), while 313 recorded LGBTI+ violations in 2025 were dominated by detentions. There is no legal protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity, official family-and-morals rhetoric has escalated since 2024–2026, and pending legislation targeting LGBT expression adds further uncertainty. Anyone detained faces placement by birth sex rather than gender-matched housing, segregation and isolation, intrusive searches, restricted healthcare, abuse, ineffective complaints in custody and a documented 2025 death of a trans prisoner, with no public coverage of hormone therapy. In Artvin an outed trans visitor would depend on local police discretion with fewer anonymity buffers and thinner recourse: any police, hospital, family or school contact is likely to default to national binary placement and hostility, and the absence of local reports does not demonstrate safety or effective local recourse.

25984515B63739470532168.name: Aydın
25984515B63739470532168.summary: Aydın is a western Aegean province centred on the city of Aydın and the resort districts of Kuşadası and Didim, whose tourism economy, university presence and visible foreign visitors give coastal hotels, beaches and promenades a comparatively secular, service-oriented atmosphere with noticeably higher street-level tolerance than Istanbul, inland or central-eastern Anatolia. There is no separate provincial entry rule, local trans-specific ordinance or protective regime, and no local pattern of targeting trans visitors, region-specific anti-trans violence, hostile ordinance or police campaign at Istanbul's scale is documented; an Aydın branch of the Human Rights Association, which has joined calls for an independent investigation into prison practices, provides some rights infrastructure but no demonstrated remedy for visitors. Local conservatism and centralized police practice remain, and informal tolerance is uneven. Under the national framework that applies here, a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed faces passport or ID checks — an active trigger for police contact at holiday destinations — leading to stop-and-document practices, GBT documentation and short detention, under an official climate framing LGBT people as a threat to the family, with no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection covering gender identity and no effective local recourse. Custody carries poor conditions, while prison placement follows a binary system bringing segregation, isolation, intrusive searches and restricted healthcare, and hormone therapy is available only privately at the visitor's own cost. Resort-area foreignness and the comparatively liberal coastal setting reduce everyday scrutiny and friction, but they do not change police, custody or proposed criminalisation risks if a visitor is outed.

25984515B55384476443375.name: Balıkesir
25984515B55384476443375.summary: Balıkesir is a province in western Turkey centred on Balıkesir city, with tourist-oriented coastal districts around Ayvalık, Burhaniye, Edremit and the Kaz Dağları area drawing domestic and some foreign visitors, while the interior remains largely conservative and Aegean-Marmara in character. The province inherits Turkey's national regime with no region-specific legal rules: there is no LGBTQ-specific entry ban, but mandatory photo-ID checks and GBT-style police stops apply, with identity checks reportedly less frequent than in Istanbul. No regional anti-discrimination ordinance, documented local protection, recorded local pride or community infrastructure, dedicated legal aid or advocacy presence, visible trans community, or documented pattern of region-specific police action against trans people was identified, and rural districts are policed by gendarmerie rather than city police. Outside the more visitor-oriented coastal towns a trans visitor is more conspicuous, with less anonymity and recourse than in Istanbul or Izmir; national stigmatising rhetoric and family-focused campaigns framing LGBT people as a threat to family and children shape official attitudes, and enforcement against trans people has been documented in 2025 and 2026 alongside reported draft legislation targeting LGBT people. Should a trans visitor be outed or discovered, the national exposure applies with no documented local exception to offset it: discretionary police identity checks and background checks that can lead to detention, no legal recourse or protection against gender-identity discrimination, and hostile state framing. 25984515B40631498613339.name: Kars
25984515B40631498613339.summary: Kars is a small, remote province in eastern Anatolia near the Armenian border, with a socially conservative and religiously observant population in which gender nonconformity draws stronger social disapproval than in Istanbul or the Aegean coast, and where low anonymity for a visibly trans foreigner makes informal tolerance or discreet avoidance harder than in larger Turkish cities. There is no documented LGBTQ community infrastructure or local advocacy presence, few support organisations or specialist lawyers, and no nearby specialised legal or medical help, with advocacy, consular assistance and any remedy at long distance in Istanbul or Ankara. Kars adds no documented local protections and shows no documented exception to the national climate, and there is no documented local authority, armed-group control or province-specific ban; at the same time, Kars-specific border practices, police targeting, facility rules, violence and effective local remedies are not documented, and that lack of information is not evidence of safety. Border-region policing adds scrutiny at checkpoints and crossings, while the province's thin support network and conservatism are described as increasing street-level exposure, service refusal and ineffective complaints. One assessment notes instead that lower police intensity in a small town cuts the frequency of documented encounters, placing the combined effect below Turkey's overall pattern; that disagreement is not resolved here. Entry is not expressly restricted on grounds of being transgender, but original photo ID must be carried, and document or checkpoint checks can escalate into police identity checks, GBT background checks, arbitrary stops of trans women and detention; local enforcement is described as discretionary and poorly documented, with discovery more likely to bring official scrutiny and community hostility than organised street raids. If detained, trans people face segregation, strip searches, isolation, violence, inadequate medical access and ineffective complaints, and hormone replacement therapy is not covered for visitors. There is no comprehensive gender-identity anti-discrimination law, official rhetoric frames LGBTQ people as a threat to family and children, recorded violations are rising, and the proposed criminalisation provisions were not included in the 2026 judicial package.

25984515B36972543372669.name: Kastamonu
25984515B36972543372669.summary: Kastamonu is a socially conservative, less urban Black Sea province in northern Turkey centred on a small city with little foreign tourism, no visible transgender community, no local LGBT organisations, pride activity or advocacy and legal-aid infrastructure, and no local anti-discrimination protections or documented local tolerance that would offset national practice. Policing outside major cities is largely gendarmerie-led, with fewer oversight bodies, lawyers and media scrutiny than Istanbul or Ankara, Izmir or the capital. Documentation for this province is essentially absent: no region-specific cases of trans visitors being targeted were identified, sweeps and recorded incidents are sparse, and the lack of such reports is not evidence of safety, since less visible enforcement also means fewer local avenues for complaint or support. No local enforcement exception to national practice is documented. Turkey's national regime therefore applies in full: there is no visa or border exclusion for transgender travellers, but carrying photo identification and routine police identity checks and GBT background checks at transit points are the entry mechanism for contact, with documented street detentions and background recording, hostile official rhetoric, and detention and prison placement under binary, birth-sex facilities involving segregation, isolation, strip searches and reported denial of care. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection on gender identity, hormone therapy must be privately and self-arranged, and proposed criminalising provisions were not enacted in the 2026 judicial package. For a trans visitor who is discovered or outed, Kastamonu's deep social conservatism, small-city setting where officials know one another, and thin civil-society and service infrastructure mean visible gender nonconformity draws immediate attention, fewer witnesses or advocates are available, rural isolation is likely to worsen rather than improve the consequences of an identity check, and the practical remedy for detention, extortion or refusal of services is thinner than in larger cities, leaving stigma-driven questioning and limited support as the operative exposure.

25984515B43172796860329.name: Kayseri
25984515B43172796860329.summary: Kayseri is a socially conservative, nationalist and religiously conservative provincial capital in central Anatolia — smaller, less cosmopolitan and less familiar with visible gender non-conformity than Istanbul, Ankara or Izmir. It has few visible LGBTQ venues, little tourist-facing nightlife, no pride events (banned under national practice in any case), no visible community infrastructure or support network a visitor could turn to, limited specialist legal or medical support, privately arranged hormone therapy, and no sanctuary rules, trans-competent public services, or other documented local protective measure. Tourism is limited mainly to transit, airport, hotel, winter-sports and Cappadocia-area visitors, and those checkpoints create no known exception: they inherit the national exposure with fewer local safeguards. There is no documented Kayseri-specific campaign of raids or organised targeting, and street enforcement is less documented than in Istanbul's Beyoğlu, where the 2025 general information-gathering stops were concentrated — but local evidence about trans visitors and enforcement is limited, so the absence of a known local incident is not evidence of safety, and local police tolerance is not known to exceed the national pattern.\n\nTurkey's national regime applies in full: no LGBTQ-specific entry bar and no execution pathway for identity, but no legal protection or anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, routine police identity checks and General Information Gathering documentation, arbitrary and trans-specific detention, custody placement by birth sex with segregation or isolation and documented abuse, a 2025 custody death of a trans prisoner with no effective investigation, and hostile official rhetoric, with public pride events banned nationally. A trans visitor who is outed or discovered in Kayseri would therefore face stronger social disapproval, public scrutiny, hostility or refusal of service, isolation and street harassment than in western Turkey, with little practical recourse locally — while police contact still carries the full national consequences, including questioning, short detention and custody conditions, though there is no record of systematic imprisonment for being trans. No local mitigating exception is documented, and the combination of national exposure with this deeply conservative setting offers nothing that improves on the national pattern and may be somewhat harsher.

25984515B30869354278170.name: Kilis
25984515B30869354278170.summary: Kilis is a small, socially and religiously conservative southeastern border province adjoining Syria, with a large refugee population, heavy military and police security, frequent checkpoints and routine document scrutiny, and far less anonymity than a major city. It has minimal tourism infrastructure and few amenities for diverse visitors, and little or no visible LGBTQ community, venues, or support and legal-aid organisations of the kind present in Istanbul, Ankara or Izmir, so a visibly trans visitor may stand out and attract scrutiny in hotels, transport and street checks. Religious and tribal norms, together with strong nationalist and Islamist currents, raise the likelihood and severity of confrontation, harassment or violence if a visitor is outed, and friction with residents can escalate without intermediaries. Trans-competent healthcare and ongoing medication are scarce locally, with specialist services generally requiring travel to larger cities, and any recourse — including in Diyarbakir — is distant. Against that backdrop, Turkey's national regime governs discovery: there is no trans-specific entry ban or explicit criminalisation, but also no legal protection against gender-identity discrimination. Carried-ID rules and document checks can bring routine contact with police, and documented practices include identity checks, detentions, background recording and privacy violations affecting trans people, including street detentions and GBT background checks in 2025, with the frequency of such contact for trans visitors in Kilis uncertain. Detention and prison practice is binary, with segregation, isolation, strip searches, inadequate healthcare, transfers and ineffective complaints, alongside a 2025 death of a transgender prisoner; official family-and-morals rhetoric and raids on support networks accompany a rising count of documented violations. No local protective protocol, effective remedy or distinct local pattern of organised targeting against trans visitors is documented, and no distinct local information on travelling minors is recorded.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's national 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page is the framework every Turkish province, Kırıkkale included, stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the military: the armed forces' health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual' illness making members unfit for service, and conscripts who declare their homosexuality have to provide photographic proof. Same-sex marriage is not recognised; a 2012 constitutional-writing request to include it was rejected by both the AKP and the MHP. Authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years and police have used tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans; on 14 June 2019 the 7th Izmir Pride, the 3rd Antalya Pride and the 27th Istanbul Pride were banned by the cities' governors. The page also records a February 2026 newspaper report that the government was considering a law criminalising publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex', with a sentence of one to three years in prison.

sources.title: Türkiye - Amnesty International country report (Report 2025/26)
sources.summary: Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) applies in any province, Kırıkkale included. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. In November a court overturned a ban in Istanbul governorate as 'disproportionate' and 'unlawful', though prosecutions involving 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an Izmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had engaged in activities outside its stated purpose and shared 'obscene' images incompatible with the law. Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible. They were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's national 'LGBTQ rights in Turkey' page is the framework a trans visitor in Kütahya stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the military, and same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised. Pride parades have been banned by local authorities since 2015 (Istanbul's 2015-2018 parades were banned and dispersed). The 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026 dropped provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people and made symbolic same-sex weddings possible, though these carry no legal marital status; in early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', which was ultimately not included in that year's package, and in September 2026 police detained dozens in raids on gay bars and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists under a 'Decade of Family and Population' crackdown.

sources.title: Human rights in Türkiye - Amnesty International

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 - which would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible - but they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Muş province stands under the national legal framework of Türkiye; no Muş-specific ordinance, incident or court decision is documented for the province. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but no comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTI people are barred from military service: conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classified under a definition of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' being leaked publicly. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and since 2015 local authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches; police used water cannon and tear gas on the 2015 and 2016 Istanbul parades. Press reports in early 2026 stated that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', a provision ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package.

sources.title: Türkiye - Amnesty International country report (Report 2025/26)
sources.summary: Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) documents the national LGBTI climate under which Muş province sits: in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. Amnesty also records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 - an unprecedented assault that would criminalize expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible - but they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Under Türkiye's national framework, which applies in Niğde: homosexuality has been decriminalised since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised, and LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military: the armed forces' health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', conscripts who declare it must provide photographic proof, and those receiving an 'unfit report' may face later discrimination in public life. Pride events have been banned in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions, and ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking placed Turkey 47th out of 49 countries. A court case to close Lambda Istanbul was overruled by the Constitutional Court. A February 2026 press report of draft legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison was not included in the 12th judicial package, whose passage removed provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people and made symbolic same-sex weddings possible. No Niğde-specific source covers these points.

Amnesty records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 - an unprecedented assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible - but they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

The draft would raise the minimum age for legal gender recognition procedures from 18 to 25 and add further conditions. These are nationwide proposals that would apply within every province including Sakarya.

25984515B95251525471141.name: Uşak
25984515B95251525471141.summary: Uşak, a smaller inland province in western Turkey's Aegean region, has no province-specific criminal statute, protective policy, enforcement pattern or documented incident that departs from the national picture: no local anti-discrimination protection, no visible trans community, no trans-specific advocacy or legal-aid groups, and few trans-friendly clinical or social venues. It lacks the activist infrastructure, lawyers, Pride visibility and tourist-facing nightlife of Istanbul and Izmir, and social norms plus weak local recourse can make accidental outing through neighbours, employers, landlords, health or school settings more consequential, especially for families travelling with minors. Local incidents are thinly reported, so the picture is inferred from the national record and the province's conservative social character rather than from local evidence — the absence of local reports is not itself evidence of safety. A visibly trans visitor may stand out more in a smaller provincial center with less anonymity than Istanbul's large, diverse districts, drawing more scrutiny, though this does not establish a local pattern of targeting; conversely, Uşak lacks the organised Beyoğlu-style street policing documented in the metropolis, and there is no documented local campaign against trans people. Once discovered or outed, the national regime applies: routine photo-ID checks at transit checkpoints and police GBT stops document visibly gender-nonconforming people, and Kaos GL recorded more than 300 rights violations in 2025, most of them detentions, including GBT background checks. There is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection covering gender identity and no legal recourse of practical value, official rhetoric frames LGBT people as a threat, and in custody trans prisoners are placed by birth sex or in segregation, isolated, subjected to strip searches and restricted care. Hormone therapy is not covered by public healthcare, requiring private arrangements, and there is no border rule or trans-specific criminal statute aimed at travellers. In a province without protective institutions and with less practical accountability for police discretion than Istanbul or Izmir, a discovered visitor faces meaningful harassment or police exposure with limited reliable recourse.

25984515B28392380114016.name: Van
25984515B28392380114016.summary: Van is an eastern Turkish border province that is largely Kurdish-speaking, socially conservative, tribal and religiously observant, with a lakeside tourist economy centred on Lake Van and Akdamar Island. Its securitized environment — sustained police and gendarmerie presence, routine identity checkpoints, heavy security operations near the Iranian border and past curfews — increases the frequency of document checks, compounding the national pattern of GBT-style background stops. A visibly trans visitor is highly conspicuous here: the anonymity available in Istanbul or Izmir is largely absent, street-level hostility, intrusive curiosity and community pressure are more likely, and there is no documented local tradition of LGBTQ tolerance, no local protective policy, no trans-specific enforcement pattern and no visible trans residents. The LGBTQ social, advocacy, legal-aid and NGO monitoring capacity found in Istanbul, Ankara and Izmir is largely absent and the nearest dedicated trans organisations are distant, so an outed visitor has thinner practical recourse; a small university presence offers only limited openness. Tourist sites and hospitality around the lake may bring some outsider tolerance and moderate day-to-day friction, but they are not documented as trans-specific protections, and Van-specific facilities, police practices and visitor cases are not documented, so local severity remains uncertain rather than presumed safe. Against that backdrop, discovery or outing exposes a trans visitor to Turkey's national regime: no LGBTQ-specific entry rule and no explicit criminalisation of being trans, but post-arrival identity checks, documented detention and privacy violations affecting trans people, and hostile official family-and-morality framing — with no gender-identity anti-discrimination law and no recognised same-sex partnership. If detained, visitors face prison placement by birth sex with segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched accommodation, restricted or inadequate healthcare, arbitrary searches, intrusive questioning and ineffective complaints procedures. Discovery is therefore more likely to bring outing, detention, eviction, extortion, street or private violence and hostile local treatment, with little reliable police or judicial recourse.

25984515B35512619552530.summary: Şanlıurfa inherits Turkey's national framework for transgender visitors: there is no trans-specific entry ban, but police identity and background-stop checks (including general information-gathering stops, with trans women recorded in detentions during 2025) expose visitors to stops, recording and privacy risks; there is no legal protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity; custody uses segregation rather than housing prisoners by gender identity, with documented concerns about treatment and healthcare in custody, a trans prisoner's death in state custody in December 2025 amid evidence of neglect, and no public funding for hormone therapy; official rhetoric frames LGBTQ people as a threat to family and children, rights-violation counts are rising, and a draft law would criminalise LGBT advocacy. Locally, Şanlıurfa is among Turkey's most religiously conservative and tribally patriarchal provinces, with strong honor-based family and gender norms, tighter community and family surveillance, low anonymity in tight-knit communities, almost no visible LGBT or trans community infrastructure, no Pride events, no documented local protections or tolerant enforcement exceptions, and far weaker civil-society and legal-aid support than Istanbul, Ankara or İzmir, alongside a stronger security-police presence in the southeast. Tourism centres on Göbeklitepe and Balıklıgöl, which draw foreigners but bring no documented accommodation of gender diversity, and visitors outside those sites have limited anonymity. 19177384B49506124846693.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires
19177384B49506124846693.summary:
Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires stands under Argentina's national framework on legal gender recognition, gender markers, health care and hate-crime law. The sources assembled for the City record no municipal statute of its own on those matters and no city-level enforcement figure.

Activists based in Buenos Aires told the Washington Blade, in reporting published on 10 April 2025, that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers in the city has become more common since the current national government took office, and that harassment and hate speech have risen. The account supplies no incident counts and no dates for individual cases, and no later City-specific instance is documented in these sources.

Emergency decree DNU 61/2025, published in February 2025, re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty and invites the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere. It prohibits people who have legally changed gender from being housed in women's prisons when they are detained for sexual offences or violence against women. FALGBT and legal experts describe the decree as illegal and unconstitutional and are seeking judicial intervention. The sources do not record whether the City has adhered or how its prisons have applied the rule.

sources.summary: The national administration eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, closed the National Institute Against Discrimination, Xenophobia and Racism (INADI), dismissed trans people hired under the Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs, and has moved to restrict the 12-year-old Gender Identity Law. Buenos Aires-based activists told the Washington Blade on April 10, 2025 that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common since the current government took office, with harassment and hate speech rising nationally.

Argentina recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, up 62% year-on-year, a ten-year record of one crime every 38 hours. According to Agencia Presentes data published on 19 March 2026, 32% of the crimes occurred in police stations and penal facilities, security-force violence multiplied from 17 cases (2024) to 64 (2025), and trans women and travestis concentrated 62.5% of victims (142 cases). Most perpetrators were security personnel and unknown assailants.

Via emergency decrees published in February 2025, DNU 62/2025 modified Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law (Law 26743) to prohibit gender-affirming interventions for persons under 18, and DNU 61/2025 re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty, inviting the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere. The latter decree prohibits those who legally changed gender from being housed in women's prisons if detained for sexual offences or violence against women. FALGBT and legal experts call the decrees illegal and unconstitutional and are seeking judicial intervention.

14911670B90188072957077.name: Santa Catarina
14911670B90188072957077.summary:
Santa Catarina stands under Brazil's national framework, and its own record shows a state legislature moving against trans and LGBTIQ people while the courts have narrowed the state's own protections.

The state constitution carries an anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002 that lists sexual orientation among the protected grounds, but as of 2019 it does not address discrimination against transgender people. Two state statutes that did cover gender identity have been stripped back: State Law No. 12,534 of 4 April 2003 was repealed on 8 October 2015 by Complementary Law No. 656, and Complementary Law No. 527 of 28 December 2010 was partially overturned on 11 October 2018 after a 2015 Supreme Federal Court challenge on labour-law grounds. What remains of Complementary Law No. 527 penalises private entities and, where applicable, state public servants who promote, permit or tolerate discriminatory acts based on gender or sexual orientation, covering violent, coercive or vexatious acts, refusal of entry to places of free public access, denial or surcharging of lodging and property transactions, and prohibition of affectionate expression permitted to others, punishable by a R$2,500 fine rising to R$5,000 on repeat, a 30-day licence suspension or revocation, and up to 30 days' suspension for state servants; complaints go to the State Secretariat of Public Security and Defense of the Citizen, with fines paid into the State Civil Police Improvement Fund. In ADI 5307 on 29 October 2018 the Supreme Federal Court unanimously declared Article 2, items VI and VII of that law formally unconstitutional.

Legislative hostility is documented in volume. From January 2019 to June 2025, state deputies introduced 19 anti-LGBTQIA+ bills against 4 pro-LGBTQIA+ bills, including proposals to prohibit neutral language in official government communications and to bar minors from hormone therapy, surgical interventions and other gender-transition care; 4 of the anti-LGBTQIA+ bills were archived and none were enacted. As of 2025 the Legislative Assembly had 19 anti-LGBTQ bills on record with 11 authored by the Liberal Party. A 2026 count recorded 271 unconstitutional laws processed since 2015 against women's or LGBTQ rights, about 70% involving the trans and travesti community and 41% ruled unconstitutional by the Supreme Federal Court. A separate report covering January 2015 to October 2025 found the Legislative Assembly and its 295 municipal chambers approved or advanced at least 271 laws, bills and normative acts already declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Federal Court, 41% attacking gender and sexuality with particular focus on LGBTIA+ people, 36% already in force and only 11% judicially annulled, concentrated in the Vale do Itajaí and accelerating in the last five years.

Restroom access is contested. On 21 January 2026 Governor Jorginho Mello signed State Law No. 19,686/2026 requiring all public and private educational institutions from preschool through higher and vocational education to maintain strictly separate male and female restrooms and changing rooms; from 18 June 2026 the Federal University of Santa Catarina installed signs indicating restrooms may be used in accordance with gender identity. In a 2014 Florianópolis shopping-mall case where a trans woman was denied access to the women's restroom, a lower court ordered R$15,000 in compensation for pain and suffering, the Court of Justice of Santa Catarina overturned it, and on 6 June 2024 the Supreme Federal Court dismissed her appeal pending since 2014 by an 8-3 vote, withdrawing its recognized general repercussion on procedural grounds that the original claim pleaded only consumer-law damages rather than constitutional provisions, thereby issuing no binding constitutional ruling on trans bathroom access; in August 2025 an extraordinary appeal was filed with the Inter-American Court of Human Rights against both courts.

Education policy has also been restricted. A decree of Governor Carlos Moises on 15 June 2021 banned gender-neutral language in state schools until it was overturned on 6 May 2025 by the Supreme Federal Court, and a Joinville law of 20 December 2021 banned it in public office until struck down on 3 August 2022 by the Court of Justice. On 15 October 2025 the Supreme Federal Court struck down a 2015 Tubarão law that had prohibited teaching of gender and sexual orientation in schools. On 1 April 2026 Governor Jorginho Mello signed a law published 6 April allowing parents to prohibit children from participating in classes on LGBTQ topics. In December 2023 the Constitution and Justice Committee of the Legislative Assembly approved a bill prohibiting transgender women from participating in women's sports, still under review as of 18 August 2026.

Document and registry practice in the state runs through the courts rather than a state statute. Since 2020 people in Santa Catarina have obtained documents recording non-binary gender through the courts or notarial offices, although no specific state law prescribes this; in 2021 Idris Kawabe became the first person in Santa Catarina to judicially change documents to reflect a neutral gender, and judicial actions are still required because no state law recognizes the marker, with legal sex still required on birth certificates. The Army provides that any person in the draft cohort expressing a gender identity other than male who holds a final, unappealable court ruling or civil registry amendment is treated as non-binary in the same manner as intersex individuals and considered exempt from mandatory military service for not meeting Federal Constitution, Military Service Law, implementing regulations and the 2024 General Conscription Plan requirements.

Violence and hostility figures for the state are recorded. In 2024 three murders of trans people were recorded in Santa Catarina. The 2024 Brazilian Public Security Yearbook reported 85 cases of intentional bodily injury against LGBTQ individuals in the state, with low rates attributed to underreporting. On 3 September 2026 the Court of Justice ordered the parents of a gay teenager in Jaguaruna to pay R$100,000 in compensation after kicking him out and exposing his sexual orientation on social media.

Florianópolis carries some protective signals. A legal guide updated 5 April 2026 names it among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction even though legal rights are identical nationwide. In a Florianópolis case, judge M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva of the 1st Civil Court blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived over ten years in a stable relationship with a lesbian Brazilian. On 29 April 2013 the Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça of Santa Catarina authorized notarial and civil-registry offices to process marriage habilitations regardless of the sex of the spouses, allowing same-sex couples where both partners reside in Santa Catarina to formalize civil marriage and expanding Article 629 of the CGJ Code of Norms beyond the stable union recognized since 2011.

Since 2020 people in Santa Catarina have obtained documents recording non-binary gender through the courts or notarial offices, although no specific law prescribes this. In Florianópolis, judge M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva of the 1st Civil Court blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived over ten years in a stable relationship with a lesbian Brazilian. Nationally, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 under CNJ Resolution 175/2013, and a 2019 Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling made discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989.

Constitutional guarantees and federal criminal provisions adopted after the 2019 Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling prohibit discrimination and hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity. A deeply conservative Congress has nonetheless generated a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals, including efforts to repeal the marriage equality recognised by the Supreme Court in 2013. These guarantees apply nationwide and cover visitors in Santa Catarina. In September 2025 the government reinstated the National LGBTI+ Health Technical Committee, a participatory mechanism dissolved in 2019, for shaping and monitoring inclusive public-health policy. The Superior Court of Justice ruled that nonbinary people may amend their civil registry to reflect their gender identity.

A legal guide updated 5 April 2026 names Florianópolis among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes. Smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction, though legal rights are identical nationwide. Foreign same-sex spouses and partners are treated identically for visa and residence categories, including the spousal residence permit, and foreign same-sex marriages are recognised for immigration purposes. Joint and second-parent adoption are confirmed by STF RE 846.102 (2015). Gender-marker changes proceed without surgery. ADO 26 (2019) criminalises homophobia and transphobia as equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989.

14911670B90188072957077.blindSummary:
This division sits within this country's national framework, and its own record shows a state legislature moving against trans and LGBTIQ people while the courts have narrowed the division's own protections.

The division constitution carries an anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002 that lists sexual orientation among the protected grounds, but as of 2019 it does not address discrimination against transgender people. Two division statutes that did cover gender identity have been stripped back: division statute No. 12,534 of 4 April 2003 was repealed on 8 October 2015 by complementary statute No. 656, and complementary statute No. 527 of 28 December 2010 was partially overturned on 11 October 2018 after a 2015 highest constitutional court challenge on labour-law grounds. What remains of complementary statute No. 527 penalises private entities and, where applicable, division public servants who promote, permit or tolerate discriminatory acts based on gender or sexual orientation, covering violent, coercive or vexatious acts, refusal of entry to places of free public access, denial or surcharging of lodging and property transactions, and prohibition of affectionate expression permitted to others, punishable by a fine of R$2,500 rising to R$5,000 on repeat, a 30-day licence suspension or revocation, and up to 30 days' suspension for division servants; complaints go to a division public security and citizen protection agency, with fines paid into a police improvement fund. In a constitutional challenge numbered 5307 on 29 October 2018 the highest constitutional court unanimously declared Article 2, items VI and VII of that law formally unconstitutional.

Legislative hostility is documented in volume. From January 2019 to June 2025, members of the legislature introduced 19 anti-LGBTQIA+ bills against 4 pro-LGBTQIA+ bills, including proposals to prohibit neutral language in official government communications and to bar minors from hormone therapy, surgical interventions and other gender-transition care; 4 of the anti-LGBTQIA+ bills were archived and none were enacted. As of 2025 the legislature had 19 anti-LGBTQ bills on record with 11 authored by a single political party. A 2026 count recorded 271 unconstitutional laws processed since 2015 against women's or LGBTQ rights, about 70% involving the trans and travesti community and 41% ruled unconstitutional by the highest constitutional court. A separate report covering January 2015 to October 2025 found the legislature and its 295 municipal chambers approved or advanced at least 271 laws, bills and normative acts already declared unconstitutional by the highest constitutional court, 41% attacking gender and sexuality with particular focus on LGBTIA+ people, 36% already in force and only 11% judicially annulled, concentrated in one named subregion of the division and accelerating in the last five years.

Restroom access is contested. On 21 January 2026 the governor signed division statute No. 19,686/2026 requiring all public and private educational institutions from preschool through higher and vocational education to maintain strictly separate male and female restrooms and changing rooms; from 18 June 2026 a public university in the capital city installed signs indicating restrooms may be used in accordance with gender identity. In a 2014 shopping-mall case in the capital city where a trans woman was denied access to the women's restroom, a lower court ordered R$15,000 in compensation for pain and suffering, the division's highest civil court overturned it, and on 6 June 2024 the highest constitutional court dismissed her appeal pending since 2014 by an 8-3 vote, withdrawing its recognized general repercussion on procedural grounds that the original claim pleaded only consumer-law damages rather than constitutional provisions, thereby issuing no binding constitutional ruling on trans bathroom access; in August 2025 an extraordinary appeal was filed with a supranational human rights court against both courts.

Education policy has also been restricted. A decree of the governor on 15 June 2021 banned gender-neutral language in division-run schools until it was overturned on 6 May 2025 by the highest constitutional court, and a law of a large city of 20 December 2021 banned it in public office until struck down on 3 August 2022 by the division's highest civil court. On 15 October 2025 the highest constitutional court struck down a 2015 law of a coastal city that had prohibited teaching of gender and sexual orientation in schools. On 1 April 2026 the governor signed a law published 6 April allowing parents to prohibit children from participating in classes on LGBTQ topics. In December 2023 the legislature's constitution and justice committee approved a bill prohibiting transgender women from participating in women's sports, still under review as of 18 August 2026.

Document and registry practice in the division runs through the courts rather than a division statute. Since 2020 people in this division have obtained documents recording non-binary gender through the courts or notarial offices, although no specific division law prescribes this; in 2021 one person became the first in this division to judicially change documents to reflect a neutral gender, and judicial actions are still required because no division law recognizes the marker, with legal sex still required on birth certificates. The armed forces provide that any person in the draft cohort expressing a gender identity other than male who holds a final, unappealable court ruling or civil registry amendment is treated as non-binary in the same manner as intersex individuals and considered exempt from mandatory military service for not meeting the national constitution, the military service statute, implementing regulations and the 2024 general conscription plan requirements.

Violence and hostility figures for the division are recorded. In 2024 three murders of trans people were recorded in this division. The 2024 national public security yearbook reported 85 cases of intentional bodily injury against LGBTQ individuals in the division, with low rates attributed to underreporting. On 3 September 2026 the division's highest civil court ordered the parents of a gay teenager in a small city to pay R$100,000 in compensation after kicking him out and exposing his sexual orientation on social media.

The capital city carries some protective signals. A legal guide updated 5 April 2026 names it among this country's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction even though legal rights are identical nationwide. In a case in the capital city, a judge of a first-instance civil court blocked immigration authorities from deporting a foreign citizen who had lived over ten years in a stable relationship with a lesbian citizen of this country. On 29 April 2013 the division's judicial administration body authorized notarial and civil-registry offices to process marriage habilitations regardless of the sex of the spouses, allowing same-sex couples where both partners reside in this division to formalize civil marriage and expanding Article 629 of that body's code of norms beyond the stable union recognized since 2011.

82249235B24619009834807.summary:
British Columbia stands under the national framework of Canada. No statute of the province restricts trans people's access to restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, to gender-affirming care, or to gender-related name use in schools, and the province has enacted no hostile legislation of its own in these areas.

British Columbia's human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds across employment, housing, and public and private accommodations. Complaints against private businesses proceed under that statute, since Charter equality guarantees do not bind the private sector directly.

Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms applies in British Columbia. The Supreme Court of Canada has interpreted the concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15 to include transsexuality, and section 15 reaches all laws and government institutions in the province, including law enforcement authorities. Those guarantees remain subject to reasonable limits under section 1 and to the notwithstanding clause in section 33.

Vital statistics, including birth certificates and other identity documents, fall under British Columbia's provincial jurisdiction, so a gender-marker change on a provincial birth certificate is governed by the province rather than by Ottawa.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in British Columbia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal, provincial and territorial law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations, and as of 2017 all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly list gender identity as a prohibited ground in their human rights acts. The Supreme Court has interpreted the concepts of sex and physical disability in Charter section 15 to include transsexuality, with section 15 applying to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities, while complaints against private businesses proceed under the applicable federal or provincial human rights statute. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules, with vital statistics including identity documents such as birth certificates falling under provincial jurisdiction. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause to require schools to obtain parental consent for students under 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, prompting calls for repeal and legal action. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024 and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges blocked when the government passed Bill 9: Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans, Transgender and Queer communities, stated police must stand together against transphobia, and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 received royal assent, and the anal-intercourse provision in section 159 of the Criminal Code was repealed on June 21, 2019 by Bill C-75, setting the age of consent at 16 for all sexual activities, 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency, with close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15. In Egan v Canada in 1995 the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under Charter section 15 as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta in 1998 it held failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law violated section 15, with all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly prohibiting sexual orientation discrimination as of 2017. Charter equality protections apply to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement but not directly against the private sector, are subject to reasonable limits under section 1 under the Oakes Test and to section 33's notwithstanding clause, which has never been used by the federal Parliament. Canada legalized same-sex marriage nationwide on July 20, 2005 through the federal Civil Marriage Act, becoming the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to do so, after court rulings between 2002 and 2005 struck down the opposite-sex common-law definition. Same-sex adoption is legal in all provinces and territories, beginning with British Columbia in 1996 and ending with Nunavut in 2011, and British Columbia, Ontario and Saskatchewan grant parental status to three or more intentional parents. In 2022 Canada became the third country in the world and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for minors and adults, making it a crime under the Criminal Code to subject anyone to it as defined by statute. On June 21, 2018 royal assent was granted to the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act allowing RCMP, federal departments, and notified provincial, municipal police and courts to destroy or remove judicial records for pre-1969 homosexual acts and section 159 convictions for living and deceased persons, distinct from a pardon or record suspension. Canada was ranked first in Asher & Lyric's LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023 indicating least dangerous, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024. The 2020 Pew Research showed 85% of Canada's general population, including 92% among Canadians aged 18 to 29, favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013. June 2013 polls showed a vast majority blessed same-sex marriage available throughout Canada since 2005, with 70% agreeing same-sex couples should have the same rights to adopt as heterosexual couples and 76% agreeing they are just as likely to successfully raise children. A 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office found 91.8% of those surveyed said they would be "comfortable" if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual. The same poll documented transgender-specific tolerance, finding that "87.6% said they would be 'comfortable' if a neighbour was a transgender person."

13589884B3780741375954.name: Antioquia
13589884B3780741375954.summary:
Antioquia stands under Colombia's national framework: the national rules on identity documents, recognition of marriages performed abroad, access to public and commercial premises, and the treatment of detainees apply in the department as elsewhere in the country, and the inventory identifies no Antioquia-specific statute, departmental decree or court ruling of its own.

The region-specific record is a killing in Bello, in the metropolitan corridor around Medellín. On 5 April 2025 a video circulated showing Sara Millerey González Borja, a 32-year-old trans woman, beaten and thrown into a waterway in daylight while onlookers filmed; her legs, arms and hands were fractured, she could not swim, and she died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon.

She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello during 2025, the two earlier victims being gay men. A clinic reportedly declined to treat her as an emergency, on the stated ground that she had not been shot. Bello city hall drew criticism for referring to her by her pre-transition name. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and protests followed in several cities.

sources.summary: El País English (14 April 2025), reporting from Bello, Antioquia: 32-year-old trans woman Sara Millerey González Borja was beaten and thrown into a waterway in broad daylight while onlookers filmed; the video went viral on 5 April, President Gustavo Petro ordered an investigation and protests were held in several cities. She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello in 2025 (the first two victims were gay men); a clinic reportedly did not treat her as an emergency 'because she didn't get shot', and she died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon. The article records 13 trans people killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 alone and notes city hall was criticised for using her pre-transition name.

The Guardian (30 July 2024), reporting from Caquetá: 41 transgender women were killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight more between February and April 2024, national figures that also cover Antioquia. Armed groups in Caquetá, where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement, distributed flyers on streets and WhatsApp announcing a 'social cleansing' plan naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets, and trans women there fled after death threats. No Antioquia-specific source covers these national 2023-24 kill tallies or the southern-department flyers.

25490228B43154843394848.name: Comunidad de Madrid
25490228B43154843394848.summary:
Madrid stands under Spain's national framework for legal gender recognition, with the Comunidad de Madrid's own statute as a layer beneath it. Madrid is one of Europe's principal LGBT urban centres, and the region was among the first in Spain to pass a gender-identity law, adopting its statute in 2016 alongside the Islas Baleares and the Región de Murcia and after Extremadura in 2015. That regional statute was later amended by Ley 17/2023. Regional law must comply with Spain's Ley 4/2023, which sets the statutory floor that a trans visitor's recognition and protection claims in the region rest on.

What the region has withdrawn since then matters to anyone relying on local antidiscrimination machinery. After the 2023 regional election, the new government of the Comunidad de Madrid repealed the region's non-discrimination law, repealed the regional ban on conversion therapy as it applies to trans people, removed the penalties that attached to conversion therapy, and repealed several trans legal recognitions. These measures act on the region's own guarantees and leave the national framework in place.

The safety picture the region's own sources report does not follow from the legal position. Homophobic and transphobic discrimination and violence are described as significant problems in Madrid, and trans people and migrants are reported to face additional barriers within the city's LGBT population.

The community is concentrated and long established. The Chueca district is the centre of the city's LGBT life, and MADO, held annually in late June or early July, is among the largest Pride events in the world and draws millions of attendees. COGAM, founded in 1986, is the city's most influential LGBT organisation; the city government maintains an Oficina de Atención a la Diversidad Sexual y de Género; and Arcopoli works against discrimination and violence.

19338628B30439183828151.summary:
Bourgogne-Franche-Comté stands under the national framework of France. Identity documents, criminal law, anti-discrimination protection, legal gender recognition and marriage are set nationally, and the national assessment applies in the region without modification.

The region's one documented restriction concerns public assembly. The Côte-d'Or prefecture barred the Dijon Pride march from the city centre in June 2025.

The Dijon march was not a new event. Pride marches have been held in Dijon, Chalon-sur-Saône and Auxerre since 2013, reported by France 3 Bourgogne, so the ban fell on a gathering with more than a decade of local history rather than a first-time assembly.

No region-specific rule on identity documents, entry, healthcare access, facilities or screening was identified in the sources. Those remain matters of national law and practice.

19338628B36302232233914.name: Hauts-de-France
19338628B36302232233914.summary:
Hauts-de-France legislates nothing of its own on detention, identity documents or anti-discrimination. The region stands under the national framework of France: custodial placement, gender markers and discrimination protections are set nationally. No regional statute, regional court ruling or regional administrative instruction on transgender detainees or visitors appears in the sources.

The single documented case in the region is Paola, a trans woman whose identity documents record her as male, transferred in 2014 to the correctional facility at Lille and held in a men's establishment. Detainees there shouted "We don't want any women here!"; a fellow inmate tried to attack her with a knife; she spent two days in solitary confinement. The account was published in a BuzzFeed News investigation of 12 January 2018.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed investigation posted 12 January 2018: under Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code men and women must be held in separate establishments, but placement follows the legal gender on identity documents, so trans women still recorded as male are held in all-male facilities - the group that, per controller-general Adeline Hazan, 'suffers the most' in prison. Region-relevant case: Paola, transferred in 2014 to Lille's northern correctional facility, was met by detainees shouting 'We don't want any women here!', a fellow inmate tried to attack her with a knife and she spent two days in solitary confinement; Kara B. was held under conditions described as worrying after her 2016 Paris protest trial; the Ministry of Justice counted 13 transgender detainees across eight facilities as of 1 November 2016.

National detention-oversight opinion of 25 May 2021 (covering every place of deprivation of liberty; prepared from referrals received since 2010 concerning transgender detainees): assignment to establishments or wards (male or female) is based exclusively on civil status, so the vast majority of transgender people are held in institutions or wards that do not correspond to their gender identity, and search procedures for persons whose civil-status sex does not match their identity add constraints such as isolation. It recommends guaranteeing every transgender detainee the possibility of choosing the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation, requires continuity of medical and hormone care with free choice of doctor, urges research funding, and faults the administration for not translating the 2016 justice-modernisation law (n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016) into prison rules.

19338628B57683459369229.name: Occitanie

Occitanie stands under the national legal framework of France. The region-specific record in the sources is the opinion issued on 25 May 2021 by the CGLPL, the national inspectorate of places of deprivation of liberty, whose visits covered two facilities in Toulouse: Toulouse-Seysses prison and the Toulouse central police station.

The opinion concerns eight transgender women held in those Toulouse facilities. It documents isolation imposed on detainees because of their trans status, and staff who had received no training on trans issues. It further finds that the depathologisation law of 18 November 2016 (n° 2016-1547) was never written into prison rules or into healthcare guidance, so the statutory change of status had no operational effect on how trans detainees were held or treated.

The inspectorate's recommendations bearing on the region call for financed research, policies against discrimination, and suitable procedures for searching and for assigning detainees whose civil-status sex does not match the identity they present. For a trans visitor, the operative exposure in Occitanie is custody: police custody at a central station and detention at a prison are the settings where the documented failures occur, and the placement and search practices described apply regardless of how a person presents in ordinary daily life.
